seeds.name: Land-promotion junior: option farmland,
seeds.memo:
## Land promotion, Round 4 re-dive (UK first, US and Australia checked)

### Frame of reference
The rung is "unconsented farmland to land with outline consent", sold to a housebuilder. A capitalised buyer exists and pays when consent is granted. But discovery is not 80% of this rung. Most of the cost and time goes into proving: a planning application, then an appeal, over 2-5 years, decided by political and legal judgement. Picking the site is the smaller part. The relaxed C3 does not change that.

I tested the variant the brief suggested: **buy Green Belt or "grey belt" farmland outright at agricultural value, then promote it under the Dec 2024 NPPF grey-belt policy.** Grey belt is a new policy, its tests are judgement calls, and the evidence sits in council Green Belt assessment PDFs. That made it the best candidate for land where the hope value is not yet priced in.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price.** Farmland is about £20-25k/ha. Green Belt farmland trades at £8-15k/acre, towards the top of that range near London, because hope value is already priced in ([urbanistarchitecture](https://urbanistarchitecture.co.uk/green-belt-land-planning-gain-uplift/)). The Upper Tribunal has held that even remote Green Belt prospects carry hope value ([DKLM](https://www.dklm.co.uk/site/library/latest/hope_value_boosts_compulsory_purchase_compensation_award.html)).
- **Proven price.** Real outline-consented sales came to about £400-490k per gross acre (prior verifier: Sudbury and Hereford). That is about 45-55x farmland before s106, infrastructure and affordable housing.
  - Grey belt is worse. The golden rules require 50% affordable housing by default, or the existing requirement plus 15 points ([LGA webinar](https://lb2.local.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/Dec%2024%20NPPF%20Webinar%2019%20March%20Golden%20Rules.pdf)). Viability assessments cannot be used to reduce this ([DHA](https://www.dhaplanning.co.uk/knowledge/the-golden-rule-for-viability)).
  - Councils' benchmark land values for greenfield run at about 14-24x existing use value, or about £370-620k/ha ([Lichfields](https://lichfields.uk/blog/2024/september/20/fool-s-gold-how-a-rigid-approach-to-affordable-housing-and-benchmark-land-values-for-green-belt-could-undermine-housing-delivery); [Rossendale viability](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/downloads/file/16410/el8-020-2-action-20-2-viability-study-update)).
  - Government floated cutting that to 3x ([BCLP](https://bclplaw.com/en-US/events-insights-news/nppf-consultation-green-belt-reform.html)).
- **Net to the company (estimate).**
  - Freehold variant: buy at about £12k/acre, spend about £30k/acre on promotion, sell at about £250-350k per gross acre after the golden rules. That is about 6-8x on capital, in 10-100x territory only before costs.
  - Promoter variant (prior evidence): the promoter keeps 10-25% of the uplift, or about 3-10x on promotion spend.
- **Transactions per year.** Gladman consented about 2,796 plots/yr (prior evidence). Grey-belt appeals produced about 1,600 homes in 8.5 months ([HBD/Marrons](https://hbdonline.co.uk/?p=363028)). The total pool is £10-20B/yr (estimate).
- **US.** Texas cropland is about $2,710/acre against about $10,200/acre for development-stage land ([Neuhaus](https://neuhausre.com/raw-land-investing/)). Generic guidance puts entitled land at about 2x raw ([RealWealth](https://realwealth.com/?p=101492)). That is a 2-6x step-up, so worse than the UK.

### Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Proving capex.** £250k-1M per site, or £25-40k per gross acre, over 2-5 years (prior evidence). This passes the "expensive" leg.
- **Hit rates.**
  - Marrons, to Aug 2025: major residential grey-belt appeals were allowed 80% of the time (16/20); all residential, 54% ([HBD](https://hbdonline.co.uk/?p=363028)).
  - Marrons, to Feb 2026: majors 75% (18/24), all residential 43%, and 2-9 dwelling schemes about 30% ([GB Chambers](https://www.greaterbirminghamchambers.com/resource/grey-belt-policy-continues-to-increase-housing-planning-permissions-research.html)).
  - Promoters win about 67-76% on the sites they choose (Gladman, Mac Mic; prior evidence).
- **With ML (estimate).** On sites already filtered, ML can cut the cost per consented site by about 1.2-1.35x at most, because failures are only 25-33% of attempts. Choosing sites before an option is signed, across all farmland, could in theory do better. But the filters that matter are legible fields, which LandTech already scores (next section). So the extra lift over existing tools is probably below 1.5x.

### Data source
- **Inputs that are partly illegible.** PINS appeal decision letters (public PDFs), council Green Belt assessments and grey-belt reviews (PDFs that score each parcel against purposes a, b and d), HELAA call-for-sites submissions, and local plan examination reports.
- **The outcome is mostly already legible.**
  - Each council's 5-year supply position, its Housing Delivery Test score and appeal outcomes are all structured fields.
  - LandTech already sells a parcel-level "Grey Belt favourability" score built on purposes a, b and d plus the footnote-7 exclusions ([LandTech support](https://support.land.tech/en/articles/9915221-understand-grey-belt-favourability); [LandTech blog](https://land.tech/blog/find-grey-belt-sites-fast-with-landinsight)).
- **Result.** The new illegible signal was turned into a product within months. C4 fails again.

### How the right is bought
- **Seller.** Farm owners, nearly always through an agent. Bruton Knowles markets a 37.8-acre Cheltenham site as "grey belt", on option or promotion terms only ([landsale](https://www.landsale.co.uk/properties/129539)).
- **Terms.** Under a promotion agreement the promoter keeps 10-25% of net proceeds. An option is exercised at a 10-20% discount to market value. Outright sales carry 30-50% overage for 20-30 years (prior evidence).
- **Freehold variant.** I found no evidence of unencumbered freehold sales at agricultural value next to settlements. Owners and agents already flag grey-belt potential. The company keeps about 100% of the uplift only if it buys outright with no overage, and the market does not offer that on edge-of-settlement land.

### Capitalised buyer
Volume housebuilders pay cash when consent is granted: Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey and Vistry. Barratt also bought Gladman outright for £250M (prior evidence).

### Integration ladder above
Promoter, then housebuilder (land plus construction margin), then build-to-rent or a rental platform. The ladder is real but bounded: UK housebuilders are worth single-digit billions each (estimate). It is not a trillion-dollar chain.

### Who else does this
- **Promoters:** Gladman (owned by Barratt), Catesby, Richborough, Hallam, Rosconn, Mac Mic and Wallace.
- **Data tools:** LandTech, Searchland and Nimbus.
- **Advisers:** Marrons and LPDF track the appeals.
- **AI-native entrant:** Tract shut in March 2025 with no revenue (prior evidence).

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Take the 224 grey-belt appeals Marrons reviewed (pull them from PINS).
2. Extract features with ML from the matching council Green Belt assessment PDFs and from earlier inspector letters.
3. Test whether this beats a baseline of LandTech favourability plus 5-year-supply and HDT status. Kill if the AUC gain is under 0.05.
4. In the same two weeks, ask 10 land agents for freehold prices with no overage on 5 candidate grey-belt parcels. Kill if the asks are above 2x agricultural value.

### Verdict: still refuted (12/25)

| Criterion | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 2 | A buyer exists, but proving, not discovery, is most of the work |
| C2 Step-up | 3 | Gross 20-55x on land, but only about 6-8x net for a freehold owner and 3-10x for a promoter |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 3 | Proving is expensive, but with 67-80% base rates on chosen sites the lever is about 1.2-1.35x |
| C4 Data + right | 1 | The outcome sits in legible fields that LandTech scores, hope value is already priced in, and rights are sold through agents with overage |
| C5 Ladder | 3 | Real, but bounded at UK housebuilder scale |

The relaxed C3 does not rescue this candidate. The old C4 problems still bind, and so does the promoter's small share of the uplift. Grey belt was the best variant to test, but LandTech had already turned it into a product within months, and the golden rules (50% affordable housing) cut what consented land is worth.

seeds.name: Mitigation-bank junior: buy drained or h
seeds.memo:
## Verdict up front
The best variant I found is a preservation-only species conservation bank on land the company owns outright, in California. It fixes two of the old killers: almost no physical work, and no exposure to Sackett. It does not fix the step-up, and demand stays the hidden variable. Even with the relaxed C3 it remains weak, at about 10/25.

## Frame of reference
The rung is buying grazing or farm land outright (fee simple) where a listed species lives (vernal pool shrimp, California tiger salamander, Swainson's hawk, giant garter snake). The company preserves it, gets a USFWS/CDFW bank enabling instrument, and then sells ESA/CESA credits or the whole entitled bank.

This fixes two old killers:
- **Physical step:** preservation needs no earthwork. At Van Vleck, preservation credits release on how much of the endowment is funded, not on growing-season performance: 15% at establishment, then 25%, 15% and 15% at 15%, 40% and 70% funded, and the rest at full funding. The endowment needed is $765 per credit (https://www.conservationfund.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Van_Vleck_Mitigation_Bank.pdf).
- **Sackett:** species credits are under ESA/CESA, not the Clean Water Act, so the 2023 ruling does not shrink demand.

What it does not fix: the work is not 80% discovery. Most of the value is still in selling credits over a decade into local permit demand, plus the capital tied up in the endowment.

## Step-up ratio
**Unproven land:**
- A San Benito County, CA horse ranch was bought for $1,400/acre in 2014.
- Santa Clara range land had a book ("Yellow Book") value of $4,000/acre.
- Thurston County, WA: The Conservation Fund offered $5,300/acre.

All three are from the EASI landowner deck (https://www.easillc.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2024-Real-Estate-Landowner-Deck_short_v-1.3.pdf).

**Realised once proven (same source):**
- San Benito: an energy company paid $4,400/acre for the mitigation land, 3x market. The same credits from a local bank would have cost about $21.7k/acre, about 15x.
- Santa Clara: sold to POST at $11,700/acre, about 2.9x.
- Vancouver, WA: about $97k/acre gross over 15 years.
- Credit prices for species run from $1,505 to $205,055 per credit in 2015 dollars (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10531-019-01747-2). Sonoma CTS credits run "as high as $200,000" (https://www.biologicaldiversity.org/news/media-archive/a2016/herp_pressdemo_6.21.16.pdf). Most banks issue about 1 credit per acre.

**Net result:**
- About 3x when the land itself is sold.
- About 10-25x gross on credits, before endowment, holding costs and a 17.5-18% discount rate (EASI's own rate).
- Only 15% releases at approval. Nothing reaches 10^3.

**Transactions:**
- USFWS approved 135 banks by Dec 2015 (https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/uploads/cb_sponsors_and_managers_survey_report_final_092716.pdf). The Springer study counts 155 by Sep 2018, so roughly 7 new banks a year.
- Whole-bank sales are rare. EIP's Appalachia portfolio drew 6-12 bids and sold for less than its $82.6M projected net revenue (https://ecosystempartners.com/eip-sale-points-to-deeper-institutional-market-for-mitigation-bank/).

## Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
**Approval time:** planning averages 13.6 months (median 12) and final approval 18.6 months (median 14.5), so about 2.7 years in total (DOI survey).

**Upfront cost:** about $1M, mostly the endowment (https://bren.ucsb.edu/media/1441).

**Approval rarely fails.** The weak point is sales: sponsors name weak credit demand as a top obstacle, and rate demand "weak" in USFWS Regions 1 and 2 (DOI survey).

**Hit-rate definition:** under the relaxed C3, I define a "hit" as a bank that sells out within 7 years. My estimate of the base rate is 30-50%.

**Where ML could help:** choosing parcels where future impacts on a species are concentrated, read from CEQA project pipelines. That could plausibly lift sell-through 1.3-1.8x (estimate, untested). The proving step is expensive, so C3 is worth about 3.

## Data source
- **CEQAnet** (https://ceqanet.lci.ca.gov): tens of thousands of notices, environmental impact reports and mitigated negative declarations. Their biology appendices are unstructured PDFs that state required mitigation ratios, species and locations. That makes them a forward demand signal that nobody aggregates.
- **Credit prices are not public.** They are negotiated, RIBITS and HabitatCAN ledgers show no prices, and sponsors say "contact the Sponsor" (https://www.habitatcan.org/local-resources/Hazel-Mitigation-Bank/69127/). Scattered staff reports carry the price points.
- **Outcome summary:** whether a bank was approved, and how many credits it has sold, is legible in RIBITS. Future demand by service area is not summarised anywhere.
- **Supply side is legible:** CNDDB occurrences, SSURGO and the CDFW approved-bank list (https://wildlife.ca.gov/conservation/planning/banking/approved-banks).

## How the right is bought
- **Seller and price:** bilateral fee-simple purchase from ranch owners at range or ag value ($1.4-5.3k/acre, EASI deck).
- **What the company keeps:** owning outright means it keeps 100% of the uplift. A promotion agreement would split it.
- **Legal mechanics:** a conservation easement plus the enabling instrument. The prospectus fee is $10k, with a 30-day completeness review (https://californiaglobe.com/articles/conservation-banks/).
- **Owners can increasingly read the data.** EASI sells eco-asset valuations directly to landowners and targets holdings of 500-20,000 acres, so the information discount is closing.

## Capitalised buyer
- Developers, Caltrans, utilities and energy companies buy credits as they need them.
- Funds buy entitled banks: EIP ($1.2B AUM, Fund V $400M), plus a 50/50 mix of financial and strategic bidders on the Appalachia portfolio (EIP article).
- They pay for banks with performance already de-risked, at a discount to projected revenue. They do not pay a premium at the moment of approval.

## Integration ladder above
1. Single bank.
2. Portfolio of banks.
3. Full-delivery and in-lieu-fee programs.
4. Regional habitat conservation plan administrator.
5. Entitlement services for developers.

This tops out around a $1-5B category (estimate). It does not lead to the whole value chain.

## Who else does this
- Sponsors: Westervelt Ecological Services, RES, Wildlands, EIP and The Conservation Fund.
- EASI: GIS-based eco-asset valuation.
- CEC: a GIS tool for choosing bank sites (https://www.cecinc.com/project/gis-based-mitigation-banking-site-selection-tool/).
- Aarden AI: land underwriting, not banks.

None of them, as far as I found, forecasts demand from CEQA filings.

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Use an LLM to extract species-mitigation requirements (species, acres, ratio, location) from Sacramento, Placer and Sonoma CEQA environmental impact reports and mitigated negative declarations, 2012-2018.
2. Aggregate the results by bank service area.
3. Check against RIBITS ledgers whether this predicts 2018-2025 credit sell-through better than a legible baseline (population growth plus existing credit supply).
4. In parallel, collect 20 credit prices from staff reports.

**Kill conditions:**
- The top quintile of service areas sells through less than 1.5x faster than the baseline.
- Median credit price divided by land price comes out below 10x.

## Scores (relaxed rubric)
| Criterion | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 2 | Preservation makes the physical step trivial, but demand and endowment carry the risk, and buyers pay after de-risking. |
| C2 Step-up | 2 | About 3x on land sold, 10-25x gross on credits. |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 3 | Proving is expensive (about 2.7 years, about $1M); the ML lift on sell-through is plausibly about 1.3-1.8x (estimate). |
| C4 Data + right | 2 | CEQA and price data are illegible, but the supply side is legible and EASI is educating owners. |
| C5 Ladder | 1 | The chain above is small. |
| **Total** | **10/25** | Still refuted. |

The hard killer is C2. No variant of mitigation banking I found produces a step-up of 100x or more.

scored.name: Air-permitted behind-the-meter power pad for DC campuses
scored.one_line: Option industrial or ag parcels on interstate gas laterals, prove a PSD/Title V or minor-source air permit for 100-500MW of onsite turbines or engines plus a gas tap agreement, and sell the permitted, fuel-secured pad to off-grid AI campus developers.
scored.unproven_right: Land option near pipeline laterals from owners unaware that attainment status and dispersion profile make the parcel permittable.
scored.proving_step: Air dispersion modelling, PSD/Title V application and approval, pipeline tap or precedent agreement: about $300k-1.5M and 12-24 months; about 40-65% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Off-grid AI campus developers, hyperscalers and IPPs building bridge power (Crusoe, xAI-type builders, Williams-style deals).
scored.public_data: State air permit databases and scanned permits (TCEQ, ODEQ, PA DEP), EPA RACT/BACT/LAER Clearinghouse, EPA Green Book nonattainment maps, PHMSA and FERC pipeline filings, EIA gas pipeline data.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-40x on site value; depends on gas-for-DC demand persisting.
scored.frame: The rung is: an optioned parcel plus an air permit plus a gas tap, sold as a pad ready for behind-the-meter power. Nothing physical is built inside the rung. It is all paperwork, dispersion modelling and negotiation. But the work is mostly proving (permit engineering and pipeline negotiation), not ML-driven discovery. Finding a parcel in an attainment area next to a lateral is maybe 20-30% of the work. The buyer is clearly capitalised: Pacifico got a 7.65 GW TCEQ permit for GW Ranch (Pecos), then the ~8,000-acre site was sold to Amazon. One catch: the permit's value depends on turbine supply and firm gas capacity, which the rung does not secure.
scored.step_up: Unproven: West Texas or Midwest industrial/ag land at ~$2-5k/acre. Proven: a Pecos TX 770-acre '2.4 GW energy campus' is listed at ~CAD 168M, which I calculate as ~CAD 218k/acre (~US$160k/acre). That is roughly 30-80x, but it is an asking price, not a closed sale. Benchmark: Northern Virginia powered land at $6M/acre vs $4M/acre for land with entitlements but no power (Avison Young via DatacenterKnowledge). That is only 1.5x between entitled and powered. Overall ~10-50x, so C2 = 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Per the candidate: $300k-1.5M and 12-24 months per attempt, 40-65% success. That meets the relaxed expense bar. But a Texas seller's listing claims expedited TCEQ permitting in 60-90 days for SCR-controlled units. So in permissive states the permit is cheap and fast, and failures come mostly from gas capacity and turbine availability, not siting. ML could pick parcels in attainment areas with headroom on laterals and few nearby PSD increment consumers. A plausible gain is ~1.2-1.5x on cost per proven pad, not clearly >=1.5x. C3 = 3.
scored.data: Mixed. EPA Green Book nonattainment areas, EIA and PHMSA pipeline maps and RBLC BACT entries are already legible GIS or database fields. Lateral capacity and tap feasibility are partly hidden in FERC filings and in negotiations with operators. Scanned state permits (PA DEP, ODEQ) are illegible, but they mostly record precedent, not the outcome for a new parcel. Landowners near laterals are cheap to option, but rural owners in Texas and Ohio know about the data center boom, and brokers are already marketing 'energy campus' land. The edge is thin. C4 = 2.
scored.right_bought: Purchase or lease options on industrial or ag parcels next to interstate gas laterals in attainment counties, bought from farmers and industrial owners. A pipeline precedent or tap agreement is negotiated, not bought.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Amazon bought GW Ranch), off-grid AI campus developers (Crusoe, xAI), IPPs and midstream companies building bridge power (Williams for Meta in New Albany, OH, 200 MW).
scored.ladder: Strong: permitted pad, then turbine and engine procurement and EPC, then an owned onsite IPP selling power under a PPA, then powered shell or campus developer, then a gas-integrated compute or energy platform. Each rung is large. C5 = 4.
scored.fatal_flaw: The binding constraint is not the permit. Gas turbines have ~5-year backlogs (GE Vernova sold into 2030, Mitsubishi sold out through 2028, 260-week lead times), and firm pipeline capacity is also scarce. Air permits are written for specific equipment and are fast to get in Texas (60-90 days expedited). A permitted pad with no turbine slot or firm gas is not where the scarce value sits. Buyers like Amazon, Crusoe and Williams permit for themselves around the turbines they have secured, so the step-up goes to whoever holds equipment and gas, not to the holder of the paper.
scored.one_line_reason: The ladder is real and the buyer is capitalised, but this is permitting and siting work, not ML discovery over illegible data. The scarce input is turbines and gas, not the permit, so the expected step-up (~10-50x) and the ML lift (~1.2-1.5x) are both modest.

scored.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Options agricultural parcels in counties whose planning records imply data center approval, obtains rezoning or special exception, and sells entitled parcels to data center developers.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no purchase discount and no 10^3 step: landowners already receive developer offers of 6-10x farmland value before any rezoning. The premium that does exist comes mainly from power availability, which planning records cannot prove, and the zoning outcome is a public, legible vote that incumbents like Tract already arbitrage.
scored.step_up: Kentucky is the clearest case. Farmland trades at about $6k/acre, and developers are already offering about $35-60k/acre before rezoning, roughly 6-10x (tweaktown.com/LEX18; USDA 2024 Kentucky cropland ~$6.2k/acre). In Northern Virginia, entitled and powered land reaches $1-4M/acre against $20-100k/acre raw, roughly 10-50x. Most of that premium comes from power and fibre, not from zoning. The increment from zoning alone, measured from a price already lifted by developer offers, is about 3-10x and at best ~10-30x. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is lower than the prior round assumed. The Data Center Watch Q2 2026 update counts 45 projects worth $68B blocked or delayed by local opposition in April-June 2026, which it calls more than half of large developments in that window. It also counts 843 opposition groups across 49 states. Many outright denials have occurred in 2025, including Pittsylvania VA, Coweta GA and Fredericksburg VA. The base approval rate is now plausibly ~40-60%. Each attempt costs about $50-300k in fees, counsel and engineering, plus option premiums and 1-2 years of carry, so proving is expensive. Under the relaxed C3, ML over planning minutes, opposition signals, comprehensive-plan text and hearing transcripts could plausibly lift the hit rate about 1.5x by picking counties and parcels before options are signed. I score C3 at 4 rather than 5 because the predictive features (board composition, organised opposition, utility capacity) are partly legible to local brokers already.
scored.frame: The rung is to option rural or agricultural land, win a rezoning or special exception for a data center, and sell the entitled parcel to a hyperscaler or developer. The paperwork is cheap and abstracted (filings, counsel, engineering). Discovery is choosing the right parcel and county and predicting political approval, perhaps 60-70% of the work. The rest is community campaigning and securing power. That is below the 80% bar, because a power and utility commitment, not zoning alone, is what makes the parcel sellable. The buyers are capitalised: hyperscalers, Tract, QTS, and other developers.
scored.data: The data is county planning records: staff reports, minutes, comprehensive plans and hearing videos. They are public and scattered, and fairly illegible across about 3,000 counties. However, each approval is written directly into a legible field, the zoning status or a published board vote, which is the pattern of regulators writing in the answer. Power availability, the main driver of value, sits mostly in non-public utility load studies.
scored.right_bought: Options are bought from farmers, but those owners are not unable to read the market. Developers are already offering 6-10x farmland value unsolicited, sellers widely know a data center premium exists, and some families refuse $26M offers. Tract and brokers run the same playbook, so there is little purchase discount for being able to read the data.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) and data center developers or REITs (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, Tract). They are deeply capitalised and actively buy entitled, powered land.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs: entitled land, then powered land (utility agreements and substations), then a powered shell, then a developed campus, then operating or leasing data centers, possibly with power generation behind it. The rungs above are real and enormous but crowded with heavily capitalised incumbents (Tract, QTS, Digital Realty).
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 helps, because rising opposition pushes approvals to ~40-60% on expensive $50-300k, multi-year attempts. But the zoning-only step-up is ~3-30x, sellers already know the premium, and power rather than zoning drives value, so C1, C2 and C4 stay weak.

scored.name: Floodway Narrowing for Urban Infill Parcels
scored.one_line: Buy urban and suburban parcels made near-worthless by sitting in the regulatory floodway, where no-rise rules ban building. Use ML to find floodways drawn from coarse old models or pre-channelisation topography, fund a corrected floodway model and LOMR, and sell now-buildable infill land to multifamily developers.
scored.unproven_right: Fee purchase of floodway-encumbered infill lots and remnant parcels, often tax-delinquent or estate-held, at 1-5% of comparable land value.
scored.proving_step: Corrected HEC-RAS encroachment model with current channel survey and LiDAR, community concurrence, then FEMA LOMR: about $100-400k and 18-30 months; about 30-50% success on ML-selected reaches.
scored.proven_buyer: Multifamily, build-to-rent and REIT-backed infill builders in supply-constrained Sun Belt metros.
scored.public_data: FEMA NFHL floodway layers versus 3DEP LiDAR, scanned FIS floodway data tables, DOT and municipal channelisation and culvert-replacement records (channel changed, map did not), tax-delinquent rolls, assessor data.
scored.rough_step_up: About 20-100x (land from ~$0.50/sqft to $20-60/sqft metro infill).
scored.frame: The rung is: buy floodway-encumbered parcels, get a LOMR floodway revision, and sell the now-buildable land. Discovery (finding reaches where the floodway is drawn too wide, from coarse models or pre-channelisation topography) is maybe 35-50% of the work. The rest is not trivial or abstracted. It needs a new HEC-RAS encroachment model and channel survey, a community finding under 44 CFR 65.7 that 'no practicable alternative' to revising its adopted floodway exists, notice to affected owners and adjacent jurisdictions, state approval where the state has floodway jurisdiction, FEMA review, and local adoption. Floodway width is an allocation along a whole reach under a surcharge cap (60.3(d)(2)). Narrowing it for my parcel can raise flood elevations on neighbours, so proving is a political and regulatory negotiation, not a drill hit. Capitalised buyers (multifamily, build-to-rent, REIT-backed builders) exist.
scored.step_up: The claimed ~20-100x (about $0.50/sqft to $20-60/sqft) is overstated. Land moved out of the floodway stays in the 100-year flood fringe (SFHA). It still needs flood insurance, elevated floors and often no-net-fill compensation. Houston requires floors 2 ft above the 500-year level and zero net fill across the 500-year floodplain; Harris County requires 24 in above the 500-year level, with no fill to reach elevation in the 100-year floodplain. Residential floodplain discounts are only ~4.6% in the LSE meta-analysis (Beltran et al. 2018), but for vacant fringe land the mitigation cost cuts net value. A realistic net step-up is ~10-30x, which fits the 10-100x band.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. The candidate puts it at $100-400k and 18-30 months per reach. Search found only an informal ~$4k LOMR review fee, plus a note that engineering fees vary widely and floodway no-rise work can mean full HEC-RAS modelling. The candidate's base success rate on ML-selected reaches is 30-50%. Comparing FEMA NFHL floodway layers with 3DEP LiDAR and DOT culvert and channelisation records to find mis-drawn reaches could plausibly lift success 1.5x+ over picking parcels naively. Under the relaxed C3 that is a near-full lever. I scored 4, not 5, because success depends heavily on community and neighbour politics, which ML cannot predict.
scored.data: Floodway status is a legible field in the NFHL. Whether the floodway is wrong is not: that sits in scanned FIS floodway data tables, old effective models, LiDAR differences and scattered DOT and municipal channel records, so the outcome is not pre-summarised. Incumbents, though, already do LOMRs one parcel at a time as a standard developer and civil-engineering tool. The edge is systematic screening, not unreadable data.
scored.right_bought: Yes. These are fee purchases of tax-delinquent, estate-held or remnant floodway lots from owners who cannot evaluate the hydraulics, so the right is bought cheaply. The catch is that the parcels are often thin strips along channels. Even when the floodway is narrowed, the buildable area may be small or bounded by setbacks and the flood fringe, and the inventory in infill metros is limited.
scored.buyer: Multifamily, build-to-rent and REIT-backed infill developers in supply-constrained Sun Belt metros. They are well capitalised, but they will discount for flood-fringe insurance, elevation and fill-mitigation costs, and for reputational risk after Harvey.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs: buy land, then entitle it (LOMR), then develop and own multifamily, then possibly do district-scale channel and flood-control improvements that unlock many parcels at once. That is a real-estate developer ladder. Its top is a big developer, not a trillion-dollar chain, and the base is capped by how many mis-drawn floodway infill parcels exist.
scored.fatal_flaw: A floodway is not a property of one parcel. It is a reach-wide allocation under a surcharge cap. To narrow it, the community must find no practicable alternative, notify affected owners and jurisdictions, accept higher flood elevations on others, and formally adopt the change. Even after a win, the land stays in the 100-year fringe with elevation and no-net-fill burdens. So the proving step is political and regulatory, not a discovery hit, and the step-up is capped well below 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive and an ML lever is plausible, but approval is reach-wide, needs community buy-in and shifts flood risk onto neighbours, and the de-floodwayed land stays flood fringe, so discovery is not the dominant work and the net step-up is about 10-30x.

scored.name: Reviving zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats)
scored.one_line: Buy or option distressed parcels in stalled or antiquated pre-recession subdivisions where vested plat rights have lapsed or are uncertain and REO desks price them as raw land, re-entitle or confirm vested rights and secure will-serve letters, and sell finished-entitled lots to national homebuilders.
scored.unproven_right: Paper lots or tracts in a stalled plat with unclear lapse, reinstatement or vesting status, sold at raw-land prices.
scored.proving_step: Vested-rights determination or replat, updated development agreement and utility capacity letters: about $100k-1M and 12-36 months; likely 50-70% success since the jurisdiction approved once.
scored.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (Lennar, D.R. Horton, Pulte) via lot-option programs and land bankers (Millrose, Varde).
scored.public_data: Scanned plat books and recorded development agreements, planning and council minutes, bond and improvement-guarantee release records, tax-delinquency rolls, imagery of partly built roads and utilities (AZ, FL, NV, ID, TX).
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 10-30x ($5-20k/acre to $100-300k/acre-equivalent entitled lots).
scored.frame: The rung is 'raw or stalled paper lots to entitled, serviceable land'. The proving work (vested-rights research, replat, development agreement, will-serve letters) is about 70-80% legal and discovery work. But builders mostly pay up for FINISHED lots, and getting there takes horizontal development (roads, sewer, water, grading), commonly $40-100k+ per lot. That physical step is large and bespoke, much like the geothermal counter-example. Land bankers (Millrose, Varde) do buy entitled land, but they price it near cost plus a carry return, not as a jackpot. So the frame where discovery is 80%+ exists but is thin.
scored.step_up: The pitch claims 10-30x ($5-20k/acre to $100-300k/acre), but that compares raw land to finished lots and counts in the value of horizontal improvements still to be paid for. Entitlement alone usually lifts value about 2-5x (industry rule of thumb). Raw land per acre fell only 2.4% YoY versus 1.1% for build-ready land (Realtor.com via MortgagePoint, 2026), which shows a modest spread, not 10^3. Acres.com gives a same-county example of $3k vs $18k/acre (6x), and it argues development costs eat much of that gap. Net step-up for the entitlement rung alone: ~2-5x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive: $100k-1M and 12-36 months per vested-rights determination or replat, plus utility capacity letters. The pitch puts the base hit rate at 50-70%, but this is weakened by Arizona's Dawe v. Scottsdale rule: a recorded plat alone does not vest rights, so you need substantial expenditure or construction in reliance. Under relaxed C3, ML that screens thousands of plats for partly built infrastructure, released bonds, utility capacity and still-valid agreements could plausibly lift cost per proven asset 1.5x or more. That counts as a full lever, docked one point because jurisdictional politics (council votes) caps what ML can predict.
scored.data: The data is public and genuinely illegible: scanned plat books, recorded development agreements, council minutes, bond-release records and imagery of half-built roads. But the outcome is partly legible already. Plat status, zoning and entitlement are usually in county GIS or planning databases, and local land brokers and entitlement attorneys already know which stalled projects are revivable. Florida's 2,600+ antiquated subdivisions (2.1M lots) have badly fragmented ownership, so assembly is the problem, not information. The 2009-2012 wave of REO-desk sales at raw-land prices has largely been absorbed by builders and land funds (2012-2022). Today's sellers are mostly individual paper-lot holders and remaining institutional owners.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought: fee title or options on lots and tracts, not free first-come claims. Single-owner stalled tracts are cheap to option. In antiquated subdivisions, though, you have to assemble hundreds of scattered owners, which is slow and full of holdouts.
scored.buyer: Public homebuilders (Lennar, D.R. Horton, Pulte) buy finished lots through option and takedown programs, and land bankers (Millrose, Varde) fund entitled land. Both are well capitalised, but they pay a premium mainly for finished, ready-to-build lots, not for entitlement alone.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: entitlement, then horizontal land development, then a land-banking fund, then vertical homebuilding and master-planned communities, then mortgage and title. These are proven, very large markets (Lennar and Horton are each worth tens of billions). The higher rungs are capital-heavy and cyclical.
scored.fatal_flaw: The jump from paper lot to finished lot comes mostly from horizontal development: physical construction at $40-100k+ per lot, which is hard, bespoke and capital-heavy. Entitlement or vested-rights proving on its own gives only about a 2-5x step-up, and land brokers and builders already price entitlement status reasonably well. So discovery is not 80%+ of the value creation in any rung a builder pays a jackpot for.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps: proving is expensive, and ML triage of stalled plats could plausibly cut cost per proven asset 1.5x or more. But the real step-up from entitlement alone is about 2-5x, not 10^3. The claimed 10-30x needs costly physical lot development. And the REO-mispricing window from the 2008 bust has largely closed.

scored.name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
scored.one_line: Take abandoned-in-place pipelines and easements from operators carrying decommissioning liabilities; ML over easement instruments proves broad 'any substance' assignable scope and continuity; sell to CO2/H2 trunkline and fiber developers.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving title does not create the value and is not where the difficulty lies. Corridors fail on all-parcels-must-pass continuity, easement lapse or reversion (now being written into state law, as in Nebraska LB1186 and Missouri HB 706), bespoke physical requalification, and a stalled CO2/H2 buyer. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode. And the owners can read their own easements and do the good conversions themselves (Tallgrass Trailblazer).
scored.step_up: The basis is near zero or negative, because the operator carries an abandonment liability (my estimate: about $10-50k/mile to abandon in place). Proven value is about $100k-1M/mile to a CO2 developer if the pipe also requalifies (new CO2 build is about $2-4M/mile, with ROW about 10-20% of that; my estimate, not sourced), or about $5-50k/mile capitalised for fiber. That is a ~10-100x step-up, and it is not realised when proving succeeds. It comes only after requalification and once a shipper commits. New laws also threaten the basis: Nebraska LB1186 would revert easements to the landowner within 3 years after a line stops operating, and Missouri HB 706 would treat an easement as abandoned after 10 years of non-use.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap for each parcel (my estimate: about $300-2,000 for title review) but expensive for a corridor: hundreds to thousands of parcels cost roughly $100k-1M+ per corridor attempt, so it clears the relaxed ≥$50k bar. My estimate is that 20-50% of parcels carry broad, assignable language. Corridor success is roughly that rate raised to the power N, so the binding constraint is holdouts and gaps, not choosing the right corridor. ML reading the instruments can cut review cost per parcel and screen corridors before acquisition, plausibly a 1.2-2x gain in cost per proven corridor. That gain is diluted because requalification and holdout cure costs dominate. I give C3 a 3, up from below threshold under the strict rubric.
scored.frame: The rung is acquiring an abandoned-in-place pipe plus its easement chain and proving the corridor is assignable and continuous for CO2, H2 or fiber. Legal discovery is only about 30-50% of the work in that rung. The rest is getting every parcel to pass (holdouts, lapsed easements, scope litigation one parcel at a time), physically requalifying the pipe (PHMSA conversion, integrity testing), and finding a buyer. The CO2 and H2 buyers are currently stalled. The physical step is not trivial, and the real conversions so far were done by the incumbent owner: Tallgrass moved 392 miles of Trailblazer from gas to CO2 itself.
scored.data: The easement instruments are recorded in county deed records, scanned and scattered, which makes them public but illegible. That is a genuine fit. But the operator owns the easements, holds its own land files and can read them, so the seller is not blind to the data. The rights also cannot be bought cheaply apart from the pipe and its liability. Landowners and state legislatures are actively pushing reversion, so the right may be void exactly when it is transferred.
scored.right_bought: You would buy the idle pipe and its easements, with the abandonment liability, from midstream operators. Nominal price is near zero, but you take on the liability and the regulatory exposure. Owners who hold good corridors convert them themselves (Trailblazer is the example).
scored.buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Tallgrass, Summit-type projects, many stalled by permitting and landowner opposition), H2 developers (early-stage and capital-light), and fiber long-haul and middle-mile builders (capitalised, but they pay low ROW values).
scored.ladder: The ladder above is strong: corridor ownership, then operating the CO2/H2 transport pipeline as a midstream operator, then sequestration hubs and fiber and power co-location in the corridors. Midstream is a very large industry, so the path to a big company exists if the first rung works.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the lever to a moderate 3, because proving a whole corridor is expensive. The frame still fails: discovery is not 80% of the work, the step-up needs physical requalification and a stalled buyer, and sellers are not blind to the data.

scored.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
scored.one_line: Option farmland next to substations ML predicts have load headroom; prove with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter; sell powered land to data-center developers. Rescore of powered brownfields with a real purchase discount.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value step-up comes from the utility's firm capacity commitment, and the utility gives that to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral (AEP's 85% take-or-pay for 12 years), not to whoever reads the data first. Study results are non-binding and lose value as others join the queue, and tariffs are now built to filter out speculative flippers. So the 100x jump needs heavy capital and upgrade risk rather than an ML-found hit. Discovery is a minority of the rung, and incumbents already screen the same fairly legible grid data.
scored.step_up: Unproven: farmland in Licking County, OH sells for about $10-15k/acre, and options run about $50-300/acre/yr. Proven: Meta paid more than $1.1M/acre near Columbus in 2025. In Northern Virginia, entitled land without power sells for about $4M/acre and powered land for at least $6M/acre (Avison Young via Data Center Knowledge). So land goes up about 70-100x, and the option premium goes up 10^3x or more. But that jump goes with committed load (an ESA plus collateral), not with a study. A study or a non-binding will-serve letter alone probably gets about 2-5x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: A study costs about $50-250k per site (Texas SB6 set a roughly $100k large-load study fee), so proving clears the C3 expense bar. Base hit rate: AEP Ohio had about 13 GW of load-study requests after its tariff, and only 5.6 GW signed ESAs (E&E News). That puts the hit rate around 40% from study to firm contract, which is inside the relaxed 30-70% band. ML ranking substations by headroom could plausibly give about 1.3-1.6x on cost per proven site against naive screening. Against incumbents who already screen the same hosting-capacity maps and queue data, the edge is smaller. I score this 3, not 5. The relaxation moves C3 up from about 1-2, but the lift is not clearly 1.5x or better against competent rivals.
scored.frame: The rung is optioned farmland plus a utility load study or will-serve letter, sold to data-center developers. Finding headroom accounts for maybe 30-40% of the work in this rung. The rest is securing firm capacity: signing an ESA, posting collateral, accepting minimum-bill commitments (for example, AEP Ohio's 85% take-or-pay over 12 years) and funding network upgrades. That step is capital-heavy and controlled by the utility, not trivial. Capitalised buyers do exist (hyperscalers, Tract-type developers). Altus Group found that committed utility load, not study results, was the strongest predictor of land price.
scored.data: Utility hosting-capacity maps, FERC 715 filings, IRP load forecasts and queue data are public and fairly legible. Incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already extract them. Farmland options can be bought from farmers who do not read grid data, which is a real purchase discount. But the outcome (available capacity) is close to being a legible field, and the utility allocates it first-come to whoever commits capital.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Option or purchase agreements on farmland near substations are bought from farmers at near-agricultural prices. Prices are rising quickly as farmers learn about the data-center demand.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft), colocation and data-center developers, and powered-land platforms (Tract, Cloverleaf). They are heavily capitalised and paying $200k to more than $1M per acre for land with committed power.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: optioned land, then studied land, then land with an ESA or firm capacity, then entitled and powered shell, then built data center or campus developer, then on-site generation or utility-like power provider. It is a real ladder toward a very large company.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 helps a little: proving costs $100k or more and the study-to-ESA rate of about 40% fits the new band. But ML lift against incumbents is modest, and the step-up comes from committing capital to the utility rather than from discovery, so the frame still fails.

scored.name: Cryptic Clusters / Legacy Actinomycete Libraries: orphaned natural-product collections re-read for novel clusters
scored.one_line: Acquire mothballed pharma and academic actinomycete/fungal natural-product strain and extract libraries cheaply, sequence them, ML-rank silent biosynthetic gene clusters for novel high-value chemotypes (anti-Gram-negative, antifungal, ADC payloads), and ferment or express the top few to prove a compound.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is both the dominant cost and the dominant failure mode, which inverts Terranox's 95-5 discovery/physical ratio into roughly 25-75: 11-32% of expressed clusters yield any detectable compound at $50-200k and 6-24 months each, and a commercially viable chemotype is <1-2% per cluster, so ML can only re-rank the cheap part and cannot touch the expensive part. This is exactly the geothermal-in-abandoned-coal-mines failure. Compounding it, the discovery edge is already commoditised: antiSMASH/antiSMASH-DB/BiG-FAM/MIBiG publicly novelty-score nearly every public BGC, and private collections are made legible by $50-200/isolate sequencing that any buyer can run, so there is no durable illegible-data moat and the sellers are sophisticated specialists rather than owners who cannot read their own asset.
scored.step_up: Right side: physical legacy libraries change hands for storage cost or effectively nothing — Sanofi transferred ~110,000 strains (~80,000 actinomycetes, ~70 years of industrial screening) to Fraunhofer IME in 2020 as a shared-resource transfer with no sale price; Ginkgo acquired Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform (>135,000 strains, >4M predicted BGCs) in 2019 on undisclosed, plausibly low-single-digit-million terms as a cast-off asset; Deinove licensed 400 of Naicons' ~45,000 strains, price undisclosed. Call the unproven right ~$10-100 per strain-equivalent, i.e. near zero. Proven side: a preclinical natural-product antibacterial or ADC-payload asset with in vivo proof-of-concept licenses in the low tens of millions upfront in a good case (single-asset preclinical anti-infective deals typically $1-20M upfront plus milestones); ADC payload/linker platform deals go higher but are platform, not single-compound, deals. So ~100-1000x on the right itself, which is C2 = 3 — but, crucially, the step-up is NOT immediate on a hit: it arrives only after the expensive expression-isolation-structure-assay-in-vivo chain, not at the moment of proving existence. A cluster shown merely to express a novel scaffold with no potency data moves value maybe 10-30x, not 10^4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is genuinely expensive, which is what the relaxed C3 rewards. Detection of any compound from a heterologously expressed silent cluster: 11-32% across four large-scale studies (2023 review, PMC10727000). Across 50 studies Jan 2018-Jun 2023, only ~63 new natural-product families emerged in total. Probability a given silent cluster yields a novel compound with commercially relevant potency, selectivity and developability: my estimate <1-2%. Cost per proving attempt: $50-200k and 6-24 months per cluster (consistent with CRO/biofoundry refactoring plus isolation, structure elucidation by NMR/MS, and assay panels); a full isolate-to-structure-to-in-vivo package is my estimate $0.5-2M per serious candidate. Comfortably above the ~$50k / years-per-attempt bar. ML lever: ranking clusters by predicted novelty and by predicted expressibility in a chosen heterologous host plausibly lifts "yields a detectable novel compound" from ~15% to ~30%, i.e. ~2x on cost per proven asset — a full-strength lever by the relaxed standard, so C3 rises from near-0 under the strict rubric to 4. It is 4 rather than 5 because a large part of that ranking is already done for free by public tools (see C4), so the *marginal* ML lift over an incumbent using antiSMASH + BiG-SLiCE is much smaller than the lift over naive random picking.
scored.frame: The sellable rung would be "a legacy strain/extract library plus one novel-chemotype compound proven to exist and hit a target," sold or licensed to a pharma/biotech partner. But inside that rung, discovery (sequence + ML-rank silent BGCs) is roughly 20-30% of the work and the "physical step" (refactor/express/ferment, isolate, elucidate structure, assay for potency, selectivity, developability) is 70-80% — the opposite of Terranox's 95-5 split. The physical step is neither trivial, cheap nor abstracted: 11-32% of heterologously expressed clusters yield any detectable compound, and each attempt is $50-200k and 6-24 months. There is a capitalised buyer (big pharma buys anti-Gram-negative and ADC-payload assets), but it buys a validated hit/lead, not a ranked cluster list, so the buyer sits several expensive rungs above the discovery output. C1 = 2 (buyer exists; discovery share and physical-step triviality both fail).
scored.data: The underlying data is partly public and partly private, but the key failure is legibility of the OUTCOME, not of the raw data. Genomes of public strains are in NCBI; antiSMASH, antiSMASH-DB, BiG-FAM/BiG-SLiCE and MIBiG already auto-annotate essentially every public BGC and attach a novelty/distance-to-known score — i.e. the regulator-equivalent has already written the answer into a legible field, exactly the failure mode prior hunts identified. The genuinely illegible asset is the *unsequenced* private legacy collection (freezer vials, paper screening logs, 1960s-80s fermentation records), and there is real latent value there — but sequencing is cheap (~$50-200/isolate), so any acquirer can make it legible in weeks, which means the illegibility is a temporary and purchasable condition, not a durable moat. Owners (Fraunhofer, Naicons, university collections, ex-Sanofi/Merck/Pfizer archives) are specialists who can read the data as well as the acquirer can; they are not naive sellers. C4 = 2.
scored.right_bought: Right bought: physical strain/extract collections plus the IP and freedom-to-operate to commercialise compounds derived from them — acquired by asset transfer, licence, or by taking over a mothballed collection's custody and storage costs. Price is near zero to low single-digit millions for 10^4-10^5 strains. This part is real: the right is cheap and the step-up on a validated compound is large. The problem is that the right conveys optionality on a very expensive, low-yield proving process rather than on a cheap, decisive one.
scored.buyer: A capitalised buyer exists and is well funded: large pharma and anti-infective-focused biotech buying preclinical-to-Phase-I anti-Gram-negative, antifungal and ADC-payload assets, plus non-dilutive funders (BARDA, CARB-X, AMR Action Fund) who pay for anti-infective development. But the buyer buys a compound with target engagement and in vivo data, not a proven-existent cluster — so the buyer is two or three rungs above the rung this company would win, and the company must fund those rungs itself.
scored.ladder: Clear rungs above: proven compound -> lead optimisation -> IND -> clinic -> commercial product, and horizontally a strain-library-as-platform business. A winner could in principle become a large pharma company, so the ladder is real. But each rung is capital-intensive, slow and failure-prone in a way mine-building is not — climbing it means becoming a drug developer with ~10-year, ~$1B+ per-approval economics, so the smallest rung does not cheaply bootstrap the whole chain. C5 = 3.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxed C3 genuinely rescues only the hit-rate leg (proving is expensive and ML plausibly gives ~2x on cost per proven asset, so C3 goes from near-0 to 4), but the structural defects are untouched: the expensive, low-yield wet-lab proving step dominates the work instead of discovery, and the discovery answer is already written into free public novelty scores while private collections are cheaply sequenced by anyone — so total 14/25 and the fatal flaw stands.
sources: 2023 review of heterologous expression success rates for silent BGCs, PMC10727000 (11-32% detection of any compound; ~63 new natural product families across 50 studies Jan 2018-Jun 2023)
Sanofi to Fraunhofer IME transfer of ~110,000 microbial strains incl. ~80,000 actinomycetes (2020), reported as a shared-resource transfer with no disclosed sale price
Ginkgo Bioworks acquisition of Warp Drive Bio genome-mining platform (2019): >135,000 bacterial strains, >4M predicted BGCs, terms undisclosed
Deinove-Naicons licence covering 400 of ~45,000 strains, price undisclosed
antiSMASH / antiSMASH-DB / BiG-FAM (BiG-SLiCE) / MIBiG: public automated BGC annotation and novelty scoring of essentially all public BGCs
Candidate's own capex figure of $50-200k and 6-24 months per cluster, cross-checked against CRO/biofoundry refactoring, isolation and structure-elucidation pricing

scored.name: DeadPatent Hits: re-proving unlicensed university compound patents against new targets
scored.one_line: ML over unlicensed university chemistry/biology patents and assay tables finds compounds hitting targets that became valuable after filing (GLP-1R small molecules, KRAS, NLRP3, Lp(a), TL1A). Option from the TTO, resynthesise and assay at a CRO, then license to biotech.
scored.fatal_flaw: Hit substitution. Validated hits are near-commodities: Enamine REAL plus docking, or DEL screening, gives unencumbered hits at about $100 per compound. So a re-proven old university patent commands little premium, and the real value step-up happens later, in medicinal-chemistry optimisation, which is not discovery-dominated. The relaxed C3 does not fix the weak C1 and C2.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a TTO option is about $10-50k. Proven: a re-validated hit with no in vivo data might get $0-1M upfront. Harvard-Merck's $20M upfront was called atypical by BioCentury, and UT-CSPC's $4.5M was for mAb candidates further along. The realistic step-up is about 3-30x and back-loaded into milestones. This is unchanged from the prior round.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $50-150k and takes 6-10 weeks at a CRO, which meets the relaxed expense threshold. Virtual-screening hit rates are typically about 5-30% at the micromolar level. Clearing potency, selectivity and ADME is perhaps 2-10% (literature estimate). ML could plausibly improve cost per proven hit about 1.5-3x by mining patent assay tables that incumbents do not cross-reference. The relaxed C3 accepts that lift, so C3 rises to about 4. It is held below 5 because incumbent docking over ChEMBL/SureChEMBL already captures part of the baseline.
scored.frame: The rung is to option an unlicensed university compound patent, resynthesise the compound, re-assay it against a newly valuable target at a CRO, then license it to biotech. Inside that rung, discovery is perhaps 60-70% of the work, and the physical step (CRO synthesis plus assays) is outsourced. The rung's output, a re-validated hit with old composition-of-matter IP, is not something capitalised buyers pay much for, because they can get hits cheaply elsewhere. The frame exists but its buyer is weak.
scored.data: The patents and assay tables are public but semi-legible: SureChEMBL and ChEMBL already extract the structures and much of the bioactivity. TTOs will option cheaply, but the rights are not uniquely valuable, because the same chemical space is buyable from Enamine REAL or DEL providers with no IP encumbrance.
scored.right_bought: An option or licence from a university TTO on an unlicensed patent, at about $10-50k.
scored.buyer: Biotechs and pharma business-development teams. They are capitalised but discount early hits heavily and pay mostly in milestones.
scored.ladder: There are strong rungs above: lead optimisation, IND-enabling studies, clinical trials, and then a full drug company. However, the rungs above are not discovery-dominated.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the hit-rate lever to 4 because CRO proving is expensive and ML gives roughly 2x, but there is still a weak 3-30x step-up and hit substitution leaves no premium buyer for the proven rung.
sources: IPWatchdog/LESI: about 60-70% of US university patents are never licensed (cited in the prior round)
BioCentury on the Harvard-Merck $20M upfront deal for preclinical inhibitors being atypical (prior round)
UT-CSPC $4.5M upfront for two preclinical mAbs (prior round)
Enamine REAL / DEL provider pricing of about $100 per compound (prior round)

scored.name: German Bauerwartungsland: picking farmland ahead of a Bebauungsplan
scored.one_line: Option arable land at farm prices next to built-up areas in German growth regions. Pick fields by reading Gemeinderat minutes, Flächennutzungsplan change procedures and Regionalplan settlement allocations to predict which will be zoned. Fund the Bebauungsplan as Vorhabenträger under a städtebaulicher Vertrag and sell Bauland to developers, who pay the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Option or purchase of Ackerland at about €5-10/m² that the Flächennutzungsplan does not yet designate as building land. Owners are farmers and Erbengemeinschaften who cannot follow about 11,000 Ratsinformationssysteme.
scored.proving_step: Planning studies and the Bebauungsplan procedure (environmental report, compensation measures) under an urban development contract. About €200k-€1M and 2-5 years, plausibly 30-60% success on picked sites. Screen out municipalities that use Zwischenerwerb or Einheimischenmodelle, which cap the private uplift.
scored.proven_buyer: Bauträger and Projektentwickler (Vonovia development arm, Instone, regional developers) and logistics developers; raw building land in growth regions trades at about €150-500/m².
scored.public_data: Ratsinformationssysteme minutes and Beschlussvorlagen (PDF), Flächennutzungsplan amendment notices in Amtsblätter, Regionalplan settlement areas, BORIS standard land values (price current status, not future zoning), ISEK and housing needs reports.
scored.rough_step_up: About 30-60x (€7/m² to €250/m²).
scored.frame: The rung is Baulandentwicklung: option Ackerland, push it through FNP and Bebauungsplan, sell Rohbauland. It can be sold, and German land developers already do this work. Discovery (picking the field) is maybe 20-35% of the effort. Most of the work is political and procedural, and picking the field does not make it easy. That work is: lobbying the Gemeinderat, the Umweltbericht, Artenschutz surveys, Ausgleichsflächen, negotiating the städtebaulicher Vertrag, and assembling several owners (Erbengemeinschaften) into one plan area. This is close to the geothermal counter-example, where executing the bespoke step is harder than finding the asset. There is a capitalised buyer (Bauträger and Projektentwickler), so the frame half-works.
scored.step_up: The headline figure is €5-7/m² Ackerland to €150-500/m² finished Bauland, about 30-60x. Three things cut that down. (1) Erschlossenes Bauland is not the output of this rung. Erschließung costs about €50-100/m², and 25-35% of the gross area is lost to roads and green space. (2) Municipal capture under SoBoN-style § 11 BauGB contracts often takes up to about 2/3 of the planning uplift (Berlin's cooperative model explicitly tests the burden against the uplift). (3) Once the FNP designates the land, Bauerwartungsland already trades at 25-60% of the Bauland value (McMakler), so the price climbs in steps and does not jump on a single hit. The realistic net step for a private owner, from Acker to sold Rohbauland, is about 10-25x. A forum example: a developer offered €11.50/m² against a €25/m² Bodenrichtwert in Sachsen-Anhalt in 2022.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about €200k-1M and takes 2-5 years per site (the candidate's own estimate, consistent with typical B-Plan costs), so it clears the 'expensive' bar. The base hit rate on picked sites is plausibly 30-60%. Under the relaxed C3, ML that reads Ratsinfo minutes and Regionalplan allocations could pick better sites before options are signed. But the zoning decision is a local political choice, often made years later, and it depends on council majorities, Flächensparziele (the 30 ha/day target) and the municipality's own land-policy model. Local developers and the farmers already track these signals in person. I estimate the lift at about 1.2-1.5x, not 2-3x. No source was found that quantifies it.
scored.data: The data is public and genuinely illegible: about 11,000 Ratsinformationssysteme of PDF minutes, Amtsblatt notices, and scanned Regionalplan maps. But the key outcome signals are fairly legible. Regionalplan settlement allocations and FNP designations are published maps. Once land is in the FNP it is priced as Bauerwartungsland, so the regulator effectively writes the answer into a status field, and the edge only exists before the FNP stage. Rights are bought, not free first-come, which is good. But owners are not naive. Farmers are advised by Bauernverband and topagrar. Option contracts with Nachbewertungsklauseln are standard, and topagrar notes that the option contract itself can be treated as evidence of Bauerwartung. Municipalities hold Vorkaufsrecht under §§ 24-25 BauGB.
scored.right_bought: Option or purchase of Ackerland at about €5-10/m² before FNP designation. Farmers often negotiate uplift-sharing (Nachzahlung) clauses that claw back much of the gain.
scored.buyer: Bauträger, Projektentwickler, logistics developers and municipal land funds. They are capitalised and active. In many growth municipalities, though, the municipality itself is the required counterparty at a capped price.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: land development, then Erschließung, then Bauträger home building, then build-to-rent and portfolio ownership (the Vonovia scale). Each rung above this one is a commoditised, low-margin, crowded construction business in a market that is down cyclically. The discovery edge does not carry upward.
scored.fatal_flaw: A municipal political decision gates the step-up, and growth-region municipalities increasingly design that decision to deny the uplift to private holders. Münster, Potsdam, Ulm, Braunschweig and others only start a Bebauungsplan in the Außenbereich if the city first owns at least 50% of the land, bought at a 'very low Bauerwartung' price. Elsewhere, SoBoN-style contracts capture up to about 2/3 of the uplift. These are exactly the growth regions the thesis targets. So the private optionholder often cannot realise the step-up, and the proving step is politics and permitting rather than discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the proving step is expensive, but the net step-up is only about 10-25x after Erschließung and municipal capture. The proving work is political and procedural rather than discovery, and growth-region municipalities increasingly require that they buy 50%+ themselves at Bauerwartung prices before zoning, which blocks private capture of the uplift.

scored.name: Australian rural-to-urban rezoning (NSW, SEQ and Victorian growth corridors)
scored.one_line: Option broadacre rural land near the growth fronts of Western Sydney, the Hunter, South East Queensland or Melbourne. Pick parcels by mining planning panel reports, council papers and state infrastructure plans. Lodge a proponent-led planning proposal or planning scheme amendment (NSW gateway to LEP amendment; Victorian PSA or precinct structure plan; SEQ scheme amendment) and sell zoned englobo land to master-planned community developers.
scored.unproven_right: Option over RU1/RU2, Farming Zone or Rural Zone land at about AUD $50-200k/ha from pastoral families who price it on agricultural yield and cannot read regional plan or servicing signals.
scored.proving_step: Planning proposal or scheme amendment: gateway or panel hearing, specialist studies (flood, bushfire, biodiversity, traffic), exhibition and state infrastructure contribution negotiation. About AUD $0.5-3M and 2-6 years; plausibly 30-60% success on sites inside state-identified investigation or growth areas.
scored.proven_buyer: Stockland, Mirvac, Lendlease Communities, Frasers Property, Peet, AVJennings, AVID/Sekisui, Satterley and land funds, paying about AUD $1-3M/ha for zoned englobo land.
scored.public_data: NSW Planning Portal planning proposal tracker and document sets, Planning Panels Victoria reports, council business papers and Local Planning Panel minutes, VPA, EDQ and ShapingSEQ investigation-area documents, Sydney Water, Urban Utilities and water-authority servicing plans, flood studies, the Government Gazette. Gateway conditions and refusal reasons sit unstructured in PDFs; which parcels inside investigation areas get zoned first is not legible.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-30x (AUD $100k/ha to AUD $1-3M/ha).
scored.frame: The rung is "hold an option on fringe rural land, get it rezoned, sell it as englobo land". Picking the parcel is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of the effort is the proving step itself: 2-6 years of specialist studies (flood, bushfire, biodiversity, traffic), council and state lobbying, exhibition, infrastructure contribution negotiation and gateway extensions. That step is political and procedural, not trivial or abstracted. The buyers are well capitalised (Stockland, Mirvac, Lendlease, Frasers and others). But these same developers option land and run rezonings in-house, so the buyer is also the main competitor for the rung.
scored.step_up: Zoned or zone-ready englobo land sells for about AUD 1.5-2M/ha (Melbourne benchmarks: $2M/ha cited in 2018, $1.5M/ha at Craigieburn). True agricultural land goes for about AUD 50-100k/ha, which would mean 15-30x. Land near a growth front already trades at hope value, though. Beveridge: 600 ha inside Melbourne's growth boundary but not yet in a precinct plan sold for $220M in 2018, about $367k/ha. Austral, Western Sydney: about $240/m2, roughly $2.4M/ha, on a $100M guide for 41 ha. So land actually inside state investigation areas costs about $300k-1M/ha, and the realistic step-up is about 2-6x before infrastructure contributions, which often run tens of thousands of dollars per lot. That puts the net step-up below 10x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about AUD 0.5-3M and takes 2-6 years. NSW gateway deadlines are 12-15 months and are routinely extended, sometimes to 4 years or more. The Kempsey case ran from lodgement in 2021 to a revised proposal in 2023. I found no published success rate. The candidate's 30-60% for sites inside investigation areas is plausible. That base rate is acceptable under the relaxed C3, and proving is clearly expensive. But ML only plausibly lifts cost per proven asset by about 1.2-1.5x. The order in which parcels get zoned is driven mostly by servicing sequencing and state priority lists that are already published, plus politics and lobbying that the documents do not capture. Sources: NSW Planning Portal gateway determinations (Tahmoor, Wyong/Central Coast) and Kempsey rezoning review documents.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: gateway conditions, panel reports and refusal reasons sit in PDFs scattered across councils and the planning portal. But the main signal is legible and published as maps: urban growth boundaries, ShapingSEQ investigation areas, the Victorian precinct structure plan program, Sydney Water growth servicing plans and state rezoning pipeline lists. Incumbents (developers' acquisition teams, land agents marketing "land bank opportunities") already read these closely. The outcome field, a zoning change, is itself legible once it happens, and the leading indicators are fairly legible too.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free first-come: a call option or put-and-call deal from the landowner. But fringe families are not naive. Developers and land bankers have been approaching them for decades, and asking prices already carry hope value, as the Nillumbik council submission and the Beveridge sale show. Cheap options are only available well outside the published growth areas, where the hit rate collapses.
scored.buyer: Master-planned community developers and land funds (Stockland, Mirvac, Lendlease Communities, Frasers, Peet, AVJennings, Satterley) paying about AUD 1-2M+/ha for zoned englobo land. They are well capitalised and transact regularly.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: zoned englobo land, then civil works and subdivision, then lot sales, then built-form housing, then master-planned communities and community or retail assets. Stockland-scale outcomes (an ASX-listed company in the tens of billions) are possible. It is a capital-intensive, cyclical, domestic market, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is already priced in. Land with any real chance of rezoning sits inside published growth or investigation areas and trades at hope value (Beveridge about $367k/ha unzoned versus about $1.5-2M/ha zoned). Developers hunt for exactly these parcels themselves. That leaves a 2-6x, multi-year, politically driven proving step, where the work is advocacy rather than discovery and ML adds only a modest edge.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but crowded land-banking trade: the planning signal is mostly published in maps, owners already price in hope value, the proving step is long political work rather than discovery, and the net step-up is about 2-6x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Texas ETJ-release plus MUD/WCID formation land
scored.one_line: Option fringe ranch and farm acreage near Texas metros, use SB 2038 (2023) to release it from a city's ETJ, form a MUD or WCID with a utility service agreement and development agreement, and sell the entitled, utility-backed tract to master-planned-community builders. The company also keeps reimbursement rights on the district's future bonds.
scored.unproven_right: Options on 200-2,000 acre ag-exempt tracts at about $5-30k/acre where the ETJ or the lack of a utility provider blocks development; many sit inside dormant CCNs the owners do not know can be decertified.
scored.proving_step: ETJ release petition, CCN decertification or release, TCEQ or legislative MUD creation, wholesale water/sewer contract, development agreement and preliminary plat. About $0.3-1.5M and 1-3 years; about 50-70% success on screened tracts.
scored.proven_buyer: Master-planned-community developers and national homebuilders (Johnson Development, Hillwood, D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, Taylor Morrison) plus land-banking funds.
scored.public_data: TCEQ water district database and scanned creation orders, PUCT CCN maps and decertification dockets, city council and ETJ-release minutes, county commissioners court minutes, wholesale utility contracts in PUC dockets, regional water plans, appraisal district rolls. Serviceability lives in scattered PDFs, not a parcel field.
scored.rough_step_up: About 4-10x on land ($8-15k/acre to $50-150k/acre entitled), plus roughly 1-2x more from MUD bond reimbursement rights.
scored.frame: The rung is real and sellable: the company sells entitled, utility-backed acreage, and homebuilders and MPC developers buy it. Discovery is not 80% of the work inside it, though. Finding the tract is maybe 20-30%. The other 70-80% is legal, political and engineering work: getting a wholesale water/sewer contract from a provider with capacity, CCN decertification, MUD creation, negotiating the development agreement, and the plat. The physical step is not a drill but a multi-year entitlement campaign. That is exactly what existing land-entitlement firms (Hillwood, Johnson Development, Bury, land funds) already do as their core skill.
scored.step_up: Unproven land: fringe ag acreage at about $8-30k/acre (generic Texas land guides put rural land at $1.5-25k/acre, with a premium on the metro fringe). Proven land: listings next to or inside MUDs with utilities ask about $120k/acre (17.97 ac in Jarrell, next to Sontera MUD, $2.15M) and about $375k/acre (93 ac in Hutto with its own MUD sewer plant, $35M list). These are asking prices, often for smaller or more advanced parcels. For large raw-to-entitled tracts the realistic step-up is about 3-8x, plus bond reimbursement of perhaps 1-2x more. The option structure gives levered equity returns, but the asset step-up itself is far below 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's own figures put proving at about $0.3-1.5M and 1-3 years per tract, with roughly 50-70% success on screened tracts. These are unverified; I found no public tally of MUD creation outcomes. Proving clearly passes the 'expensive' bar. The ETJ release leg is cheap and ministerial: Austin's FAQ says the city has no discretion once a compliant SB 2038 petition is filed, and Leander charges $590 in fees, so it carries no information edge. Failures come mainly from wholesale utility capacity, city or provider politics and market timing. Reading wastewater capacity, CCN dockets and regional water plans with ML might lift the hit rate about 1.2-1.5x, not reliably 1.5x or more. Score 3.
scored.data: The data is partly public and illegible: TCEQ creation orders, PUC wholesale contract dockets, council and commissioners court minutes, and regional water plans sit in scattered PDFs. Key outcomes, however, are already in legible fields. The TCEQ Water District database lists every existing district, and PUCT CCN boundaries are downloadable GIS shapefiles. Sophisticated land developers and brokers already track utility capacity by hand, and it is a relationship-driven local market. ML has some edge in reading capacity and politics, but it is not a hidden-signal edge. Score 2.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Options or purchase contracts are bought from ranch and farm families who generally cannot read the dockets. But fringe acreage near Austin, DFW, Houston and San Antonio is heavily solicited by land brokers, builders' land teams and land-banking funds, and owners increasingly price in 'MUD potential' (for example a Jarrell ranch family selling 200 acres directly to a national builder). The discount exists, but it is competed down.
scored.buyer: Capitalised and deep: national homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, Taylor Morrison) via land-light option and land-banking structures, MPC developers (Johnson Development, Hillwood), and land-banking funds. They routinely pay for entitled, utility-served acreage.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: entitlement leads to horizontal development (finished lots, reimbursed by MUD bonds), then MPC master developer, then vertical homebuilding and build-to-rent, then owning and operating utilities and districts, then commercial town centers. Howard Hughes, Hillwood and Johnson Development are proof that the path builds very large companies. Score 4.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is the existing Texas land-entitlement business. The rung's work is legal, political and utility-negotiation execution, not discovery, and the step-up is only about 3-8x on land. Key status data (TCEQ district database, CCN shapefiles) is already legible, so ML adds at most a modest screening edge in a market where sophisticated incumbents compete for the same fringe tracts.
scored.one_line_reason: The ladder and buyer are real, but discovery is a minority of the work, the step-up is about 3-8x not 10^3, and the ML edge over experienced Texas land entitlers is thin. The relaxed C3 only lifts the hit-rate lever to about 3.

scored.name: Retired fossil plant sites with reusable interconnection (surplus/replacement rights)
scored.one_line: Buy or option retired or retiring peaker and coal plant sites from co-ops, munis and IPP estates who see only a decommissioning liability, prove FERC/RTO replacement or surplus interconnection rights for co-located generation, storage or large load before they lapse, and sell the energised brownfield to hyperscalers or power-plus-DC developers. Adjacent to the killed powered-brownfields idea; the edge is ML on which sites keep deliverable MW, and remediation must be screened.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or option on a retired plant parcel near salvage value, plus the at-risk right to reuse interconnection service that lapses about 1-3 years after retirement.
scored.proving_step: MISO, PJM or SPP replacement or surplus interconnection application and study, local use permit and Phase I/II baseline: about $0.1-3M and 12-24 months; roughly 40-70% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, power-to-DC developers and IPPs (Constellation, Vistra, NRG, Crusoe) and BESS developers, paying about $50k-3M per deliverable MW.
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary interconnection agreements and study PDFs, EIA-860 and 860M retirements, RTO deactivation notices, scanned RTO tariff filings, state PUC and environmental closure filings, county assessor records.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-50x all-in; retirement lists are legible, so the ML edge is moderate and cleanup costs can eat the uplift.
scored.frame: The rung is 'site control plus a confirmed reusable interconnection right' (replacement or surplus interconnection service), sold to a powered-land buyer. Discovery is perhaps 30-40% of the work inside this rung. Most of the effort goes to negotiating with the plant owner, running the RTO study, local permitting, and Phase I/II plus remediation scoping. Remediation (ash ponds, asbestos, demolition) is a large physical step and is not abstracted.
