Capitalised buyers do exist: hyperscalers, Constellation/Vistra/NRG, Crusoe, TeraWulf, and the Homer City Redevelopment-style developers.
scored.step_up: I found no reliable per-MW price for retired-plant or powered-land sales. Avison Young puts Northern Virginia powered land at about $6M/acre against about $4M/acre for entitled land without power, only about 1.5x. Rural coal-plant parcels at salvage value are near zero after netting decommissioning liabilities, and a confirmed few-hundred-MW interconnection plausibly sells for $50k-500k/MW. Homer City is the showcase: a 3,200-acre retired coal site whose PJM and NYISO interconnections anchor a $10B+ project with 4.5 GW of planned gas generation. All-in, the step-up is about 5-50x, and less where remediation liabilities are large. That is far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step costs about $0.1-3M and 12-24 months, so it passes the 'expensive' test. Base success is about 40-70% (candidate estimate; I found no published hit-rate data). The ML lever is predicting which sites keep deliverable MW: transmission headroom, how long the right can be retained, and remediation burden. But the grant mostly follows from the existing ISA/CIR values plus a load-flow study, and RTO engineers' power-flow models already answer the deliverability question. A plausible lift is 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven site. MISO's ERAS and PJM's RRI fast-track lanes also show that the binding constraint is the RTO process and queue politics, not prediction.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. EIA-860/860M gives the retirements and nameplate MW, RTO deactivation notices are public and structured, and the interconnection agreements in FERC eLibrary state the MW and point of interconnection in a field. The outcome (MW that can be reused) is largely written into the ISA or CIR, the same pattern that killed the grid-queue idea, where a lookup table matched ML. The illegible residue is scanned closure/ash-pond filings and assessor records, which inform remediation risk rather than the core signal.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought in principle (fee title or an option), but the sellers are not illiterate about its value. Since 2024, IPP estates and utilities have actively marketed retired sites to data-centre developers: GenOn sold Morgantown to TeraWulf, Homer City went to a developer consortium, and Brandon Shores-type sites sit in a crowded field. Co-ops and munis are slower but are advised by consultants and the RTOs. The interconnection right also attaches to the generator owner and lapses by tariff, and utilities often reserve it for their own replacement generation. The discount to salvage value is shrinking fast.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (via power-plus-DC developers), IPPs such as Constellation, Vistra and NRG, Crusoe, bitcoin/AI hosts such as TeraWulf, and BESS developers. They are well capitalised, but their willingness to pay depends on firm deliverable MW and a clean environmental baseline. Market-monitor and FERC opposition to co-location and to retiring resources (the PJM IMM challenge to Morgantown) adds regulatory risk.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong. Site control plus interconnection leads to building replacement gas, storage or generation on site, then a powered shell or data-centre campus, then owning and operating power-plus-compute (the Homer City model, $10B+). That is a credible path to a very large company, but every rung above the first is capital-heavy construction, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry. Retired-plant interconnection is now the most-shopped asset in US power: the retirement lists and ISA MW values are legible fields, and the owners and their advisors already price the right at data-centre value. Meanwhile, the remediation and build steps, not discovery, decide whether a deal works.
scored.one_line_reason: The capitalised buyers and the ladder are real, but discovery is a minority of the rung, the outcome sits in legible ISA/EIA fields, sellers are now value-aware, and the step-up is only about 5-50x. The relaxed C3 raises it only to a moderate 3.

scored.name: Foreign-only drugs to a US 505(b)(2) NDA
scored.one_line: License US rights to drugs long approved in Japan, the EU or Korea but never filed with the FDA, bridge with a 505(b)(2) relying on foreign data, and sell the approved US NDA to a specialty pharma.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive US license or option for about $0.2-2M upfront from a mid-size Japanese, EU or Korean firm lacking FDA know-how.
scored.proving_step: 505(b)(2) approval, often with one bridging PK study or modest confirmatory trial: about $10-30M and 2-4 years; likely 50-70% approval.
scored.proven_buyer: US specialty pharma (Jazz, Supernus, Harmony, PE-backed rollups).
scored.public_data: PMDA review reports (Japanese PDFs), EMA EPARs and Article 57 database, MFDS approvals, J-STAGE and Ichushi, Drugs@FDA, CMS claims.
scored.rough_step_up: 5-20x on capex and 100x+ on the right.
scored.frame: The rung is "exclusive US rights to a foreign-approved drug, carried to a US NDA" and then sold. Buyers do exist with money: US specialty pharma pays for approved, exclusive NDAs. But finding the drug is only about 20-30% of the work inside this rung. Most of it is the proving step: a $10-30M, 2-4 year program covering bridging PK or confirmatory trials, US-standard GCP data audits, CMC and tech transfer, facility inspection readiness and FDA negotiation. This is the opposite of trivial drilling. Landiolol is the example: licensed for US rights in 2021 on existing Japanese and EU data with "no additional clinical work expected", it still took until Nov 2024 to get approved, and the sponsor changed (Eagle to AOP) along the way.
scored.step_up: Unproven US right: about $0.2-5M upfront. The Eagle/AOP landiolol US license was $5M upfront plus milestones, above the candidate's $0.2-2M. Proven right: an approved NDA with 5-year NCE exclusivity (or 3-year for a new clinical investigation) sells for roughly $30-300M, depending on the US market. Precedent: Amneal paid $100M upfront for Kashiv Specialty, a whole 505(b)(2) pipeline company. That is about 30-300x on the right but only about 3-10x on all-in capex once the $10-30M proving cost is counted. The step-up is not immediate: buyers still discount for commercial risk, and many old foreign drugs have small US markets. Scores 3, not the 10^3-10^4 of the rubric.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $10-30M and 2-4 years per attempt, so it clears the "expensive" bar. The base approval rate for 505(b)(2) with an existing foreign efficacy package is roughly 50-70% (the candidate's own estimate; CRLs on CMC or facilities are common, as with landiolol). Under the relaxed C3, ML can lift cost per proven asset by screening PMDA, EPAR and MFDS reports for packages likely to meet FDA standards (randomised placebo-controlled trials, ICH-GCP era, population comparability) and for US commercial size. A 1.2-1.5x gain is plausible. A 1.5x+ gain is doubtful, because the main failure modes (FDA wanting new US trials, CMC and inspection problems, weak commercial uptake) are judgment and execution risks that review-report text predicts poorly. Score 3.
scored.data: PMDA review reports (Japanese PDFs), EMA EPARs and Article 57, MFDS approvals and J-STAGE are public and partly illegible. But the core candidate list is fully legible: joining PMDA, EMA and MFDS approval lists against Drugs@FDA by active ingredient produces it, so the outcome sits in a status field (approved there, absent here). ML would only add the second-order call on whether the foreign data will satisfy FDA. Text extraction can help with that, but regulatory consultants and in-licensors (AOP, Eagle, Nobelpharma, Eton and others) already do this work by hand.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, not claimed first-come, which fits the rubric. But the sellers are sophisticated pharma companies that fully understand their own data. They lack US infrastructure, not the ability to read their data. Many now file in the US themselves (Mitsubishi Tanabe with edaravone, Nobelpharma with Hyftor, Kyowa Kirin with istradefylline), and the good assets attract competing in-licensors. That pushes upfronts above $0.2-2M (landiolol was $5M) and adds royalties and milestones that take back much of the step-up. There is no information-asymmetry discount like the one on a Saskatchewan claim.
scored.buyer: US specialty pharma and PE-backed rollups (Jazz, Supernus, Harmony, Amneal, ANI, Eagle), plus the licensor itself buying back US rights. Real and well funded, but they price commercial risk, so payments come mostly as milestones and royalties rather than a clean lump sum on approval.
scored.ladder: Several rungs sit above: keep the NDA and commercialise it in the US, which means building a specialty pharma company with sales, market access and distribution. Then build a portfolio of in-licensed foreign assets, then own manufacturing, then move to global rights or lifecycle management. Specialty pharma can reach multi-billion scale (Jazz is about $10B+). There is no obvious trillion-dollar path, and every rung up is a conventional, crowded pharma business.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the dominant work in the rung. The proving step is a $10-30M, multi-year regulatory, CMC and clinical program in which execution and FDA judgment set success, not finding the asset. And the candidate list is already legible: a simple join of foreign approval lists against Drugs@FDA produces it, and the owners know their drugs well. So ML neither shrinks the dominant cost nor exploits an illegible-data asymmetry.
scored.one_line_reason: A real, financeable 505(b)(2) arbitrage with buyers who pay, but it is an execution-heavy regulatory business: discovery is under 30% of the rung, the "approved abroad, absent in the US" signal is a legible join, and the step-up is about 3-10x on capex, not 10^3-10^4.

scored.name: Poland plan-ogólny rezoning arbitrage (agricultural to MPZP residential / logistics land)
scored.one_line: Option agricultural plots on the edges of growing gminas (Warsaw, Wrocław, Poznań, Kraków, Tricity, A2/S8 corridors) while plany ogólne are being finalised (due 31 Aug 2026, many late, WZ frozen), pay for an MPZP or ZPI, and sell buildable land to housebuilders or logistics developers.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on agricultural or unzoned plots at roughly PLN 5-15/m² from farmers or heirs who cannot read where the POG puts development zones.
scored.proving_step: Designation inside a POG development zone, then MPZP or ZPI with developer agreement: about PLN 300k-1.5M and 1.5-3 years; maybe 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Dom Development, Atal, Develia, Murapol, Panattoni, P3, MDC2, Hillwood.
scored.public_data: Draft and adopted plany ogólne in the Rejestr Urbanistyczny and gmina BIPs, scanned consultation comments, council minutes, archived WZ decisions, GUGiK Geoportal/EGiB, GDDKiA road documents.
scored.rough_step_up: About 15-30x on land (PLN 10/m² to PLN 150-400/m²), 100x+ on option premium.
scored.frame: The rung is buying land and getting it entitled: option the plot, get it inside a POG development zone, get an MPZP or ZPI adopted, then sell it to a housebuilder or logistics developer. The physical step is trivial because nothing gets built. Discovery (picking which plot) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is political and procedural: lobbying the gmina council, negotiating the developer agreement, sitting through consultations, and paying the planning levy (opłata planistyczna, up to 30% of the value gain). That is execution, not discovery, so this falls short of the 80%+ bar. The buyers (Dom Development, Atal, Panattoni, P3) do have capital and buy entitled land routinely.
scored.step_up: Agricultural land on a gmina edge sold at its real farm value is roughly PLN 3-10/m². But land near growing metros already trades with hope value priced in, often PLN 30-150/m², so the candidate's PLN 5-15/m² entry price is optimistic. Entitled land: Otodom 2025 puts the average Mazovia building plot at about PLN 397/m². AXI IMMO puts warehouse-ready land around Warsaw at PLN 450-650/m² in the inner zone, 250-350 in the second zone (Pruszków, Nadarzyn) and about 100 in the outer zone. A realistic land step-up is about 3-30x, near 10x on average. The return on the option premium alone can exceed 100x, but that is leverage, not a change in the asset's value. This sits in the C2 10-100x band, low end.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's own figures: PLN 300k-1.5M (about $75k-375k) and 1.5-3 years per MPZP or ZPI, with 40-60% success. That clears the 'expensive' bar under the relaxed C3, and the hit rate is in the newly acceptable 30-70% range. ML could plausibly reach about 1.5x on cost per entitled hectare in the window before a POG is adopted: reading draft POGs, consultation comments and council minutes to predict where zones land and which councils will pass MPZPs. After adoption that edge mostly disappears, because the zones are published as machine-readable data. Scored 3 because the lever is real but fades fast. These cost and success figures are the candidate's own assumptions; I did not verify them.
scored.data: Drafts and consultation material are scattered across gmina BIPs as scanned PDFs, which is illegible. But the outcome itself, the adopted plan ogólny, must be published in the Rejestr Urbanistyczny as vector GML with typed planning zones (strefy planistyczne) and infill areas (obszary uzupełnienia zabudowy, OUZ). A validation report for the Świerklany gmina POG, for example, lists 330 zones and 86 infill areas, and e-mapa.net serves every gmina's POG. That is exactly the pattern from prior hunts: the regulator writes the answer into a legible field. The only edge is time-limited, roughly 2025-2026 while plans are being drafted. Many gminas, especially in fast-growing metro areas, have already adopted. The legal deadline of 31 Aug 2026 has passed (it was moved from end-2025 to 30 Jun 2026, then to 31 Aug 2026), so the window is now closing or closed.
scored.right_bought: Partially. A conditional sale agreement or option is possible, but the Agricultural System Act (ustawa o kształtowaniu ustroju rolnego) generally limits who can buy farmland above 0.3 ha: the buyer must be an individual farmer, and KOWR (the state agricultural land agency) holds a pre-emption right. Exemptions cover land inside city limits and land planned for non-agricultural use, which is circular here, because the land qualifies only after the zoning you are trying to win. Owners near growing metro areas are not naive: land agents and developers' acquisition teams already work these edges, and asking prices carry hope value.
scored.buyer: Housebuilders (Dom Development, Atal, Develia, Murapol) and logistics developers (Panattoni, P3, MDC2, Hillwood) have plenty of capital and buy entitled land routinely. They usually price in the remaining planning risk and pay in tranches tied to permits.
scored.ladder: Land entitlement, then development (housing or warehouses), then owning the built stock as a build-to-rent or logistics REIT. The ladder exists, but every upper rung is a crowded, commodity-margin real estate business with no ML moat. That makes it a path to a large Polish property developer, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is written into a legible field. The plan ogólny is published as machine-readable GML with typed planning zones, so once a gmina adopts it the 'where will development go' answer is free to everyone, and farmers and developers already price hope value at metro edges. What remains is a narrow pre-adoption timing window that the 31 Aug 2026 deadline is now closing, plus a farmland purchase restriction (individual-farmer requirement and KOWR pre-emption) that makes cheap optioning awkward.
scored.one_line_reason: This is real land arbitrage with capitalised buyers and an expensive proving step, but the zoning outcome is published as machine-readable GML, entry land already carries hope value, the step-up is only about 10x, and most of the work is political rather than discovery.

scored.name: Haryana / Maharashtra agricultural land conversion with DTCP licence or CLU
scored.one_line: Buy or JDA-option agricultural land near new expressways (Dwarka Expressway, Samruddhi nodes, Navi Mumbai airport zone), secure the change-of-land-use or colony licence, and sell or JDA licensed land to listed developers.
scored.unproven_right: Agricultural land or agreements to sell at about Rs 1-3 cr/acre assembled from smallholders who cannot read draft development plans.
scored.proving_step: Title clean-up and assembly to minimum licence area, then DTCP licence or CLU with EDC/IDC payments: Rs 1-5 cr and 1.5-3 years; about 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: DLF, Godrej Properties, Lodha, Signature Global, M3M.
scored.public_data: Scanned Hindi and Marathi Development Plans and gazettes, DTCP licence registers and LOIs, Jamabandi and 7/12 extracts, NHAI/MSRDC alignments, RERA filings.
scored.rough_step_up: About 7-20x (Rs 2 cr/acre to Rs 15-40 cr/acre); title risk is the main failure mode.
scored.frame: The rung is "licensed land aggregator": assemble the parcel, clean up title, get a DTCP licence or CLU, then sell or JDA the land to a listed developer. Discovery (finding R-zone parcels before the price moves) is maybe 15-25% of the work. The rest is physical and bureaucratic: chasing smallholder title one owner at a time, consolidating to the minimum licence area (about 5 acres for group housing in Haryana), getting through DTCP, and paying EDC/IDC. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted, so the work ratio is close to the reverse of Terranox's. A capitalised buyer does exist (DLF, Godrej, Signature, M3M and others buy licensed land).
scored.step_up: Licensed group-housing land on Dwarka Expressway traded at about Rs 14.5 cr/acre: Indiabulls sold about 40 licensed acres in Sector 106 to Elan for Rs 580 cr in January 2022. Prime Gurugram was Rs 28-40 cr/acre in 2024 (DLF about Rs 28 cr/acre, Oberoi about Rs 40 cr/acre in Sector 58). Agricultural land inside the R-zone near the expressway already lists at Rs 5-10 cr/acre, because the zoning is already priced in. The licence also costs Rs 3+ cr/acre in EDC (DTCP letters show an interim rate of about Rs 312 lakh/acre for group housing), plus IDC and internal-works bank guarantees. Net of those, the real gross step-up is about 1.5-4x where the plan is known, and 5-10x only in peripheral sectors bought at Rs 1-3 cr/acre. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims about 40-60% success. Each attempt costs Rs 1-5 cr+ (land advances plus licence fees and EDC instalments, Rs 3 cr/acre EDC alone) and takes 1.5-3 years. That passes the "expensive" bar easily, and base rates of 30-70% are acceptable under the relaxed C3. ML could plausibly lift the hit rate by screening title chains (Jamabandi/7-12 mutation histories, litigation, ceiling or Section 4/6 acquisition notifications) before advances are paid. Failures come mostly from title, litigation and politics, though, not from information, so a 1.2-1.5x gain on cost per licensed acre is more plausible than more than 2x. Sources: DTCP licence letters on haryanarera.gov.in. The hit rate is the candidate's own estimate, not verified.
scored.data: This is weak, and it is the same pattern earlier hunts found. The outcome-relevant field (land-use zone in the Final or Draft Development Plan 2031) is a legible, widely circulated map. Brokers, aggregators and developers' land teams read it in detail, and portals such as 1acre.in publish DTCP master-plan zone-check layers. Haryana's Jamabandi is digitised and online. Some illegible signal remains: Hindi gazettes, mutation chains, court records, and LOI and licence registers that show nearby pipeline. That is incremental, not decisive, and the main buyers of these signals already extract them.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought. They come through agreements to sell, collaboration agreements or JDAs with farmers, not first-come claims. But smallholders near new expressways are not unable to read the data: aggregators and broker networks have saturated these corridors since about 2007, and owners price R-zone status in quickly. Some discount remains in peripheral or draft-plan sectors.
scored.buyer: Listed developers and well-funded private ones: DLF, Godrej Properties, Signature Global, M3M, Oberoi, Birla Estates, Lodha. They regularly buy licensed parcels or sign JDAs on them, for example Elan buying 40 licensed acres from Indiabulls for Rs 580 cr, and Oberoi and DLF buying in Gurugram in 2024.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong. Licensed land, then development or JDA revenue share, then construction, then sales, then rental or commercial assets, then a full integrated developer. DLF itself began as a colony licensee and land aggregator, and Indian developers are worth tens of billions of dollars. So a path exists in principle, though it is capital-intensive and depends on relationships at every rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck, and the signal is not illegible. R-zone land-use in the published Development Plans is legible and already priced in by a dense aggregator and broker market. The real work, and the real failure mode, is physical and political execution: smallholder title clean-up, assembly to the minimum area, the DTCP process, and Rs 3+ cr/acre in EDC. After those costs the step-up is about 2-5x, not 10^4. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines problem: the hard part is not finding the asset.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the Terranox shape. Zoning is public and priced in, proving means title, assembly and paying EDC rather than discovery, and the step-up net of fees is about 2-5x. The relaxed C3 helps a little (proving is expensive and title-screening ML could give 1.2-1.5x), but the frame and the data edge are weak.

scored.name: Continuation Forge: live patent families with pending continuations
scored.one_line: Buy patent families with a still-pending continuation from small inventors, robotics or materials startups and bankruptcy estates for $5-100k; ML finds written-description support in the spec for claims reading on products shipping today; prosecute to allowance with an EoU chart and sell.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is already the standard NPE playbook. IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, IV and Acacia, plus brokers who screen for live continuations, already buy families with pending continuations and draft claims to read on shipping products. Pending status is a legible field, and claim-charting is commoditising. Value is not realised on allowance: it depends on years of litigation exposed to IPR and Alice. That caps the immediate step-up at about 10-50x and leaves no illegible-data moat.
scored.step_up: Unproven: small-inventor, auction and bankruptcy families clear at about $5-50k (my estimate). Richardson Oliver puts the average brokered asking price at about $100k per asset in 2022, down from about $150k in 2020-21. The 2019 average was $194k and the 2018 average was $124k (LexisNexis IP podcast with Kent Richardson; Richardson Oliver 2019 preview). Proven: a family whose allowed claim has a strong EoU chart against a high-volume product might sell for $250k-$2M (my estimate). That is about a 10-50x step-up, not 10^3-10^4. The larger outliers need years of litigation and survival at IPR and Alice.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Allowance itself has a high base rate. My estimate is 70-90% for continuations, which is not sourced this run but matches overall USPTO allowance rates. A real hit means a valid, infringed claim that survives a buyer's diligence. Commonly cited figures say only about 1-5% of patents are ever licensed or asserted (also unsourced). Cost per attempt: $5-100k to buy plus $3-60k to prosecute, about $20-150k in all, over 1-3 years. That only borderline meets the relaxed bar of at least $50k or years per attempt. ML could plausibly lift the sellable-hit rate 1.5-3x by picking families whose spec supports claims on current products. But LLM claim-charting is already common among NPEs and brokers, so the relative edge is smaller. Score 3, not 5, because the proving step is cheap at the low end and incumbents already use similar tools.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a live family with a pending continuation, then draft and prosecute a claim that reads on a shipping product until it is allowed with an EoU chart. Inside that rung, finding the spec support and the target product is roughly 70-80% of the work. Prosecution is a cheap physical step that patent counsel can handle. Capitalised buyers exist: NPEs, Acacia, IV, and defensive aggregators such as RPX and AST. But they pay for the litigation or licensing value they expect, and an allowance on its own does not settle that. The frame only partly holds.
scored.data: Partly illegible. Spec text and file wrappers sit in USPTO Patent Center and are full text, so they are not truly illegible, just large. Matching them to product features is the hard part. Pending-continuation status is a legible PAIR field, and brokers already screen on it.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Rights are bought from inventors, startups and bankruptcy estates, often cheaply, so this leg passes. But the sellers are often represented by brokers who flag live continuations as a selling point, which shrinks the discount.
scored.buyer: NPEs and litigation funders (IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, Acacia, IV), defensive aggregators (RPX, AST) and operating companies. They are capitalised, but they price on expected litigation or licensing value, discounted for IPR and Alice risk.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are assertion, litigation and licensing. That is the NPE model, which is capped by litigation economics and reputational and legal headwinds. It offers no path to a vertically integrated trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the lever to a modest 3, because ML can plausibly pick 1.5-3x better families. But the 10-50x step-up, a legible pending-status field, crowded NPE incumbents and a litigation-gated ladder keep this weak.

scored.name: DuctFind / Dark Conduit Recovery: abandoned urban and long-haul conduit
scored.one_line: Buy abandoned or forgotten conduit (old telegraph/telephone ducts, defunct CLEC and 1998-2002 long-haul builds) from estates and successors at ~zero book value; ML over scanned franchises, as-builts, permits and bankruptcy schedules proves continuous routes and title; rod/mandrel tests confirm; sell or IRU to carriers and hyperscalers.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up comes from legal and physical remediation, not discovery, and the valuable inventory is not actually lost. The 2001-03 long-haul conduit was cleared through legible bankruptcy orders and absorbed by Zayo, Lumen and others, and ILEC duct is mapped. In what remains, the binding questions are whether the easement or franchise survived abandonment and is assignable, and whether the duct is intact. ML over scans resolves neither, so this shares the killed telco-copper and rail-title failure mode and adds a bespoke physical step. The relaxed C3 helps only marginally.
scored.step_up: Nominally 10^2-10^3: a near-zero acquisition price per foot against a proven value capped by new-build cost. Two benchmarks: a 2014 Lawrence, KS memo puts fiber and conduit installation at $15-20/ft (about $80-105k/mile), and dense-urban builds run $1-3M/mile (my estimate). Comparable values are opaque because dark fiber and conduit are priced route by route. For example, Centennial CO's municipal IRU rate is $2,750 per pair per fiber-mile, a lease rate that says little about what conduit sells for. In practice the multiple shrinks to roughly 10-100x. The right is not free: successors and municipalities lease rather than sell, as in the Helendale CSD case where an existing conduit system was leased long-term. Remediation also eats the uplift, and vacant long-haul conduit traded at a fraction of build cost during the glut.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Physical proving costs about $2-5k per block for rodding, mandrel or camera tests (my estimate). A camera survey of a multi-mile route, plus a title opinion, permits and traffic control, plausibly reaches $50-150k per route. That is near the relaxed C3 cost threshold, but well below the years and dollars an exploratory drill takes. Base hit rates are moderate: about 30-60% for physical continuity, and lower, perhaps under 20%, for title and rights continuity (my estimates, not sourced). Under the relaxed rubric, ML that ranks routes before options are signed could plausibly give about 1.5x on cost per proven route. The constraint is that the binding uncertainty is legal and physical condition, which scans only partly reveal. One commentator notes that cost estimates for unmapped conduit contain 'a considerable element of hope'. Scored 3: proving is only borderline expensive and the lift is moderate.
scored.frame: The rung is to acquire the right to a forgotten conduit route, prove it continuous and titled, then sell or IRU it to a carrier or hyperscaler. Discovery (finding the route and reconstructing its title) is perhaps 40-60% of the work inside that rung, not 80% or more. The rest is legal remediation (franchise or easement survival, assignability, removal-on-abandonment statutes) and physical remediation (cleaning out old cable, fixing collapsed or blocked sections, connecting segments). The buyers are well capitalised, but they buy proven, contiguous, clean-title routes rather than raw finds.
scored.data: Partly illegible public data exists: scanned franchises, as-builts, permits and bankruptcy schedules. But the high-value 2001-03 long-haul inventory was resolved in legible bankruptcy sale orders and absorbed by Zayo, Lumen and others, and ILEC duct is actively owned and mapped. The leftover inventory consists of short, fragmented urban or municipal segments, often government-owned and leased rather than sold. Owners can sometimes be found, but abandonment may extinguish the easement or trigger removal duties, as in Missouri HB1135. So the right that can be bought cheaply is often not a valid or assignable right.
scored.right_bought: Conduit rights acquired from estates, defunct CLEC successors and bankruptcy trustees, or leased from municipalities and special districts. There is no clean first-come claim system.
scored.buyer: Carriers, fiber altnets, hyperscalers and dark fiber operators such as Zayo, Lumen and regional ISPs. They have capital but pay only for contiguous, clean-title, usable routes.
scored.ladder: Conduit route, then lit fiber and IRUs, then a metro or long-haul dark fiber network operator, then data-center interconnect and edge. The path is real but leads to a mature fiber-infrastructure business (Zayo-scale, tens of billions of dollars), not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the hit-rate lever to a borderline 3, since route-level proving costs about $50-150k and ML can plausibly give about 1.5x on route selection. The frame, the data edge and buyable rights stay weak, because remediation and title, not discovery, drive the value.

scored.name: Orphan Game IP Title Clearing
scored.one_line: Buy rights to 1985-2010 games of defunct studios from estates and trustees; ML rebuilds chain of title; sell or license cleared IP to remaster publishers.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is about 10x, not 10^4, and most cleared orphan games are worth almost nothing. The few valuable ones are blocked by third-party rights that no amount of discovery can clear, and the buyers who can pay are the same incumbents already chasing those assets.
scored.step_up: Unproven claims are cheap. In the 2025 Tequila Works bankruptcy auction, bids for RiME and GYLT topped out at about EUR 15k per franchise. In 2013, Nordic Games bought a bundle of THQ franchises (Darksiders, Red Faction and others) for about $4.9M in total. That puts the median dormant IP in the low tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands. A cleared mid-tier IP licenses for about $10k-100k up front plus royalty, or sells for $50k-500k. A rare top asset like the System Shock line was worth enough to anchor Atari's $10M (plus up to $10M earn-out) purchase of Nightdive, but that price covered the whole studio and its KEX engine, not the IP alone. Typical step-up is about 5-50x and about 100x+ only for the rare top title. That is well short of 10^3-10^4, and the value mostly arrives over years of remaster sales, not on the day title is cleared.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: 20-40% of clearing attempts end in a clean, sellable chain. A failed attempt costs about $5k-50k in legal and outreach work and takes months to a year or more. That only partly meets the relaxed rule that proving must be expensive (at least about $50k or years per attempt). ML over scattered filings, court dockets, copyright records and credits can plausibly lift the success rate about 1.3-1.6x by picking claims with fewer encumbrances before money is spent. Failures caused by third-party rights limit how far that goes. Score 3: the relaxed C3 helps a little, but the attempts are cheap enough to brute-force without ML.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a dormant 1985-2010 game IP claim and deliver a clean chain of title. Inside that rung, discovery work makes up about 60-80%: finding the owner, the estate, the trustee, or the asset buyer in bankruptcy, and rebuilding the contracts. The physical step is cheap legal paperwork, not a bespoke build. But the remaining 20-40% is negotiating third-party rights (music, licensed brands, co-developer shares, engines), and ML cannot do that part. Capitalised buyers do exist: Atari/Nightdive, Embracer/Plaion, Limited Run and Piko. They are few, though, and they also compete for the same assets.
scored.data: The signal is public but illegible: bankruptcy dockets, scanned asset purchase agreements, US Copyright Office records, trademark assignments, probate files, old credits and manuals. Fan wikis and retro publishers already map much of the high-value catalogue by hand, so incumbents do extract the valuable part. The outcome (who owns it, and whether it is clean) is not written into any single legible field, which helps. Rights are bought, not claimed first-come, from estates and trustees who often do not know what they hold. That part fits.
scored.right_bought: Copyright, trademark and source-code rights to dormant games, bought or optioned from estates, bankruptcy trustees, liquidated parent companies or original founders. Cost is about $1k-20k per claim (e.g. Tequila Works franchises bid at about EUR 15k).
scored.buyer: Remaster and retro publishers: Atari/Nightdive, Embracer/Plaion/THQ Nordic, Limited Run Games, Piko Interactive, Digital Eclipse, and occasionally a large publisher reviving a brand. The pool is small and these buyers also bid against you for the assets.
scored.ladder: The rungs run: clear title, then license, then publish the remaster yourself, then build an engine and porting tools (like Nightdive's KEX), then run a catalogue publisher and develop new sequels. The top of that ladder is a retro or catalogue publisher. Comparables: Atari is worth roughly a few hundred million dollars, and the catalogue publishers fold into multi-billion holders like Embracer. That is sub-$1B for a pure-play, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the hit-rate lever only to about 3, because clearing attempts are cheap ($5k-50k) and ML lifts the success rate only about 1.3-1.6x. Evidence like EUR 15k franchise bids and Atari's $10M Nightdive deal confirms a 5-50x step-up and a sub-$1B ladder.

scored.name: Replication-Proven Lab Materials Licences (ShelfLicense, Dormant Lab Option Book, Materials Claim Matcher)
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive or field-of-use options on unlicensed university and DOE/NASA/AFRL/NRL materials patents (catalysts, electrolytes, cathodes, alloys, magnets); ML over papers, SI data, citations and DFT screening (Materials Project/OQMD) picks claims that really work or contain untested winning compositions; a small contract-lab replication or synthesis run proves them; sublicense or sell to chemical and cell majors.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proof a buyer pays for is not the cheap bench replication. It is cell-scale or reactor-scale validation and scale-up, at $0.5-3M over months, and literature or DFT ML predicts that poorly. So discovery is not 80%+ of the rung, there is no immediate 10^3-10^4 step-up, and payment comes mostly as deferred royalties.
scored.step_up: No new evidence. Unproven: a federal-lab or university option at about $5-50k upfront plus patent costs; TTOs often waive or defer upfront fees (CASRAI licensing guide). Proven at bench: a sublicence at about $50-500k upfront plus a 1-10% royalty (2-6% is typical for early engineering inventions) that only pays years later, if the material reaches product. That is about 5-30x on cash, sometimes, and far from 10^3-10^4. Compare Terranox at about 10^4 on $/ha, payable immediately.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rates: commonly cited estimates put materials-result reproducibility at 30-60%, which the relaxed C3 now allows. My estimate is that well under 5% survive commercial-format testing. Cost per proving attempt: $20-60k for bench synthesis plus FTO, but $0.5-3M over 6-18 months for buyer-grade cell or pilot data (my estimates). Proving is expensive, so the relaxed C3 applies. Literature and SI mining can plausibly filter out irreproducible claims and lift bench-replication hit rate about 1.5x. But the success that sets the price is at scale, and DFT or literature features predict scale-up poorly, so the lift on cost per sellable proven asset is realistically about 1.2-1.5x. Score: 3, up from the effectively low prior C3.
scored.frame: The rung is an exclusive or field-of-use option on a dormant materials patent, proved by replication and then sublicensed. Discovery, meaning ML triage of claims, papers and DFT data, is maybe 30-50% of the work. The other 50-70% is the physical proof a chemical or cell buyer actually accepts: cell-scale or reactor-scale validation, scale-up and freedom-to-operate (FTO). That proof is bespoke and not abstracted. The buyers (chemical and cell majors) do have money, but they buy proof at scale, not bench replications.
scored.data: The data is public: papers, supplementary information (SI), patents, Materials Project and OQMD. It is semi-legible. Big chemical R&D groups and TTO analytics vendors already mine it, so this is partly illegible, not dark data. The outcome (does it work at scale?) is not written in any field, which is good. The weakness is that the data barely contains the scale-up signal.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Exclusive options and licences are bought cheaply from TTOs and federal labs (37 CFR 404 for federal labs) that cannot evaluate their own portfolio. The licences come with diligence milestones and march-in or reversion risk.
scored.buyer: Chemical, battery-cell and catalyst majors. They have money but are conservative, pay mostly in deferred royalties, and discount anything not proven at scale.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are licence, then pilot validation, then toll manufacturing of the material, then own production and cell or component supply. Each rung up is a capex-heavy chemical-manufacturing business. The path exists but it is a slog, not a clean climb.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 raises the lever to about 3 because proving is expensive and ML can filter irreproducible claims. But the frame and step-up still fail: buyers pay only for scale proof, which is costly, physical and not ML-predictable, and they pay in royalties.

scored.name: Orphan Lazarus: dormant orphan-designated assets with positive data
scored.one_line: Buy shelved compounds with orphan designation and positive signal from divestitures or dead biotechs; get FDA alignment on accelerated or single-trial path; sell, or approve for orphan exclusivity plus a rare pediatric PRV.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a clinical trial costing $20-100M+ and taking years, not a cheap discovery step. Discovery (asset selection) is well under 80% of the rung, and the FDA-alignment sub-rung is not a sellable step-up. Relaxing C3 helps only a little, since ML on asset selection plausibly gives about 1.2-1.5x over crowded expert BD and rescue funds (Roivant, BridgeBio, Fortress, pharma BD). ML does nothing to the trial cost, which dominates.
scored.step_up: Unproven: shelved orphan assets from dead biotechs change hands for about $0.1-3M upfront plus milestones (estimate). After FDA alignment, about 10-30x, mostly paid as contingent milestones (estimate). On approval, the rare pediatric PRV alone now sells for $150-160M (2025: Zevra $150M, Abeona $155M, Bavarian Nordic $160M) and $200-210M (2026: Jazz $200M, Ultragenyx $203M and $210M), plus commercial value. That is about 100-1000x+ over the purchase price, but it arrives only after a multi-year trial costing $20-100M+, not immediately on a cheap hit. The PRV program's reauthorization was also still in limbo in these reports.
scored.hit_rate_capex: BIO/Biomedtracker found that rare disease programs succeed at higher rates than average in every phase. An Amplion analysis of non-oncology orphan designations found about 25% overall likelihood of approval and about 50% Phase 2 success. For a rescued asset with positive Phase 2 data, the chance of reaching approval is about 30-50%, which is inside the relaxed 30-70% window. Each proving attempt (pivotal or single-arm trial) costs about $20-100M+ and takes years (estimate), so proving is clearly expensive. ML can help with asset selection by reading scattered FDA briefing documents, publications and failed-company filings. A 1.5x gain over expert BD diligence is unproven, and about 1.2-1.5x is more defensible. ML cannot cut the trial's cost. Relaxed C3 = 3.
scored.frame: The rung is to buy a shelved orphan asset and prove it, by getting FDA alignment and then running a pivotal or single-arm trial to approval. Discovery here means picking the right asset from the public record, and it is about 10-20% of the work. The physical step is the trial itself: years of work and $20-100M+, not trivial. The cheap sub-rung, an FDA Type C alignment meeting, does not give a step-up that buyers pay proven prices for. So no frame exists where discovery is 80% or more of the work.
scored.data: Some signal sits in illegible public sources: FDA briefing documents, conference posters, bankruptcy and divestiture filings, and publications. But the key outcomes are already legible in ClinicalTrials.gov results fields, the FDA orphan designation database and press releases. Specialist rescue funds and BD teams already mine these, so the extraction edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought rather than claimed for free. They come from bankruptcy estates, wind-downs and pharma divestitures, often cheaply, with milestones and royalties attached. But sellers are usually sophisticated (biotech boards, pharma BD teams, bankers) and auctions are competitive, so the discount does not come from sellers being unable to read the data.
scored.buyer: Large and mid-size pharma is well capitalised and in-licenses or acquires de-risked orphan assets. A liquid secondary market buys PRVs at $150-210M. Royalty funds (Royalty Pharma and others) also buy.
scored.ladder: Strong. Asset rescue leads to in-house development, then a commercial orphan franchise, then a platform company. Precedents include BridgeBio, Roivant's Vant model and Fortress. The path to a very large company is real, but those incumbents also make the space crowded.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 lifts it to 3, because base rates of 30-50% and expensive trials now qualify. The candidate still fails C1: the work inside the rung is clinical development, not discovery, and the outcomes are already legible and competitively mined.

scored.name: Orphan Sole-Source Defense Parts (SoleSource Shells, Orphan Tooling, stranded DLA NSN sources)
scored.one_line: Buy the drawings, tooling, TDPs and CAGE/approved-source standing of tiny closing or defunct machine shops and military electronics suppliers at scrap value; ML over DIBBS, FLIS/PUB LOG and scanned SAR/J&A records finds NSNs with recurring sole-source demand and dead approved sources; novate or SAR-qualify, deliver first awards via contract shops, and sell proven part families to aftermarket roll-ups.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is mostly manufacturing and government requalification, not discovery. Approved-source status is tied to the manufacturer, facility and process, so it does not transfer cleanly with an asset purchase. The key outcome signals (AMSC sole-source codes, approved CAGE, inactive CAGE, demand history) are already legible in DIBBS, SAM and FLIS, so ML gives only about 1.2-1.5x over a lookup table. The relaxed C3 raises the lever score modestly but does not fix the frame: discovery is not 80% of the rung, and the 10^3-10^4 step-up on a hit is absent. It is the same shape as the killed FAA PMA candidate.
scored.step_up: Unchanged from r1 and still my estimate, unverified. An unproven TDP and tooling purchase runs about $1k-200k. A proven part family with about $0.3-2M a year of DLA revenue at 25-40% EBITDA, sold at 10-15x for private tuck-ins (20-30x for public TransDigm/Heico), is worth about $1-10M. That is about 10-200x. The value is not immediate: it arrives 1-3 years after purchase, once approval is granted and awards are delivered. C2=3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $20-150k per attempt: TDP, legal and novation work, SAR package, first article of about $10-50k, and tooling refurbishment or a first lot. A DLA/NDIA industry briefing gives 12-18 months to full approval; that figure sits under the RPPOB-to-SAR program, so it is approximate for SAR review alone. That meets the relaxed "expensive or years" bar at the upper end, but only marginally at the lower end. The base hit rate for the whole chain (asset purchase through to a profitable award stream) is my estimate of about 20-40%. A DLA presentation reports that once a SAR is submitted it usually succeeds: 40 approved, 4 rejected and 11 pending out of 55 since 2014, about 90% of decided cases. So the main losses are not at qualification. They come from picking NSNs whose demand evaporates, from losing price competition, and from manufacturing problems. ML ranking of NSNs and target shops plausibly lifts cost per proven asset about 1.2-1.5x, not more. The outcome-relevant fields (AMSC/AMSC-R codes, approved CAGE, CAGE status, demand history in DIBBS/FLIS) are already legible, so a lookup table captures most of the edge. Under the relaxed rubric C3=3, up from an effective weak score.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a qualified sole-source position on a family of NSNs and sell it." Inside that rung, discovery (finding NSNs with recurring demand and dead or weak approved sources, and finding the defunct shop holding the TDP and tooling) is perhaps 30-40% of the work. The other 60-70% is manufacturing and government qualification: SAR or novation packages, first-article testing, contract-shop production and price competition on awards. The physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. There is a capitalised buyer (aftermarket roll-ups like TransDigm, Heico and PE platforms), but it buys proven revenue streams, not proven rights.
scored.data: Mostly legible. AMSC codes, approved-source CAGE, inactive CAGE status in SAM, and award and demand history in DIBBS/FPDS/FLIS are structured fields that already summarise the outcome. The illegible parts are scanned TDPs, J&A documents and old drawings, and shop records. They help with valuing an asset, not with finding the opportunity. Rights can be bought cheaply from closing shops, but approved-source status attaches to the manufacturer, facility and process and does not transfer cleanly. C4=2.
scored.right_bought: Drawings, tooling and TDP ownership, plus possible novation of existing contracts or CAGE standing, bought by asset purchase from closing or defunct machine shops and military electronics suppliers at near-scrap prices. Government approved-source standing usually has to be re-earned through a SAR or first article rather than bought.
scored.buyer: Defense aftermarket roll-ups and consolidators (TransDigm, Heico, private-equity-backed spares platforms). They pay 10-30x EBITDA, but for proven recurring revenue, not for an approved but unproduced right.
scored.ladder: Moderate. The path runs from a single NSN family, to a multi-family sole-source spares portfolio, to in-house manufacturing, to a TransDigm-style proprietary aftermarket platform, to possibly OEM subsystem work. The chain is real and large (TransDigm is a $70B+ business), but each step up is M&A and manufacturing execution rather than a discovery advantage compounding. C5=3.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the lever to 3, since proving is fairly expensive and takes 12-18 months. The candidate still fails the core thesis: the rung is mostly manufacturing and qualification, the outcome data is already legible, and the step-up is about 10-200x and delayed.

scored.name: Billboard Permit Hunting / Grandfathered Wall: dormant legal-nonconforming sign rights
scored.one_line: Buy or lease parcels and building walls in capped jurisdictions (highways, NYC, LA, SF, Chicago, Houston) where an old sign right may still be legally valid; ML over scanned DOT permits, council minutes, NYC 1940/1980s tax photos and DOB/BSA records proves legal establishment and continuity; sell or lease to outdoor operators.
scored.fatal_flaw: The continuity and abandonment rules. NYC ZR 52-61 uses 2 years, and many codes and state programmes use 12 months. So most truly dormant sign rights are legally dead, and the ones still alive are usually still in use, already registered in a legible DOT or DOB status field, and already known to operators. The proving step is a slow, expensive legal fight, and its outcome turns on facts (continuous use) that ML over documents often cannot establish. The relaxed C3 gives the lever partial credit but does not fix the tiny pool of real hits.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an option or lease on a wall whose owner thinks the right is dead, roughly $0-10k (my estimate). Proven: real lease examples are a Lamar lease in Muskegon, Michigan at $7,800 a year, a California county digital lease at $40,000 a year, and a New Jersey borough RFP with a $48,000 a year minimum. Industry guides put typical site rents at $200-$1,000 a month (about $2.4k-$12k a year), or 15-20% of the sign's net ad revenue. Capitalised at 8-15x, a highway face is worth roughly $20k-$700k, and a prime NYC or LA wallscape possibly $1M+. Against a $5-10k option that is about 10-100x typically and 1000x only at rare prime walls, so C2 is 3. Against the property's existing value the uplift is much smaller.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate, my estimate: probably under 10% of 'dormant' candidates survive, because codes commonly extinguish a non-conforming use after 12 months of non-use. Woodinville and Stanwood, Washington both use 12 months, and Stanwood lets an owner rebut the presumption with evidence of continued utilities or leasing efforts. Utah lets a municipality terminate a billboard abandoned for 12 months, after notice and a cure period. NYC ZR 52-61 uses 2 years. California requires intent to abandon plus an overt act, which is friendlier. Cost per proving attempt: about $25k-$150k and months to years (expediter, attorney, filings, appeals), which meets the expensive bar. Under the relaxed C3, ML screening of scanned permits, photos and minutes before signing options could plausibly lift the hit rate 1.5-2x, mostly by targeting friendly jurisdictions like California and rebuttal-evidence cases. But the hit is decided by a legal fact (was the sign actually used continuously?) that the documents often cannot show, so the lever is real but uncertain. I score it 3, not 5.
scored.frame: The rung: optioning a wall or parcel, then proving that a legal-nonconforming sign right still exists so it can be leased or sold to an outdoor operator. Discovery is maybe 60-70% of the work: finding the permit trail and proving the sign was legally established and used without a break. The physical step (putting up a structure or vinyl) is cheap, and the operator does it. The proving step is not abstracted, though. It is a legal and administrative fight (expediter, attorney, DOB or DOT filings, possibly a BSA or BZA appeal), not a quick drill hit. There are capitalised buyers (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel), but they mostly buy rights that are already proven.
scored.data: The signal is in scanned DOT permits, council and BZA minutes, NYC 1940 and 1980s tax photos and DOB/BSA records, which is public and illegible. But many state DOTs and NYC DOB keep legible sign permit and registration status fields (NYC's outdoor advertising company registration, state ODA permit lists), and live rights are usually already in them.
scored.right_bought: In principle the right is bought cheaply by optioning a wall or parcel from an owner who thinks the sign right is dead, so it is bought, not free first-come. In practice owners are routinely approached by operators, and the right attaches to the specific parcel, so the buying edge is narrow.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront Media and Clear Channel Outdoor, who are capitalised and buy or lease sign sites. They pay well mainly for rights that are already proven and permitted.
scored.ladder: Proven sign rights, then building and owning structures, then a regional outdoor operator, then digital conversion. That leads to a roll-up of a mature, roughly $9B-a-year US out-of-home industry with tightly capped supply. A real ladder, but bounded: not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough to earn partial credit under the relaxed C3, but abandonment law kills most dormant rights, live ones sit in legible registries, and the step-up is mostly 10-100x, so this is a weak candidate.

scored.name: SiteSeed: entitled build-to-suit tower sites
scored.one_line: Take cheap ground-lease options on parcels in coverage deserts; ML predicts which will clear zoning, FAA, NEPA/SHPO and RF need; entitle only those and flip permitted sites to tower companies.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value comes from the anchor carrier tenant, which is driven by private carrier RF plans and search rings, not from entitlement. Entitlement succeeds about 70-85% of the time under federal shot-clock and substantial-evidence rules (my estimate). So even with the 'usually fails' requirement dropped, ML on public zoning data gives only about 1.3x on a step that neither fails much nor creates the value. A permit-only flip lands near breakeven on total spend.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a 2-3 year ground-lease option at about $500-2,000 (candidate's figure). Entitled but with no tenant: about $10-50k plus reimbursed costs (my estimate), so about 10-25x on the option and close to 1x on total spend. Entitled with an anchor tenant: about $300-600k (15-25x tower cash flow), but that value belongs to the carrier lease, not to the entitlement. One industry guide puts new tower builds at $150k-1M, so the buyer still has to put in heavy capex after buying.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is borderline expensive. Entitlement and site acquisition run about $30-90k per site (candidate's figure; a PTTG-style cost guide gives about $90k average for permitting and zoning, but its sourcing is weak). Approval rates are high, about 70-85% (my estimate, not verified). Section 332(c)(7) substantial-evidence rules and FCC shot clocks push localities to approve. Under the relaxed C3, a 70-85% base is acceptable, but the most ML can add on entitlement is about 1/0.75, roughly 1.2-1.35x. Public coverage and crowd-sourced speed data might nudge the chance of getting a tenant, but carrier search rings are private. Score 3, raised from the prior effective level.
scored.frame: The rung is a parcel option plus entitlement (zoning, FAA, NEPA/SHPO), sold as a permitted site. Discovery and proving are maybe 50-60% of the work in that rung. Paperwork, site acquisition, legal work and hearings make up most of the rest. The rung's value is not set by discovery. It is set by an anchor carrier lease, which depends on private carrier RF plans. A permit-only site has no capitalised buyer paying a large premium for it.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scattered county zoning minutes, SHPO files and FAA obstruction records. Much of it is legible, though. FCC ASR and FAA OE/AAA hold structured determinations, and the deciding signal (carrier demand) is private. Ground-lease options can be bought cheaply from landowners, but tower companies and site-acquisition firms already compete for the good parcels.
scored.right_bought: A ground-lease option from a rural landowner, about $500-2,000 for 2-3 years. It is cheap and bought (not first-come), but its value hinges on a carrier wanting the location.
scored.buyer: Tower companies (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge) are well capitalised, but they buy tenanted sites or build-to-suit under carrier contracts. They pay little for speculative permitted sites with no tenant.
scored.ladder: Option, then entitlement, then building and owning the tower, then signing anchor and co-location tenants, then a tower portfolio. That ladder leads to a REIT-scale business (AMT is about a $90B+ company). The ladder is strong, but rungs 1-2 do not capture the value.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 lifts the hit-rate lever only to about 1.3x (score 3). The frame, the step-up and the data edge stay weak, because the value step is the private carrier lease, not entitlement.
sources: 47 U.S.C. 332(c)(7); FCC 2009/2014/2018 shot-clock orders (from memory, not searched)

scored.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
scored.one_line: Buy patents from Chapter 7/11 estates, ABC sales, dead startups (fabless, LiDAR, photonics, quantum, microLED) and lapse-bound owners for $2-50k; ML maps claims against FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, SEM cross-sections, datasheets, driver code and papers to build evidence-of-use charts; sell charted patents to NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools and funders.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An EoU chart is a contestable opinion, and the value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation at about $2-5M per case. About 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidate all challenged claims. So the step-up is only about 10-30x on an asset that is not near zero, and each charting attempt costs about $10-35k, below the relaxed C3's expense threshold.
scored.step_up: Proven side: Richardson Oliver puts the asking price for brokered US-issued patents at about $177k-$360k per patent across 2013-2019, and a secondary source (a Korean news article, not checked against the report itself) cites about $286k per patent for 2024. These are asking prices, not sale prices; on my unverified recollection only about a quarter to a third of listed packages sell, at a discount. Unproven side: lots from distressed estates and ABC sales are estimated at about $2k-$30k per patent, not verified this run. Realistic step-up is about 10-30x, with outliers near 100x. It is far from the 10^3-10^4x the rubric wants, because the unproven patent is not near zero. Score unchanged at 2.5.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Under the relaxed C3, the proving step must still cost at least ~$50k or take years per attempt. An EoU attempt costs roughly $3k-$15k for the attorney chart plus $5k-$20k for a teardown or SEM, so about $10k-$35k in total. That is below the threshold, though the real proof, litigation at $2-5M per case, is expensive and slow. Base hit rate is roughly 1-5% (my estimate). The ML triage lever is real and probably 5-20x, but it was never blocked by the "usually fails" leg, so relaxing C3 changes little. Proving per attempt is cheapish, and several AI patent-analytics startups are already automating charting, so the lever is not proprietary. Score 2 (no C3 was given for the prior candidate).
scored.frame: The rung is buying an orphan patent and attaching an evidence-of-use (EoU) chart, then selling the charted asset. Inside that rung, discovery (finding which claim reads on which shipping product) is roughly 80-90% of the work, and the physical step (a teardown or SEM cross-section) is cheap or can be outsourced. NPEs, aggregators such as RPX and AST, and litigation funders are capitalised buyers. Two things weaken the frame. Buyers apply their own heavy diligence, and the value is only realised later through licensing or litigation, so the rung is not truly self-contained. Score unchanged at 3.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, datasheets and driver code. Claims are legible, and incumbent analytics firms (Unified Patents, PatentSight, the AI charting startups) already mine them. The outcome is not written into a status field; the USPTO only records maintenance and assignment status. Score unchanged at 3.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought outright from Chapter 7/11 trustees through 363 sales, from ABC assignees and from owners about to let them lapse, often cheaply. The catch is that trustees run auctions in which NPEs already bid, so the discount is partly competed away.
scored.buyer: NPEs and patent assertion entities, defensive aggregators such as RPX and AST, litigation funders, and occasionally operating companies looking for counter-assertion ammunition. The pool is thin, and only about 25-30% of listed packages sell (my recollection, not verified this run).
scored.ladder: The rungs run from a charted patent, to the company running its own licensing and assertion campaigns, to a litigation-funded fund or NPE (Intellectual Ventures at its peak, roughly $5B of capital). That tops out at a few-$B IP fund. It does not climb into owning the physical value chain, so there is no trillion-dollar path. Score unchanged at 2.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 barely helps. The base hit rate was never the constraint; the problems are that charting is cheap per attempt, the step-up is only 10-30x, and real proof comes only from slow, invalidation-prone litigation, with a ladder that tops out at an IP fund.

scored.name: German Wind Zone Land Optioning (Windvorrangflächen)
scored.one_line: Option farmland inside draft regional-plan wind zones that ML ranks most likely to survive final designation and get a BImSchG permit, obtain the permit, and sell the permitted project to a utility or IPP at EUR 100-200k/MW. The company keeps the uplift.
scored.unproven_right: Land-use option and lease on agricultural or forest parcels inside draft or likely wind priority zones (WindBG requires ~2% of land by 2027/2032), costing roughly EUR 1-5k/ha up front, from owners who cannot read 100+ regional plan drafts and objections.
scored.proving_step: Wind measurement, bird and species surveys (1-2 years), BImSchG application and grant: about EUR 300k-1M and 2-3 years per site; roughly 40-70% success inside designated zones.
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities and IPPs buying permitted onshore wind (RWE, EnBW, Enercity, Statkraft, Energiekontor, infra funds).
scored.public_data: Draft and final Regionalpläne and Teilflächennutzungspläne (scanned maps and objection files) from ~110 planning regions, Marktstammdatenregister, BNetzA EEG auction results, state Natura 2000 and Rotmilan nest registers, DWD wind data, military radar exclusion zones.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 100-300x on the land right (EUR 2-5k/ha option to EUR 300k-1M/ha permitted value); ML adds ~1.5-2x on cost per permit.
scored.frame: The rung is: secure land and get it to a BImSchG-permitted, ready-to-build project that can be sold to IPPs. Picking the site is maybe 20-30% of the work. The remaining 70-80% is paid, procedural proving: wind measurement, 1-2 years of species surveys, noise and shadow studies, a radar check and the permit process. That is commodity consultant work, not discovery. No construction is needed, but the proving step is not trivial or abstracted the way an exploratory drill hole is.
scored.step_up: Measured against the option fee alone (EUR 2-5k/ha), a permitted site looks like a ~100x step-up. But the right is a lease, not a purchase. The landowner keeps the land and takes a revenue-share rent of about EUR 20/kW/yr (Deutsche WindGuard 2025 average, cited by topagrar; EUR 50-100k per turbine per year). The company never holds the land at near-zero. The real comparison is sunk development cost (EUR 0.3-1M per site) against permitted-project value (about EUR 100-200k/MW, roughly EUR 0.6-1.2M per 6 MW turbine). That is roughly 2-5x on capital in, not 10^3-10^4. Auctions are now ~2x oversubscribed (first 2026 round: 7,858 MW bid, average award EUR 55.4/MWh), which squeezes premiums for permitted projects.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about EUR 300k-1M and 2-3 years per site, so it meets the C3 cost bar. The base hit rate inside designated zones is already 40-70% or higher, and section 6 WindBG simplifies species review inside designated Vorranggebiete, so permit risk inside final zones is low and mostly known. Where ML could help is in predicting which draft zones survive to the final plan, and in flagging Rotmilan or radar conflicts before an option is signed. That plausibly gives about 1.2-1.5x on cost per permit, not 2x or more, because nest registers and radar zones are already legible GIS layers that every developer screens. These figures are the candidate's own estimates; I found no independent hit-rate data.
scored.data: Partly illegible: about 110 regional-plan drafts with scanned objection files. But the outcome is written straight into a legible field, because the final Regionalplan designates the Vorranggebiet and that designation is a public GIS layer. Developers already track every draft as it is published. The Marktstammdatenregister and BNetzA auction results are fully structured. The ML edge is limited to the window between draft and final plan.
scored.right_bought: Not cheap and not bought from owners who cannot read the data. Once a draft zone is published, dozens of professional Projektierer (ABO Energy, Juwi, enercity, local cooperatives) approach every landowner. Municipalities organise Flaechenpools that run competitive bids. Owners get offers of EUR 3-5k/ha/yr and revenue-share leases, so they capture most of the uplift. The market is a competitive auction for land, not an information-asymmetric purchase.
scored.buyer: Strong and well capitalised: RWE, EnBW, Enercity, Statkraft, Energiekontor and infrastructure funds actively buy permitted projects (RtB) in Germany.
scored.ladder: Real: develop, then build (EPC), then own and operate as an IPP, then sell power through PPAs or direct marketing. Integrated developers such as Energiekontor and ABO Energy show the path, but it leads to a crowded, low-margin multi-billion-euro IPP business rather than a uniquely defensible trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is neither cheap nor information-asymmetric. Wind priority zones are published and legibly designated, and every parcel is contested by dozens of developers. Landowners extract revenue-share rents of about EUR 20/kW/yr, so the company never captures a near-zero-to-proven step-up. Net of EUR 0.3-1M of procedural development spend, the multiple is about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little (expensive proving, modest ML edge on predicting which draft zones survive), but the option is a competitive public land race with landowner revenue-share and a ~2-5x step-up on development capital, so it fails C2 and C4.

scored.name: UK Gate-2 BESS/Solar Ready-to-Build Land
scored.one_line: Option land near National Grid and DNO substations that ML predicts will pass both Gate 2 connection readiness and local planning, secure the connection offer and consent, and sell RTB projects to funds at GBP 50-150k/MW.
scored.unproven_right: Option agreements at about GBP 500-2k/acre per year on farmland near substations; Gate 2 requires land rights as readiness proof, raising the value of early options.
scored.proving_step: Grid connection application plus planning application (LVIA, ecology, flood, heritage), then committee or appeal: about GBP 150-500k and 1-2 years per site; roughly 40-70% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Infrastructure funds and IPPs (Gresham House, Harmony Energy, Field, Zenobe, NextEnergy, Octopus).
scored.public_data: ~330 LPA portals (committee reports, free-text refusal reasons), Planning Inspectorate appeals, NESO TEC register and Gate 2 outcome lists, DNO capacity registers and heatmaps, ALC maps, flood zones.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 100x (option worth GBP 1-3k/acre to RTB value GBP 100-400k/acre); ML adds ~1.5-2x on cost per consent.
scored.frame: The rung is real and sellable: developing a site to ready-to-build (land option, grid offer, planning consent) and selling it to funds. But maybe 20-30% of the work is 'discovery' (picking the site). Most of it is the slow grind of permits and grid allocation: the grid application, Gate 2 readiness and strategic-alignment tests, the planning studies (landscape/visual, ecology, flood, heritage), committee hearings, appeals, community objections and capacity fees. That paperwork-and-politics step is the expensive part, the opposite of Terranox, where proving (the drill) is trivial.
scored.step_up: Enerdatics European BESS developer premiums: about $20k/MW early stage, about $50k/MW with a provisional grid connection, at least $80k/MW ready-to-build (megaproject.com/Enerdatics, June 2026). An option at £1-2k/acre/yr on about 5-10 acres for 50MW works out to roughly £200-400/MW/yr, so the gross step-up from option to RTB is about 100-300x. But by the time it is 'proven' the developer has spent £150-500k plus commitment/security fees (Ofgem proposed £3k-25k/MW for oversubscribed technologies). Net of the proving cost, the uplift on capital deployed is about 3-10x. The jump from secured grid connection to RTB is only about 1.6x. Roughly 10^2, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: £150-500k and 1-2 years per site (candidate estimate, consistent with the cost of a full planning application plus grid studies). Base success is about 40-70%, so under the relaxed C3 it qualifies on cost. The ML lever is weak, though. The binding constraint is NESO's centralised capacity rationing, not site quality. The Dec 2025 Gate 2 results gave offers to only 83GW of BESS, leaving it about 62GW oversubscribed against Clean Power 2030 pots. 153GW of BESS was pushed to Gate 1, and 217GW of Gate-2-ready projects were 'not prioritised' as strategically misaligned. ML on planning-refusal text might lift consent odds about 1.2-1.5x, but it cannot create grid capacity in a closed, oversubscribed window. Hence 3.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: about 330 local planning authority portals, committee reports and free-text refusal reasons, plus Planning Inspectorate appeal decisions. But the outcomes sit in legible fields. Planning decisions (approved/refused) are status fields. The NESO TEC register and Gate 2 outcome lists state outright who got capacity. DNO heatmaps publish headroom. This is the 'regulator writes the answer into a status field' failure mode. Hundreds of incumbents (Field, Harmony, Zenobe, FRV, Gresham House pipelines) already mine the same registers and planning portals, and land agencies systematise it.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought (an option), not free first-come, which suits the model. But owners do not lack information. Farmland near substations has been canvassed by dozens of developers since 2020, so land agents run competitive option rounds and option fees and rent shares get bid up. There is no market of uninformed owners for cheap rights. On top of that, Gate 2 readiness requires land rights, which makes options near substations more contested, not cheaper.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and active: infrastructure funds and IPPs such as Schroders Greencoat (Yarnton 50MW), Field (Hartmoor 200MW), Fidra (1GW), Sosteneo (Sheaf £210m), Gresham House and Zenobe. They are moving earlier in the pipeline to buy grid-ready assets.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: EPC/build, owning and operating, trading/optimisation (Habitat, Arenko-style), and becoming an IPP. But every rung above RTB is a capital-intensive commodity infrastructure business with thin, falling margins (BESS revenues compressed in 2023-25) and well-funded incumbents. A path exists but there is no technical moat carrying upward, so it is credible rather than trillion-dollar.
scored.fatal_flaw: The scarce input is grid capacity, and NESO rations it centrally in a closed, about 3x oversubscribed process: 83GW of BESS got Gate 2 offers against a CP2030 need of roughly a third of that, and 217GW of ready projects were 'not prioritised'. Site selection is not the bottleneck. On top of that, both outcomes (consent, connection) are written into legible public status fields, and landowners near substations are already heavily courted, so ML neither unlocks a hidden asset nor buys it cheap. This is the counter-example pattern again: the hard part is the permitting and grid-allocation step, not the discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is a real, sellable development-premium business with capitalised buyers, but the hard part is gaining grid capacity that NESO rations centrally, not discovery. Outcomes are legible status fields and land near substations is already competitively optioned, so ML adds at most about 1.2-1.5x. Score 12/25.

scored.name: US County-Permit-Predicted Solar Site Control
scored.one_line: Option farmland for utility solar in counties and townships that ML predicts will grant a CUP and not pass moratoria, win the CUP and site studies, and sell NTP-track projects to IPPs. The edge is the political permit signal, not the interconnection queue.
scored.unproven_right: Solar lease options at about $10-50/acre per year on 500-2,000 acre assemblies in PJM/MISO counties where landowners and developers misread ordinance trajectory.
scored.proving_step: County CUP or zoning approval plus state siting certificate (e.g. Ohio OPSB), environmental surveys, title and ALTA: about $200k-1M and 1-2 years; roughly 40-65% success, with moratoria the main killer.
scored.proven_buyer: IPPs and utilities (NextEra, AES, Invenergy, Lightsource bp, EDF) paying about $50-150k/MW for permitted, queue-positioned projects.
scored.public_data: County and township minutes and agendas (scanned PDFs, video transcripts), zoning ordinance amendments, local newspaper archives, state siting board dockets, ISO queue reports, LBNL local opposition and ordinance datasets.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 100x+ (option cost ~$50-200/acre to ~$15-50k/acre permitted value); ML adds ~1.5-2x on cost per permitted MW.
scored.frame: The rung is a CUP-permitted, site-controlled solar project sold to an IPP. Inside that rung, picking the jurisdiction is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is hands-on execution: land agents signing options on 500-2,000 acre assemblies, community engagement, public hearings, environmental and cultural surveys, ALTA/title work, and above all an interconnection position, which buyers price as heavily as the permit. Winning a CUP is political labor, not a cheap step you can hand off. It works like a bespoke build, much as in the geothermal counter-example, not like a drill hit. A capitalised buyer does exist (IPPs and utilities).
scored.step_up: Unproven: option rents of about $10-50/acre/yr, or roughly $30k per year for a 1,000-acre assembly. Proven: industry rule of thumb, not verified by search, is about $50-150k/MW for an NTP-track US project with a queue position, and much less ($10-30k/MW) for a CUP without a strong interconnection position. At ~5-7 acres/MW that is about $10-25k/acre, so 100-500x on option cost per acre. Against total proving spend ($200k-1M + options) it is only ~10-50x. The only hard comp I found was Italian: Zenith Energy's March 2026 appraisal values permitting phase at EUR 300k/MWp and RTB at EUR 500k/MWp, a ~1.7x step between those stages. US values are pressured: under OBBBA, a project starting permits now misses the July 2026 begin-construction and 2027 placed-in-service credit deadlines. FTI also reports pricing pressure on pure-play solar because midday capture rates are falling, and that solar-plus-storage commands the premiums.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $200k-1M and 1-2 years per project, which passes the relaxed 'expensive' bar. On base rate, LBNL's 2024 developer survey found about a third of applications cancelled because of community opposition and about half delayed 6+ months, which fits the 40-65% CUP success in the brief. The Sabin Center counts 865 local restrictions, 22 projects cancelled in 2025 (9.8 GW), and new restrictions slowing from 165 (2023) to 112 (2024) to 70 (2025). Under relaxed C3 a 1.5x lift from forecasting moratoria is plausible. But Paces says sentiment is negative in most jurisdictions, and the cheaper, more decisive filter is the existing ordinance data. So the marginal ML lift over that data is likely ~1.2-1.5x, and I score 3.
scored.data:
The signal is already being extracted, and much of the outcome is already in legible fields:
- NREL's 2025 U.S. Solar Siting Regulation and Zoning Ordinances dataset (public, LLM-built, county and township level, includes bans and moratoria).
- The Sabin Center's annual restriction database.
- LBNL opposition surveys.
- Commercial siting/permitting-risk products (Paces AI, and others such as Transect and LandGate) sold to developers.
CUP decisions and moratoria are recorded votes, not hidden. Scanned minutes and video transcripts add some leading signal, but incumbents and startups are already mining them with LLMs. The edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought: lease options from farmers, cheap upfront ($10-50/acre/yr). But land is contested by many developer land agents who already use Paces-style tools. Landowners compare offers and increasingly know about solar. In hostile counties, neighbors and boards make the assembly hard to put together at all. There is no first-come mechanism and no deep information asymmetry with the land seller.
scored.buyer: IPPs and utilities (NextEra, AES, Invenergy, Lightsource bp, EDF) buy late-stage projects. Their appetite for greenfield, post-credit, pure-play solar is reduced. The premiums go to solar-plus-storage and to projects with secured interconnection, especially for data-center-driven demand.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: early-stage developer, then NTP/RTB seller, then EPC and construction, then IPP ownership of operating assets and power sales (NextEra-scale path). The upper rungs, though, are capital-intensive and commoditized build-and-own. Many developers already climb the same ladder, and permitting skill does not compound into a moat on construction or financing.
