scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not cheap discovery but slow, political, hands-on execution, and its value is gated by interconnection. Meanwhile the permit signal is already extracted into legible public and commercial datasets (NREL's LLM-built ordinance database, the Sabin Center, Paces AI). So ML adds little over a lookup, and the permitted asset's step-up is modest and policy-exposed (post-OBBBA credit loss).
scored.one_line_reason: Expensive, risky permitting that a buyer pays for does pass the relaxed C3. But it is a crowded developer business: county ordinance data is already structured and sold, permitting is execution rather than discovery, and value depends on queue position and shrinking tax credits.

scored.name: Merchant Transmission Corridor Easement Assembly
scored.one_line: Assemble easement options along an ML-picked corridor where state CPCN siting is predicted to succeed, prove the route with the routing study and permit, and sell the permitted corridor to a merchant HVDC developer or utility.
scored.unproven_right: Easement options at about $100-500/acre along 100-300 mile corridors, from thousands of owners identified through scanned county deeds and plats.
scored.proving_step: Routing and environmental study, state CPCN or siting application, FERC and ISO studies: $2-10M and 2-4 years; roughly 30-50% success with an assembled route.
scored.proven_buyer: Transmission developers and utilities (Invenergy Grain Belt, Grid United, NextEra Transmission, hyperscaler-backed lines).
scored.public_data: Scanned county deed and plat records, state PUC CPCN dockets (Grain Belt, Clean Line history), BLM and NEPA documents, rail and pipeline corridor data, ISO transmission planning reports.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 25-100x on option cost, over a long timescale; ladder extends to owning the line and wheeling revenue.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted HVDC corridor: a route, assembled easements and a CPCN, sold to a builder. Picking the corridor (the discovery part) is maybe 20-30% of the work in this rung. Most of it is a multi-year political, regulatory and landowner fight: county opposition, state laws limiting eminent domain (Arkansas killed Plains & Eastern; Missouri pushed back on Grain Belt), and offtake. Plains & Eastern was stalled when TVA declined to buy its power. These steps cannot be abstracted the way an exploratory drill can. Buyers for development-stage corridors do exist: NextEra bought Plains & Eastern's Oklahoma assets, Invenergy bought Grain Belt, and Pattern bought Western Spirit. But those were distressed exits with undisclosed terms, not a liquid market that pays a step-up.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims 25-100x on option cost, but that compares an option premium to a permitted asset. The real easement cost is far higher. Grain Belt pays 110% of county market value per acre (one Missouri PSC sheet says 150%), with a $2,000 minimum per parcel, plus $6k-18k per structure. Invenergy reports about $105M in agreements with about 1,500 landowners: $19M already paid and $86M due at construction. So an option at $100-500/acre must be exercised at roughly $3k-10k+/acre. On total development spend (more than $100M at Clean Line), a permitted corridor plausibly sells for about 2-10x, not 10^3. Clean Line appraised its Oklahoma assets at over $1B, but the actual sale price was never disclosed and the sale was distressed.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is clearly expensive. The candidate's estimate is $2-10M and 2-4 years; Clean Line actually spent more than $100M over about 9 years on Plains & Eastern alone (Arkansas Business), and Grain Belt has taken over 10 years. History suggests a base hit rate of about 30-50% or lower: Plains & Eastern, Rock Island and Grain Belt (under Clean Line) all failed or stalled, and only Western Spirit was built. Under the relaxed C3, ML over dockets, deeds and opposition signals might pick better corridors by about 1.2-1.5x. Failures are driven by legislatures, offtake (TVA) and federal politics (DOE ended its Clean Line partnership; the LPO commitment for Grain Belt was terminated), which are poorly predictable from documents. Score 3.
scored.data: Scanned county deeds and plats are illegible and scattered, so there is some real extraction work. But the signal that matters, whether siting succeeds, sits in PUC CPCN dockets, legislative votes and ISO plans that are already legible and closely watched by every transmission developer. This is the same pattern that killed earlier hunts. Ownership lookup from deeds is commodity title-abstract work.
scored.right_bought: The rights are bought, not claimed first-come, but not cheaply from uninformed owners. Once a corridor is public (it must be, for the CPCN filing), landowners organize (Block Grain Belt Express groups, the Kansas fights) and become holdouts. Easements end up priced at 110-150% of market value plus structure payments. A few holdouts on a linear route destroy the option value unless eminent domain is granted, and that is the political battle itself. The owners' information gap closes at the moment of proving.
scored.buyer: Invenergy Transmission, NextEra Energy Resources, Pattern, Grid United, and utilities. They have capital and have bought development-stage Clean Line assets, but at undisclosed, distressed terms after the original developer failed.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: permitted corridor, then construction and ownership of the HVDC line ($2-10B+ capex), then wheeling and tolling revenue, then renewable generation at the sending end. Owning transmission is a large regulated or merchant business, so a winner could become very large.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving a corridor is not a discovery problem. It is a decade-long political and holdout fight that ML cannot predict well (legislatures, eminent-domain limits, offtake, federal loans). Easements cost about 110% of land value once exercised, and landowners learn the corridor exactly when it is proven. So there is no cheap illegible right and no 10^3 step-up; at best this is a 2-10x development business with a 30-50% base rate.
scored.one_line_reason: The ladder is attractive and proving is expensive, but discovery is a small share of the work, the easements are bought at full market price from owners who organize once the route is public, the siting outcomes are already legible in PUC dockets, and Clean Line's $100M+ failures show the risk is political and cannot be read from documents.

scored.name: FEMA floodplain overmapping land bank (Zone A / old-study LOMR, scaling to watershed PMR)
scored.one_line: Use ML to compare old FEMA flood studies, especially approximate Zone A drawn from 1970s-80s USGS quads, against modern 3DEP LiDAR and find land in homebuilder growth corridors mapped into the 1% floodplain that actually sits above it. Option or buy at the floodplain discount, fund a detailed HEC-RAS restudy and CLOMR/LOMR, and sell entitled out-of-SFHA land to production homebuilders. The higher rung assembles options across a whole HUC-12 watershed and funds one Physical Map Revision that rezones hundreds of parcels at once, then moves into lot development.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase option or fee title on floodplain-encumbered raw land bought at ag or 'unbuildable' prices (about $2-10k/acre), from owners whose lenders and builders treat the zone as a stop sign.
scored.proving_step: Detailed hydrology and hydraulics restudy using LiDAR, survey, local floodplain administrator sign-off, CLOMR submittal and FEMA LOMR issuance: about $50-300k and 9-24 months per tract (or $0.5-2M and 2-3 years for a watershed PMR); roughly 40-60% success on ML-picked sites.
scored.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Taylor Morrison), build-to-rent funds, industrial developers and land bankers (Millrose, Varde-backed vehicles).
scored.public_data: FEMA NFHL Zone A polygons with no BFE, scanned Flood Insurance Study PDFs and water-surface profiles, effective models from the FEMA Engineering Library (often missing), LOMC case histories and determination letters (training labels and a density signal of overmapping), Risk MAP Discovery reports, USGS 3DEP LiDAR versus original quad contours, NOAA Atlas 14, county parcel, plat and sales data showing the floodplain discount.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x on removed acreage ($3k/acre to $40-150k/acre entitled residential), higher where it unlocks a whole subdivision; the company keeps the uplift as owner.
scored.frame: Rung: optioned floodplain-encumbered raw land plus a FEMA LOMR that removes it from the SFHA. Inside this rung, most of the work is analysis: picking the tract, H&H modelling, and getting the LOMR through FEMA. On genuinely overmapped land there is no physical step (no fill). That makes roughly 70-85% of the rung discovery and paperwork. The output is sellable to capitalised buyers (public homebuilders, land bankers such as Millrose). The weakness is that this is not hidden work. Homebuilder land teams and their civil engineers already run floodplain feasibility and CLOMR/LOMR on every tract in due diligence, so the rung is a standard step in their pipeline rather than a frontier.
scored.step_up: Unproven: floodplain-mapped raw land. Texas rural land averaged about $5,158/acre in Q3 2025 (TX A&M Real Estate Research Center, via a broker). Measured floodplain discounts are modest: Harris County homes -2.3% (Freddie Mac); an inland meta-analysis -4.6%; anecdotal 80-90% on fully mapped parcels. Proven: unentitled out-of-SFHA raw land in the same corridor. The pitched $40-150k/acre is finished or entitled lot value, and that needs zoning, utilities and development capital that the LOMR does not supply. The realistic uplift that comes from the map change alone is about 2-5x on removed acreage, and it is often far less because growth-corridor owners already price at developer comps. This falls well short of 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's own figures put a detailed H&H restudy plus CLOMR/LOMR at about $50-300k and 9-24 months per tract, so proving is expensive and passes the relaxed C3 cost bar. The 40-60% base success rate is the candidate's claim and was not verified. ML lift over the baseline is weak. FEMA Base Level Engineering (BLE) already publishes free LiDAR/2D-model 1% floodplains for Zone A. The Texas Water Development Board's statewide BLE covers all 268,000 sq mi of Texas, with new maps for about a third of it. FEMA Region 6 explicitly accepts BLE data for LOMAs. A simple BLE-vs-effective-Zone-A overlay therefore captures most of the screen, and ML on top plausibly adds about 1.2-1.4x on cost per proven acre, not 1.5-3x.
scored.data: This is where the candidate fails. The core signal (effective Zone A versus a modern LiDAR floodplain) is already extracted and published by the regulator as BLE estimated-BFE layers, with Texas covered statewide. LOMC determinations are a structured, legible database. FIRM panels in the NFHL are vectorised GIS rather than scanned images. Some illegible layers do remain (old FIS PDFs, missing effective models), but the outcome-relevant answer, whether the land is really in the 1% floodplain, is written into a public BLE layer: exactly the 'regulator writes the answer' kill pattern from prior hunts.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The right is bought, not free first-come: an option or fee title from private landowners, so this leg passes. Two things blunt the discount. Owners in builder growth corridors are courted by builder land teams and brokers who read the maps. And measured floodplain price discounts are small (single-digit percent in most hedonic studies), so the land is rarely available at 'unbuildable' prices where demand exists.
scored.buyer: Public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Taylor Morrison), land-banking vehicles (Millrose), build-to-rent funds and industrial developers. They are well capitalised and buy land continuously, but they also have in-house teams that do this exact LOMR diligence.
scored.ladder: Tract LOMR, then watershed-scale PMR assembly, then land banking and entitlement, then lot development, then homebuilding or BTR. The ladder is real and the endpoint is large (homebuilding is a $500B+/yr US market), but every rung above the first is a mature, low-margin, capital-intensive business where incumbents are strong. The first rung's 'discovery' edge does not compound up the chain the way a mineral discovery feeds a mine.
scored.fatal_flaw: FEMA and state Base Level Engineering programs (statewide in Texas, accepted by FEMA for LOMAs) already publish the modern LiDAR-based floodplain for approximate Zone A. The overmapping signal is therefore a free, legible public layer, and builder land teams already use it. On top of that, removing land from the floodplain yields only about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4. Most of the claimed uplift comes from entitlement and development, not from the proving step.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive and analysis-heavy, but the regulator has already written the answer into public BLE floodplain layers, and the map change alone is worth about 2-5x, not orders of magnitude.

scored.name: Florida Coastal 'Unbuildable' Lot Permitting (CCCL / setback)
scored.one_line: Buy vacant coastal lots trading at distressed prices because owners assume they are seaward of the Coastal Construction Control Line or 30-year erosion line, use ML over historic shoreline surveys and permit files to pick lots where a DEP CCCL permit or variance is likely, and sell permitted lots to luxury builders.
scored.unproven_right: Fee purchase of vacant beachfront and near-beach lots (heirs' parcels, post-hurricane forced sales) at 2-10% of permitted-lot value.
scored.proving_step: Coastal engineering study, DEP CCCL permit and local variance, sometimes dune enhancement: about $75-250k and 9-24 months; about 40-60% success on selected lots.
scored.proven_buyer: Luxury custom and spec home builders and high-net-worth buyers in Florida Gulf and Atlantic markets.
scored.public_data: FDEP CCCL permit database and scanned historic permits and denials, DEP R-monument shoreline profiles since the 1970s, beach nourishment records, county parcel and sales data, post-storm FEMA damage inventories.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x ($50-150k distressed lot to $1-4M permitted).
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a vacant coastal lot, get it entitled (CCCL permit, 30-year erosion projection study, local setback variance) and sell the entitled lot. There is no physical step (no construction), so it looks clean. But the work inside the rung is not mostly discovery. Probably only ~30-40% is picking the lot. The other 60%+ is the entitlement fight: engineering studies, hearings, appeals and litigation. The Boca Raton 2600 N. Ocean case shows the pattern: the City Council denied the variance, then circuit court ordered a new hearing, taking years. Luxury builders and HNW buyers are a real, capitalised buyer for the entitled lot.
scored.step_up: Roughly 10-50x. One real example: Boca Raton 2600 N. Ocean, where the Property Appraiser valued the lot at $165k assuming it is unbuildable, versus a 2018 appraisal of about $7.2M if buildable (about 44x). The candidate's own range is $50-150k to $1-4M (10-50x). This is 10^1-10^2, not 10^3-10^4, and the value does not arrive the moment a permit issues: the challenge window and appeal risk remain.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive enough: about $75-250k and 9-24 months, often longer when there is litigation. The base hit rate is less clear. A CBS12/CoastalCare analysis found the state CCCL permit almost never fails: of 236 applications since 2010, only 4 were denied, 2 of those for being incomplete (about 98% approval). So the uncertainty sits in two other places: (a) the 30-year erosion projection, a deterministic engineering calculation from R-monument history that any licensed coastal engineer reproduces, and (b) local council variance votes, which are political (Boca denied 2600 N. Ocean but approved Azure with 17 conditions). ML over shoreline data cannot predict a council vote, and it adds little over an engineer on (a). A plausible lift is about 1.2-1.5x on cost per entitled lot, mostly from filtering lots before buying. Score 3 under the relaxed C3.
scored.data: The data is public but only partly illegible: scanned historic CCCL permits and denials, and R-monument profiles since the 1970s. The deciding inputs, though, are legible or not in data at all. The 30-year erosion projection is computed site by site from published shoreline change rates under rule 62B-33.024, at a default 1 ft/yr in stable areas, and seawalls truncate it. The local variance outcome lives in council politics and hardship law: the self-created-hardship doctrine weighs against a buyer who purchased knowing the lot was seaward of the line. On top of that, the state permit's outcome is close to a constant, about 98% approved. So the signal ML could add is thin.
scored.right_bought: The lots can be bought as fee purchases from heirs or after a hurricane, so the right is bought, not claimed. But the sellers are often sophisticated: the Boca owners hired appraisers and litigated. The discount reflects legal and political risk, not owners being unable to read data. Inventory is thin, probably hundreds of genuinely 'unbuildable' vacant beachfront lots statewide. And buying a lot with knowledge of the constraint weakens the hardship case for the variance, so ML-informed buying actively hurts the variance argument.
scored.buyer: Luxury custom and spec builders and high-net-worth end buyers on Florida's Atlantic and Gulf coasts. They are capitalised and pay $1-7M+ for entitled beachfront lots, provided no appeal is pending.
scored.ladder: Short. Rungs above are: building the spec homes, then a coastal residential development and homebuilding business, possibly expanding to other states' setback regimes (the Carolinas, the Gulf). That is a solid real-estate firm, not a trillion-dollar chain. The asset class is also shrinking: climate pressure tightens setbacks, nourishment funding is politically contested, and insurance (Citizens) is retreating from the coast.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome that decides value is not hidden in illegible data. The state CCCL permit is approved about 98% of the time. The 30-year erosion line is a deterministic engineering calculation. The real gate is a political, litigated local variance, and the self-created-hardship doctrine weakens it when the buyer knowingly bought an 'unbuildable' lot. ML has little to discover, the discount prices legal risk rather than ignorance, and the inventory is a few hundred lots.
scored.one_line_reason: A 10-50x step-up with an expensive proving step, but the hit rate turns on council politics, hardship law and a deterministic erosion calculation, not illegible data; the state CCCL permit itself is about 98% approved, so the ML edge and C4 collapse.

scored.name: Senior surface-water right change-of-use decrees (Colorado and Western prior-appropriation states)
scored.one_line: Buy dormant or under-documented senior agricultural surface-water rights (pre-1900 ditch shares, direct-flow decrees, partially used rights) at ag or abandonment-risk prices, using ML on a century of diversion records and imagery to predict the consumptive-use yield a court will accept. Win a water-court or state-engineer change-of-use decree to municipal or industrial use, and sell the decreed acre-feet to Front Range and Southwest cities, developers and data centres. This is surface-water adjudication, not groundwater exploration.
scored.unproven_right: Senior ditch-company shares or direct-flow decrees whose historic use is patchy, contested or at abandonment risk; they trade at ag value (about $1-15k per acre-foot) or near zero when abandonment risk is high.
scored.proving_step: Historic consumptive-use engineering plus a water-court change case through trial or stipulation against objectors: $150k-2M and 2-6 years; about 50-80% success, but decreed yield is often cut. ML picks rights with clean, well-documented histories to raise yield per dollar.
scored.proven_buyer: Municipal water providers (Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Colorado Springs, Parker), metro districts, master-planned developers needing tap dedication, and data-centre developers that must show firm water supply; they pay about $30-80k per decreed acre-foot.
scored.public_data: CDSS/HydroBase diversion records, scanned state engineer field books and ditch-rider logs, water court resumes, case files and decrees back to the 1880s, ditch company minutes and reports, NAIP, historic USDA/USGS aerials and Landsat irrigation history, abandonment lists, opposer filings; similar archives in AZ (ADWR), NM, UT, ID and TX (TCEQ).
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-10x against clean ag value and 10-50x (up to ~100x) on rights bought at abandonment-risk discounts; C2 is the weak point.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy a senior ag right, win a change-of-use decree, sell the decreed acre-feet". Discovery, meaning choosing which right to buy and predicting its historic consumptive use, is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is a contested legal and engineering case: years of objector litigation, dry-up covenants, revegetation, return-flow and augmentation terms. On top of that, delivery infrastructure (storage, exchanges, pipelines) is usually needed before a city can actually use water from a Weld County or Arkansas Valley ditch. The physical and legal step is neither trivial nor abstracted, so this is closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example than to Terranox. A capitalised buyer does exist (Front Range municipal providers). The frame does not reach 80%+ discovery.
scored.step_up: About 2-4x on clean rights. Colorado-Big Thompson units, which transfer without water-court review, sold for about $85k/AF in 2025 (peak $101k in 2022, WestWater Research via Colorado Sun, April 2026). AgWeb commentary says rights that need complex review trade at 1/3 to 1/4 of CBT prices in the same area, so a successful change case realises roughly a 3-4x uplift, minus the cut in decreed yield. Front Range ag rights already carry municipal option value, because cities are the dominant buyers even at ag auctions (KUNC 2016). The 10-100x figure on abandonment-risk rights is mostly illusory: rights at real abandonment risk lose their historic consumptive-use credit, so the decreed yield shrinks toward zero. Nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $150k-2M and 2-6 years per change case. Single contested South Platte cases have cost parties millions in legal fees (BizWest, Gazette). The base success rate for getting some decree is high (~50-80%), so under the relaxed C3 the lever is yield per dollar. ML on HydroBase diversion records and Landsat/NAIP irrigation history could plausibly pick rights with cleaner, defensible historic consumptive use and fewer objectors, for perhaps 1.2-1.5x better decreed acre-feet per dollar. Incumbent water engineers already do historic-consumptive-use analysis from the same digitised HydroBase data, so the gain is modest.
scored.data: The data is largely legible. CDSS/HydroBase diversion records are digitised and structured. Water-court resumes and decrees are public. Ditch companies know the historic yield per share, and the share itself is the legible field in which the outcome is mostly summarised. The illegible parts (field books, ditch-rider logs, old aerials) give only an incremental edge. Counterparties are sophisticated: municipal water departments with in-house engineers and specialised brokers such as WestWater.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought rather than claimed first-come: ditch shares and decrees are purchased from farmers. But they are not cheap relative to their proven value. Sellers price in the municipal exit, and cities bid directly at ag auctions. Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains A&M v. Southeastern Colorado WCD, 2005) bars a change decree without a specific, non-speculative end use and user. So a pure speculator cannot prove the right and then sell it; it must line up the buyer first, and that buyer captures much of the spread.
scored.buyer: Front Range municipal providers (Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Colorado Springs, Parker), metro districts, master-planned developers and data-centre developers, paying roughly $30-85k per firm decreed acre-foot. These buyers are highly capitalised. Demand softened after 2022: CBT prices fell 16% from peak as housing slowed.
scored.ladder: There are moderate rungs above: storage reservoirs, augmentation plans, exchanges, conveyance pipelines, wholesale water utility, and water-as-a-service for data centres and industry. That is a credible path to a large regional water utility, but it is capital- and politics-heavy (buy-and-dry backlash, county 1041 permits) and not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 3-4x, not 10^3-10^4. Proving takes years of contested litigation and infrastructure, not a trivial physical step. Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains 2005) forbids changing a right without a committed end user, so the company cannot independently prove the asset and capture the jump: the sophisticated municipal buyer must be in from the start and already prices the change option.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded: this is surface-water adjudication, not exploration. But it is a 3-4x legal-arbitrage play on largely legible HydroBase data, against sophisticated city buyers, and the anti-speculation rule blocks proving the right on spec.
sources: High Plains A&M, LLC v. Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District, 120 P.3d 710 (Colo. 2005) (anti-speculation doctrine in change cases; from background knowledge, not fetched)

scored.name: Sewer/water capacity-constrained parcels with recoverable legacy allocations
scored.one_line: In jurisdictions under sewer or water connection moratoria, use ML over decades of utility board minutes and recorded agreements to find parcels carrying forgotten prepaid capacity reservations, EDU allocations or development-agreement rights. Buy the parcels or allocations at moratorium prices, get the allocation reconfirmed, and sell serviceable parcels to builders.
scored.unproven_right: Parcels or recorded capacity rights in moratorium areas (parts of CA, the FL Keys, MD/VA septic-limited counties, Utah and Idaho growth fringes) priced as unserviceable.
scored.proving_step: Title and agreement research, then petition, administrative hearing or litigation to confirm and assign the allocation: about $50-300k and 6-24 months; about 40-60% success on ML-flagged candidates.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders and multifamily developers blocked by the moratorium.
scored.public_data: Scanned utility district board minutes, recorded development and capacity agreements, sanitary district EDU ledgers via public records requests, regional water quality board orders.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x per parcel, higher in severe moratoria.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a parcel or EDU allocation in a moratorium area, getting the allocation confirmed, and selling a serviceable lot to a builder. Finding the parcel is perhaps 40-50% of the work. The proving step is not trivial or abstracted: it is a petition, hearing or lawsuit against the capacity-constrained utility, the party that most wants to deny the claim. The result is decided by law and politics, not by a physical fact the way a drill core is. Builders are real, capitalised buyers, but the frame where discovery is 80% or more does not exist.
scored.step_up: Usually 2-5x, about 10-20x at the extremes. Bonner County, ID: sewer-blocked 0.137-acre lots argued down to $50k against $79k-$118k assessed values (about 2x), and existing LID members who had prepaid hookups were exempt from the moratorium. Island County, WA: lots denied septic sell as recreational lots for $5-7k, far below buildable lots (roughly 10-20x where buildable lots sell for about $100k). Hernando County, FL: parcels in a moratorium area sold for $1.0M against $2M+ assessed (about 2x). A wastewater EDU can be bought privately for about $16.7k in Bayside, MD, which caps what an allocation is worth where a transfer market exists. This is well short of 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's own figure is $50-300k and 6-24 months per attempt for legal research and a hearing or lawsuit, at about 40-60% success on ML-flagged candidates. I found no outside source for that success rate. Proving is expensive, so it passes the relaxed C3 cost bar. ML lifts the hit rate only on finding forgotten agreements in scanned minutes. Whether a found right is honoured depends on the forfeiture, transfer-ban and reservation-fee terms in the ordinance, which ML cannot change. I put the plausible improvement in cost per proven asset at about 1.2-1.5x, so C3 = 3.
scored.data: Partly illegible: decades of scanned board minutes and recorded development agreements. But the outcome is usually already a legible field. Utilities keep EDU and allocation ledgers: St. Mary's County, MD keeps formal records of inactive EDUs and transfer notices that state a price per EDU, and Bonner County treats prepaid LID members as a known class. Many codes also forfeit an allocation that is not connected within about 18 months unless a reservation fee is paid, or ban transfers outright (for example a North Shores ordinance). So the forgotten-but-valid allocation is narrower than pitched. This is the same failure as prior hunts: the regulator has already written the answer down.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Parcels in a moratorium area are bought from private owners at depressed prices. Bought EDUs need the utility's approval and a demonstrated need, such as a filed site plan or permit (St. Mary's County SOP).
scored.buyer: Homebuilders and multifamily developers blocked by the moratorium. They are capitalised and motivated, but they also discount for legal risk and for a moratorium possibly lifting on its own.
scored.ladder: Land banking leads to entitlement and lot development, then homebuilding, and possibly to building private or package wastewater capacity. That is a real ladder, but it ends in commodity homebuilding with thin margins, and moratoria are local and temporary.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is decided by the utility that is short of capacity and wants to deny claims, not by a physical test, and valid allocations are usually already in the utility's legible EDU ledger or have lapsed under forfeiture or transfer-ban rules. So the ML edge is small, and the 2-20x uplift is set by politics and law rather than discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive (it passes the relaxed C3), but the step-up is only about 2-20x, it is decided in an adversarial hearing rather than by finding something, and the outcome is often already in the utility's own allocation ledger.

scored.name: Licensing hydropower at distressed and orphaned non-powered dams
scored.one_line: Buy (often for $1 plus liability) or option private or municipal dams whose owners want to shed dam-safety costs, win the FERC license or exemption plus 401 certification at ML-screened sites, and sell the licensed project to an IPP or infrastructure fund.
scored.unproven_right: Title to or long-term option on a small dam with high-hazard deficiencies and no hydropower license.
scored.proving_step: FERC preliminary permit, then license or 10MW exemption, 401 water-quality certificate and interconnection study: about $0.5-3M and 2-5 years; roughly 50-70% success on screened sites.
scored.proven_buyer: Hydro IPPs and infrastructure funds (Brookfield-type, Rye Development, Enel) and utilities buying firm clean MWh for data-centre PPAs.
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary (including surrendered and lapsed licenses), USACE National Inventory of Dams, scanned state dam-safety inspections, USGS streamgage hydrology, ORNL non-powered dam assessments.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x on all-in cost for a 3-10MW site and far more on purchase price (licensed value ~$1-3M/MW).
scored.frame: The rung (hold the dam, win the FERC license, 401 certificate and interconnection study, then sell the shovel-ready project) does exist and does trade. Rye Development has filed to sell three unbuilt Pittsburgh lock-and-dam licenses to an affiliate of the turbine maker Mavel. Inside this rung, though, discovery is perhaps 20-30% of the work. Most of the work is regulatory process: consultation with agencies, fish passage studies and water-quality certification. That is grinding through procedure, not finding something nobody else can see. The buyer still faces the hard physical step of building a bespoke powerhouse at $2,200-34,000/kW, with most ORNL sites under $12,000/kW. This is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the build is harder than the find, so the licensed rung is worth little.
scored.step_up: The candidate's "licensed value ~$1-3M/MW" is the value of an operating asset, not of a license. Comparables: Romanian operating small hydro sold at about EUR 0.7M/MW, and Brazilian operating plants at roughly BRL 2.6-5.9M/MW. Unbuilt licenses for non-powered dams usually change hands for development fees. My estimate (no transaction price found) is ~$30-200k/MW, so $0.1-2M for a 3-10MW site, against $0.5-3M spent to prove it. That is roughly 0.5-3x on all-in cost. The multiple only looks enormous against a $1 purchase price, and that ignores the liability taken on with the dam (a high-hazard dam can need millions in repairs).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $0.5-3M and 2-5 years per site, so the relaxed C3 test is met. The base success rate on screened sites is about 50-70% (the candidate's figure, which I find plausible). But many licenses are won and then go unbuilt. FERC refused to extend five of Rye's Kentucky preliminary permits because Rye had not started prefiling consultation in 35 months. A Bates College thesis found that licenses at small-capacity dams are the most likely to be surrendered. ML that screens for LCOE, permitting risk and the cost of fixing deficiencies could plausibly improve cost per sellable license by about 1.3-1.6x. The lift is limited because ORNL already publishes site-level non-powered-dam cost models (2020 cost analysis; 2024 reduced-form model ORNL/TM-2024/3299).
scored.data: Partly illegible: scanned state dam-safety inspections and FERC eLibrary dockets for surrendered licenses. But the core value drivers are already in legible fields: capacity potential, head and flow in the ORNL non-powered dam assessments, and hazard class and condition in the USACE National Inventory of Dams. FERC eLibrary itself is searchable. Incumbents such as Rye and ORNL already use this data.
scored.right_bought: Mixed. The FERC preliminary permit is free and first-come, which is the anti-pattern: competitors can file at any site you reveal. Private or municipal dams can be bought cheaply, often for $1, but the buyer inherits liability for dam-safety deficiencies. Most of the high-value non-powered dam potential is at federal USACE locks, which cannot be bought at all. Those sites are reached through the free permit queue, so there is no owner who fails to read the data and can be bought out cheaply.
scored.buyer: Thin and price-sensitive. Mavel-affiliated buyers, a few hydro IPPs and infrastructure funds buy licensed projects only when the economics pencil out. ORNL puts most non-powered-dam LCOE under $400/MWh at lake dams and under $200/MWh at locks. That is far above the price of firm clean power from alternatives, even with data-centre premiums. Buyers are capitalised, but they do not pay the large step-up for permits.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are real: build, operate, own a portfolio, sell power to data centres. But the total market is small (US non-powered dam potential is about 12 GW, mostly at sites with uneconomic LCOE), so the chain caps out as a mid-size hydro IPP, not a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical build dominates, as in the geothermal counter-example. Retrofitting a dam costs $2,200-12,000+/kW and LCOE is $79-790/MWh, so licenses routinely go unbuilt, get surrendered or are resold cheaply. Winning the license (discovery plus permitting) does not unlock a large step-up, because the buyer's real problem is building the plant economically, not finding the site.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough for the relaxed C3, but a licensed, unbuilt non-powered-dam project is worth roughly 1-3x what it cost to prove. The bespoke powerhouse build, not site discovery, is the bottleneck, and the key site data is already legible in ORNL and NID datasets.

scored.name: Stranded Paragraph IV first-filer rescue
scored.one_line: Acquire first-to-file Paragraph IV ANDAs carrying 180-day exclusivity from undercapitalised filers about to forfeit them, fund the patent litigation or IPR that ML rates winnable, and sell the approved exclusivity-bearing ANDA to a large generic company.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of a pending first-filer ANDA bought cheaply from a sponsor unable to afford Hatch-Waxman litigation or CMC fixes.
scored.proving_step: Winning or settling the Paragraph IV case or IPR plus tentative or final approval: about $5-15M over 2-3 years; historically about 40-60% favourable outcome.
scored.proven_buyer: Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's, Sun and others paying heavily for exclusivity on $200M+ brands.
scored.public_data: FDA Paragraph IV list, Orange Book patent and exclusivity data, USPTO file wrappers, PTAB IPR filings, PACER Hatch-Waxman dockets, FDA forfeiture decisions.
scored.rough_step_up: 5-30x on capex and up to about 100x on the right.
scored.frame: The rung is owning a pending first-filer Paragraph IV ANDA and taking it to a favourable litigation or IPR outcome plus tentative or final approval. That rung is sellable, and there is precedent: Par paid Handa upfront plus a profit share for its first-filer Dexilant ANDA. Discovery, meaning picking which stranded ANDA has a winnable patent challenge, is maybe 20-30% of the work. The other 70-80% is the proving step itself: 2-3 years of Hatch-Waxman litigation run by trial counsel, plus CMC and bioequivalence fixes, while racing the 30-month forfeiture clock. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted. It is the hard, bespoke part, much like the bespoke plant in the geothermal counter-example. The buyer is clearly capitalised (Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Par).
scored.step_up: There is no public price for stranded ANDAs; the Par/Handa price was not disclosed. On the brief's own figures, roughly $1-5M to acquire plus $5-15M to prove gives an asset worth about $20-150M, with the upper end for $1B+ brands such as Celebrex, where 'hundreds of millions' went to the 180-day holder. That is about 5-30x on capital, and up to about 100x only on the bare right. Exclusivity is often shared among several same-day first filers (common for NCE-1 date filings, per Health Affairs 2026), which cuts the value of each holder's share several-fold. Most cases settle into licensed entry dates rather than clean wins. This is about 10-100x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $5-15M over 2-3 years (the candidate's own estimate; full Hatch-Waxman cases commonly run several million dollars in legal fees alone), so the expensive-step leg is met. The base favourable-outcome rate is about 40-60%, and most cases settle. ML that predicts patent or IPR outcomes from file wrappers and PTAB records plausibly gives a modest lift. Litigation outcomes depend on claim construction, judge and expert testimony, and the sophisticated opposing side already prices these well. A realistic gain is about 1.2-1.5x in cost per proven asset, not 2-3x. Score 3.
scored.data: Most of the signal is in legible, structured public data: the FDA Paragraph IV list, Orange Book patent and exclusivity fields, PTAB decisions and PACER dockets. File wrappers are long but routinely read in full by every generic company's IP group. Brand and generic legal teams already extract this information, so there is no illegibility gap. Outcomes are logged clearly in PTAB final decisions, docket judgments and FDA forfeiture letters.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought: ANDAs, with their exclusivity, are transferable, as Par/Handa shows. The sellers, however, are generic firms that know what first-filer status is worth. They are capital-constrained, not unable to read the data. Large generics and specialty litigation funders already compete for these assets, so a deep discount comes only from the seller's distress, not from an information edge. Forfeiture risk under the 30-month and failure-to-market rules, and the 2026 D.C. Circuit Norwich ruling that exclusivity is all-or-nothing for a first applicant, both add risk to the transaction.
scored.buyer: The buyers are Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Par/Endo, Dr. Reddy's, Sun, Aurobindo and Amneal. They are capitalised and active, and they pay upfront plus a profit share for first-filer ANDAs (Par/Handa Dexilant precedent).
scored.ladder: The ladder runs: first-filer rescue, then own ANDAs and contract manufacturing, then a full generic company, then 505(b)(2) and complex generics or biosimilars. That is a real path to a multi-billion-dollar generics company. But US generics is a low-margin, price-deflating industry; Teva and Viatris trade well below $50B. It is not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegibility edge. Both the sellers and the buyers are sophisticated generic companies whose IP litigators already read the same Orange Book data, file wrappers and dockets. The proving step is bespoke, multi-year patent litigation rather than a cheap, trivial physical step. So discovery is a minority of the work, and any discount comes from the seller's capital distress, not from ML insight.
scored.one_line_reason: Expensive proving and an active capitalised buyer exist, but the data is legible to expert incumbents, the proving step is hard litigation rather than discovery, and the step-up is about 10-30x and often diluted by shared exclusivity.

scored.name: Orphaned 510(k) clearance revival
scored.one_line: Buy 510(k) clearances, design history files and IP from defunct device startups, use ML to find clearances needing only a modest new 510(k) to address a large CPT-coded market, file it, and sell the cleared reimbursable product to a strategic medtech.
scored.unproven_right: Clearance plus design and IP files bought from ABC sales or Chapter 7 auctions for $50-500k.
scored.proving_step: New 510(k) with bench, biocompatibility and sometimes small clinical data plus a quality system: about $1-5M and 12-24 months; typically 60-80% clearance.
scored.proven_buyer: Medtronic, Stryker, BD, Teleflex and PE platforms.
scored.public_data: FDA 510(k) database and decision summaries, MAUDE, recalls, establishment registration (to detect defunct holders), PACER bankruptcy dockets, CMS CPT/HCPCS utilisation.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x on capex and 50-200x on the right.
scored.frame: The rung is "cleared, reimbursable device design sold to a strategic". Discovery (picking which orphaned clearance fits a large CPT-coded market) is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of the work is engineering and regulatory: rebuilding the quality system, verification and validation, biocompatibility, sometimes clinical data, plus the 510(k) itself. That physical and regulatory step is neither trivial nor abstracted. Strategic buyers exist, but they mostly buy revenue and commercial traction, not a bare clearance.
scored.step_up: Unproven: bankrupt-estate packages that include clearances and design history files go for roughly $0.6-7M in total (Electro-Catheter's assets including 510(k) K854511 sold for $625k; Diomed's assets to Biolitec for $6-7M; Surgalign's US hardware to Xtant for $5M). Proven: a newly cleared device with no revenue is worth only a little more than what it costs to re-clear it, about $1-5M, because a strategic can file its own 510(k) on the same predicate. Investors say acquirers want sales, reimbursement and revenue first; general medtech multiples are 3-6x revenue, and revenue here is zero. The realistic step-up is about 2-5x on total capex. The candidate's 50-200x figure on the right alone ignores the $1-5M proving spend and the buyer's option to build the product itself.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $1-5M and takes 12-24 months, which meets the "expensive" bar. The base regulatory hit rate is 60-80%, per the candidate and typical 510(k) clearance rates. ML can raise the regulatory hit rate only a little, about 1.1-1.3x. The bigger lift is in choosing clearances that map to large reimbursed markets. That improves commercial value, not proving cost, and it is plausibly about 1.2-1.5x on value per proven asset. Score 3 under the relaxed C3.
scored.data: The FDA 510(k) database is structured and legible, and the clearance outcome is already a status field (decision and date), which is the usual killer. Decision-summary PDFs, MAUDE and recall records are semi-structured and are already mined by regulatory-intelligence vendors. The one fairly illegible signal is spotting defunct holders by joining registration lapses with PACER dockets, and that is modest. CMS utilisation data is fully legible and is what every strategic already uses.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Clearances, design history files and IP can be transferred and are bought from ABC (assignment for the benefit of creditors) sales, Chapter 7 auctions and 363 sales. Examples: Premier Laser auctioned more than 50 510(k)s, and NovoSource sold design history files with its clearances. Prices are low, about $50k-$600k for small packages. But sellers and bankruptcy trustees are not unable to read the data. These sales are brokered and often sold to strategics directly, so the information edge is thin.
scored.buyer: Medtronic, Stryker, BD, Teleflex and PE roll-ups. All are well capitalised, but they buy revenue-generating products. A pre-revenue 510(k) holder is a low-interest asset to them, and they can re-clear the same device in-house for the same $1-5M.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: contract manufacturing, then commercialising the device yourself with a sales force and reimbursement, then a portfolio medtech company. It is a real ladder, but each rung is capital- and sales-heavy, and there is no compounding information advantage from the first rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: A 510(k) clearance is not a scarce asset. Any strategic can file its own substantial-equivalence 510(k) on the same predicate for the same $1-5M and 12-24 months. A cleared device with no revenue therefore sells for about the cost of re-clearing it, not at a 10^3x step-up. Medtech acquirers pay for revenue and sales traction, not for clearance.
scored.one_line_reason: The rights are cheap and buyable, but the proving step is regulatory engineering rather than discovery, the outcome is already a legible FDA status field, and a clearance is easy to replicate, so the step-up is about 2-5x on capex and the strategic buyer can simply build the product itself.

scored.name: BC Agricultural Land Reserve exclusion and inclusion swaps
scored.one_line: Option ALR parcels next to urban containment boundaries in Metro Vancouver, the Fraser Valley and the Okanagan, win an ALC exclusion (often by offering compensating inclusion elsewhere) plus RGS and OCP amendments, and sell developable land to Lower Mainland builders.
scored.unproven_right: Options on ALR parcels at about C$100-250k/acre where adjacent non-ALR land is worth C$2-5M/acre.
scored.proving_step: ALC exclusion application with local support, agrology reports, inclusion swaps, then RGS and OCP amendments: C$300k-1.5M and 2-4 years; about 30-50% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Polygon, Qualico, Anthem, Beedie and other residential and industrial developers.
scored.public_data: ALC decision archive (decades of scanned reasons PDFs), ALC application portal, council minutes, Metro Vancouver RGS amendment files, Canada Land Inventory soil capability, BC Assessment.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-25x; higher for industrial exclusions in Delta and Richmond.
scored.frame: The rung is an entitled, excluded parcel sold to a developer. Nothing physical is built, which is a good sign. But almost all the work inside this rung is political and procedural, not discovery. Since Bill 15 (in force Sept 30, 2020), a landowner can no longer apply for exclusion; only a local government, a First Nation or another prescribed body can. So council has to agree to forward the application, often Metro Vancouver's board has to amend the RGS and the urban containment boundary, and then the ALC has to approve. Choosing the parcel with data is maybe 15-25% of the work; lobbying, agrology reports, inclusion swaps and hearings are the rest. Developers who would buy the result do exist.
scored.step_up: ALR parcels near the urban edge list at about C$100-270k/acre (Langley: a 44-acre parcel at C$12M is about C$270k/acre; a blueberry farm at about C$100k/acre). Nearby industrial land sells for C$2-3M/acre (BIV 2018 Surrey/Langley) and peaked at about C$6.7M/acre (Port Kells, 2022), then fell 15-20%. Excluded but unserviced raw land is worth less than serviced comparables, so a realistic step-up is about 8-20x, at most about 25x. That is a 10-100x step-up, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs C$300k-1.5M and takes 2-4 years, which counts as expensive. Base rates: IntegrityBC found about 72% of ALC decisions approved in the Kootenays (2006-2012). The South Coast panel approved 59% of all application types in 2007. In Metro Vancouver, councils filter applications out before they reach the ALC; Richmond refused to forward the Burrows Road exclusions in 2019, and Surrey staff recommended denial for the 56 Ave/Hwy 10 sites. A WUR logit study found success depends on soil capability, distance to a highway, and parcel and portion size. Those are legible variables, so a simple model captures most of the signal. The biggest driver, local political support, is not in the data. My estimate for ML lift in cost per proven asset is about 1.2-1.5x.
scored.data: ALC decision PDFs and council minutes are public and partly unstructured. But the outcome is already written down in legible form (decision: approved or refused, plus conditions), and the main predictors are mapped (CLI soil class, RGS designation, distance to the urban containment boundary). Local planners, land brokers and the developers themselves already read this material closely.
scored.right_bought: Options can be bought, but not cheaply relative to the information. Farmland at the urban edge already carries hope value: it trades at C$100-270k/acre against an agricultural value of perhaps C$30-80k/acre. The owners are often speculators or developer land-bankers who know the exclusion game better than an outsider does. Developers such as Beedie, Polygon and Qualico option this land themselves.
scored.buyer: Lower Mainland residential and industrial developers and industrial REITs: Beedie, Polygon, Qualico, Anthem, PC Urban. They are well capitalised and buy entitled land.
scored.ladder: Entitle, then service and subdivide, then build industrial or residential, then hold income property. This is the ladder of a regional master-planned developer, the Beedie or Qualico scale: billions of dollars, but geographically capped by the ALR and limited by politics. It is a real path, but not trillion-dollar scale.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a political permission, not a discovery. Since 2020 only the local government can file the exclusion. The RGS and urban containment boundary amendment needs a regional board vote, and the ALC weighs local support and agricultural benefit. ML cannot predict or change those votes. Meanwhile the parcels where ML could help already trade at hope-value prices to sophisticated owners, and the edge is in lobbying, not in reading data.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical step is trivial and there are real buyers. But the value of a C$0.3-1.5M, multi-year attempt is set by council and regional board politics, not by illegible data. The step-up is only about 10-20x, and edge-of-boundary ALR land is already priced with hope value. ML gives at most about 1.2-1.5x.

scored.name: Romania PUZ rezoning (extravilan to intravilan) around Bucharest, Cluj and Iasi
scored.one_line: Buy extravilan agricultural land on peri-urban corridors (Bucharest A0 ring, Cluj northwest), win intravilan inclusion through a PUZ, and sell to residential and logistics developers.
scored.unproven_right: Extravilan plots at about EUR 5-15/m² from post-restitution heirs with fragmented, often undocumented ownership.
scored.proving_step: PUZ with environment, roads and utility approvals, council vote and intravilan inclusion: EUR 100-500k and 1.5-3 years; about 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: One United Properties, Impact Developer, CTP, WDP, Speedwell.
scored.public_data: Scanned HCL council decisions on primarie sites, ANCPI eTerra cadastre, CNAIR motorway documents, draft PUG updates.
scored.rough_step_up: About 8-20x (EUR 10/m² to EUR 80-200/m²).
scored.frame: The rung is land entitlement: buy extravilan land, get a PUZ approved, sell intravilan plots to developers. This is a real, sellable rung, and developers such as One United, CTP and WDP do buy entitled land. But discovery (choosing the plot) is perhaps 20-30% of the work. The other 70-80% is the proving step itself: the PUZ, which means sequential endorsements, roads and utilities studies, political lobbying of the local council, and clearing fragmented heir titles. Unlike a drill hole, that is the bulk of the job, not a trivial physical step. It is closer to the geothermal counter-example, where the hard part is building the thing, than to Terranox.
scored.step_up: About EUR 10-17/m2 unproven to about EUR 60-200/m2 entitled. That is 5-15x, roughly 10x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. Peri-urban extravilan near Bucharest is already priced speculatively: a forum seller cites EUR 17/m2 for a sought-after area, while plain agricultural land in Bucharest-Ilfov averages about EUR 12,000/ha (about EUR 1.2/m2, per Capital.ro 2025). So the cheap EUR 1/m2 land is not on the corridors, and corridor land already carries the rezoning option premium.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate states EUR 100-500k and 1.5-3 years per PUZ with about 40-60% success, so proving is expensive. Sources say 6-18 months in practice for simple cases (Playtech 2025 guide). The Cluj chief architect says there is no guarantee of approval and that many PUZs stop at the opportunity endorsement stage. Bucharest city hall has reportedly approved almost no private PUZs in about 4.5 years, with 42 approved PUZs waiting about 4 years for a council vote (BusinessForum, Nov 2025). Whether a PUZ succeeds depends mainly on politics, council timing and moratoria, not on features ML can read. ML can screen plots against draft PUG expansion zones, motorway nodes and utility reach, which plausibly gives about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven asset, not 2-3x.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned HCL council decisions on primarie sites, eTerra cadastre and CNAIR motorway documents. But the key outcome signal is largely legible. Draft PUGs map the proposed intravilan extensions explicitly, and approved PUZs appear in the HCLs. Local brokers, speculators and developers' land teams already track A0 ring nodes and PUG drafts closely, so the edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the land is bought freehold from post-restitution heirs. But fragmented, undocumented ownership (succession not finalised, no intabulation) makes assembly slow and legally risky. Owners near the corridors are price-aware and anchor to intravilan prices, so the discount to fair value is modest.
scored.buyer: Capitalised and real: residential developers (One United Properties, Impact Developer) and logistics REITs and developers (CTP, WDP) buy entitled land. The Bucharest PUZ freeze is pushing them toward Ilfov and regional cities, which supports demand for entitled Ilfov and Cluj land.
scored.ladder: Entitlement leads to infrastructure and parcelling, then vertical development, then build-to-rent or logistics asset ownership. The ladder exists, but it is ordinary real-estate development in a mid-sized market: large (possibly a multi-billion-EUR developer), not a trillion-dollar chain, and the higher rungs are crowded with capitalised incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step (getting a PUZ through a council) is itself the hard, political, bureaucratic work, not a cheap physical step after discovery. It delivers only about 5-15x, because land on the peri-urban corridors already carries the speculative rezoning premium.
scored.one_line_reason: This is ordinary land-entitlement speculation. Discovery is a small share of the work, the step-up is about 10x rather than 10^3x, and success depends on council politics that ML cannot read. The relaxed C3 lifts it only to a middling 3.

scored.name: Masterless: defunct-label masters via MMA
scored.one_line: Buy masters of defunct small labels from trustees, successors and heirs; ML proves chain of title and matches to streams; claim SoundExchange and Content ID; sell catalogues.
scored.fatal_flaw: Unit economics on the typical hit are too small, and proving is cheap. A defunct small-label master earns hundreds of dollars a year and sells at 5-10x, so the typical step-up is 1-5x. Proving title costs only about $2-10k, below the $50k threshold, so the relaxed C3 adds nothing. The valuable orphans are already flagged by SoundExchange's unregistered-owner lists and by public play counts.
scored.step_up: Small and lesser-known catalogues trade at about 5-10x net share (deal-focused sources). Guides for independent artists give 2-8x annual net royalties (RouteNote), and established catalogues get 10-15x. A typical defunct small-label master earns roughly $100-2,000 a year (my estimate). Bought at $1-5k, it sells for about $1-15k, so the typical hit is 1-5x. Only rare sampled or breakbeat masters reach about 100x. The tail is fat, but there is no reliable 10^3. Score unchanged at 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Relaxing C3 does not help here, because it still requires an expensive proving step (at least ~$50k or years per attempt). Proving costs about $2-10k per master (archival research, tracing heirs and trustees, a chain-of-title opinion; my estimate, no source found). That is cheap. Base hit rate is roughly 5-15%. ML might improve cost per proven asset by 2-4x, but the rubric scores a cheap proving step near 0. C3 = 1.
scored.frame: The rung is 'acquire a defunct-label master plus clean chain of title, register it, and claim SoundExchange and Content ID.' Discovery and proving (who owns it, does it earn) is roughly 70-80% of the work. The physical step is trivial because the recording already exists. But the human legal work of closing title (heir signatures, trustee releases, exposure to termination rights under 17 USC 203) is a big share, and ML does not shrink it. The buyers are catalogue aggregators and funds, but they only want bundles above about $1M NPS. Unchanged from r1.
scored.data: The signal sits in scattered public sources: Copyright Office records (pre-1978 records are scanned card catalogues), bankruptcy dockets, Discogs, probate files and play counts. That part is illegible enough. However, the outcome is partly written into legible fields already. SoundExchange publishes lists of unregistered sound-recording owners: in 2012 these named more than 50,000 artists and labels and over $31M in royalties three or more years old. Public streaming play counts also show which masters earn. So the valuable orphans are already visible and contested.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Masters are bought from bankruptcy trustees, successor companies and heirs, who usually cannot value them, so they can be bought cheaply. But closing the deal is slow, human legal work, and 17 USC 203 termination rights can claw back value.
scored.buyer: Catalogue aggregators and funds (Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Hipgnosis/Recognition, Kobalt-type funds) and major-label catalogue arms. They are well capitalised, but they buy at 5-15x net share and only at scale, so small orphan masters have to be aggregated into a bundle first.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: aggregated orphan catalogue, then an administration and distribution business, then a sync and licensing desk, then an independent label or publisher. The ladder is real but leads to a mid-sized music company, not a trillion-dollar path. Score 3.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 does not help. Proving costs about $2-10k, the typical hit is 1-5x, and the valuable orphans are already flagged in legible public lists. Total 12/25.

scored.name: Tracebird / Back-to-Birth: records-orphaned engines and LLPs
scored.one_line: Buy engines, gear and LLPs at scrap because traceability is broken; ML over registries, bankruptcy schedules, EETC/ABS filings and AD records rebuilds back-to-birth history; sell certified green time.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proof sits in private records, not public ones. Back-to-birth cycle history is either documented in operator and OEM files or it cannot be rebuilt, and regulators and buyers will not accept ML-inferred cycles for safety-critical LLPs, especially after AOG Technics. ML can find leads but cannot prove a part. Each proving attempt is also cheap (about $5-20k of records work, below the roughly $50k floor), so even the relaxed C3 does not create a lever.
scored.step_up: Unchanged from r1, which used estimates from prior knowledge. A part without trace has to be treated as having zero life remaining, which industry guidance confirms (IATA LLP Traceability guidance; LLP tracking literature). That puts it at scrap or metal value, about $2-20k. A serviceable CFM56-7B or V2500 LLP with remaining cycles is worth about $100k-$1M, and a full -7B stack lists around $4-5M. The step-up is therefore about 20-300x, which is real but short of 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimated; no published figures were found. A trace-recovery attempt costs roughly $5-20k per part in records-specialist labour, OEM and operator data requests and sworn statements. That falls below the relaxed C3 floor of about $50k per attempt, even though a whole-engine records package could approach it. The base success rate is perhaps 10-30%. ML over public registries, bankruptcy schedules and EETC/ABS filings can rank leads. It cannot raise the success of the proving step itself, because success depends on whether a private document exists. Relaxing the base hit rate does not help when proving is cheap and the lever cannot close the gap.
scored.frame: The rung is buying records-orphaned LLPs, gear and engines at scrap, re-establishing back-to-birth trace, and selling certified green time to lessors and MROs, who are capitalised buyers. Inside that rung, the proving step (finding the history) is perhaps 60-70% of the work, because it is document archaeology. However, the proof has to be paper from operators, OEMs and shops, and once trace exists, inspection, overhaul and recertification at a repair station are real and costly. The rung is discrete and sellable, but discovery is not 80%+ of it, and the asset still needs physical work and paperwork after the history is found.
scored.data: Public sources such as FAA registry, bankruptcy schedules, EETC/ABS prospectuses and AD records are illegible and scattered, so they can locate where a part flew and which entity owned it. The outcome itself (the back-to-birth cycle history) is not in any public source. It sits in private operator, OEM and MRO records, and those records either exist or they don't. Regulators and buyers will not accept ML-inferred cycles for safety-critical LLPs, and after AOG Technics (forged CFM56 paperwork) scrutiny of trace documents has risen, not fallen.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Untraceable parts and engines are bought cheaply at scrap or teardown pricing from lessors, part-out shops, liquidators and bankruptcy estates, and those sellers have written them off. The right being bought is clean and cheap. The weakness is that the edge from public data does not prove the asset.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: engine lessors (AerCap, Willis Lease, SES/FTAI), airline MRO shops, USM distributors (AAR, AerSale, GA Telesis) and engine overhaul shops building green-time stacks. FTAI's strategy shows strong demand for CFM56 green time.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from orphaned-LLP trace recovery to USM part-out and distribution, then whole-engine teardown, green-time engine leasing, and module and engine overhaul (FTAI-style). That is a credible multibillion-dollar aftermarket chain, but it is capital-heavy and competitive, and each rung above the first is ordinary aftermarket business, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap orphaned assets with a real 20-300x step-up exist, but proving depends on private paper that ML cannot create, and each proving attempt is too cheap for the relaxed C3 to help, so it stays weak.

scored.name: ShelfClear: rescuing compounds shelved for species-specific tox findings
scored.one_line: Buy shelved preclinical or Phase 1 compounds dropped over tox flags that probably do not apply to humans (rodent liver enzyme induction, PPAR-alpha, alpha-2u-globulin, dog-specific CV). ML predicts which flags are irrelevant; a cheap human-relevant in vitro package clears the flag and the asset is licensed.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal is not in public, illegible data. The tox package is private and held by a seller who can read it, and clearing the tox flag is not what buyers pay for: efficacy, competitive position and patent life set the price. So no rung exists where discovery from public data is 80%+ of the work and the output can be sold on its own. Relaxing C3 does not fix this, because ML has nothing proprietary to work on before the deal is signed.
scored.step_up: Unproven: shelved assets cost $0-1M upfront plus royalties from tech transfer offices or biotech estates. Big pharma rarely sells at nominal prices. Proven: the 2024 median upfront for preclinical deals was $47M (JP Morgan via BioStock), but that median comes from efficacy-differentiated assets in hot modalities. An old small molecule whose tox flag was cleared would more likely fetch $1-10M upfront. That is a 10-100x step-up and only on a licence, not right after the proving step. No new evidence found; prior C2=3 kept.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive at $0.5-3M per attempt (well above the $50k bar). The mechanistic package probably succeeds 30-50% of the time for textbook rodent mechanisms such as PPAR-alpha and alpha-2u-globulin (estimate). But only about 5-15% of tox-cleared compounds get licensed for real money (estimate), because shelving is often really about efficacy or strategy. ML cannot see the private tox data before the deal is signed, and the mechanisms that matter are already well known. So the lift on cost per proven asset is probably 1.1-1.3x, not 1.5x or more. Even under the relaxed C3 that scores only 2.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a shelved compound, running a human-relevant in vitro or mechanistic tox package to clear a species-specific flag, and licensing the asset out. Discovery (working out which flag is irrelevant) is maybe 30-50% of the work in this rung. The rest is lab and bridging work ($0.5-3M, sometimes with in vivo studies), plus showing efficacy and position, which is what licensees actually pay for. Clearing the tox flag does not make the asset sellable on its own, so the rung is not discrete.
scored.data: The signal sits in private tox packages that the seller holds and can read. Public sources (patents, posters, ClinicalTrials.gov terminations) are thin, and they often record the stated reason in a legible field. Rights are bought from sophisticated owners who know the asset's history, so there is no information asymmetry.
scored.right_bought: Licence or assignment of a shelved compound's IP and data from a pharma company, a biotech estate or a tech transfer office. It is bought, but from sellers who understand it.
scored.buyer: Big pharma or mid-size biotech in-licensing groups. They are well capitalised but pay for efficacy, differentiation and remaining patent life, not for a cleared tox flag.
scored.ladder: Strong in principle: tox rescue, then IND, then Phase 1/2 development, then late-stage development and commercialisation as a full pharma company. This is the familiar drug-rescue path (for example BridgeBio-style asset aggregation).
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 lifts it only slightly, because proving is expensive but ML has no public, illegible data to improve the hit rate. The flags are private, licensing depends on efficacy, and this is essentially the already-killed stranded drug rescue idea.
sources: JP Morgan biopharma licensing data via BioStock (2024 median preclinical upfront $47M, down from $75M in 2022) - cited in prior round
Goodwin biopharma deal analyses 2024-2025 (early-stage upfronts 1.5-3.7% of deal value) - cited in prior round
No new web searches run this round; estimates are marked as such

scored.name: Freezer Estate / Liquidation Strains / Strain Salvage: bankrupt synbio and fermentation strain banks
scored.one_line: Buy the strain and plasmid freezers, cell banks and notebooks of bankrupt or wound-down industrial biotech, synbio and ag-bio companies at scrap value; ML over dockets, patents and sequence data identifies the few strains that make molecules or traits with a live market, then a bench titer, assay or greenhouse test proves them for sale or licence to ingredient and ag majors.
scored.fatal_flaw: A bench-proven strain is not the valuable asset. Value appears only after scale-up and techno-economic de-risking, which is expensive, bespoke and usually fails, so discovery is never 80% of a sellable rung. And the strain-level outcome (titer) is already written in the debtor's notebooks and LIMS, so ML adds little beyond reading the records.
scored.step_up: Unproven: trustee lots, which I estimate at $10k to low $100ks. This is not sourced, and the Zymergen Chapter 11 (Del. 23-11661) auction to Ginkgo and Pivot Bio disclosed no per-asset price. Proven: Givaudan paid $200M upfront plus up to $150M earnout for Amyris's cosmetic ingredients, but that was a commercial portfolio with about $30M in sales, not a strain proven at the bench. I estimate a bench titer lifts one strain's value about 3-10x: from a few $k in a lot to perhaps $50-500k as a licence option. That is far short of 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Bench proving costs about $10-100k per strain at CROs (the candidate's figure; plausible). That is at or below the ~$50k expense threshold, so proving is only borderline expensive. No published base rate exists. My estimate is that 5-20% of strains revive and reproduce their recorded titers, and under 1-2% are commercially relevant. The relaxed C3 removes the low-hit-rate penalty, but the lever is still weak. Once a lot is bought, the debtor's own notebooks and LIMS already record which strains hit which titers, so triage is a matter of reading records rather than prediction. Before purchase that data is private. ML over patents and dockets might pick slightly better estates, which I put at about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven strain. Score: 2.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a bankrupt company's strain bank, prove one strain at the bench (titer or assay), then sell or license it. Discovery and triage might be 30-50% of the work within this rung. Most of the rest goes on the bench proving itself, and the asset becomes valuable only after scale-up and techno-economic de-risking. That later work is bespoke, expensive and usually fails. So no rung where discovery is 80%+ has a capitalised buyer: ingredient and ag majors buy de-risked processes, not shake-flask strains.
scored.data: Partly public and illegible: bankruptcy dockets, patents and deposited sequences. The key outcome data, the titers in notebooks and LIMS, is private until purchase and legible after it. So the edge either does not exist before the buy or is trivial after it.
scored.right_bought: Yes, rights can be bought. Trustees sell strain banks and IP in 363 sales or by abandonment, at near-scrap prices for minor estates. But capitalised strategics such as Ginkgo and Pivot Bio show up at the auctions for the good estates, as in Zymergen.
scored.buyer: Ingredient majors (Givaudan, DSM-Firmenich, IFF), ag-bio companies (Pivot Bio, Corteva) and CDMOs. They pay real money only for scaled, de-risked processes or commercial portfolios, not for bench-proven strains.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is strong in principle: strain to scale-up to contract manufacturing to an owned ingredient brand or product. But each rung above the bench is capital-heavy, and that is exactly where Amyris and Zymergen died.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 barely helps: proving is only borderline expensive at $10-100k, and the titer records already give the answer. The step-up is about 3-10x and the buyers want scaled processes, not strains. Total score 12/25.
sources: Amyris 8-K 2023, Givaudan cosmetic ingredients sale ($200M upfront + up to $150M earnout)

scored.name: Corridor Title / Orphan Easement / EasementGraph: dormant utility, pipeline and telegraph easement corridors
scored.one_line: Buy forgotten assignable easements in gross and corridor strips from successors of dissolved utilities, co-ops, interurbans, telegraph and pipeline companies; ML over scanned deed books stitches continuous corridors and proves scope (communications or any lawful purpose) and survival; sell insured corridors to HVDC and long-haul fiber developers.
scored.fatal_flaw: Scope, overburden and continuity. Old telegraph, telephone and pipeline easements are narrow and limited to their original use. Courts and class settlements (T-Cubed at $6k per mile, Sprint/Qwest/Level 3/WilTel at $2 per foot) gave the value of new uses to the fee owners, not the easement holders. On top of that, every gap in a corridor must be cured by negotiation or condemnation. The hard work is legal assembly, not discovery, so the ML edge does not reach the part that decides value.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $10-5,000 per instrument by quitclaim (the candidate's figure, not checked). Proven, for fiber (the only use where old telegraph and telephone scope plausibly carries over): real comparables are the landowner settlements for fiber laid in railroad and telegraph rights of way. T-Cubed/Norfolk Southern (2001) paid $6,000 per mile plus a 10-15% revenue share. The Sprint/Qwest/Level 3/WilTel class settlement (2003, $142.5M, about 360k landowners) paid $2 per linear foot, about $10.6k per mile. That puts fiber corridor rights at roughly $6-11k per mile. Those courts also held that the value belonged to the fee owners, not the easement holder. For HVDC, about $100-300k per mile is avoided, but old 10-33 ft single-purpose easements mostly cannot carry it. Per instrument the realistic step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per attempt: title opinions and abstracting at about $500-3,000 per parcel (estimate), at 5-15 parcels per mile, comes to about $250k-4.5M for a 100-mile corridor. That is expensive, so the relaxed C3 cost bar is met. Base hit rate: no published figure. My estimate is well under 5% for an easement that is alive, assignable, wide and broad enough in scope, and continuous, and about 0% for HVDC. That is far below the 30-70% band the relaxed C3 accepts. ML can lower abstracting cost and screen chains, but the binding failures are legal (scope, overburden, abandonment, gaps), which ML does not move. Cost per proven corridor improves maybe 1.2x at best. Raised from the prior score only because proving is expensive.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying dormant easements in gross, proving they survive and what they allow, and selling an insured continuous corridor. Discovery (finding instruments in scanned deed books and stitching chains) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is legal: title opinions, defending against abandonment and marketable-record-title-act claims, fighting overburden and scope suits, and curing every gap by negotiation or condemnation. That legal assembly is the physical-step equivalent, and it is neither trivial nor abstracted. HVDC and fiber developers are capitalised buyers, but they buy whole corridors, not fragments, and they already hold eminent domain or negotiation teams.
scored.data: Scanned county deed books, dissolved-utility and co-op records, and old telegraph right-of-way grants: public, illegible, scattered, and not summarised in any status field. That is a real data edge. Rights can be bought by quitclaim from successors who do not know what they hold. However, the fee owners, not the easement successors, generally win the value for new uses (the fiber overburden settlements confirm this). So the cheaply bought right is often worth little.
scored.right_bought: Assignable easements in gross and corridor strips, quitclaimed from successors of dissolved utilities, interurbans, telegraph and pipeline companies. Survival, scope and apportionability are uncertain, and they are frequently lost to fee owners in overburden and abandonment suits.
scored.buyer: HVDC transmission developers (for example Grain Belt-type merchant lines) and long-haul fiber builders, plus title insurers wrapping the corridor. They are capitalised, but they already have condemnation or negotiation capacity, so they pay at most their avoided acquisition cost of about $6-11k per mile for fiber.
scored.ladder: Corridor fragments, then insured continuous corridors, then a corridor-owning infrastructure company (dark fiber or a transmission right-of-way REIT), then building and operating the lines. The ladder is plausible but capped by the overburden law at the bottom rung.
scored.one_line_reason: Illegible public data is real, but the value step-up is about 3-10x per instrument, the base hit rate is near zero, and fee-owner overburden law moves the payoff to the landowners, so the relaxed C3 only lifts this to a weak 12/25.

scored.name: University and National-Lab Patent Evidence-of-Use (Shelfware, Bayh-Dole sweep, LabOption)
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive licences or options with enforcement rights on unlicensed university and DOE/NASA lab patents (incl. robotics, photonics, superconductors); ML finds the few already practised in large shipping products; prove with EoU charts and sell or sublicense.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap proving step (the EoU chart) does not prove the asset. Value is realised only through multi-million-dollar litigation, and about 70% of patents reaching a PTAB final decision lose all claims. ML on use does not predict validity, so the real expensive proving step has no ML hit-rate lever. On top of that, AUTM and university policy restricts supply.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an exclusive option or licence costs about $0-50k upfront plus a revenue share. Proven but unlitigated, on the brokered market: Richardson Oliver average asking prices were $124k-194k per asset in 2018-2019, about $150k in 2020-21 and about $100k in 2022. Asking prices are above closing prices, and many listings never sell. So a hit is roughly 10-100x on the upfront cost, or about 3-10x net of the revenue share.
