Litigated jackpots (around $100M+) are rare and often reversed (WARF v. Apple, Caltech v. Apple/Broadcom). Score C2=3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base rate of unlicensed university patents being practised in a large product is an estimate of about 0.5-5%; I could not verify it. An EoU chart costs about $5-20k per patent, below the relaxed C3's roughly $50k threshold, so the discovery and proving step is cheap. The expensive step is litigation at about $2-5M per case. ML gives that step little lift, because the binding risk is validity. In FY2024, about 68-70% of patents reaching a PTAB final written decision had all claims held unpatentable (USPTO FY2024 roundup; Finnegan's cumulative claim-cancellation rate is about 74%). An ML screen for use does not predict validity well. Relaxing C3 does not help: proving is either cheap (the EoU chart) or expensive but not lifted by ML (litigation and the PTAB). C3 stays low at 2, credited only for better choice of patents before options are signed.
scored.frame: Rung: take an exclusive licence or option on an unlicensed university or national-lab patent, then prove it with an evidence-of-use (EoU) chart against a large shipping product. Discovery is about 80-90% of the work only until the EoU chart is done. But a capitalised buyer (an aggregator, a non-practising entity or a litigation funder) pays only modestly for EoU-charted but unlitigated assets. The step that actually realises value is litigation plus surviving PTAB review. That step is bespoke and expensive, and it is legal work, not discovery. Measured over the whole rung that sells at a high price, discovery is probably 20-30% of the work.
scored.data: The data is public but illegible: patent claims, product teardowns, datasheets, FCC filings and firmware. Incumbents (non-practising entities, IP Bridge, aggregators, and the universities' own tech transfer offices with Unified Patents-style tools) already run EoU tools at scale, so the ML edge is partial. The outcome is not written into a status field. Licensing status is partly visible through AUTM or tech transfer office listings.
scored.right_bought: Rights are bought through exclusive licences or options from university tech transfer offices and lab licensing offices, cheaply and with enforcement rights. Supply is restricted: the AUTM "Nine Points" guidance and many university policies discourage licensing to assertion entities. DOE and NASA licences come with Bayh-Dole government licence and march-in strings, and some labs refuse licences whose main purpose is enforcement.
scored.buyer: Patent aggregators (RPX, AST), non-practising entities, litigation funders (Burford and others) and accused infringers settling. The capitalised buyers exist, but they discount heavily for PTAB risk and pay brokered prices of about $100-200k per asset.
scored.ladder: Weak ladder. The possible path runs from option, to EoU-charted asset, to a funded assertion vehicle, to a portfolio non-practising entity or licensing company. Patent monetisation is a capped, reputationally constrained niche of a few billion dollars a year, not a vertical chain toward building the products. Score C5=2.
scored.one_line_reason: C3 only moves from about 1 to 2 under the relaxed rule, because the EoU chart is cheap (well under $50k). The expensive step, litigation plus surviving the PTAB, carries roughly a 70% all-claims invalidation risk that ML on evidence of use does not reduce, and the other scores stay unchanged.

scored.name: Surplus Military and Government Aviation Lots to Serviceable (Scrap-to-Serviceable, Surplus Lift, Bone Yard Records)
scored.one_line: Buy DLA Disposition, GSA, GovPlanet and foreign-military surplus aircraft, engines, rotables and avionics priced as scrap; vision/NLP over listing photos, NSN text, scanned logbooks and FLIS finds civil-certifiable, high-life, traceable items; reconstruct records, get 8130-3 tags via Part 145 shops; sell to USM distributors, MROs and firefighting operators.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Value is created by physical and regulatory proving (overhaul or inspection plus the AC 20-142 eligibility determination for military surplus parts), which ML cannot abstract. The supply ML could find is either competed away at auction by brokers using the same structured FLIS cross-references, or barred from sale by DoD FSCAP and demil mutilation rules. For most items proving costs only $1k-$10k, below the relaxed C3 threshold.
scored.step_up: No new numbers. The search found only regulatory documents, no prices. Estimate carried from round 1: scrap or by-weight lots clear at roughly 1-10% of the serviceable USM price. One rotable bought for about $100-$1k might sell tagged for $5k-$100k, so 10-100x gross and roughly 3-20x net of overhaul, tagging and records work. Outliers reach about 1000x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. A lot costs hundreds to low thousands of dollars to buy. Proving a typical rotable or LRU costs about $1k-$10k for repair-station inspection or test. That is below the relaxed C3 floor of about $50k per attempt, so the lever is weak for most items. Only engine teardowns or overhauls ($100k+) and whole airframes under AC 21-13 clear the floor. The base share of items that end up civil-eligible is maybe 5-20%, because of FSCAP, demil mutilation and missing traceability. ML screening could plausibly lift that 2-4x. On cheap rotables, though, cost per proven asset is driven by acquisition volume, not by the cost of proving. The relaxed C3 changes the score only for the engine and airframe slice, so C3 is 2.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a surplus lot and turning it into a tagged, civil-eligible part to sell. Discovery, meaning spotting the civil-certifiable, high-life, traceable items in DLA, GSA or GovPlanet listings, is maybe 30-40% of the work. Most of the work is physical and regulatory proving. That means Part 145 inspection or overhaul, rebuilding a records trail, and the FAA eligibility determination under AC 20-142 for military surplus flight-safety-critical parts. There are capitalised buyers (USM distributors, MROs, firefighting operators), but no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
scored.data: Listings on DLA Disposition, GSA and GovPlanet, plus FLIS/NSN text, are public but only partly legible. Listing photos and scanned logbooks are illegible. But NSN-to-civil part-number cross-references are structured and already worked by experienced surplus brokers. DLA demil and FSCAP codes act as a legible status field that already answers much of the eligibility question.
scored.right_bought: Lots are bought at competitive public auction, not by private option from owners who cannot read the data. Experienced surplus brokers bid against each other, which narrows the discount. DoD FSCAP and demil rules bar resale of a large share of the most valuable flight-critical items, which must be mutilated.
scored.buyer: USM distributors (AAR, AerSale, GA Telesis and others), MROs, operators of ex-military types such as firefighting and utility helicopters and restricted-category operators, and foreign militaries.
scored.ladder: Parts trading leads on to an owned Part 145 repair station, then whole-airframe and engine teardown, then restricted-category aircraft conversion and leasing (for example, firefighting fleets). It is a real but mid-sized aftermarket ladder, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 helps only the small engine and airframe slice. The core problem stands: proving is regulatory and physical, the right is auction-competed, and demil codes already put the answer in a legible field.

scored.name: Ghost Offsets / OffsetBank: unclaimed emission reduction credits from shut-down sources
scored.one_line: Buy for a nominal fee or revenue share the unexercised right to bank NOx/VOC/PM ERCs from closed or curtailed boilers, turbines, kilns and small industrials in nonattainment areas; ML matches shutdowns (ECHO, NEI, WARN, bankruptcies) against ERC registries and reconstructs defensible baselines from scanned permits and stack tests; certify and sell to data-center turbine, peaker, refinery and LNG projects that cannot permit without offsets.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is cheap paperwork with a short filing deadline, done against legible registries that brokers already watch. Under the relaxed C3 the expensive-proving requirement still fails (about $10-50k per attempt), the step-up is only 10-100x, and the whole market is thin. This is a niche origination business, not a 10^4 discovery engine.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $0-25k for an assignment, option or revenue share. Proven: the SJVAPCD 2025 ERC cost report shows 5 NOx trades at $9,500-16,500/ton. The volume-weighted average is about $15.7k/t (my calculation from the report's table) on only about 128 tons traded in the whole year. VOC traded at $4,500/t. Ventura County shows one 1 tpy NOx deal at $65k/t, and South Coast is higher. A typical 5-50 tpy shutdown is therefore worth about $50k-$800k, a step-up of roughly 10-100x over the acquisition cost, far short of 10^3-10^4. The value also only appears if a buyer exists in that district, and the market is thin.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the candidate's 20-40% from shutdown identified to credit certified (unverified). Cost per attempt: about $10-50k (my estimate) for a consultant baseline, legal assignment and district filing fees. That is at or below the relaxed C3 threshold of about $50k per attempt, and it takes months, not years. ML could plausibly lift the hit rate about 1.5x by screening out ineligible sources (surplus or baseline failures, sources already past the banking window) before options are signed. But the proving step itself is cheap, so the lever is weak even under the relaxed rule. Score 2 (up from roughly 1 under the strict rubric).
scored.frame: The rung is: get assigned the right to bank credits from a source that shut down or cut output, have the credit certified, and sell it to a project that needs offsets to get its permit. About 70-80% of the work is finding and proving eligibility: matching shutdowns to sources that have not banked, and rebuilding a baseline from permits and stack tests. The physical step is trivial because nothing is built. Capitalised buyers exist (peaker, data-center turbine, refinery and LNG projects). The weak points are that the "discovery" is mostly paperwork and filing deadlines, and the market is very thin.
scored.data: Shutdown signals (ECHO, NEI, WARN notices, bankruptcies) and the ERC registries are public and legible. Only the baseline reconstruction from scanned permits and stack tests is illegible. The outcome (whether a source banked its credits) sits in legible registry fields, and the short deadlines to apply for banking (about 180 days in many districts) remove most "ghost" sources from old shutdowns. Brokers already canvass large shutdowns.
scored.right_bought: Partly. The right to bank sits with the source owner, who must apply within the district's window, and it can be bought or assigned cheaply only for small, overlooked, recent shutdowns. Large sources are already approached by brokers and their own consultants, so the purchase discount is small where the tonnage is.
scored.buyer: New or modified major sources in nonattainment areas that need offsets: gas peakers, behind-the-meter data-center turbines, refinery expansions, LNG projects, cement plants. They are well capitalised, but the volume traded per district is small (SJV NOx was about 128 t/yr in 2025).
scored.ladder: Limited. Possible rungs above: an offset brokerage or bank, then permitting-as-a-service for developers, then maybe co-developing peaker or data-center power projects. Each step up is a different business, and the ERC market is capped at tens to hundreds of millions of dollars a year across US districts. There is no clear path to a very large company.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 changes little, because proving is cheap (about $10-50k) and mostly succeeds when a source is eligible. The step-up is only about 10-100x, at a verified SJV NOx price of about $15.7k/t on about 128 t/yr traded, so the scores stay low (3/3/2/2/2).

scored.name: Function-Category Arbitrage: US/EU devices into Japan STM reimbursement
scored.one_line: Take Japan rights to cleared devices from small makers; ML maps them onto MHLW function categories with fixed prices; get Shonin approval without new trials; sell to Japanese distributors.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not where the value is. The function-category answer sits in legible MHLW price tables, and a cleared device succeeds at Shonin at a high base rate. ML therefore barely improves cost per proven asset, about 1.1-1.3x. Most of the work is regulatory, QMS and commercial, and the capitalised buyers already run the same in-licensing playbook.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: an exclusive Japan option from a small maker, about $20-100k (candidate's figure, not verified). Proven right: Japan distribution rights to an approved device. The one sourced comparable is the Japan exclusive Medikit signed with Cardiovascular Systems in 2016. It paid $10M upfront, and part of that was refundable (CSI 10-Q FY2016). That device was already a large FDA-approved product, not a small maker's device. A Boston Scientific–Japan Lifeline deal is reported at about 3B JPY for 10 years of exclusivity, but the only source is an unconfirmed Substack post. For small-maker devices, my estimate is $0.5-5M, which is roughly a 10-100x step-up. Japan's two-yearly reimbursement price cuts and foreign-average-price rules then erode it. This is well short of 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt is expensive. My estimate is $0.3-1M including MAH/DMAH, QMS and translation (I found no source for Shonin fees). Review takes about 9-12 months for Class III and 12-24 months or more for Class IV (meddeviceguide, Freyr; vendor sources). So the relaxed C3 cost test is met. The base hit rate is high, an estimated 50-80%, because foreign clinical data is usually accepted and the category is predictable from the predicate. ML's lift on cost per proven asset is therefore small. Category mapping is close to a lookup, and the main source of failure is commercial uptake, which public filings do not reveal. A plausible lift is about 1.1-1.3x, below the 1.5x full-strength bar. Under the relaxed rubric C3 rises from roughly 1 to 2, not to 3-5.
scored.frame: The rung is the exclusive Japan rights to a US/EU-cleared device, carried to Shonin approval plus a reimbursement (B or C1) category. Discovery here means choosing the device and mapping it to a function category, and it is maybe 15-25% of the work. The rest is not trivial and cannot be abstracted. It covers the MAH/DMAH setup, Foreign Manufacturer Registration, QMS audits, the PMDA dossier with translations, the 9-24 month review, and commercial launch. Capitalised buyers do exist (Japan Lifeline, Century Medical/Itochu, Medikit). But they run in-licensing themselves, so they compete with the company more than they buy from it.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible and the outcome is already written down. MHLW publishes function-category price tables (STM reimbursement lists) and PMDA approval lists. FDA 510(k)/PMA summaries are structured and searchable. Incumbent distributors already read all of this. Some value may sit in unstructured clinical evidence that supports a C1 or C2 innovation premium, but that is a thin seam.
scored.right_bought: Yes, Japan rights are bought through an option or exclusive license from small US/EU makers. They are not free on a first-come basis. Small makers can probably value them cheaply, but not because they cannot read the data. The reason is that Japan market entry is costly for them. Sophisticated distributors also scout these same makers, which narrows the discount.
scored.buyer: Japanese device distributors and trading houses (Japan Lifeline, Century Medical/Itochu, Medikit) and the Japan arms of multinationals. They are capitalised, as Medikit's $10M upfront to CSI shows. But they run this in-licensing playbook themselves, so they are competitors as much as buyers.
scored.ladder: MAH/DMAH rights holder, then a Japan distributor holding a portfolio of approved devices, then local manufacturing/OEM, then a Japan/APAC medtech platform. The ladder is real but bounded at Japan Life-scale medtech distribution, a company in the low billions, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 rescues this only slightly. Proving is expensive (about $0.3-1M and 1-2 years), but mapping is a near-lookup against published price tables, so ML lift is under 1.5x. The step-up is about 10-100x, and incumbent distributors compete for the same rights.

scored.name: Captive Scent (natural odorant discovery from public GC-MS spectra)
scored.one_line: Mine public GC-MS and NMR spectra of plant, fungal and insect volatiles for unassigned peaks whose predicted structure is a high-impact odorant (musk, ambergris, sandalwood). Make a few mg and run an odour panel. File composition-of-use IP and sell the captive molecule to a fragrance house, which pays $5-50M for a patented captive.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no defensible owned asset. Natural odorants found in public spectra generally cannot be patented as compositions, and the publication itself may anticipate them. So the 'captive' is a weak use patent and not a bought right. Osmo ($130M raised) already holds the ML-discovery lever and uses synthetic novel scaffolds, which avoids this patent problem. The relaxed C3 does not help, because each proving attempt is cheap ($10-30k), not expensive.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $0, plus about $20-50k for synthesis and a filing (my estimate). Proven at the panel-hit stage: there are no public licence prices. My estimate is $0.5-5M upfront plus royalties for an odorant that has not been scaled up or tox-tested. That is about 10-100x on the cost of proving, or 10^2-10^3 only at the top of the range. The $5-50M figure applies only after tox and scale-up. Nothing new changes this, so the prior C2 of 3 stays.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: 0.25% of molecules tested become commercially interesting (Osmo's own Jan 2026 figure, not verified). Osmo claims about 10x on hit rate and 5-10x on discovery cost. Cost per proving attempt: about $10-30k for CRO synthesis plus an odour panel (my estimate), which is below the relaxed C3 bar of about $50k per attempt. The years-long cost (tox and scale-up, 7-10 years) falls after the screening hit, where ML adds little. Under the relaxed C3 the per-shot proving is cheap, and Osmo has already captured the ML lever. So C3 scores 2, not 5.
scored.frame: The rung is finding, making and panel-testing a candidate odorant molecule, then selling or licensing it as a captive. Discovery is perhaps 70-80% of the work at the screening stage. But a fragrance house will only pay once scale-up, stability, IFRA/RIFM safety and toxicology work, and regulatory registration (REACH) are done. That work is physical and regulatory, not trivial, and it takes most of the 7-10 years to a commercial captive. So the cleanly sellable frame is weaker than it looks. The buyers (Givaudan, IFF, dsm-firmenich, Symrise) are well capitalised.
scored.data: Public GC-MS and NMR spectra of natural volatiles: NIST, MassBank, GNPS, and supplementary files of papers. These are partly legible and already structured in spectral libraries. Peaks with no assigned structure are an illegible signal. But the outcome is often already written down: published papers report the odour descriptors of identified compounds. And the incumbents' internal headspace programmes (Givaudan ScentTrek) already mine natural volatiles.
scored.right_bought: There is no right to buy. In the US, natural products cannot be patented as compositions, and the source publication may anticipate a use patent. The asset is a weak use patent that the company files itself, not an unproven right bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. This is why C4 stays at 1.
scored.buyer: Fragrance houses: Givaudan, IFF, dsm-firmenich, Symrise. They pay for captives that are protected, safe and scalable, not for molecules that have only passed a panel.
scored.ladder: Captive molecule, then scale-up and process chemistry, then supplying aroma ingredients, then fragrance compounding, then consumer brands. The ladder exists, but the top rungs are dominated by four incumbents. The path is real but crowded, so C5 stays at 3.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 does not rescue this: proving each molecule is cheap and Osmo already owns the ML lever. The owned asset is still a weak, likely anticipated use patent, and there is no cheaply bought right. Total 12/25.
sources: Osmo press release, Jan 2026 (0.25% base hit rate; claimed ~10x AI hit-rate gain) - from prior round, not re-verified
Osmo blog (7-10 years to a captive) - from prior round
Prior r2 scoring of this candidate (C1 3, C2 3, C4 1, C5 3); no new searches run this round

scored.name: Ontario settlement-boundary expansion and draft plan approval on GTA-fringe whitebelt farmland
scored.one_line: Buy or option whitebelt farmland just outside settlement boundaries in Ontario's Golden Horseshoe (outside the Greenbelt). The 2024 Provincial Planning Statement now allows private boundary expansion requests at any time, not only in municipal reviews. File an Official Plan Amendment and zoning amendment, take it to the Ontario Land Tribunal if needed, and sell designated or draft-plan-approved land to GTA homebuilders.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold or option on agricultural parcels outside the urban boundary and the Greenbelt, at farm prices (about CAD $30-300k/acre depending on location). Owners are mostly farm families and estates who do not track OLT case law or servicing allocations.
scored.proving_step: Privately initiated OPA, ZBA and draft plan of subdivision with servicing, transportation, agricultural impact and natural heritage studies, often followed by an OLT appeal. About CAD $0.5-2.5M and 2-6 years; plausibly 35-60% success on well-sited, serviceable parcels.
scored.proven_buyer: GTA builders and land developers (Mattamy, Brookfield Residential, Tribute, Minto, Fieldgate) plus REIT and pension-backed land funds, paying about CAD $1-3M per acre for designated or draft-plan-approved land.
scored.public_data: Ontario Land Tribunal decisions and case files (PDF), municipal comprehensive review and land needs assessment reports, council and committee agendas with scanned staff reports, Environmental Registry of Ontario postings, regional water and wastewater servicing master plans, conservation authority mapping, MZO records, MPAC parcel data. ML predicts which parcels fall inside future servicing catchments; the outcome is in no field until the boundary moves.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-15x to designated unserviced land and up to 20-50x after draft plan approval; 50x or more on option capital.
scored.frame: The rung is entitlement: whitebelt farmland goes to designated or draft-plan-approved land, and there is a capitalised buyer (GTA builders, land funds). Discovery, meaning picking the parcel that lands inside a future servicing catchment, is maybe 25-40% of the work inside this rung. Most of the work is the proving step itself: 2-6 years of OPA/ZBA studies, negotiation with council and the region, a servicing allocation fight and often an OLT hearing. That proving step is the hard, bespoke and political part, the opposite of an abstracted drill hole. It looks more like the geothermal counter-example (execution dominates) than like Terranox.
scored.step_up: Whitebelt land near the GTA already sells far above farm value. Examples: a Caledon East farm sold to a developer for about $97M on 150 acres (~$650k/acre); Milton-area asking prices near $364k/acre; Simcoe farmland bought by developers at $54k/acre as early as 2014, double the farm price. Draft-plan-approved GTA low-rise land runs roughly $1-3M/acre at the peak, and the market has softened: Urbanation reports GTA residential development land transaction value down 25% YoY in Q4 2025 and total land sales down 20% in 2025. The realistic land-value step-up is therefore ~3-10x, not 10^3-10^4. Higher multiples exist only on option capital, which is leverage, not a step-up in the asset's value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about CAD $0.5-2.5M and 2-6 years per attempt (studies, planners, lawyers, OLT), which clears the relaxed C3 cost bar. The candidate's base hit rate of 35-60% on well-sited parcels is plausible but unsourced. What decides approval is mostly politics, servicing allocation and the region's land needs assessment. Those documents are published and are read closely by every land developer and planning law firm, so ML parcel selection plausibly gives ~1.2-1.5x on cost per approved acre, not >=1.5x. My source is PPS 2024 commentary (Aird Berlis, Osler, WeirFoulds) on private expansion requests now being allowed at any time and appealable to the OLT under Bill 185. The hit-rate figure is the candidate's own estimate.
scored.data: The signal is public: OLT decisions, servicing master plans, land needs assessments, ERO postings and MPAC data. But it is only moderately illegible, and it is exactly what Mattamy, Brookfield, Tribute and dozens of land-banking funds and planning firms already read. The servicing master plans and land needs assessments state close to directly where growth and pipes will go, so the answer is semi-written into planning documents. That is the same "regulator writes the answer down" problem seen in earlier hunts.
scored.right_bought: The rights are bought, not free first-come, so that part passes. But the sellers are not naive. GGH whitebelt (~46,000 ha, mostly in Peel, Halton and Durham) is the most heavily speculated farmland in Canada. Land agents approach farm families constantly, brokers (e.g. CBRE) market parcels explicitly as boundary-expansion bets, and much of the best-located land is already owned or optioned by builders. Asking prices already price in expansion option value, so there is no reliable illegibility discount to capture.
scored.buyer: GTA low-rise builders and land developers (Mattamy, Brookfield Residential, Tribute, Minto, Fieldgate, Metrus/Condor and others) plus pension- and REIT-backed land funds. They are well capitalised, but the market is currently soft, with development land transaction volumes down 20-25% in 2025.
scored.ladder: The path above the rung is real: entitled land, then servicing and lot creation, then homebuilding, then master-planned communities and rental (Mattamy-scale, multi-billion). The rungs above are commodity, capital-heavy construction with thin margins, and incumbents already own the whole chain. Winning the entitlement rung gives no structural advantage higher up.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is not illegibly priced and the proving step is not trivial. GTA whitebelt is Canada's most picked-over land-speculation market: farm owners and developers already price in boundary-expansion option value (sales at $300-650k/acre), so the step-up is only ~3-10x. The proving step is a multi-year political and legal entitlement fight in which execution, not discovery, dominates.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the lever to a modest 3 because proving is expensive. But the rung is dominated by political and legal execution, not discovery, the land is already speculatively priced by sophisticated incumbents, and the step-up is ~3-10x rather than 10^3-10^4.

scored.name: ERCOT Substation-Adjacent BESS Pads
scored.one_line: Buy or option 5-20 acre parcels next to ERCOT substations that ML predicts have congestion value and will pass the full interconnection study, run the study and county steps, and sell interconnection-ready BESS projects. The edge must come from congestion and revenue prediction, not the queue.
scored.unproven_right: Small parcels at about $5-20k/acre next to transmission substations, from ranchers who cannot see nodal congestion or study results.
scored.proving_step: ERCOT full interconnection study, signed IA and county abatement: about $100-300k and 12-18 months; roughly 50-70% success under connect-and-manage.
scored.proven_buyer: BESS developers and owners (Jupiter Power, Plus Power, Key Capture, Engie, Hunt) paying about $30-80k/MW for IA-ready sites.
scored.public_data: ERCOT GINR reports and study PDFs, nodal LMP and DAM price history, SSWG and CDR planning cases, PUCT filings, county appraisal parcels.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 30-150x (about $100k of land to $3-15M for 100-200 MW IA-ready).
scored.frame: The rung (early-stage BESS development: site, full interconnection study, signed IA, county abatement, sold as ready-to-build) is discrete and sellable. Discovery, meaning picking the node, is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of it is execution: running ERCOT studies, posting IA financial security, abatement negotiations, landowner deals, and marketing to buyers. ERCOT's connect-and-manage regime makes the physical interconnection fairly routine, so the step is abstracted, but it is process and capital, not discovery. Fails the 80%+ test.
scored.step_up: Land: about 10 acres at $5-20k/acre, so $50-200k. Ready-to-build value: Solvent Energy expects ERCOT RTB deals at 7-9% of capex, about $59.5-76.5k/MW, so roughly $6-7.6M for 100 MW. That is about 30-100x on land alone, but only about 10-30x on all-in capital (land, $100-300k studies, IA security, legal). Buyers' prices are also falling: energy-storage.news says acquirer appetite is softer, and Modo says new queue applications fell 50% in H2 2025. And the value arrives at RTB, not immediately at study completion.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive enough: about $100-300k and 12-18 months per site (candidate's estimate), which meets the relaxed threshold. The base hit rate is already high, since under connect-and-manage most projects pass the study. Modo says about 85% of battery capacity with a signed IA reaches COD. The real risk is revenue and congestion value, not study success, and every incumbent already models that with Modo, Enverus, Yes Energy and PLEXOS nodal forecasts. Realistic ML lift on cost per proven sellable asset is about 1.1-1.3x.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible and heavily mined. ERCOT's GINR is a structured monthly spreadsheet, nodal LMP and DAM history is clean and API-accessible, and SSWG cases are standard planning files. Commercial vendors (Modo, Enverus, GridStatus, Yes Energy) sell congestion and revenue analytics to every BESS developer. Outcomes are summarised in legible fields: queue status, IA signed, and realised revenue indices. No illegibility moat exists.
scored.right_bought: Parcels next to ERCOT substations can technically be bought or optioned. But with about 148-178 GW of storage in the ERCOT queue, landowners near substations get approached constantly by developer landmen, and substation-adjacent land already carries a premium. The rancher-cannot-see-the-value asymmetry largely no longer exists. Rights are bought, not free, but not cheaply from uninformed owners.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: Jupiter Power, Plus Power, Key Capture, Engie, Hunt, and Korean and Japanese strategics (for example Apex's Korean partners). They are increasingly disciplined. ERCOT battery revenues fell about 84% from the 2023 peak (Modo puts 2025 at about $29/kW versus $193/kW in 2023), and ancillary revenues fell about 90%, which compresses what buyers will pay per MW.
scored.ladder: The ladder goes site/IA, then RTB development, then EPC/build, then own and operate, then merchant trading/optimisation, then a multi-GW IPP. The rungs are real, but each upper rung is a commodity, capital-intensive, low-margin infrastructure business already crowded with well-funded IPPs. It is a plausible path to a large IPP, not a trillion-dollar chain the edge compounds into.
scored.fatal_flaw: No illegible-data edge in a saturated market. Congestion and revenue signals sit in clean, structured ERCOT data that every competitor already buys analytics on, and with 150+ GW of storage queued the substation landowners already know their land's value. Cheap rights plus a proprietary signal is the core of the thesis, and here neither holds. The ERCOT BESS revenue collapse in 2024-25 is also shrinking the step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the previously killed queue-position idea relabelled as congestion prediction. The proving step is expensive, but base success is already high and every incumbent models the revenue risk from the same legible data, so the relaxed C3 changes little. Low score.

scored.name: Behind-the-Levee Option Portfolio (levee accreditation)
scored.one_line: Option land behind non-accredited or de-accredited levees that maps as Zone AE or AR/A99 and is frozen for development and mortgages. Fund the levee district's 44 CFR 65.10 certification where ML on old construction records says the levee likely already meets the standard, and sell the land once remapped to shaded Zone X.
scored.unproven_right: Long-dated purchase options on ag or industrial land inside levee-protected areas, plus a reimbursement agreement with the levee owner for certification work.
scored.proving_step: Borings, seepage and stability analysis, freeboard hydraulics, O&M manual, then FEMA accreditation and PMR/LOMR: about $300k-2M per system and 1-3 years; about 40-60% success on ML-selected levees.
scored.proven_buyer: Industrial and logistics developers, data-centre site buyers and homebuilders who need Zone X for financing.
scored.public_data: USACE National Levee Database and scanned periodic inspection reports, USACE as-builts and boring logs, FEMA PAL lists, 3DEP LiDAR crest elevations versus BFE plus 3 ft.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-30x (ag at $5-10k/acre to $50-250k/acre), with cost spread over thousands of acres per levee system.
scored.frame: The rung is: certify the levee, then sell the land as Zone X. The engineering and paperwork of certification are perhaps 60-80% discovery-like. But most levees lack accreditation because they have real deficiencies: of 744 USACE ratings, only 73 were Acceptable, 585 Minimally Acceptable and 86 Unacceptable. Physical remediation can cost 10-100x as much as the certification, as at Natomas (hundreds of millions of dollars and a multi-year building moratorium). Turning ag land into industrial land also needs rezoning, utilities and power. Across the whole rung, discovery is only about 20-40% of the work.
scored.step_up: The claimed 5-30x (ag land at $5-10k/acre to $50-250k/acre) is driven by entitlement and location, not by the flood zone. Remapping from AE to shaded X by itself removes mandatory insurance (about $1.5-3k per home per year in Natomas) and the cost of elevation and fill. That plausibly lifts land value about 1.1-2x, or unlocks development only where demand and zoning already exist. I found no study that measures the price uplift from remapping. At best this is 3-10x on a favourable subset of parcels.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. Certification runs from $45k/mile (Rapides LA, 2014) to more than $250k/mile excluding remediation (STC NY, 2024); Hastings MN cost about $75k. So $300k-2M and 1-3 years per system is plausible, which clears the relaxed C3 cost bar. The 40-60% success rate claimed for ML-selected levees has no source. The base rate of levees that already pass without remediation looks low (about 10% of systems are rated Acceptable). ML on scanned inspection reports could plausibly improve selection about 1.2-1.5x over simply sorting by the legible USACE rating.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned USACE inspection reports, as-builts, boring logs and 3DEP LiDAR. But the outcome is largely summarised in legible fields. The NLD shows accreditation and PAL status, and USACE assigns each segment an overall Acceptable / Minimally Acceptable / Unacceptable rating, which FEMA uses. Incumbents (levee districts, FEMA, USACE) already read this data. This is the usual pattern of the regulator writing the answer into a status field.
scored.right_bought: Options on ag land can be bought, but owners know their land sits behind a levee and price it on location. The bigger problem is free-riding: certification benefits every parcel behind the levee. You capture only the parcels you optioned, and you need the levee district's consent and a reimbursement agreement. Neighbours and the district will tend to hold out once work starts.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: industrial and logistics developers, data-centre site buyers and homebuilders. But they buy entitled, serviced, in-demand land. Flood status is one gating item among many (in California, SB 5 also requires 200-year protection for urban development).
scored.ladder: The ladder is moderate: levee finance and assessment districts, then land entitlement and master development, then flood-protection infrastructure. It is a real-estate and civil-works roll-up, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Most non-accredited levees are deficient and need costly physical remediation (a bespoke-construction problem like the geothermal counter-example). The value step-up mostly comes from rezoning and demand, not the flood map. The flood-map uplift (about 1.1-2x) also spills over to every parcel behind the levee.
scored.one_line_reason: Certification is expensive enough to satisfy the relaxed C3. But the real bottleneck is levee remediation and entitlement, the remap uplift is modest and shared with free-riders, and USACE ratings already summarise the outcome in legible fields.

scored.name: Tropical-disease PRV harvester (foreign-approved neglected-disease drugs to a US NDA)
scored.one_line: Option US rights to an old drug approved only ex-US or WHO-prequalified for an FDA-listed tropical disease, file an NDA on the existing foreign data, collect the tropical disease priority review voucher and sell it to big pharma (precedents: miltefosine, benznidazole, moxidectin).
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive US marketing and data-reference rights licensed cheaply ($0.1-1M) from a small Indian, Brazilian or African-market maker, NGO or academic sponsor with no FDA plans.
scored.proving_step: FDA NDA approval of a new chemical entity for a qualifying tropical disease (bridging CMC, US-grade dossier, often a PK study, inspection): about $10-40M and 2-4 years; maybe 40-70% approval when efficacy data exist.
scored.proven_buyer: Large pharma buying PRVs (recent sales ~$100-160M), plus a specialty pharma for the US commercial tail.
scored.public_data: WHO Prequalification reports, EMA EU-M4all opinions, CDSCO and ANVISA files, ClinicalTrials.gov and PACTR, DNDi/MMV papers, the 21 USC 360n tropical disease list, FDA review packages for past PRV grants.
scored.rough_step_up: About 200-300x on the right and 3-10x on all-in capex; NCE eligibility is the binding filter.
scored.frame: The rung is a US NDA approval that earns a voucher. Finding the drug is perhaps 10-20% of the work. The other 80-90% is the regulatory and clinical proving: a new trial the sponsor must run itself, bridging CMC, a US-grade dossier and inspections. The physical step is the hard part, not a trivial one, which makes this structurally like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. A capitalised buyer exists (big pharma buys PRVs), but the frame is not one where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
scored.step_up: The right costs about $0.1-1M. A proven voucher sold for $150-205M in 2025-26 (Zevra $150M, Abeona $155M, Bavarian Nordic $160M, Rocket $180M, Jazz $200M, Ultragenyx $203M, Cyprium $205M). That is about 150-2000x on the right. On all-in capex of roughly $15-50M (now including a mandatory new trial) the step-up is only about 3-10x. The jump comes at approval, not when the drug is found. Scored 4 on the right-level step-up, generously.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $10-40M plus a new essential clinical study, over 2-4 years, with maybe 40-70% approval odds where efficacy data exist. That passes the relaxed cost test. ML gives little lift, though. Only 14 tropical vouchers were awarded in 2007-2024, so the candidate pool is a few dozen drugs that a pharmacologist can list by hand from the WHO PQ list, DNDi/MMV pipelines and the statutory disease list. Approval risk depends on CMC, trial execution and FDA review, which document mining does not change. Plausible ML gain on cost per proven asset is about 1.1-1.3x. Source: FDA TDPRV program page; PMC12911920 (14 vouchers through 2024).
scored.data: The data are mostly legible, curated and small. The WHO Prequalification list is a clean table. The 21 USC 360n disease list and the FDA voucher list are public and short. The question that matters, whether the active ingredient was ever approved in the US, can be answered from Drugs@FDA in minutes. The new-study rule also makes existing foreign efficacy data insufficient on its own. ANVISA and CDSCO files are messier, but they do not hold the binding answer.
scored.right_bought: US rights can in principle be licensed from Indian or Brazilian generic makers or academic sponsors. The most valuable assets, however, sit with DNDi, MMV, Sanofi, Novartis and Bayer, which now know what a voucher is worth: Sanofi and DNDi split the fexinidazole voucher. Owners are not blind to the value, so rights will not be cheap at $0.1-1M on good candidates.
scored.buyer: Big pharma buys PRVs at $150-205M (2025-26) through a liquid, repeated market. This part is strong. The US commercial tail for tropical drugs is negligible.
scored.ladder: The ladder above this rung is weak. The next steps are a neglected-disease specialty pharma or a broader regulatory-arbitrage drug developer. US markets for tropical drugs are tiny, the voucher supply is capped by a pool of a few dozen qualifying NCEs, and rare-pediatric and medical-countermeasure vouchers are a different game with real R&D risk. There is no clear trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Since FDARA 2017, any application filed after Sept 30, 2017 must include one or more new clinical investigations (other than bioavailability studies) that are essential to approval and were conducted or sponsored by the applicant. The applicant must also attest that the data were not filed with India, Brazil, Thailand or PIC/S regulators before Sept 27, 2007. This closed the "file on existing foreign data" arbitrage behind the miltefosine-era precedents. The proving step is now real clinical development rather than discovery, and the candidate pool is small and legible, so ML has nothing illegible to extract.
scored.one_line_reason: The voucher market is real ($150-205M per voucher), but FDARA 2017 requires a new trial run by the sponsor. Proving therefore dominates the work, the pool of about 14 vouchers in 17 years is hand-enumerable and legible, and sophisticated NGO owners know what vouchers are worth, so the ML discovery edge is small.

scored.name: Dormant ANDA revival for shortage drugs
scored.one_line: Buy discontinued or dormant ANDAs for off-patent sterile injectables on the FDA shortage list from small or bankrupt holders, transfer them to a CMO with a prior-approval supplement, and sell the reactivated approved product to a capitalised generic buyer.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an approved but discontinued ANDA bought for $50-500k from an exited sponsor, liquidator or foreign parent.
scored.proving_step: Site-transfer PAS or CBE-30 with exhibit batches, stability and pre-approval inspection: about $1-4M and 12-24 months; likely 50-70% first-cycle success.
scored.proven_buyer: Hikma, Fresenius Kabi, Amneal, Civica, Sandoz and similar.
scored.public_data: Orange Book discontinued list, FDA and ASHP shortage databases, Drugs@FDA letters and review packages, FDA 483s and warning letters, DMF lists, NADAC and 340B pricing.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x on capex and 50-200x on the right.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy the dormant ANDA, do the site transfer, and sell the reactivated approved product. Inside that rung, discovery (picking which ANDA) is maybe 10-20% of the work. The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory: scarce sterile-fill CMO slots, tech transfer, media fills, three exhibit batches per strength, stability, and a pre-approval inspection. This is the geothermal pattern, where the hard part is building the asset, not finding it. The capitalised buyers (Hikma, Fresenius, Civica, Amneal) are real, but they are buying a manufacturing result, not a discovery.
scored.step_up: Unproven: discontinued ANDAs trade cheaply in bundles. Lannett sold a set of discontinued ANDAs for about $3M total in 2022. Amphastar sold 14 injectable ANDAs for $6.4M ($1M at closing, the rest in milestones, plus a 2% royalty), so roughly $0.1-0.5M each. Proven: a reactivated, marketed shortage injectable might fetch $2-15M, but I found no clean comps for that figure. Against total capex (right plus $1-4M proving) that is about 2-5x. Against the right alone it is about 10-50x. Either way it is far below 10^3. Erosion of sterile-injectable ASPs (about -9% CAGR per Pfizer) and sole-source GPO contracts cap what a reactivated product is worth.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $1-4M and 12-24 months per attempt (candidate estimate; FDA expects three exhibit batches per site per strength for sterile transfers, and I found no public dollar figures). That clears the relaxed C3 expense bar. The base first-cycle success rate is about 50-70%, but it depends mainly on how well the CMO executes and on its inspection history, not on information hidden in the ANDA. ML over 483s and review packages might filter out bad formulations or CMOs, but a realistic gain in cost per proven asset is about 1.1-1.3x, not 1.5x or more. An experienced regulatory consultant gets most of that edge.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible, and the key fields are structured. The Orange Book discontinued section, the FDA and ASHP shortage lists, NADAC prices and DMF lists already state which drugs are in shortage, discontinued and profitable. This is the 'answer written in a status field' failure. Review packages and 483s are illegible-ish PDFs, but incumbents' regulatory teams already read them.
scored.right_bought: The rights are bought, not claimed first-come: you buy title to the ANDA from the exiting sponsor, liquidator or foreign parent, and the LOE/Orange Book listing transfers with an FDA letter. But the sellers are generic companies that understand the ANDA's value well. Brokers and bankruptcy auctions (Akorn, Lannett) set market prices, so there is little 'owner can't read the data' discount.
scored.buyer: Hikma, Fresenius Kabi, Amneal, Sandoz, Civica, Xiromed, Gland and similar: real, well-capitalised and active acquirers of injectable ANDAs. But low and falling margins on shortage injectables limit what they will pay.
scored.ladder: There is a plausible ladder: rented CMO capacity, then owned sterile fill-finish plants, then API backward integration, then a portfolio-scale injectable company, Civica-style, possibly with government or hospital offtake contracts. It is real but low-margin, and capped at a multi-billion-dollar generics company, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates. Restarting a sterile injectable (CMO capacity, tech transfer, exhibit batches, pre-approval inspection) is most of the work and risk, while picking the ANDA is easy from legible shortage and discontinued lists. The products were discontinued because their margins are structurally thin, which caps the step-up at roughly 2-5x on capex.
scored.one_line_reason: This fits the geothermal counter-example: manufacturing and regulatory execution, not discovery, is the bottleneck. The outcome signals sit in legible FDA fields, and the step-up is about 2-5x on capex, not 10^3.

scored.name: Off-patent pesticide registration packaging (FIFRA data compensation)
scored.one_line: Buy dormant or thinly supported EPA Section 3 registrations and state labels for off-patent active ingredients, use ML over scanned labels and data-submission records to pick those with cheap data-gap cures and growing demand, complete registration review or amendments, and sell the registered line to an off-patent agchem consolidator.
scored.unproven_right: Lapsed, at-risk or thinly supported registrations and data-compensation positions bought from small registrants for $50-500k.
scored.proving_step: Curing data call-ins, adding crops or uses, or a new end-use registration citing data with offers to pay: about $0.5-3M and 1-3 years; 50-70% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Albaugh, AMVAC, UPL, Nufarm, Gowan and similar consolidators.
scored.public_data: EPA PPLS scanned labels, PRIA tracker, registration-review dockets, Federal Register cancellation notices, data call-in lists, CA DPR and NPIRS.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-10x on capex and 25-100x on the right; the weakest step-up of the regulatory set.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a lapsed or thinly supported registration and curing it into a sellable registered line. Picking which registrations to buy is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of the work is regulatory execution: running GLP studies to answer data call-ins, negotiating data compensation, filing PRIA submissions and amending labels. That execution is the expensive "physical" step, and it is not trivial or abstracted the way drilling is for Terranox. Capitalised buyers do exist (Albaugh, AMVAC, Nufarm, UPL, Gowan). AMVAC, for example, bought four Syngenta US brands in 2026 (registrations plus trademarks, expected to add more than $7M a year in sales), and Nufarm paid $490M for Syngenta and Adama's off-patent European portfolio.
scored.step_up: About 3-10x on the capital put into the cure, and 25-100x only against the nominal $50-500k paid for the right. A registered off-patent product line sells for a few times its annual sales. Deal multiples are rarely disclosed: the Nufarm deal ($490M plus $50M of inventory) and the AMVAC/Syngenta deal (more than $7M a year in added sales, price undisclosed) give no clean multiple. Nothing like Terranox's 10^4 jump from $1/ha to $10k/ha.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's own figures: proving costs $0.5-3M and takes 1-3 years, with a 50-70% success rate. That passes the "expensive" test under the relaxed C3. ML over PPLS labels and data call-in dockets could plausibly screen out registrations whose cures need costly new tox or environmental-fate studies. That might give about 1.2-1.5x on cost per cured registration. It is unlikely to reach 2-3x, because the main risk is regulatory (EPA findings in registration review, mitigation demands), which documents do not predict, and experienced registration consultants already triage these files well. I found no source for the success rate; it comes from the candidate description.
scored.data: The data is weak for an ML edge. EPA PPLS, the PRIA tracker, data call-in lists, registration-review dockets and Federal Register cancellation notices are mostly searchable and structured. Registration status, cancellations and outstanding data call-ins sit in legible fields, so the outcome is largely already written down. Some illegibility remains in scanned labels and old data-submission records, but incumbents' regulatory teams already work through it.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but it is not scarce. Under FIFRA, studies submitted more than 15 years ago can be cited free, and the 10-year exclusive-use period only covers data for new active ingredients. So for an off-patent active ingredient, any consolidator can get its own me-too registration for PRIA fees plus product chemistry, with a written offer to pay for any data still under compensation rights. That puts a ceiling on what a buyer will pay for the right we bought.
scored.buyer: Off-patent agchem consolidators: Albaugh, AMVAC (American Vanguard), UPL, Nufarm, Gowan and Adama. They are well capitalised and actively buy registration-plus-trademark bundles from larger companies.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: registered product line, then a brand and distribution channel, then sourcing and formulation of the active ingredient, then manufacturing. That path leads to a company the size of Albaugh or AMVAC (low single-digit $B in revenue), but the market is commoditised and margins are thin. It is not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is not scarce. Off-patent data older than 15 years can be cited free under FIFRA, so any consolidator can file its own me-too registration for PRIA fees and avoid paying our step-up. That keeps the value gain at a few times capital, with no 10^3-10^4 jump. The outcome signal also already sits in legible EPA status and data call-in fields.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive and the relaxed C3 earns a middling 3, but the step-up is only about 3-10x, the right is not scarce because consolidators can file free me-too registrations, and EPA's legible status fields leave ML little edge.

scored.name: Closed-file product-defect subrogation buyouts (fire and water losses)
scored.one_line: Buy written-off subrogation rights from small P&C insurers, mutuals and self-insured landlords for losses ML flags as likely caused by a defective product, fund forensic proof, and sue or settle against the manufacturer's carrier.
scored.unproven_right: Paid-but-uninvestigated subrogation claims bought at 1-5% of paid loss.
scored.proving_step: Cause-and-origin forensic engineering plus suit: about $50-250k per claim cluster over 1-3 years; about 40-60% success if evidence survives (buy early to avoid spoliation).
scored.proven_buyer: Manufacturers' liability insurers and specialty receivables funds.
scored.public_data: CPSC recalls and SaferProducts reports, NFIRS free-text equipment fields, fire-marshal reports, state court dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-30x on purchase price; shallow ladder.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a subrogation right and proving product causation. Picking the claim (discovery) is maybe 30-40% of the work. Proving it takes forensic cause-and-origin work, expert battles and 1-3 years of litigation against a well-funded defense carrier, and that is the bulk of the effort. It is not trivial or abstracted the way a drill is; it can only be handed to contingency subrogation counsel. The payer is a capitalised manufacturer's liability carrier, but it pays because it loses or settles, not because it wants to buy. Receivables funds will buy claims that have survived spoliation and Daubert challenges, but that resale market is thin.
scored.step_up: The candidate assumes purchase at 1-5% of paid loss. A successful product-defect recovery typically returns 30-70% of paid loss after comparative fault and fees, which is about 10-30x on the purchase price. Market pricing for recoveries that are close to proven is far tighter. Hippo sold its Eaton/Palisades fire subrogation rights for about $15M against roughly $42M in losses, i.e. tens of cents on the dollar, not 1-5 cents (Carrier Management 2025; Baupost bought PG&E Camp Fire claims at a similar order). The step-up is about 10^1, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate estimates the base hit rate at 40-60% if evidence survives, and $50-250k plus 1-3 years per claim cluster. That meets the 'expensive' bar under relaxed C3. ML could plausibly pick better claims (better defect match, more solvent defendant, evidence still intact), but only about 1.2-1.6x. Industry figures say 15% of P&C claims close with missed subrogation, worth $15-20B a year (Shift Technology, Clara Analytics, PC360). However, many of those misses are unrecoverable because evidence or the limitations period is gone (Ethos Risk). For closed files, spoliation sets the hit rate, not ML: whether the product was kept is decided by facts that ML cannot change.
scored.data: The data is partly public: CPSC recalls and SaferProducts, NFIRS, fire-marshal reports and dockets. But NFIRS already codes 'equipment involved in ignition' and 'factors contributing' as structured fields, and CPSC recalls are legible lists. So the outcome-like signal sits in legible fields, which matches the earlier failure pattern where regulators write the answer into status fields. The decisive data (claim file, photos, whether the product was retained) is private to the seller. Sellers are not blind: carriers run AI subrogation screening at first notice of loss (Shift, Clara, CCC) and work with specialist subrogation firms (Cozen, Rimkus). The information gap therefore mostly runs against the buyer, not the seller.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Subrogation rights are assignable and are bought for cash: Baupost and others bought PG&E fire claims, Hippo sold its 2025 LA fire rights, and Subrogation Capital Group funds were set up to buy them in 2003. Small mutuals and self-insured landlords will sell written-off files cheaply, but they are cheap mainly because evidence is gone or the statute is close. Adverse selection is severe, because sellers know whether the toaster was kept.
scored.buyer: Manufacturers' product-liability carriers pay through settlement or judgment. They are capitalised payers, but adversarial ones. Specialty litigation and receivables funds (Baupost-type, litigation finance) buy portfolios of claims that are mostly proven.
scored.ladder: Shallow. Possible next steps are portfolio litigation finance, an in-house forensic lab and subrogation law operation, or reinsurance or MGA underwriting priced with recovery data. None of these leads to owning a large physical chain. It caps out as a specialty finance and litigation shop, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Spoliation plus adverse selection. Written-off closed fire and water files are cheap precisely because the physical evidence (the failed appliance, wiring or supply line) has been discarded or the limitations period is near. Without the artifact, product-defect causation cannot be proven, whatever ML predicts. The fresh files where evidence survives are already screened at first notice of loss by carriers' own AI subrogation tools and sell at tens of cents on the dollar, not 1-5 cents, so there is no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, because proving is expensive and ML can pick better claims. But the step-up is only about 10-30x, the key signal is private or already in structured fields, cheap closed files are cheap because spoliation makes them unprovable, and the ladder is shallow.

scored.name: Hand Match / Marginalia: unrecognised historic letters and annotated books
scored.one_line: Buy bulk estate letters, unattributed autographs and early printed books with unidentified marginalia; handwriting-recognition ML matched against digitised archives identifies famous writers or readers; paleographer sign-off proves association copies.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step (expert sign-off, $500-5k) is cheap, so it fails C3 even under the relaxed rubric. ML does not buy more shots at an expensive jump; it only triages a tiny, fixed supply. Value also comes from scholarly consensus and provenance, not from the ML match, which caps the business at a boutique dealer in a market of about $1-2B a year with no ladder.
scored.step_up: Unchanged from r1. An unproven lot costs about $50-5k (estimate). Proven comparables: a Poe letter sold for $125,125 in 2020 (Inquirer). A Steinbeck letter sold for about $32k (RR Auction). Tolkien letters sold for $2.7-13k (Locus, 2018). A Kerouac letter sold for $11k. That gives about 10^2-10^3x on a famous-hand hit and roughly 3-30x on a typical minor figure.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. My estimate is under 0.1% of "unidentified hand" lots having market value. The relaxed C3 does not help, because it still requires proving to be expensive. Here an attempt costs a $50-500 lot plus imaging, and the expert opinion that proves it costs about $500-5k (estimate). That is far below the $50k-per-attempt threshold. ML triage saves only small sums, and the bottleneck is how many lots exist and how much expert time is available. Score 0, because proving is cheap.
scored.frame: The rung is buying unattributed letters or annotated books, attributing them, and reselling them as authenticated. Discovery (working out whose hand it is) is roughly 80% of the work. The physical step is trivial: buy the lot, photograph it, consign it. Auction houses, dealers and institutional libraries are the buyers. They have money but are not deep-pocketed in the way a mine developer is. Value depends on expert and scholarly consensus, so the ML match alone cannot be sold.
scored.data: The signal sits in illegible public data: digitised manuscript archives (Folger, British Library, university special collections) and auction lot photos where the hand is not identified. Nothing writes the outcome into a legible field, which is good. Rights are bought cheaply from estate sellers who cannot read the hand. The weaknesses: the supply of reference exemplars is scattered, and specialist dealers already triage by eye.
scored.right_bought: Title to the physical object is bought outright at estate sales, house clearances, eBay and minor auctions, usually as an "unidentified" or "archive" lot at a low price.
scored.buyer: Major auction houses (Sotheby's, Christie's, Bonhams, RR Auction, Heritage), rare-book dealers, university and national libraries, and private collectors. The market is about $1-2B a year (estimate).
scored.ladder: Weak. The possible next steps are becoming a dealer and auction house, an authentication service, or moving into adjacent collectibles (art attribution). None of them leads to a very large company, and the supply of valuable unrecognised hands is fixed and small.
scored.one_line_reason: Under the relaxed C3 the step-up per hit is still large, but proving is cheap and the supply of findable famous hands is tiny and fixed. The ML lever saves little money and there is no path to a large company.
sources: Philadelphia Inquirer 2020: Poe letter sold for $125,125
Kerouac letter to Robert Lax, $11,000 (prior r1 research)

scored.name: Gores: claiming title gaps from deed-description errors
scored.one_line: ML reconstructs every metes-and-bounds description in a county's scanned deeds and finds slivers no current deed covers; buy quitclaims from heirs or successors of the last owner of record and sell the strip to the blocked adjoiner, developer or title insurer.
scored.fatal_flaw: The hold-up value is capped by cheap alternative cures, and proving is cheap rather than expensive. A blocked party can quiet title for $1.5k-10k, buy an insurer endorsement, or rely on the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or acquiescence. That caps the step-up at about 10x on deals worth a few thousand dollars, and ML has no expensive proving step to make cheaper.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a quitclaim from heirs costs about $100-1,000 (the candidate's figure, not verified). Proven: the price is capped by what the blocked party would pay to cure another way. That is about $1.5k-10k for an uncontested quiet title (prior-round figures from Alabama Extension and LegalClarity), or an insurer's strips-and-gores endorsement, or the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or acquiescence. The realistic step-up is about 3-30x, roughly 10x. The $10k-500k hold-up figure only applies in rare cases with a tight closing deadline.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Relaxing C3 does not help here, because proving is cheap. A title search or abstract costs about $200-500 and a quitclaim plus recording a few hundred dollars (both my estimates, carried from the prior round). That is far below the ~$50k-per-attempt threshold. ML does find gaps humans miss, but it does not lower the cost of an expensive proving step, because no such step exists. Score 1 only because ML triage of which gores matter commercially saves some search labour.
scored.frame: The rung is acquiring and curing title to one sliver (a gore) and selling it to the adjoiner. Discovery (rebuilding the deed geometry and finding the gap) is roughly 80% of the work. The physical step is trivial: a quitclaim plus recording. The buyers are blocked adjoiners, developers and title insurers. Developers are capitalised, but they have cheap alternatives, so the rung is real and only weakly sellable.
scored.data: Strong and illegible. The signal sits in scanned metes-and-bounds deed text in county recorder archives, and the gap appears in no legible status field. The right can be bought cheaply from heirs or successors who are unaware of the gap. The weakness is the defences above, which reduce the value of what is found.
scored.right_bought: Quitclaim deeds bought from heirs or successors of the last owner of record, typically for a nominal $100-1,000.
scored.buyer: Blocked adjoining owners, developers assembling sites, and title insurers. All of them can cure the defect cheaply without buying the strip.
scored.ladder: Weak. A possible path runs from gore claims to site assembly, title data or title insurance, but none of these compounds from owning the slivers. Each strip is a one-off small transaction and there is no natural chain toward a very large company.
scored.one_line_reason: The data and the right are good, but proving costs only hundreds of dollars and the cheap cures limit the proven value to about 10x a nominal quitclaim. The relaxed C3 changes nothing material.
sources: Prior r1 evaluation: Alabama Extension, uncontested quiet title about $1,500-5,000
Prior r1 evaluation: LegalClarity, quiet title $3k-10k, 2-6 months
Strips-and-gores presumption and title insurer gaps/gores endorsements (prior r1 evidence)
No new web searches run; scores carried from the prior round with C3 rescored under the relaxed rule

scored.name: LapseEdge: materials patents bought before maintenance-fee lapse
scored.one_line: Buy battery, magnet and catalyst composition patents for $2-10k from owners about to let them lapse; ML matches claim ranges to teardown literature; one ICP-MS/XRD teardown produces a claim chart; sell to funders, aggregators or the infringer.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value is realised through litigation, not through a cheap proving step. The cheap step (buying the patent plus a teardown claim chart) gives only about a 10-50x step-up, to brokered prices of about $100-200k. The step that reaches 10^3x is expensive, bespoke, takes years, and is exposed to PTAB invalidation, so it dominates the economics just as building the plant does in the geothermal counter-example. Under the relaxed C3 this gets worse, not better: proving costs under $15k, below the expensive-proving threshold, so there is no expensive shot for ML to make cheaper.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $2-10k, roughly the owner's walk-away value. The third-stage USPTO maintenance fee is about $7.7-8k for a large entity and about $3k for a small one. Proven and claim-charted, in the brokered market: Richardson Oliver average asking prices were $269k in 2013-14, $190k in 2014-15, $124k rising to $194k in 2019, and about $100k in 2022 (about $150k in the years just before). Prices have stabilised since, and many listed packages never sell. That puts the step-up at about 10-50x. Only a litigation verdict or settlement reaches 10^3x, and that is not immediate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from prior knowledge, not verified this round. Base hit rate: probably under 5% of lapse-bound materials composition patents have infringement that a teardown can detect and a US damages base big enough to fund. Cost per proving attempt: about $2-10k to buy plus $1-3k for the teardown, so under $15k. That is far below the relaxed C3 floor of about $50k or years per attempt. The relaxed C3 accepts a base hit rate of 30-70% but still requires proving to be expensive. Here proving is cheap and the expensive step is litigation, which ML does not make cheaper. So the relaxed rubric does not help this candidate. C3 = 1.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a lapse-bound materials composition patent and claim-charting it against a teardown (ICP-MS/XRD). Inside that narrow rung, discovery (matching claim ranges to teardown literature and products) is perhaps 70-80% of the work, and the teardown itself is cheap. But that rung's output, a claim-charted patent, does not realise the value. It mostly sells at a modest broker price. Real value needs litigation or a credible threat of it, which is bespoke, takes years and costs $2-4M+, and is often blocked by PTAB validity challenges. Counted over the steps where value is actually realised, discovery is well under half the work.
scored.data: The data is public and somewhat illegible: claim text, teardown and materials-characterisation papers, and product spec sheets. Incumbents do partly extract it; litigation analytics firms, PAEs and claim-charting shops already exist. Lapse status is a legible field in USPTO maintenance-fee data, but infringement is not written into any field, so the outcome is not pre-summarised.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought cheaply from owners about to let them lapse, mostly universities, small firms and abandoned assignees who will not do teardown matching themselves. These are genuine purchases, not free first-come rights.
scored.buyer: The buyers are litigation funders, aggregators (RPX-style), PAEs, or the infringer through a licence. They are capitalised but price-disciplined and increasingly wary of PTAB risk. Damages bases are limited because most infringers are Asian cell and magnet makers with modest US sales.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. The rungs above are running the litigation, then licensing programmes, then perhaps a materials IP holding company. None of them leads into owning production of batteries or magnets. It is a capped IP-monetisation business, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving (purchase plus teardown) is cheap and lifts value only about 10-50x to brokered-patent prices; the real step-up needs expensive litigation, so the relaxed C3 adds nothing and the prior scores stand.

scored.name: Black Box Publishing / Catalog / Claimant: orphan compositions behind unmatched royalties
scored.one_line: Buy writer and publisher shares from heirs and defunct small publishers whose compositions earn unmatched or unclaimed royalties at the MLC, SoundExchange, PROs and foreign CMOs; ML matches usage to works; register, collect accrued money, resell.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and the proving step is cheap. The MLC, SoundExchange and PROs publish unclaimed status and already match about 92% of usage. Proving a work costs hundreds of dollars, not $50k+, so even under the relaxed C3 ML has no expensive attempt to improve on. And a hit yields only about 2-20x because the remaining unmatched money (about $80M of the MLC's historical pool) is spread thin over millions of works.
scored.step_up: Unchanged from r1. Small catalogs trade at about 5-12x NPS (r1 estimate, not re-searched). A share bought for $500-10k that is in fact under-claimed yields its accrued money (likely $200-2k per long-tail work, my estimate) plus a resale at 6-10x ongoing NPS. That is roughly a 2-20x step-up on the purchase price, nowhere near 10^3. The remaining MLC historical pool is small: about $397M was transferred in Feb 2021, about 79% (~$317M) had been matched by Nov 2025, and about $229M (58%) had been distributed. That leaves roughly $80M unmatched, spread across millions of works. Progress is slowing: only about $5M more was distributed between July and Nov 2025.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The relaxed C3 does not help here, because it still requires the proving step to be expensive (>= ~$50k or years per attempt), and this one is cheap. Proving a work is a database match plus a claim filing, about $50-500 per work (estimate). Per-estate title work is about $1-5k (estimate). Hit rates may be in the 30-70% band now allowed, but it does not matter: with proving this cheap, ML lifting the hit rate does not materially change the cost per proven asset. The MLC's own matching already reaches a 91.9% overall match rate (Nov 2025 filing to the USCO), so incumbent matching captures most of the value.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy an orphan or under-claimed writer or publisher share, match it to usage, register it, collect the accrued money, then resell or hold. Inside that rung, discovery (matching usage to works and finding orphan shares) is maybe 50-60% of the work. Title and heir clearance is the other half. That half is legal and grinding, not trivial or abstracted, and ML does not solve it. Capitalised buyers do exist: catalog funds and marketplaces such as Royalty Exchange, Concord and Reservoir. They pay roughly 5-12x NPS for small catalogs. The frame is real but does not reach 80% discovery.
scored.data: The signal is partly illegible: messy DSP usage metadata, foreign CMO statements, and old publisher contracts and probate records. But the outcome is already written into a legible field. The MLC, SoundExchange and the PROs publish searchable unclaimed and unmatched portals and status. The MLC actively matches works itself, and admin publishers such as Songtrust and Sentric already scrape this money.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Shares can be bought from heirs and defunct small publishers who do not know the money exists, and that is the one genuine edge. But the purchase is gated by clearing the chain of title, and an heir can find the same portals once contacted. Unclaimed MLC money is also eventually distributed by market share after the hold period, so the pot decays.
scored.buyer: Music catalog funds (Concord, Reservoir, Primary Wave, Round Hill), Royalty Exchange-style marketplaces, and the larger publishers rolling up the long tail.
scored.ladder: Climb from orphan shares to a long-tail catalog aggregator, then to an admin publisher and collection society alternative, then to a full publisher, with masters and rights-tech above that. A path to a large company exists (comparable to Concord or Reservoir), but it is not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 changes nothing, because proving is a cheap claim filing rather than an expensive attempt, the step-up stays at 2-20x, and the regulators already publish the unclaimed status.

scored.name: NSW Biodiversity Stewardship credit banking (Western Sydney / Hunter threatened ecosystem credits)
scored.one_line: Option rural land whose vegetation is likely to generate scarce ecosystem or species credits (e.g. Cumberland Plain Woodland, koala habitat), pay for the BAM assessment and register a Biodiversity Stewardship Agreement, then sell the credits to developers, infrastructure agencies or the Biodiversity Conservation Fund. The company keeps credit revenue less the Total Fund Deposit.
scored.unproven_right: Option or purchase of rural or peri-urban land at farmland/lifestyle prices (~A$5-30k/ha) whose credit yield (plant community type, condition, threatened species) is unassessed.
scored.proving_step: Accredited BAM site assessment, BSA application, BCT approval and TFD calculation: ~A$80-250k and 12-24 months per site; ~40-70% of shortlisted sites yield high-value credits.
scored.proven_buyer: Developers and state infrastructure agencies (Transport for NSW, Sydney Water) with retirement obligations, plus the Biodiversity Conservation Fund.
scored.public_data: Thousands of BDARs on the NSW Planning Portal (plot data and credit obligations), State Vegetation Type Map, BioNet Atlas, NSW credit supply and price registers, the 'credits wanted' register, historic aerial imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-30x per ha net of the TFD, up to ~50x for rare PCTs near the Western Sydney growth areas.
scored.frame: The rung is 'land option to registered BSA credits'. It is discrete and sellable, and the buyers are real: developers, Transport for NSW and the Biodiversity Conservation Fund. Discovery (finding which PCT, condition and species are present) is only about 30-40% of the work inside it. The rest is negotiating land tenure, the BAM assessment and agreement process, setting aside the Total Fund Deposit, and committing to in-perpetuity management. Credit sales are also slow and lumpy, so the 'proving' step does not by itself turn the asset into cash. The physical and administrative obligation is not trivial; it works like a 20-year-plus conservation liability attached to the land.
scored.step_up: Gross yield is high for rare PCTs. A government retirement ratio of 680 credits per 63.3 ha of Cumberland Plain Woodland implies about 11 credits/ha. CPW credits have sold for up to A$37k each (NSW dashboard via S&P Global, 2025), and the April 2025 Cumberland reverse auction averaged under about A$45k per credit. That gives roughly A$200-400k/ha gross. But CPW land sits in peri-urban Western Sydney, where it costs hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars per hectare, not A$5-30k, and the TFD takes a large share of gross revenue. Cheap rural Hunter land generates common PCT credits worth about A$200-3,000 each; one example is White Box Blakely's Red Gum at about A$212. Net, the step-up is about 2-10x typically, perhaps 10-30x in rare cases. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate states a proving cost of about A$80-250k and 12-24 months per site (BAM plots, BSA application, BCT approval, TFD calculation), which meets the 'expensive' bar. The candidate also states a base hit rate of 40-70% for shortlisted sites. ML over BDAR plot data plus imagery could plausibly lift high-value hits by 1.2-1.5x. But a landholder or ecologist can already shortlist directly from the public State Vegetation Type Map (PCT polygons) and the credits-wanted register, so the extra lift over that baseline is modest. I score it 3, not 5.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: thousands of BDAR PDFs on the Planning Portal contain plot-level vegetation integrity scores and species surveys. But the core signal is already legible. The State Vegetation Type Map is a public, state-wide map of plant community type, and BioNet holds the threatened species records. The demand side (the credits-wanted register, the price dashboard, IPART reports) is also public and structured. Landholders are increasingly aware of the scheme because the BCT runs EOI tenders and reverse auctions. So the asymmetry is thinner than in uranium assessment files.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought: an option or purchase on freehold land. It is not free first-come. But owners of high-value CPW land are in peri-urban growth areas and price their land on urban hope value. Rural owners with cheap land mostly hold low-value common PCTs. A purchase discount exists only at the margins.
scored.buyer: Developers and state agencies (Transport for NSW, Sydney Water) with credit retirement obligations, the Biodiversity Conservation Fund (which also sets the effective price ceiling), and the Biodiversity Credits Supply Fund. Demand is created by regulation. The NSW Audit Office found that 97% of species credits have never traded, and that developers routed about A$90m into the BCF rather than buy credits. Reforms are under way to narrow the pay-in route.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short.
