From credit banking a company could add offset-delivery-as-a-service for developers, BAM consulting, and perpetual land management, and could expand to the national Nature Repair Market and other state offset schemes. The total market is policy-capped at hundreds of millions of AUD a year. There is no path to a whole chain worth trillions.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is created by a regulator-made, thin, lumpy market in which the BCF pay-in sets a price ceiling, and most of the per-hectare uplift is consumed by the in-perpetuity Total Fund Deposit and by peri-urban land prices. The step-up is about 2-30x, not 10^4, and the public State Vegetation Type Map already makes the 'discovery' largely legible. Structurally it repeats the failure of the previously killed wetland mitigation banks.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real bought-right, regulator-created market with expensive proving that ML could improve modestly, but the step-up is only about 2-30x net of the TFD and land cost, discovery is largely legible from the SVTM, and the ladder is policy-capped; it is a wetland-mitigation-bank analogue.

scored.name: England BNG off-site habitat bank, sited by ML on LPA demand deficit
scored.one_line: Option farmland in LPAs and National Character Areas where a planning-pipeline model forecasts a shortfall in off-site biodiversity units, create the baseline and HMMP, sign a s106 or conservation covenant, register on Natural England's register, and sell units to housebuilders. The company owns the site and unit revenue.
scored.unproven_right: Option or 30+ yr lease on low-grade arable or improved grassland at ~£10-25k/ha whose uplift potential and local unit demand the farmer cannot price.
scored.proving_step: Ecological baseline, statutory metric, HMMP, legal agreement and register entry: ~£60-200k and 9-18 months with high approval likelihood. The real risk is local demand and habitat-type match, which the ML picks.
scored.proven_buyer: Volume housebuilders and promoters with conditioned BNG obligations they cannot meet on site (Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, Taylor Wimpey), plus NSIPs from 2026.
scored.public_data: Planning portal PDFs for every major application since Feb 2024 (BNG metric spreadsheets, off-site requirements by habitat type), Natural England off-site gain register, Priority Habitat Inventory, LNRS maps, local plan allocations and housing trajectories.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-15x per ha net of 30-yr management; higher for scarce medium/high distinctiveness habitats.
scored.frame: The rung is a registered off-site habitat bank: an optioned site, a baseline survey, a habitat management and monitoring plan (HMMP), a s106 agreement or covenant, and a register entry. Picking the site and the local demand is perhaps 20-30% of the work. The rest is physical and long-tail: actually creating the habitat, then a legally binding 30-year duty to manage and monitor it, which is the main cost and the main delivery risk. Registration is close to certain once the paperwork is done, so the 'proving' step proves almost nothing, and value only arrives as units sell over time. This is the US wetland mitigation bank (killed in an earlier round) under a UK name. Discovery is well short of 80%, and the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted.
scored.step_up: Unproven: arable or improved grassland at about £10-25k/ha. Proven: an arable-to-grassland or woodland uplift gives roughly 3-6 units/ha. Brown & Co (undated) puts other neutral grassland units at about £25k each and orchard/woodland at about £35-45k, so gross is about £75-200k/ha. Net of 30-year management, monitoring, the legal agreement and sales costs (around £20-60k/ha), that is about 3-8x, and it comes in over years of sales, not in one step. RICS Land Journal (Apr 2026), citing a Biodiversity Units UK report built on 165 habitat banks, says prices for the abundant habitat types are softening. That is far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about £60-200k and 9-18 months, so it passes the 'expensive' test. But the registration hit rate is around 90%, so ML cannot raise it much. The real variable is how fast units sell and whether the habitat type matches local demand. Demand is already fairly legible from LPA requirements and Natural England register allocations, and incumbents such as Environment Bank and the big land agents already site banks on it. An optimistic ML gain is about 1.2-1.4x on cost per sold-out bank. The HBF 2026 survey shows a sharp rise in respondents saying off-site supply is sufficient, and there are now 268 habitat banks (Mondaq, citing Biodiversity Units UK). Both point to supply catching up, which limits any siting edge.
scored.data: The metric spreadsheets attached to planning applications are semi-unstructured PDFs and xlsx files spread across about 300 LPA portals, which is real illegibility. But the outcome that matters (units allocated, habitat type, which bank supplied them) is already written into Natural England's legible off-site gain register, and data firms like Biodiversity Units UK already publish market reports from it. This is the same 'regulator writes the answer into a field' problem seen before.
scored.right_bought: Leases or options are bought, not free first-come. But farmers are not blind: Savills, Strutt & Parker, Bidwells and Brown & Co all actively advise them on BNG pricing, and many farmers register their own banks. So the information gap with landowners is small, and any discount is modest.
scored.buyer: Volume housebuilders with BNG conditions they cannot meet on site, plus NSIPs later. They are capitalised, but they treat BNG as a compliance cost to minimise and buy the cheapest units that satisfy the trading rules. The market is about £100m a year (Mondaq/BUUK). From 6 August 2026, sites of 0.2ha or less are exempt from mandatory BNG, which trims demand at the small end.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs above: stacking nutrient neutrality, carbon or woodland credits on the same land, buying land outright, LNRS delivery contracts, and possibly promoting development sites that need the units. Every one of these is a small, policy-made environmental credit or land business. None leads to a very large company; the whole BNG market is about £100m a year.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery-dominated jump in value. Registration is near-certain, and the value comes from 30 years of physically delivering habitat in a small policy market (about £100m a year, 268 banks, prices softening). So the asset gains only about 3-8x net, gradually, and ML siting adds at most about 1.3x over a demand picture that is already largely visible in Natural England's register. This is the wetland mitigation bank flaw again.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a UK wetland mitigation bank. Proving is a near-certain registration, the value is in 30 years of habitat delivery, and the gain is about 3-8x in a £100m-a-year market where supply is catching up. The relaxed C3 does not rescue it.

scored.name: England nutrient neutrality credit sites (Solent, Somerset Levels, Tees, Wye)
scored.one_line: Buy or option arable land in catchments where nitrogen/phosphorus neutrality blocks housing, convert it to wetland or woodland, secure the mitigation by legal agreement with LPA and Natural England sign-off, and sell kg-N or kg-P credits to housebuilders stuck in the planning queue.
scored.unproven_right: Arable land in affected catchments at ~£15-25k/ha whose owner cannot price nutrient-offset yield (soil, drainage, leaching, WwTW permit interaction).
scored.proving_step: Nutrient budget modelling, an Appropriate Assessment-compatible mitigation plan, s106 or covenant and monitoring regime: ~£50-150k and 6-18 months, mostly approved once hydrology is confirmed.
scored.proven_buyer: Housebuilders and promoters with schemes blocked on neutrality, and LPA or Natural England credit schemes that buy third-party supply.
scored.public_data: Planning application nutrient budget calculators and HRA appropriate assessments, EA WwTW permits and storm-overflow data, Farmscoper and catchment leaching layers, soil series maps, Catchment Data Explorer.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-20x per ha. Policy risk: the Nature Restoration Fund under the Planning and Infrastructure Act may cap prices.
scored.frame: The rung is: option arable land, take it out of production (woodland, fallow or constructed wetland), secure it by s106 or covenant, and sell credits. Discovery (picking the land and modelling its nutrient yield) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is legal agreements, Appropriate Assessment negotiation with the LPA and Natural England, monitoring for 80-125 years, and, for wetlands, real civil works. So discovery is not 80%+. There is a capitalised buyer (housebuilders blocked on neutrality), but the buyer pays a regulated, per-kg price set against public council schemes.
scored.step_up: Arable land costs about £15-25k/ha. Credits are priced per kg/yr in perpetuity. Approximate prices: Eastleigh/Solent nitrate about £3,000/kg (2021); Kent Stour about £2,350/kg N and about £35,000/kg P; Somerset P-credit £34,061 (June 2025, down from £53,652); Herefordshire Lugg about £14,000/kg P. Arable-to-woodland in the Solent saves roughly 20-40 kg N/ha/yr, so £60-120k/ha of gross credits. Arable P loss of about 0.3-1 kg P/ha/yr gives about £10-35k/ha. Wetlands remove more but need capex. Net of land, legal, monitoring and perpetuity costs, that is about 2-5x on the land, and nowhere near 10^3. Prices are also falling: Somerset fell 37%, and the Nature Restoration Levy is £2,675/home under the first draft EDP (Norfolk, Sept 2026), which caps prices.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about £50-150k over 6-18 months (candidate's figure; consistent with consultancy, legal and AA costs). The approval rate is high once hydrology and land use are confirmed, so the base hit rate is likely 60-80%. ML has little room to raise it. Credit yield is set by Natural England's nutrient budget calculator, which applies standard Farmscoper leaching coefficients by soil, rainfall and land use. Any analyst with GIS can compute it, so the extra yield ML could pick out is marginal. Estimated benefit is about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven site. That is slightly expensive proving with a weak ML edge, so C3 is 2.
scored.data: The data is public but largely legible. The NE nutrient calculator is a published spreadsheet, and soil series, rainfall, land cover, WwTW permits and Catchment Data Explorer are all structured GIS. The outcome (kg N or P saved per ha) is a deterministic formula output from legible inputs. That is exactly the 'regulator writes the answer' failure mode. Demand-side data (which schemes are blocked) is scattered across planning portals, but that is market intelligence, not a hidden asset value.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Arable land or options can be bought or leased from farmers. But landowners are now well informed: land agents (Foot Anstey, Savills, Strutt & Parker) publish guides to nutrient credits. Many farmers sell credits directly through brokers and council schemes (Somerset, Wiltshire, Stour, Lugg) or platforms such as EnTrade and Natural England's own scheme. There is little discount to capture from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Housebuilders and promoters whose schemes are blocked in the Solent, Somerset Levels, Tees, Wye/Lugg, Stour and Norfolk catchments, plus LPA or NE credit schemes buying third-party supply. They are capitalised but price-capped by public schemes and, increasingly, by the Nature Restoration Levy (£2,675/home in the first draft EDP), which developers can choose instead of private credits.
scored.ladder: Weak. Adjacent rungs exist: BNG units, carbon, catchment-scale wetland delivery, and possibly becoming an EDP delivery partner. Those are other credit markets with the same structure, not a vertical chain toward a very large company. The market itself is policy-created and policy-shrinking: the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 and the NRF move delivery to Natural England, and the total market is capped by the number of blocked homes (about 160k historically).
scored.fatal_flaw: The credit price is set by a policy ceiling and the yield comes from a public, legible formula. The value step-up is about 2-5x (not 10^3), credit yield per hectare can be computed from Natural England's own calculator (no ML edge), and the Nature Restoration Levy (£2,675/home, first EDP Sept 2026) is now a state-run alternative that undercuts and caps private credit prices.
scored.one_line_reason: A policy-capped, formula-priced credit market with a ~2-5x land uplift, high base approval and legible yield data, so relaxing C3 does not rescue it.

scored.name: Post-Sackett wetland de-encumbrance via Approved Jurisdictional Determinations
scored.one_line: Buy land priced as wetland-encumbered on NWI or local maps that ML flags as no longer federally jurisdictional after Sackett v. EPA (2023), obtain an Army Corps Approved Jurisdictional Determination plus any state clearance, and sell it as developable to homebuilders or industrial developers.
scored.unproven_right: Fee or option on parcels mapped as wetland or 'potentially jurisdictional' in states without strong state wetland programs (TX, much of the Southeast, Mountain West), discounted 70-95% on old maps.
scored.proving_step: Delineation, AJD request and any state or local sign-off: about $30-120k per parcel cluster and 6-18 months; about 40-70% success on ML-screened parcels lacking continuous surface connection to relatively permanent water.
scored.proven_buyer: National homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte), industrial and logistics developers, and land bankers such as Millrose/Varde.
scored.public_data: USACE ORM2/JD database with scanned AJD PDFs and rationale memos, NWI polygons (wrong after Sackett), USGS 3DEP LiDAR, SSURGO hydric soils, NHD flowlines, county appraisal rolls showing the wetland discount.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-30x on encumbered acreage ($2-5k/acre to $30-100k/acre).
scored.frame: The rung is buying raw land that carries a wetland encumbrance, then selling it with an AJD showing the land is not federally jurisdictional. Inside that rung, discovery (the desktop screen plus delineation) is maybe 60-80% of the work, and the physical step (field delineation, the AJD request) is cheap and done by outside contractors. Homebuilders and land bankers do buy land. But they routinely run the same desktop wetland screen and delineation themselves as standard due diligence (Kimley-Horn and others sell exactly this), so the rung adds little that buyers cannot do in-house. The rest of the work is holding the land and waiting on the Corps.
scored.step_up: Overstated. The candidate's 5-30x compares encumbered raw land ($2-5k/acre) with entitled land ($30-100k/acre). Most of that gap comes from zoning, utilities and lot development, not from clearing the wetland. The fair comparison is encumbered versus unencumbered raw land in the same submarket: probably 2-5x on the affected acres. Those acres are often a slice of the parcel, so the uplift on the whole parcel is lower still. Kimley-Horn/Taft note that pre-Sackett mitigation could cost up to ~$1M per impacted acre, which shows the size of the encumbrance for projects that needed fill permits. But raw land in TX and the Southeast was rarely discounted 70-95% because of NWI maps alone. Nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap in dollars. A delineation runs about $3-5k for a 1-acre lot and roughly $4-30k for larger commercial or agricultural tracts (Oregon legislative testimony; consultant rates of $100-150/hr covering about 10 acres a day). The Corps charges nothing for an AJD. The real costs are time (months, with district backlogs and pauses after Sackett) and the cost of holding the land. Claimed success on ML-screened parcels is 40-70%, so ML might lift the hit rate about 1.5x. But the relaxed C3 still requires proving to be expensive (at least ~$50k or years per attempt), and this mostly is not, so the lever is weak.
scored.data: The inputs are legible public GIS layers (NWI, NHD, 3DEP LiDAR, SSURGO hydric soils), and every civil and environmental consultant already runs them as a desktop screen. Past AJD outcomes are written into structured jurisdictional-status fields in the USACE ORM2/JD public listings, which is the 'answer in a status field' problem. The rights can be bought rather than claimed first-come. But the edge disappears once the pending WOTUS rule is final: the Nov 2025 NPRM projected about an 81% cut in federally regulated wetland acreage, and the Sept 2026 supplemental proposal is narrower still (perennial water only). The rule will reprice encumbered land across the board, publicly, for everyone.
scored.right_bought: A fee purchase or option on rural or exurban parcels mapped as wetland, in states with weak state wetland programs. The rights are bought from farmers or estates. But land brokers and builder acquisition teams in TX and the Southeast already know about Sackett, and the pending rule is widely publicised, so sellers are quickly pricing the upside in.
scored.buyer: D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, industrial and logistics developers, and land bankers (Millrose, Varde). They are well capitalised, but they mostly do the wetland screen in-house and buy on contingency, paying for entitlement rather than for the AJD alone.
scored.ladder: There is a reasonable ladder: land banking, then entitlement and horizontal lot development, then building homes or warehouses. It is a large market, but it is crowded and margins are thin. Winning the wetland-screen rung gives no compounding advantage on the higher rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: A regulatory change, not discovery, reprices this land. The pending WOTUS rule (Nov 2025 NPRM and Sept 2026 supplemental, about 81% less federal wetland acreage) will clear most of these parcels by rule and in public. And the remaining 'which parcels are non-jurisdictional' screen is a cheap ($5-30k), legible GIS exercise that builders' consultants already run. There is no hidden information and no expensive proving step to build an ML lever around, and the real uplift on raw land is only about 2-5x.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is cheap, the inputs and AJD outcomes are legible public GIS and status fields, and the pending WOTUS rule will reprice the land for everyone, leaving a 2-5x arbitrage that is closing fast with no ML moat.

scored.name: CBRS Boundary Error Parcels
scored.one_line: Buy developable-looking parcels mistakenly drawn inside Coastal Barrier Resources System units on the hand-drawn 1982/1990 maps (no NFIP insurance, so no mortgage, so a deep discount), use ML to match old maps against development status at designation, fund the FWS technical-correction or map-revision case, and sell once removed.
scored.unproven_right: Fee purchase of parcels inside CBRS units priced for NFIP ineligibility.
scored.proving_step: Evidence package to FWS (infrastructure existing at designation, historic aerials, title), FWS recommendation and enacted map revision: about $100-300k per unit cluster and 2-5 years; about 30-50% success with legislative risk.
scored.proven_buyer: Coastal developers, homebuilders and individual buyers who can now get financing.
scored.public_data: FWS CBRS Mapper and scanned 1982/1990 maps, USGS EarthExplorer historic aerials, scanned county utility and road permits, FWS digital-conversion pilot findings.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a CBRS-encumbered parcel, getting it removed, and selling it. Building the evidence package (historic aerials, utility and road permit dates, title) is perhaps 50-60% of the work. The rest is not a cheap or abstracted physical step. It is a political one: FWS must recommend removal, and the corrected map only takes effect if Congress enacts it in legislation. That step is slow and outside the company's control, so discovery is well short of 80% of the work. A capitalised buyer (homebuilders, coastal developers) does exist once a parcel is removed.
scored.step_up: The pitch claims 5-20x. The evidence cuts against a deep discount. Druckenmiller et al. (Nature Climate Change, 2024; Lincoln Institute working paper 2023) compared CBRS units with statistically matched tracts. Units had 83% lower development density, but dwellings inside them sold for higher average prices and per-acre assessed values rose, i.e. no measurable discount on what does trade. Private flood insurance and cash buyers also weaken the 'no NFIP, so no mortgage' logic. My estimate of a realistic gain on removal is about 1.5-4x on land that is truly developable and was wrongly mapped. That is far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $100-300k and 2-5 years per unit cluster, with the vote in Congress on top. FWS publishes no aggregate success rate. Its stated rule is that it 'generally does not recommend removals... unless there is clear and compelling evidence' of a technical mapping error. It has declined well-documented claims, for example Unit P32 in Destin, where owners argued infrastructure was in place in 1982 and FWS held the area was undeveloped when designated. The recent enacted correction, P.L. 118-117 (Nov 2024), removed under 4 acres in total. So the candidate's 30-50% is optimistic for requests that pass the screen; I would put it at 10-30%. ML that screens 1982/1990 maps against the development status at designation could plausibly lift precision about 1.2-1.5x. Under the relaxed C3 that scores 3, not 5, because FWS's 'clear and compelling' bar and congressional timing set the outcome more than the quality of the selection does.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned 1982/1990 maps, USGS historic aerials, scattered county permit records. But FWS itself does this discovery. Its digital remapping projects (Hurricane Sandy pilot appendices, NC/FL/SC proposed unit binders) systematically find and propose fixes for mapping errors. It also publishes every technical-correction assessment with its outcome, so the answer is increasingly written down in legible FWS documents. The legal test, whether the area was 'undeveloped at designation', is well defined, which leaves little hidden signal for ML to find.
scored.right_bought: Fee simple purchase from private owners. Unlike first-come claims, the right is genuinely bought, but these owners often know about CBRS and lobby for removal themselves (FWS says it receives 'numerous requests from property owners'), and the evidence suggests prices are not deeply discounted.
scored.buyer: Coastal homebuilders, developers and individual buyers once the parcel can get NFIP coverage and conventional financing. They are capitalised, but the volume is small and confined to a few places.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are entitlement, horizontal development and coastal homebuilding: a fragmented, cyclical business exposed to climate risk. The supply of wrongly mapped CBRS parcels is finite and small, and FWS remapping keeps shrinking it. There is no trillion-dollar chain here.
scored.fatal_flaw: Each hit needs an act of Congress, and the regulator (FWS) already does the error discovery itself and declines removals without 'clear and compelling' evidence. Meanwhile peer-reviewed evidence shows no deep price discount inside CBRS units, so there is neither a 10^3-10^4 step-up nor an information edge that ML can monetise.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive (which earns C3 a 3 under the relaxed rule), but each hit needs an act of Congress, FWS already finds and publishes the mapping errors, and published evidence shows no discount inside CBRS units, so the step-up is about 2-4x and not 10^3+.

scored.name: Digital billboard conversion rights
scored.one_line: Option static billboard sites and their state DOT or nonconforming permits (about $50-300k each) where digital conversion is legal but contested, fight the conversion permit and variances with ML-picked jurisdictions, and sell the permitted digital face to Lamar, Outfront or Clear Channel. Distinct from dormant-permit hunting: the right is an active static sign and the proving step is the conversion approval.
scored.unproven_right: Static billboard structure and ground lease with an outdoor advertising permit, held by mom-and-pop owners or landowners.
scored.proving_step: Digital conversion permit via sign code variances, DOT approval, hearings and sometimes litigation: $75-250k and 1-3 years per site; roughly 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Lamar, Outfront Media, Clear Channel Outdoor and PE-backed regional operators buying digital faces at about 10-14x cash flow.
scored.public_data: State DOT outdoor advertising permit inventories, municipal sign ordinances, council and zoning board minutes, FHWA HPMS/AADT traffic counts, sign litigation dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10x on the asset ($100-300k to $1.5-4M) and 10-20x on conversion spend.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted digital billboard site. Winning the entitlement (variance, DOT approval, hearings) is maybe 50-60% of the work. The physical step is not trivial: an LED face costs a little over $200k per unit (Lamar CEO Sean Reilly), which is about the same as the $75-250k proving spend. A capitalised buyer exists (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel, PE roll-ups), but those buyers do the conversion fights themselves and have their own in-house legal teams. So discovery is well short of 80% of the rung.
scored.step_up: Static board: about $3k/month revenue (Reilly), roughly $15-20k/yr cash flow after ground lease and commissions. At 10-14x that is about $150-300k. A converted digital board earns about $15k/month (5-6x the revenue), roughly $90-110k/yr cash flow, so about $1.0-1.5M at 10-14x, less $200k+ of hardware. Net step-up on the asset is about 3-6x, not 10^3-10^4. The asset never starts near zero because it is already priced as a cash-flowing static board. Sources: Billboard Insider (Reilly interview); Digital Signage Pulse (24-32% return on conversion capital).
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims proving costs $75-250k and 1-3 years per site, with about 40-60% success; I found no hard source for the success rate. Proving is expensive, so it clears the relaxed C3 bar. But the outcome mostly turns on legible rules: spacing, cap-and-replace removal ratios (Baltimore requires 3 faces removed for each new digital board), Highway Beautification Act corridor status (Watertown NY), and grandfathering (Indianapolis). Billboard lawyers already know these rules jurisdiction by jurisdiction. An ML lift of 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven site is plausible; 1.5x+ is doubtful.
scored.data: DOT permit inventories are structured databases. Sign ordinances are text and searchable, and many say explicitly whether digital is allowed and under what cap-and-replace terms. Council minutes and dockets are scattered but readable, and nothing deep sits in them that incumbents miss. The traffic data (AADT/HPMS) is fully legible. The key outcome, whether digital is allowed here, is largely written into the code itself. The data edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought from mom-and-pop owners and landowners, but not cheaply. Static boards trade at full cash-flow multiples through brokers. Lamar says it can buy almost anywhere in the US as a fill-in and keeps a standing acquisition programme. Owners know digital upside exists, and Lamar, Outfront and Clear Channel solicit them constantly. There is no illegibility discount.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront Media, Clear Channel Outdoor and PE-backed regional operators, who buy at about 10-14x cash flow. They are real and capitalised, but they are also the most competent conversion entitlers in the market.
scored.ladder: Site entitlement leads to owning and operating digital faces, then a regional operator, then a national OOH company. US out-of-home is roughly a $9B revenue market, and Lamar's market cap is about $15-20B. That is a large company, but nowhere near a trillion-dollar chain. Further rungs (programmatic DOOH ad tech, media sales) are mostly selling services to incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is never near zero, and the incumbents already capture the upside. Static boards are already priced at 10-14x cash flow by sophisticated buyers who do conversions themselves. Conversion legality is mostly written into ordinances and DOT rules in legible form. After about $200k of LED hardware, the net step-up is only about 3-6x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real, modestly profitable billboard roll-up trade, but there is no near-zero asset, the hardware cost is about the same as the proving cost, and the rules are legible. The relaxed C3 only lifts the hit-rate score to middling; the rest of the rubric still fails.

scored.name: UK NHS pharmacy contract creation
scored.one_line: Use ML over Pharmaceutical Needs Assessments and NHS Resolution appeal decisions to find gaps left by the 2023-26 pharmacy closures, take a cheap retail lease option, win a new NHS pharmaceutical list entry, and sell the contracted pharmacy.
scored.unproven_right: A retail unit lease or option (near-zero premium) in a locality with a PNA gap or 'unforeseen benefits' case.
scored.proving_step: Market-entry application under the 2013 Regulations, including appeals: £20-80k and 1-2 years; roughly 30-50% success when targeted.
scored.proven_buyer: Pharmacy groups and PE-backed roll-ups and well-financed independents.
scored.public_data: ~150 Health and Wellbeing Board PNAs, NHS Resolution Primary Care Appeals decisions, NHSBSA dispensing data, NHS closure notices.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-30x on application spend (£150-600k contract plus goodwill); buyer market weak due to distressed margins.
scored.frame: The rung is "win an NHS pharmaceutical list entry and sell it". Discovery is maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung, not 80% or more. The rest is regulatory advocacy: the application, representations from competitors and the LPC, then appeals. A granted entry also usually has to open as a working pharmacy within about 6 months, extendable to 12, or it lapses. That means a fit-out of roughly £100k+, a pharmacist, a GPhC registration and stock, so the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. Buyers (multiples, PE roll-ups, independents) do exist, but they price pharmacies on dispensing history, not on bare permissions.
scored.step_up: Goodwill is priced on turnover. Hutchings puts the 2025 average at £0.76 per £1 of turnover, down from £0.80 in 2024 and £0.88 in 2023 (London and South East £0.86). Christie & Co reports more distressed and administrator-led sales. A newly granted contract has no turnover and no items history, so on day one it is worth much less than an established £150-600k pharmacy. Its value builds over 1-3 years of trading. Even on the candidate's own figures, £150-600k against £20-80k of spend plus fit-out is roughly 3-10x on the cost of proving, not 10^3-10^4, and it is not immediate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs £20-80k in applications, consultants and lawyers and takes 1-2 years. That clears the expensive-proving bar, barely on cash and fully on time. Base rates: of 103 appeals against rejected applications (Oct 2021 to Sep 2024), NHS Resolution granted 41 (40%) and refused 62 (Pharmaceutical Journal analysis), and refusals rose in 2024. First-instance targeted success rates of 30-50% look plausible. ML over appeal decisions could reasonably help pick localities and frame unforeseen-benefits arguments, so I estimate roughly a 1.2-1.5x improvement in cost per granted entry. It is hard to go above that because the decisive facts (a gap stated in the PNA, the regulatory test) are already explicit.
scored.data: The data is public but largely legible. PNAs are statutory documents whose conclusions state explicitly whether there are gaps in provision; "no gaps identified" is the usual finding. NHS Resolution decisions are published, searchable text that specialist pharmacy consultants and solicitors already read closely. Closure notices and NHSBSA dispensing data are structured. In effect the regulator writes the answer into the PNA conclusion, the same legible-outcome problem that killed earlier hunts.
scored.right_bought: The right cannot really be bought from owners who cannot read the data. The list entry is applied for, and competing applications in the same area are handled in order of receipt. The retail lease is not the constraining asset: landlords near GP surgeries and health centres already know what pharmacy use is worth, and options are cheap only in weak locations. So the edge is first-mover filing, not buying cheaply from uninformed owners.
scored.buyer: PE-backed pharmacy roll-ups, regional multiples and well-financed independents. They have capital, but sector margins are distressed after 2023-26 funding pressure: closures have pushed the count toward or below 10,000, and goodwill multiples are falling. They pay for established items volume, not for fresh permissions.
scored.ladder: The ladder above this rung is thin: operate pharmacies, roll up a chain, then perhaps clinical services under Pharmacy First, wholesale and distance-selling. It is a low-margin, NHS-tariff-capped UK retail sector with a ceiling in the low billions, not a trillion-dollar path. Volume is also tiny, with only about 30-40 granted appeals a year nationally.
scored.fatal_flaw: A granted NHS list entry has no immediate standalone value. Pharmacies sell on turnover (about £0.76 of goodwill per £1, falling), so the step-up only appears after you physically open and trade a pharmacy for years. The supposed gap signal is also written explicitly in the PNA conclusions that consultants already read.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, since applications are expensive and slow with a 30-50% base rate, but the asset is worth about 3-10x its proving cost, not 10^3x, and only after operating a pharmacy. The signal sits in legible PNA conclusions. Rights are first-come applications, not bought cheaply, and the ladder sits in a distressed, tariff-capped sector.

scored.name: FM radio move-in and upgrade chains
scored.one_line: Buy cheap rural FM stations, use optimisation and ML over FCC engineering data to find feasible chains of community-of-license changes and class upgrades into metro rimshots, win FCC grants, and sell the upgraded facility to radio groups.
scored.unproven_right: Low-value rural FM licence or construction permit bought for $100-500k.
scored.proving_step: FCC Form 301 or rulemaking for community change or upgrade, often needing coordinated moves: $50-200k and 1-3 years; decent success once technically clean.
scored.proven_buyer: Radio groups (iHeart, Cumulus, Audacy, Salem, Spanish-language), religious broadcasters (EMF), metro owners.
scored.public_data: FCC LMS/CDBS records, allotment tables, contour and terrain data, ECFS rulemaking dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-20x ($200k to $1-5M); data fairly legible and industry declining.
scored.frame: The rung is real and sellable: buying a rural FM licence or construction permit, winning an FCC grant to change its community of licence or upgrade its class, and selling the result. A construction permit after a move-in does sell (Threshold sold its Clatskanie-to-Napavine permit for $250k). But discovery is maybe 40-50% of the work, not 80%+. The rest is the FCC process itself: Form 301 or a rulemaking, protests from neighbouring licensees, paying other stations to make coordinated moves, plus siting, tower leases and building the facility. The KBGY Faribault-to-Elko New Market move, for example, depended on forcing another station to change facilities. The physical step is not trivial and the process is adversarial, though it is not as bespoke as a geothermal plant.
scored.step_up: Roughly 5-20x on a good outcome, often less. Purchase side: BIA counted 629 radio stations traded in 2025 for $255M combined, about $405k per station on average. Sale side: the Clatskanie-to-Napavine permit sold for $250k after a five-year FCC fight, which is a weak multiple. Older metro move-ins reached $7.1M (Riverside, cut from a $10.5M contract). Recent rimshot deals are priced in tiers by power (an AM move-in at $200-250k). Brokers forecast lower valuations for 2025 and beyond. This is 10^1, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $50-200k in engineering and legal costs and 1-3 years, sometimes 5+ (Threshold's Napavine move took more than five years). That passes the relaxed C3 cost bar. Base hit rate is decent once a filing is technically clean, about 50-70%. That figure is my estimate; I found no published grant-rate statistic. The hit rate is set by FCC spacing and contour rules that are deterministic and already computed by commercial tools (V-Soft Probe, ComStudy) and by consulting engineers. So ML or optimisation mostly adds search breadth across multi-station chains, not a 1.5x lift in grants per filing. A plausible lift in cost per proven asset is about 1.1-1.3x, though finding multi-hop chains could add something.
scored.data: The data fails the illegibility test. FCC LMS/CDBS, the allotment tables and the terrain and contour data are structured, machine-readable and already modelled by commercial allocation software. The FCC's own spacing rules largely decide feasibility. The ECFS dockets are unstructured, but they contain the outcomes, not hidden signal. Incumbents extract all of this routinely. The rights can be bought: rural licences come from willing sellers at depressed prices. But many of those sellers are sophisticated about move-in value because brokers and engineers pitch it to them, so the information gap is small.
scored.right_bought: A low-value rural FM licence or construction permit, bought for about $100-500k from small owners. The seller side is weak (2025 average about $405k per station), but owners and brokers commonly know a station's move-in potential and price it in, sometimes through tiered prices that depend on whether the FCC grants the upgrade.
scored.buyer: Radio groups (iHeart, Cumulus, Audacy, Salem), religious broadcasters such as EMF, and Spanish-language and metro owners. These buyers are capital-constrained: iHeart, Cumulus and Audacy are heavily indebted or post-restructuring, credit is tight (per BIA and brokers), and valuations are falling. The buyer is real but not well capitalised, and nothing like the cash-rich developer that pays $10k/ha for a drill hit.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short and pointed down. The rungs above are owning and operating stations, then clusters, then a radio group, in an industry with secular decline in revenue and valuations. There is no credible trillion-dollar path. At best this builds a mid-sized station portfolio or an asset-flipping shop.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal is not hidden. FCC allocation data is structured and is already searched by specialist move-in engineers and firms (Threshold Communications, consulting engineers using V-Soft or ComStudy). The FCC's deterministic spacing rules effectively write down which moves are feasible. That leaves no illegible-data edge, and the 5-20x step-up lands on a shrinking, debt-burdened buyer base.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough to pass the relaxed C3, but the data is fully legible and already exploited by specialist engineers and move-in firms. The step-up is only about 10x, and the buyers and the ladder sit in a declining, capital-starved radio industry.

scored.name: Improved-forest-management carbon rights
scored.one_line: Lease carbon rights on non-industrial family forests that inventory data marks as high-stock, high-additionality, take the project through registry validation, and sell issued and forward credits to corporates. The company owns the carbon right.
scored.unproven_right: Carbon-rights leases at near-zero upfront cost from family owners who cannot value carbon.
scored.proving_step: Baseline, field inventory, third-party validation and verification (Verra/ACR/CAR): $100-300k and 1-2 years; about 50-70% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Corporate net-zero buyers, CORSIA-eligible airline programmes and carbon funds.
scored.public_data: USFS FIA plots, state LiDAR, Landsat harvest history, county harvest permits and parcels, registry project documents.
scored.rough_step_up: From near zero to about $200-1,500/acre of credit value; high voluntary-market price and integrity risk.
scored.frame: The rung is carbon-rights lease to registered and issued IFM credits. About 50-60% of the work in this rung is selection/proving: inventory, baseline modelling and validation, which is mostly protocol paperwork rather than discovery of hidden value. The 'physical step' is not trivial. It is the landowner forgoing or deferring harvest for 20-40 years, which has to be paid for every year and monitored, with reversal and buffer risk. Corporate and CORSIA buyers exist, but the voluntary market is shrinking, and buyers now discount IFM for integrity reasons.
scored.step_up: There is no immediate step-up on a 'hit'. US IFM credits traded around $17/t in late 2025 (Weyerhaeuser sold at about $29 in 2023). At roughly 1-3 additional t/acre/yr, after a 10-20% buffer, gross credit value is about $200-1,000/acre, and it arrives as a 20-40 year annuity, not at validation. Against that, the developer pays family owners annually for forgone harvest; FFCP-style programmes commit about $45M to 1,200+ owners on 178k acres, about $250/acre. The net step-up on the right is roughly 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4. Sources: forestsource FFCP page; reported 2025 IFM pricing.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $100-300k and 1-2 years per project (expensive, as the candidate states). The base validation success rate is about 50-70%, and failures are mostly protocol and eligibility problems, not asset quality. ML (FIA + LiDAR + Landsat) could raise credits per acre perhaps 1.3-1.5x by choosing high-stock, high-harvest-threat parcels. That edge is also what the over-crediting literature calls adverse selection: Badgley et al. found about 29% over-crediting in CA IFM, and Song/Aldy et al. 2025 found market-entry selection effects. Registries are tightening baselines (dynamic baselines in VM0045) to remove exactly that edge. Under the relaxed C3 this rates about 3.
scored.data: The signal sits in FIA plots, state LiDAR and Landsat harvest history. These are public but already legible and heavily mined; NCX, Pachama, Renoster, CarbonPlan, Finite Carbon and AFF/TNC all use them. Registry project documents are public PDFs, but the outcome (issued credits) is already a legible registry field. There is no illegible-data moat.
scored.right_bought: Carbon rights can be leased from family owners with little upfront payment. But owners price their timber, not the carbon, and demand annual payments that track the forgone harvest. Competing programmes (FFCP, NCX formerly, Finite Carbon, Aces) actively recruit the same owners, so the discount is thin.
scored.buyer: Corporate net-zero buyers, carbon funds and CORSIA airlines. They are capitalised but price-sensitive and integrity-averse. IFM is mostly not CORSIA-eligible today, and voluntary-market volumes have fallen since 2022.
scored.ladder: Carbon rights could lead to timberland ownership, then a combined timber-plus-carbon REIT, then forest products or biomass removals. That is a real ladder, but it ends in a commoditised, low-return timber asset class worth tens of billions, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is not discovery. Validation turns a lease into a slow 20-40 year annuity of roughly $17/t credits, which must be shared with landowners paid every year for forgone harvest. The step-up is about 2-5x net, not 10^4. The ML edge of picking 'high additionality' parcels from legible public FIA/LiDAR data is the adverse-selection over-crediting that registries and buyers are now designing out. NCX already ran this playbook with the same data, and Mississippi State Extension now lists its programme under 'former' forest carbon programmes.
scored.one_line_reason: This is an integrity-challenged annuity business built on legible, already-mined data with a 2-5x net step-up, not a discovery rung with a 10^4 jump.

scored.name: Auckland / NZ Future Urban Zone private plan changes and Fast-track consents
scored.one_line: Option Future Urban Zone and rural land on the Auckland, Waikato and Tauranga fringes, run private plan changes under the RMA or apply under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024, and sell live-zoned or consented land to NZ developers.
scored.unproven_right: Options on FUZ or rural land at about NZ$300-800k/ha.
scored.proving_step: Private plan change or fast-track referral and consent with infrastructure funding agreements, geotech and ecology: NZ$1-3M and 1.5-3 years; about 40-65% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Fletcher Living, Winton, Classic Group, Templeton and KiwiSaver-backed land funds.
scored.public_data: Auckland Unitary Plan private plan change records and decisions, Fast-track panel decisions, Watercare and NZTA plans, council future development strategies, LINZ titles.
scored.rough_step_up: About 6-12x, higher on option premium.
scored.frame: The rung is: option fringe land, rezone or consent it, then sell it. That rung is discrete and has buyers, but finding the right parcel is perhaps 20-30% of the work. Most of the work is the consent process itself: planners, lawyers, geotech, ecology and transport reports, consultation with iwi (Māori tribal groups), and negotiating infrastructure funding agreements with Watercare (Auckland's water utility), NZTA (the transport agency) and the council. That work is the expensive, bespoke step, which is the same failure shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, not the cheap drill hole in the Terranox model.
scored.step_up: The candidate's own estimate is 6-12x, from about NZ$300-800k/ha for FUZ land. Grimes and Liang (Motu, 2010) found land just inside Auckland's Metropolitan Urban Limit was worth about 10x land just outside it. Newsroom, reporting Infrastructure Commission work, gives an urban-zoning premium of about $1,274/m2 over rural land, net of the cost of preparing it for housing. FUZ land already prices in much of the expected rezoning uplift, so the gain on a hit is probably 2-5x on FUZ land and about 10x on truly rural land. Nothing gets near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about NZ$1-3M and takes 1.5-3 years, with a base success rate of about 40-65% (candidate's estimates), so proving is expensive enough to qualify. Fast-track results so far: Milldale was approved in October 2025, and Queenstown, Havelock North (Arataki) and an Auckland project were approved in early 2026. Delmore at Orewa was withdrawn after the panel released a draft decision to decline. A political article quotes Chris Bishop: 35 of 149 listed projects (all types) approved so far. Outcomes are driven mostly by infrastructure servicing, whether the council has the land sequenced in its development strategy, and politics, all of which are already in legible documents. My estimate is that ML lifts the success rate about 1.1-1.3x, mostly by screening sites before options are signed.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible and the outcome is already in legible fields. Zoning is in the Auckland Unitary Plan GIS layers, Future Development Strategy timing is published, plan change decisions are public documents with clear reasoning, Fast-track decisions and the reasons for them are published, and LINZ titles are structured data. There is no large scanned or illegible corpus that only ML can read. The data that predicts success (servicing capacity and the council's growth sequencing) is exactly what council and Watercare publish.
scored.right_bought: Options on fringe land can be bought, but FUZ owners and land bankers are sophisticated. FUZ zoning itself tells them the land is expected to urbanise, and options are priced to the expected value of rezoning. There is no seller who is blind to the value because they cannot read the data. Truly rural land outside the FUZ is cheaper but has much lower odds of approval.
scored.buyer: The buyers are real and well funded: Fletcher Living, Winton, Classic Group, Templeton, CDL Land and land funds backed by KiwiSaver (NZ retirement savings). NZ house prices are soft and buyer demand is cyclical.
scored.ladder: Above the land rung sit civil works and subdivision (titled lots), then homebuilding, then build-to-rent or master-planned communities, and NZ developers already do all of these. The ladder is real but capped by the size of the NZ market. Becoming a large company would mean exporting the playbook to Australian greenfield land, where the rules differ.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a long, bespoke regulatory, infrastructure-funding and political process, not discovery. The value at stake is already visible in legible zoning and growth-strategy maps that the landowners can read. So there is no illegible data for ML to exploit, and the step-up on FUZ land is only about 2-10x.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving costs enough to qualify, but the work is consenting and infrastructure negotiation rather than discovery, the outcome is driven by legible council and infrastructure plans, FUZ sellers price in the uplift, and the step-up is about 10x at best.

scored.name: Die Hunter: finding rare die varieties and errors in bulk coin and stamp lots
scored.one_line: Buys bulk unsearched coins (at melt or face value) and estate stamp lots by the pound. ML on high-resolution imaging detects rare die varieties, doubled dies, overdates and printing errors described in scanned variety catalogues. PCGS, NGC or PSE certification ($20-60) proves the find, and Heritage-type auctions buy at once.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is cheap (about $20-75 in grading fees), not an expensive shot, so ML cannot lower the cost per expensive proven asset even under the relaxed C3. Most hits are $5-50 minor varieties that grading fees wipe out. Hits in the 10^4x class, such as the 1955 DDO at about $3k, are roughly one in a million or rarer in circulation. The diagnostics are already public and legible to every roll hunter. The result is a profitable hobby business with no ladder.
scored.step_up: The cost basis is face value ($0.01-$1). Verified: a 1955 DDO cent (FS-101) sold at Heritage on Jan 15, 2026 for $3,050 (PCGS AU58), $3,660 (PCGS MS62 BN CAC) and $2,806 (NGC MS61 BN). That is about 3x10^5 on a 1-cent base, but such coins are essentially absent from modern circulation. My estimate is that the typical attributable hit is a minor DDO, RPM or VAM worth about $5-50, so 10-100x before a roughly $20-60 grading fee. The weighted median hit is about 10-100x, so the score stays at 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is PCGS/NGC grading at roughly $20-75 per coin. PCGS has historically charged a $15 variety attribution add-on on top of grading, and that figure is old and unverified for 2026. That is orders of magnitude below the relaxed C3 floor of about $50k or years per attempt. Proving is also only paid on suspected hits that a loupe has already mostly confirmed. ML lowers screening labour per coin, which is a throughput lever and not a cost-per-expensive-proven-asset lever. The relaxed C3 does not help, because the 'expensive' leg still fails, so the score is 0.
scored.frame: The rung is buying bulk unsearched coins or stamp lots, identifying varieties, certifying them and consigning them to auction. Discovery (screening and attribution) is about 90% or more of the work. The physical step is imaging plus a TPG submission, which is trivial. Auction houses and dealers are the liquid, capitalised buyers. The frame is real, but each item is small.
scored.data: The diagnostics are public and legible (Cherrypickers' Guide, VAMWorld, Wexler doubled-die listings, stamp catalogues). Every roll hunter and every app reads them, so the answer key is not illegible. The signal is in the physical object, not in illegible public records. Bulk lots are cheap (melt or face value, or by the pound), and sellers such as banks and estates do not search them, so the 'buy cheaply' leg holds. The edge, though, is labour and throughput, not unread data.
scored.right_bought: Bulk bank-wrapped rolls at face value, unsearched estate hoards and stamp lots by the pound or kilogram. Ownership is outright, with no option or lease needed.
scored.buyer: Heritage, Stack's Bowers, GreatCollections, eBay and variety dealers. The market is liquid but small. Total US rare-coin auction volume is on the order of low single-digit billions, and the variety niche is a small fraction of that.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. The next steps are dealer, then auction house, then grading service. Those are services and marketplaces, not a vertically integrated chain toward a very large asset, and there is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.one_line_reason: C3 stays at 0 under the relaxed rubric because the proving step costs about $20-75 and not $50k or more. The other scores are unchanged, and it remains a small hobby-scale business with no ladder.

scored.name: Natural Pearls in Estate Jewellery (Nacre / NaturalPearl / Nacre Lab)
scored.one_line: Buys antique pearl strands and jewels sold as 'cultured', 'costume' or generic 'pearls' at US, European, Indian and Gulf provincial estate auctions, uses ML over catalogue photos and text (pre-1930 dating, clasp hallmarks, drilling, lustre, size gradation, provenance words) to pick likely natural saltwater pearls, gets GIA/SSEF/Gübelin/LFG X-ray reports, and resells at Christie's and Sotheby's Geneva/Hong Kong.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a $50-500 X-ray, so it is cheap. Blanket testing of plausible lots beats ML, and the relaxed C3 still requires expensive proving. On top of that, the deciding signal (internal structure) is not in the public data, typical hits are $3-30k, and the market is too small to scale.
scored.step_up: Unchanged from r3. A typical hit is a small natural strand worth $2.5k-30k: Skinner $2,500-3,500 estimate; Bonhams £7,680 (Sept 2025); Woolley & Wallis £31,500 (Apr 2025). It is bought as untested at about $200-1,000 (my estimate), so roughly 10-50x. The 10^3x results (Cowdray Pearls $3.35M at Christie's, 2024; $5M four-strand record, 2016) are rare tail cases with known provenance.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap. GIA's pearl schedule (April 2025) is $50 for a strand up to 25in and $60 over 25in; SSEF and Gübelin cost a few hundred dollars. Under the relaxed C3, the proving step must still cost at least ~$50k or take years. At $50-500 per test, a buyer can X-ray every plausible lot, so ML's capex lever is close to nothing. Base hit rate (my estimate): 1-3% of all 'pearl' lots, 10-20% of pre-1930 strands with period clasps. Relaxing the hit-rate rule does not help, because the cost condition fails. C3 = 0.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a mislabelled antique strand and proving it natural with a lab report. Discovery (picking the lot) is most of the work, perhaps 70-85%, and the physical step (a lab X-ray, then consigning to Christie's or Sotheby's) is trivial. There is a capitalised buyer: the Geneva and Hong Kong jewellery sales and high-net-worth collectors. But the market is narrow, and dealers already work this same arbitrage by eye.
scored.data: Catalogue photos and text are public, scattered and unstructured, across thousands of provincial auction sites. They hold the priors (dating, clasp, gradation, provenance words) but not the deciding signal, which is the internal growth structure. Only an X-ray shows that. Auction catalogues do not write the outcome into a legible field unless the lot was already tested, and tested lots are already priced correctly.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The lot is bought outright at auction from estates and provincial houses that cannot tell natural from cultured. The company owns the asset and sells it on itself.
scored.buyer: The Christie's and Sotheby's Geneva and Hong Kong jewellery sales, Gulf and Asian collectors, and natural-pearl dealers.
scored.ladder: Weak. Beyond resale there is a natural-pearl dealer or jewellery-house brand, plus re-stringing and design. No path to a very large company; the global natural-pearl secondary market is likely in the low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 changes nothing: a $50 GIA test makes proving cheap, so ML has no capex lever. The market is small and typical hits are 10-50x.
sources: GIA USD pearl report fee schedule, April 2025 ($50 single strand up to 25in, $60 over 25in)
Christie's 2016 natural pearl four-strand necklace record, ~$5M
Bonhams natural pearl three-row strand, Sept 2025, GBP 7,680
Woolley & Wallis natural pearl strand, Apr 2025, GBP 31,500

scored.name: CON-state nursing home and ASC entitlements
scored.one_line: In certificate-of-need states (NC, GA, VA, KY, TN), option land and file CON applications against published need determinations, using ML on past agency findings, then sell the CON-entitled site to hospital systems or PE operators who otherwise cannot enter.
scored.unproven_right: Land option plus applicant standing; some states allow non-provider applicants or nominal-operator partnerships (verify state by state).
scored.proving_step: CON application and contested review or appeal: $150-500k and 1-2 years; about 40-60% approval in competitive batches.
scored.proven_buyer: Hospital systems, ASC roll-ups (USPI, SCA), skilled nursing operators and REITs.
scored.public_data: State Medical Facilities Plans, CON decision PDFs and hearing transcripts, license renewal utilisation reports, CMS cost reports.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x on spend ($3-15M scarcity value); weak point is that many states tie CONs to the operator.
scored.frame: The intended rung is an entitled site with a CON that can be sold. That rung does not exist as sellable property. NC law lets the Department withdraw a CON if ownership or control of the certificate, project or facility is transferred before the project is completed or operating (good-cause exception only). The value is realised only after a roughly $17-23M facility is built and licensed, about $190k per bed in a 2022 NC approval for 122 relocated beds. Inside a frame that ends at a realisable asset, discovery (picking the need determination and the site) is maybe 10-20% of the work. Construction, licensure and operation are the rest, which is the geothermal counter-example. Buyers (hospital systems, USPI/SCA, SNF REITs) are well capitalised, but they buy operating facilities or joint applications, not a third party's pre-build CON.
scored.step_up: If a CON could be sold, $150-500k of application spend against a claimed $3-15M scarcity value is about 10-50x on spend. On the land it is about 2-5x, since the option land is ordinary commercial land. I found no published per-bed or per-CON transfer prices, and the only NC figures are development budgets ($17.7M for 96 beds in 2016; $23.1M for 122 beds in 2022), which are costs, not premiums. Because the CON cannot be transferred before completion, the step-up that can actually be captured right after a hit is close to zero. Scored 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive enough: $150-500k plus 1-2 years including contested appeals (per the candidate; Becker's reports competitors' appeals stalling about 1,100 NC hospital beds). The base approval rate is about 40-60% in competitive batches (candidate estimate, not verified; I found no tallied NC rate). The relaxed C3 accepts that rate, but a 1.5x lift is not plausible. NC competitive reviews score applicants on published comparative factors in the findings (access, cost per patient, operator quality and experience, Medicaid share), so specialist CON law firms and consultants already optimise against the rubric. A non-provider applicant also starts at a structural disadvantage on the experience and quality factors. ML likely gives about 1.1-1.3x at best.
scored.data: Mostly legible. Need determinations are explicit numeric tables in the State Medical Facilities Plan (county, service, number of beds or ORs), and every competitive review produces a findings PDF with a comparative analysis and a named winner. The outcome is written down in plain text, the same way prior hunts found regulators recording the answer in status fields. Decision PDFs and transcripts could be scraped, but the main signal (where need exists) is published, and incumbents' CON counsel already read the findings closely.
scored.right_bought: The land option is cheap, but the real right, applicant standing and the CON itself, is not a property bought from uninformed owners. It is a regulatory award that is effectively tied to the operator and cannot be transferred before completion (NC GS 131E-189 withdrawal on transfer). The only route is a joint application with a nominal operator, which hands most of the value to the operator. There is no class of owners who cannot read the data and would sell the right cheaply.
scored.buyer: Hospital systems (Novant, Atrium, UNC), ASC roll-ups (USPI, SCA) and SNF operators and REITs are well capitalised. They usually file their own applications, or buy operating facilities after licensure, rather than buying a third party's pre-build CON.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: entitlement, then development and construction, then operating the ASC or SNF, then owning the real estate as a REIT or roll-up across CON states. That is a large market, but the lowest rung is not separable, so the company would have to start as a developer-operator, which is the hard physical rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: A CON cannot be transferred before the project is completed or operating. NC lets the Department withdraw it if ownership or control changes first, and other CON states tie it to the operator the same way. So the entitled-site step-up cannot be sold to a capitalised buyer. Value is realised only by building and running a roughly $20M facility, which makes discovery a small share of the work, as in the geothermal counter-example. Need determinations and outcomes are also already published in legible form.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is costly enough, but the CON is tied to the operator and cannot be transferred before the facility is built, so it cannot be flipped. Need and outcomes are published in plain text, and ML is unlikely to beat CON counsel by 1.5x.
sources: https://info.ncdhhs.gov/DHSR/coneed/decisions/2025/mar/findings/2024 Mecklenburg Acute Care Bed Competitive Review Findings.pdf

scored.name: Investment-treaty claim vehicles for small foreign investors
scored.one_line: Find SME foreign investors harmed by host-state measures (licence revocations, tariff clawbacks, permit cancellations), acquire equity in the treaty-national holding entity, fund ICSID/UNCITRAL arbitration, and sell the award to enforcement funds.
scored.unproven_right: Unfiled treaty claims; bare-claim assignment is usually barred, so the company must own the claimant entity before the dispute (nationality and abuse-of-process risk).
scored.proving_step: Arbitration at about $5-15M and 3-7 years; investors win roughly 45-50% of decided cases and settlements are common.
scored.proven_buyer: Award-enforcement and sovereign-claim funds (Tenor, Burford, Gramercy-type) at 20-70 cents, or the sovereign via settlement.
scored.public_data: National gazettes and regulatory decrees, UNCTAD treaty texts, ITA/ICSID awards, company registries with foreign ownership chains.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-100x on equity paid; high structuring risk.
scored.frame: The rung would be: own a treaty-protected claimant and take it to an award. Discovery (finding harmed SME investors) is maybe 5-15% of the work. The proving step is the arbitration itself: about 4 years, a team of counsel and experts, jurisdictional fights and annulment risk. That is the bulk of the work and is neither trivial nor abstracted. It inverts the Terranox shape and looks like the geothermal-plant counter-example, where the bespoke build is harder than the find. A capitalised buyer does exist (award-monetisation funds and the sovereign via settlement), but owning this rung means being a litigation funder plus a claimant law shop.
scored.step_up: Equity in an SME whose licence was revoked might be bought for a few hundred thousand dollars against a possible award of $10-50M. That is 10-100x on the equity check, but only after adding $3-7M of claimant costs (Kluwer FY2011-15: mean $5.6M, median $2.9M; Burford 2018: $7.05M mean plus about $1M tribunal fees). Awards then sell at a substantial discount (Gramercy/Tenor prices are undisclosed; the candidate assumes 20-70 cents). Measured on total capital at risk, a win returns roughly 2-5x. It arrives 3-7 years later, not immediately, and enforcement against the sovereign is a second long step. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive: $3-15M and about 47 months on average at ICSID (HSF Kramer 2026 study). Base hit rate: about 49% of ICSID awards uphold claims in whole or part, and 53% in 2025 (Enyo). But 60% of 2025 cases got no damages, so the real money-win rate is about 40%. Settlements before award were 33% in 2025. Under the relaxed C3, ML case selection over decrees and awards could plausibly lift the success rate from about 40% to 50-60% (1.2-1.5x). Funders already screen hard, and outcomes turn on tribunal composition, legal theory and quantum, which public text predicts weakly. That gives a score of 3, not 5.
scored.data: Gazettes, decrees, UNCTAD treaty texts and ITA/ICSID awards are public and scattered. Some are in local languages, so there is some illegibility. But the key signal is not hidden from the owner: an SME whose licence was revoked or whose tariff was clawed back knows it was harmed, and treaty law firms and funders actively canvass these measures. The outcome is not in a status field, which is fine. The fatal part is the right itself. A bare claim cannot be assigned, and acquiring or restructuring into a treaty-national position after the measure, once the dispute is foreseeable, is abuse of process (Philip Morris v Australia; Pac Rim v El Salvador; Tidewater). So the right cannot be bought cheaply after discovery from an uninformed owner. Your only route is to fund or co-own the existing claimant, which is just third-party funding.
scored.right_bought: In practice, only a minority equity stake in, or a funding agreement with, an existing claimant that already holds treaty nationality. Buying in after the measure risks jurisdiction. The owner is the harmed investor, who knows the claim exists and will price it, often with a funder's term sheet already in hand. That is not a cheap purchase from someone who cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Award-monetisation and sovereign-claim funds (Tenor, Gramercy, Burford-type) buy at substantial undisclosed discounts. Sovereigns sometimes settle; for example, Uruguay settled with a Tenor affiliate over its collapsed state airline. These buyers are real and capitalised but thin. Venezuela, Argentina and Spain-renewables awards show how slow and lossy enforcement is.
scored.ladder: The rungs would be claim origination, funding, award enforcement, and then sovereign distressed debt and political-risk insurance. That ladder tops out as a litigation-finance or distressed-sovereign fund (Burford is roughly a $3B company). It does not lead to owning a large physical value chain, and there is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right cannot be bought after discovery. Bare treaty claims cannot be assigned, and acquiring treaty-national standing after the harmful measure, once the dispute is foreseeable, is abuse of process (Philip Morris v Australia, Pac Rim). That collapses the model into ordinary third-party litigation funding: a $3-15M, 4-year arbitration, which is the majority of the work, bought from an owner who already knows they were harmed.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step (arbitration) is most of the work and costs $3-15M. Abuse-of-process doctrine bars buying the claim cheaply after the harm. Award discounts hold net step-up to about 2-5x. ML lifts the 40-50% win rate only modestly. It is litigation finance in disguise.

scored.name: Rails-to-trails takings: buy adjoining parcels before the NITU
scored.one_line: ML predicts which rail lines will file abandonment or railbanking at the STB and whether original right-of-way grants were easements rather than fee; the company buys the adjoining parcels before a NITU issues, so it owns the property and the Fifth Amendment takings claim, and wins it in the Court of Federal Claims.
scored.unproven_right: Adjoining parcels at ordinary prices with an unrecognised reversionary interest; buying land is required because the Anti-Assignment Act bars buying the claim.
scored.proving_step: Title abstracting plus Court of Federal Claims litigation and appraisal: about $100k+ per corridor class over 3-8 years; >60% win rate once deeds show an easement; URA fee-shifting.
scored.proven_buyer: US Treasury pays judgments with interest; parcels and strips resell to trail authorities, utilities and fibre companies.
scored.public_data: Scanned county railroad deeds and grant books, STB abandonment and exemption filings, scanned ICC valuation maps, state rail plans.
scored.rough_step_up: Only about 2-5x on capital deployed; C2 weak.
scored.frame: The rung is: own an adjoining parcel when the NITU issues, then prove the takings claim. Discovery (predicting the abandonment or railbanking filing and reading the deeds to see easement vs fee) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is the "physical" step: title abstracting, appraisal, 3-8 years of litigation in the Court of Federal Claims, and the cost of owning and reselling whole parcels. None of that is trivial or abstracted. A capitalised buyer exists (the US Treasury Judgment Fund pays), but it buys a lawsuit outcome, not a rung of a value chain.
scored.step_up: Awards are small next to the land you have to buy. Ecusta Trail NC: $5.04M for 164 landowners, about $31k each. Tabor-Platte SD: about $128k for 7 landowners, about $18k each. Legacy Trail FL: $1.4M settlement. Outliers exist: Greensboro, $6.4M for 8 owners; St. Petersburg, $17.9M for 3, one getting $12.9M. Because the Anti-Assignment Act forces you to buy the whole parcel at market price (often $100k-$500k) to collect a claim of about $20-50k plus interest and URA fees, the gain on capital deployed is about 1.1-1.5x per typical parcel, not 10^3. Even the candidate's own 2-5x looks optimistic. A 10^2x-plus step only appears if you could buy just the underlying strip fee for close to nothing, and title, notice and court-scrutiny risk make that doubtful.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $100k+ per corridor class for title work, appraisal and litigation, over 3-8 years, so the cost bar is met. The base win rate is already above 60% once the deeds show an easement. ML that reads the scanned grant deeds and ICC valuation maps could plausibly lift the share of proven claims among purchased parcels about 1.2-1.5x, so 3 under the relaxed C3. The edge is limited because plaintiff firms (Lewis Rice and others) already screen deeds by hand corridor by corridor. The base rate comes from the candidate's stated >60% and the pattern of practitioner case wins.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: scanned county deed and grant books, ICC valuation maps, STB filings. But the timing signal (an STB abandonment or exemption filing, public with notice periods) is legible and arrives months before the NITU, so predicting it with ML adds little. Specialist contingency firms already canvass every adjoining owner and read the deeds once a NITU issues. Owners cannot read the data before the filing, so parcels could be bought at ordinary prices, but that is only ordinary residential or farm land, not a discounted right.
scored.right_bought: Whole adjoining parcels at market price, with an unpriced reversionary interest in the corridor strip attached. The claim itself cannot be bought (Anti-Assignment Act).
scored.buyer: The US Treasury Judgment Fund pays judgments plus interest and URA attorney fees. The parcels resell to the ordinary market. The strips could go to trail authorities, utilities and fibre companies, but under railbanking the trail sponsor already holds the corridor.
scored.ladder: Weak. The government pays out once; it does not lead to owning a chain. A possible extension is assembling corridor title for fibre or utility easements, but railbanked corridors are held by the trail sponsor and the railroad's reactivation right, so there is no clear path from here to a very large integrated company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Ownership has to come through whole adjoining parcels bought at market price, while the takings award covers only a strip worth about $20-50k per typical owner. That caps the gain on capital at about 1.1-2x, against a 10^3-10^4 target, and the only buyer is a one-time Treasury judgment with no ladder above it.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive and ML on the deeds helps a bit (C3=3). But the asset you must buy dwarfs the claim, specialist law firms already read the deeds, and the Treasury payout is a dead end, so there is no 10^4 step and no ladder.

scored.name: National Register plus historic tax credit certification of distressed buildings
scored.one_line: Buy vacant, distressed or condemned pre-1975 commercial buildings at teardown prices, win National Register eligibility and NPS Part 1/2 certification to unlock 20% federal plus state credits, and sell the certified project to rehab developers and tax-credit investors.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a distressed building whose historic significance is undocumented.
scored.proving_step: Significance research, SHPO nomination and NPS Part 1/2 approval: about $50-150k and 12-24 months; 60-80% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Historic-rehab developers, tax-credit syndicators and bank CRA investors.
scored.public_data: Sanborn maps, building permits, historic newspapers, SHPO survey files, NPS NRHP database, code-enforcement and condemnation lists.
scored.rough_step_up: About 1.5-4x; modest.
scored.frame: The rung is a Part 1/Part 2 certified building, which is sellable to rehab developers. Discovery and significance research is maybe 30-50% of the work and cost in that rung. The rest is the Part 2 rehab design package, done to the Secretary of the Interior's Standards, which needs architects and engineers. The credit is only realised after the physical rehab is built and Part 3 is certified, and that rehab is far larger than the research. So discovery is not 80%+ and the physical step is not trivial. Buyers have capital: about 1,463 Part 1 and 1,187 Part 2 approvals a year (FY2022).
scored.step_up: The candidate's own estimate is about 1.5-4x, and this looks generous. The federal credit is 20% of qualified rehab expenditures, not of the building's value, and it is claimed only after rehab is complete and Part 3 is certified. A teardown bought for, say, $300k might be worth $450-900k to a developer once Part 1/2 approval removes entitlement and credit risk. That is roughly 1.5-3x, nowhere near the 10^3-10^4 the rubric looks for. State credits add some value, but the value created by certification is bounded by credit dollars spread over the rehab cost.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate says $50-150k and 12-24 months per attempt with a 60-80% success rate, but those cost and success figures are unsourced. A Part 1 significance case or an NRHP nomination usually costs a consultant roughly $5-30k; the bigger cost is the Part 2 architectural package, which is design work, not discovery. So the expensive part of proving is not where ML helps. ML could screen buildings for likely significance before purchase, maybe 1.2-1.5x better cost per certified asset. But many buildings are already contributing resources in listed districts, where significance is already known. Under the relaxed C3 this is borderline: expensive only once design is included, with a modest lift.
scored.data: Sanborn maps, historic newspapers, permits and SHPO survey files are public and partly illegible, which fits the rubric. But the outcome is often already written into a legible field: NRHP listings, contributing or non-contributing status in district inventories, and SHPO survey eligibility ratings. Any building over 50 years old in a district is already on developers' radar. The real undiscovered signal is individually eligible buildings outside districts, which is a narrower pool.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee title to distressed or condemned buildings can be bought cheaply, including from tax sales, land banks and municipalities with condemnation lists. Sellers often do not pursue credits. But the buyer takes on carrying costs, insurance, demolition-order risk and possible environmental liabilities (asbestos and lead) while holding the building for 12-24 months.
scored.buyer: Historic-rehab developers, HTC syndicators (Novogradac ecosystem), bank CRA investors. Real and capitalised, but they buy credits at completion more than certified-but-unbuilt shells.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are rehab development, credit syndication, then owning and operating the property, so the ladder exists. But it is fragmented local real estate development, capped by the size of the HTC program (about $6-7B of rehab spending a year qualifying). It is not a path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Certification creates little value. The credit is 20% of rehab spending and only arrives after the costly physical rehab is built (Part 3), so proving gives a modest 1.5-3x step-up, and the real work is construction, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but ordinary value-add real estate play. Certification adds about 2x, not 10^3x. The physical rehab dominates the work, significance is often already in legible survey fields, and the relaxed C3 helps only slightly.

scored.name: UK Peatland Code restoration units on degraded upland
scored.one_line: Buy or long-lease drained, eroding upland peat at hill-land prices, validate under the Peatland Code with Pending Issuance Units, restore with grip-blocking, and sell PIUs to UK corporates for insetting. The company keeps unit revenue net of restoration grant.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase or 100-yr lease of rough grazing or grouse moor at ~£2-6k/ha whose peat depth and condition category are unmeasured.
scored.proving_step: Peat depth survey, condition mapping, project design document and accredited validation: ~£50-150k and 1-2 years, with high validation likelihood once depth and erosion are confirmed.
scored.proven_buyer: UK corporates with net-zero claims buying high-integrity domestic units (utilities, banks, supermarkets) and intermediaries.
scored.public_data: UK Peatland Code registry project documents, Natural England and NatureScot peat depth and carbon maps, LiDAR and aerial imagery of gullies and grips, historic moorland drainage records.
scored.rough_step_up: ~3-10x per ha net of restoration cost.
scored.frame: The rung is a validated Peatland Code project on land you own or lease. Discovery (depth survey, condition mapping, PDD, validation) is maybe 20-35% of the work.
