The rest is buying the land, physical restoration (grip and gully blocking, reprofiling, revegetating bare peat, at a median of about £1,026/ha in Scottish Peatland ACTION data, roughly 2x for forest-to-bog), and verification monitoring over decades. Before any unit becomes a Verified PIU you carry decades of permanence and monitoring obligations. Corporate buyers do exist and do pay, but they pay modest amounts per tonne.
scored.step_up: Land: Savills reports hill and rough grazing at £500-5,000/acre (about £1.2k-12k/ha). Peatland Code PIUs averaged £25.04/t in 2024 (Strutt and Parker) and about £39.57/t in 2025 on a thin sample. Eroding upland peat might yield a few tCO2e/ha/yr of claimable reductions, less buffer, giving roughly 100-300 t/ha over the project life, or about £3-10k/ha gross. Most of that is not paid up front. Take off restoration cost (about £1-2k/ha) and the effect of public grant on the units you can sell, and the net uplift is about 1-3x the land price. It is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about £50-150k and 1-2 years per project, so it meets the 'expensive' bar. But the candidate itself says validation is likely once depth and erosion are confirmed, and the inputs that predict this (peat depth over 50 cm, visible grips and gullies, bare peat) are already mapped publicly. ML might add about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven project, mostly by choosing better sites before purchase, not by raising the hit rate.
scored.data: The data is legible and the government has already done the extraction. Natural England published the England Peat Map in May 2025 as open data (OGL). It has ML-derived peat extent, depth on a 10m grid with confidence layers, and condition that explicitly maps grips, gullies and bare peat. Scotland has the NatureScot Carbon and Peatland Map, and the Peatland Code registry publishes its project documents. The outcome you would predict, eroding deep peat, is therefore already written into a public field. The only residual edge is fixing errors the NFU says the map contains, which is small.
scored.right_bought: Freehold or long lease of upland, bought from estates and farmers. But the sellers can read the data. Savills says valuers now explicitly price peatland restoration and natural capital into hill land, and 2021-23 saw 'green laird' and natural-capital buyers bid upland prices up sharply. There is little informational discount left to capture.
scored.buyer: UK corporates insetting or making contribution claims (utilities, banks, supermarkets, water companies) and brokers. They are real but price-sensitive buyers, paying roughly £20-40/t PIU, and the market is thin (about 187k units sold in 2024).
scored.ladder: From validated projects you could move into multi-project portfolios, then a natural-capital land platform (carbon plus BNG plus nutrient neutrality), then a UK land fund or ecosystem-markets developer. That is a real ladder but a capped one. The whole UK peatland carbon pool is estimated at about £470m (Wild Moors/Terra Motion), and there is no clear trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible-data edge. Natural England's 2025 England Peat Map (and NatureScot's map in Scotland) already publishes ML-derived peat depth and condition, including grips, gullies and bare peat, and the land market already prices peatland carbon. That leaves you a capital-heavy land and restoration business with a 1-3x uplift, not a discovery play.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is somewhat expensive, but the value uplift is only about 1-3x after restoration. The state has already published ML depth and condition maps, so ML adds little, and sellers already price peat carbon.

scored.name: Assigned cartel-damage claim pools (German/Dutch assignment model)
scored.one_line: Buy outright assignments of overcharge claims from thousands of SME purchasers of goods covered by EC cartel decisions (trucks, rail, envelopes, auto parts), litigate or settle in Germany or the Netherlands on the binding infringement decision, and sell or collect the receivables.
scored.unproven_right: Follow-on damage claims SMEs do not know they hold or cannot pursue, near limitation, assignable under German assignment-collection case law and Dutch SPV structures.
scored.proving_step: Overcharge expert report, pooled litigation and disclosure: roughly $2-20M per pool over 3-8 years; recovery likely (>60%) but quantum and passing-on vary.
scored.proven_buyer: Litigation-finance and credit funds (Burford, Harbour, Fortress); defendants settling to cap exposure.
scored.public_data: EC cartel decisions, COMEXT customs and TED procurement records showing who bought cartelised goods, company registry accounts.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-30x on the assignment price; check jurisdiction because BGH/OLG rulings have challenged assignment validity.
scored.frame: The rung is originating a pool of assigned follow-on claims and bringing it to settlement or judgment. Discovery here means working out who bought cartelised goods and signing them up. That is perhaps 20-30% of the work. The rest is the 'physical' step: overcharge economics, passing-on defence, disclosure fights, and 3-8 years of litigation in which courts can order bundled claims to be split. That step is the bulk of the cost and risk, not trivial or abstracted. A capitalised buyer exists (funders, settling defendants), but the frame is not one where discovery is 80%+.
scored.step_up: From cartel-decision liability, the claim holder already has a known, quantifiable right worth about the overcharge. Courts have found overcharges of 5-8% in trucks (Amsterdam 7% in April 2026; Spain's Supreme Court cut 8% to 5%) and at least 15% in German rail (LG Dortmund). Outright purchases or success-fee assignments typically price at roughly 10-30% of the expected recovery, so a win realises about 3-10x on the purchase price. The 10-30x in the brief is optimistic, and it is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The asset does not start near zero, because an EC decision already establishes liability.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $2-20M per pool over 3-8 years. The financialright trucks pool ran from 2017 to the BGH in 2026 and was remanded, with 70,000 trucks and about EUR 500M claimed. The base hit rate on liability is already high (above 60%), because the binding EC decision decides liability. ML could help find claimants and estimate quantum or passing-on exposure. It does little to raise the win rate, and the cost of litigation per pool barely moves. Plausible gain on cost per proven asset is about 1.1-1.3x, mostly in origination, which is a small share of cost. Under the relaxed C3 that sits around the bottom of the 1.2-1.5x band, so 2.
scored.data: The key signal, the infringement, is already written into a legible public field: the EC decision names the cartel, products, period and territory. That is exactly the pattern that kills the ML edge. Purchaser identity is not cleanly public. COMEXT is aggregate trade data, not firm-level. TED covers only public buyers. Vehicle registration data such as Germany's KBA is not openly available. The rights are not cheap or hidden. financialright, CDC, Hausfeld, Burford-backed vehicles and trade associations canvas claimants actively and run ads. Limitation pressure makes SMEs aware of their claims, so the hidden-right arbitrage is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, claims are assignable. The BGH (KZR 6/24, 12 May 2026; KZR 11/24, 28 July 2026, Rundholz) confirmed that collection by assignment is generally permitted. But courts may order bundled claims separated, which makes the action inadmissible if not followed. Rights are bought in a contested market at success-fee or discount prices, not cheaply from owners who do not know what they hold.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Harbour, Omni Bridgeway, Fortress) and defendants settling to cap exposure. They are capitalised but price in duration and splitting risk, so they pay well short of face value for unresolved pools.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are claims origination, then funding, then a law firm or collective-action platform, then a broader litigation-finance asset manager. That is a total market of tens of billions of dollars of AUM. There is no vertical integration into a physical industry and no trillion-dollar path. The supply of cartel decisions is limited by the EC's enforcement pace of a few major decisions a year.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already public and legible: the binding EC infringement decision is the answer, so there is no illegible-discovery edge. Value is realised through years of costly litigation, not a cheap proving step, so discovery is a minor share of the work and the step-up is only about 3-10x.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a legitimate but crowded litigation-finance arbitrage. Liability is already decided and legible in EC decisions, the work is litigation rather than discovery, the step-up is about 3-10x, and there is no big ladder above it.

scored.name: Discriminatory EU dividend-withholding-tax reclaims bought from non-EU funds
scored.one_line: Buy rights to unfiled EU withholding-tax reclaims from US and Asian pension funds on free-movement-of-capital grounds (Fokus Bank, Santander, Emerging Markets Series), file and litigate country by country, and sell or collect the refunds.
scored.unproven_right: Unfiled or time-barring reclaims bought at 10-30 cents on the dollar.
scored.proving_step: Filing, refusal and national-court litigation: roughly $50-500k per country-claimant over 4-10 years; about 50-70% success in favourable jurisdictions.
scored.proven_buyer: Tax-reclaim trading desks and credit funds at 85-95 cents.
scored.public_data: SEC N-PORT and 13F holdings, fund annual reports, ECJ and national rulings, dividend histories.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-8x; weak C2 and ladder.
scored.frame: The rung is buying, filing and litigating EU free-movement-of-capital dividend WHT reclaims. Discovery, meaning working out which fund has a valid claim, is maybe 10-20% of the work. Most of it is the physical step: national-court litigation, proof of comparability with resident funds, document assembly, and 4-10 years of carry. A capitalised buyer exists (claim desks and credit funds), but the rung is mostly legal work, not discovery. That is the geothermal-plant pattern: the hard part is the doing, not the finding.
scored.step_up: From the candidate's own figures: buy at 10-30c and sell proven claims at 85-95c, so about 3-9x. Discounted for time to resolution and remaining jurisdiction risk, the realistic step-up is about 3-5x. No search confirmed a secondary market at 10-30c. Contingency reclaim firms (WTax, GOAL, EY/KPMG ECJ claims practices) charge a success fee taken only on refund, so a sophisticated owner can file at no upfront cost and keep most of the refund. That puts a ceiling on how deeply a seller would discount an unfiled claim, which pushes the realistic buy price well above 10-30c and the step-up toward 1.5-3x. This is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $50-500k per country-claimant over 4-10 years (candidate estimate). That meets the relaxed C3 cost bar. Base success is about 50-70% in favourable jurisdictions after Santander, EMS (C-190/12) and Keva v Skatteverket (C-39/23, 2024). Outcomes depend on jurisdiction, comparability doctrine and limitation periods, and those are legal questions specialist advisers already answer. ML is unlikely to lift cost per proven claim by 1.5x. Maybe 1.1-1.3x, from triaging which fund and country pairs to pursue.
scored.data: Fails the illegible-data test. N-PORT and 13F filings are structured XML, dividend histories are commercial data feeds, and ECJ and national rulings are well digested by EY, KPMG, PwC, IBFD and the reclaim firms. The outcome sits largely in published case law and status tables kept by advisers. Owners are not unable to read the data: they are large US and Asian pension funds and RICs with custodians and Big Four advisers who already pitch ECJ claims to them. Reports of unreclaimed tax (e.g. GOAL's UK estimates) show some money is left on the table, but that comes from operational neglect, not hidden information.
scored.right_bought: In principle the claims are bought, by assignment of the refund claim. Several EU tax authorities limit or refuse to recognise assignment of tax refund claims, or require the original beneficial owner to litigate. The seller then stays in the process, and that weakens ownership. Also, sellers who have a no-upfront-fee contingency alternative will not sell at 10-30c.
scored.buyer: Tax-claim and litigation-finance credit funds and claim trading desks, plus collecting the refunds directly. Capitalised, but niche, and they price in time value.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Adjacent rungs are reclaim servicing (a service to incumbents, which the rubric excludes), litigation finance, and maybe VAT or other tax-claim purchasing. Each is a horizontal claims-arbitrage business with no path to owning a large physical or operating chain. The pool is also finite and shrinking as member states amend discriminatory rules after rulings and limitation periods expire.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry and no big step-up. The claimants are sophisticated institutions with no-upfront-fee contingency reclaim providers and Big Four ECJ practices already offering to file for them. That keeps the purchase price far above 10-30c, so the step-up shrinks to about 1.5-5x. The work is litigation, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: This is legal-claims arbitrage: about 3x at best, slow litigation, legible data, sophisticated sellers with contingency-fee alternatives, and no vertical ladder. The relaxed C3 does not rescue it.

verified.name: Reviving zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats)
verified.one_line: Buy or option distressed parcels in stalled or antiquated pre-recession subdivisions where vested plat rights have lapsed or are uncertain and REO desks price them as raw land, re-entitle or confirm vested rights and secure will-serve letters, and sell finished-entitled lots to national homebuilders.
verified.unproven_right: Paper lots or tracts in a stalled plat with unclear lapse, reinstatement or vesting status, sold at raw-land prices.
verified.proving_step: Vested-rights determination or replat, updated development agreement and utility capacity letters: about $100k-1M and 12-36 months; likely 50-70% success since the jurisdiction approved once.
verified.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (Lennar, D.R. Horton, Pulte) via lot-option programs and land bankers (Millrose, Varde).
verified.public_data: Scanned plat books and recorded development agreements, planning and council minutes, bond and improvement-guarantee release records, tax-delinquency rolls, imagery of partly built roads and utilities (AZ, FL, NV, ID, TX).
verified.frame: The rung is 'raw or stalled paper lots to entitled, serviceable land'. The proving work (vested-rights research, replat, development agreement, will-serve letters) is about 70-80% legal and discovery work. But builders mostly pay up for FINISHED lots, and getting there takes horizontal development (roads, sewer, water, grading), commonly $40-100k+ per lot. That physical step is large and bespoke, much like the geothermal counter-example. Land bankers (Millrose, Varde) do buy entitled land, but they price it near cost plus a carry return, not as a jackpot. So the frame where discovery is 80%+ exists but is thin.
verified.step_up: The pitch claims 10-30x ($5-20k/acre to $100-300k/acre), but that compares raw land to finished lots and counts in the value of horizontal improvements still to be paid for. Entitlement alone usually lifts value about 2-5x (industry rule of thumb). Raw land per acre fell only 2.4% YoY versus 1.1% for build-ready land (Realtor.com via MortgagePoint, 2026), which shows a modest spread, not 10^3. Acres.com gives a same-county example of $3k vs $18k/acre (6x), and it argues development costs eat much of that gap. Net step-up for the entitlement rung alone: ~2-5x.
verified.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive: $100k-1M and 12-36 months per vested-rights determination or replat, plus utility capacity letters. The pitch puts the base hit rate at 50-70%, but this is weakened by Arizona's Dawe v. Scottsdale rule: a recorded plat alone does not vest rights, so you need substantial expenditure or construction in reliance. Under relaxed C3, ML that screens thousands of plats for partly built infrastructure, released bonds, utility capacity and still-valid agreements could plausibly lift cost per proven asset 1.5x or more. That counts as a full lever, docked one point because jurisdictional politics (council votes) caps what ML can predict.
verified.data: The data is public and genuinely illegible: scanned plat books, recorded development agreements, council minutes, bond-release records and imagery of half-built roads. But the outcome is partly legible already. Plat status, zoning and entitlement are usually in county GIS or planning databases, and local land brokers and entitlement attorneys already know which stalled projects are revivable. Florida's 2,600+ antiquated subdivisions (2.1M lots) have badly fragmented ownership, so assembly is the problem, not information. The 2009-2012 wave of REO-desk sales at raw-land prices has largely been absorbed by builders and land funds (2012-2022). Today's sellers are mostly individual paper-lot holders and remaining institutional owners.
verified.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought: fee title or options on lots and tracts, not free first-come claims. Single-owner stalled tracts are cheap to option. In antiquated subdivisions, though, you have to assemble hundreds of scattered owners, which is slow and full of holdouts.
verified.buyer: Public homebuilders (Lennar, D.R. Horton, Pulte) buy finished lots through option and takedown programs, and land bankers (Millrose, Varde) fund entitled land. Both are well capitalised, but they pay a premium mainly for finished, ready-to-build lots, not for entitlement alone.
verified.ladder: Strong ladder: entitlement, then horizontal land development, then a land-banking fund, then vertical homebuilding and master-planned communities, then mortgage and title. These are proven, very large markets (Lennar and Horton are each worth tens of billions). The higher rungs are capital-heavy and cyclical.
verified.fatal_flaw: The jump from paper lot to finished lot comes mostly from horizontal development: physical construction at $40-100k+ per lot, which is hard, bespoke and capital-heavy. Entitlement or vested-rights proving on its own gives only about a 2-5x step-up, and land brokers and builders already price entitlement status reasonably well. So discovery is not 80%+ of the value creation in any rung a builder pays a jackpot for.
verified.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps: proving is expensive, and ML triage of stalled plats could plausibly cut cost per proven asset 1.5x or more. But the real step-up from entitlement alone is about 2-5x, not 10^3. The claimed 10-30x needs costly physical lot development. And the REO-mispricing window from the 2008 bust has largely closed.

verifiers.evidence:
The search budget ran out after the first query (shared 200-call cap), so this verdict rests on direct fetches of primary and known sources plus domain knowledge.

1) Millrose Properties FY2025 10-K (SEC, filed 2026-03-02). Millrose is the main capitalised buyer and land banker named in the pitch, and it buys at cost, not at a step-up. The takedown price is "the acquisition price of the property that Millrose paid and the predetermined budget" for development. Its yield is 8.5% weighted average on Lennar's master program and 11% on other counterparties. It "has not obtained independent appraisals." It buys land "in most cases" with entitlements already obtained. So the land-banker exit pays cost plus carry, as the finalist said, and is no jackpot buyer.

2) Implied per-lot values from the same 10-K:
- Whole portfolio: $16.1B of future takedown proceeds over 142,139 homesites, about $113k per finished homesite including horizontal development.
- Rausch acquisition: about 25,000 homesites for about $859M, about $34k per homesite. This is a mix of entitled and partly developed land.
- Landsea/New Home: 4,186 homesites for $522.8M of land assets, about $125k per homesite.
Read together, entitled lot to finished lot is about 3x, and that gap is mostly paid-for horizontal development at about $40-80k per lot. A distressed or unclear-vesting paper lot moving to an entitled one is plausibly 2-5x. Raw-to-finished could look like 10-30x on a per-acre basis, but only by counting in physical development capital, and that is not the proving step.

3) Realtor.com via MortgagePoint (Apr 2026): median land is $62,365 per acre. Raw land is +86.5% since 2019 and build-ready land +53.3%. Over the past year raw fell 2.4% and build-ready 1.1%. These moves are similar, which points to a modest, efficiently priced raw/build-ready spread, nowhere near 10^3.

4) Acres.com gives a same-county example of $3k vs $18k per acre (6x). It says utility extension alone runs from tens of thousands to over $100k.

5) The Lincoln Institute 2012 zombie-subdivisions paper deals with legal remedies and vacating plats, not value uplift. The distressed paper lots that were mispriced in 2009-2012 were a cyclical opportunity, since absorbed, not an information-arbitrage step-up.

Market size: lot demand is large (Millrose alone funded about $5.5B in 2025, and US builders take on about 1M lots a year). But the zombie or uncertain-vesting slice is a small, fragmented subset, and its revival trades are priced by brokers near entitled-land comps.

Net step-up for the actual proving rung (vested-rights determination or replat plus will-serve letters): about 2-5x, below the ~30x refutation threshold. Revised scores:
- C1 = 1: the buyer pays cost plus carry, and the physical step is large.
- C2 = 2: about 2-5x.
- C3 = 3: proving is expensive, but council politics limits how far ML can lift results.
- C4 = 2: entitlement status is fairly legible, and brokers already know it.
- C5 = 4: the homebuilder ladder is real.
verifiers.killer: The capitalised buyers pay cost, not a step-up. Millrose's 10-K says its takedown price is its own acquisition cost plus the development budget, at an 8.5-11% yield, with no appraisals. Implied values are about $34k per entitled homesite (Rausch: 25k homesites for $859M) against about $113k per finished homesite ($16.1B over 142k). So entitlement or vested-rights proving yields roughly 2-5x. The claimed 10-30x needs about $40-80k per lot of physical horizontal development. That is far below the 10^3-10^4 jump and below the 30x refutation threshold.

verifiers.evidence:
Evidence was limited: the shared web-search budget ran out before this agent made a search, so only 4 direct fetches of the finalist's own cited sources succeeded. The rest is domain knowledge, flagged as such.

(1) Step-up is small. Realtor.com via MortgagePoint (Apr 2026): raw land is up 86.5% since 2019 (-2.4% YoY), build-ready lots up 53.3% (-1.1% YoY), and the all-listing median is $62,365/acre across 426,986 listings. That points to a modest raw-to-ready spread, not 10^3. Acres.com gives only one same-county pair ($3k vs $18k/acre, 6x), and it cites utility extension costs of 'tens of thousands to over $100,000', so physical work eats the gap.

(2) Hit rate and vesting. Dawe v. Scottsdale (AZ Sup. Ct.): recording a plat alone does not vest rights; vesting needs substantial reliance and tangible action. So many 'paper lot' plats have no vested right to prove. Proving remains political (council or rezoning), which caps how much ML can predict.

(3) Outcome is already legible. The Lincoln Institute paper on Intermountain West zombie subdivisions frames the issue as known to municipalities, with tools for vacating or amending entitlements. Cities actively track these subdivisions and often move to vacate them rather than revive them. From domain knowledge, not verified this session: Zonda (formerly Meyers Research) and John Burns sell lot-pipeline data by subdivision (vacant developed lots, lots under development, future and stalled lots) to every public builder. Regrid, Zoneomics and Gridics sell parcel and zoning layers. Land Advisors Organization and builder land teams canvass stalled communities in AZ, TX, NV and FL. Plat recordation and expiry dates sit in county recorder and planning-portal fields. So 'which plat is stalled and what its status is' is already summarised and sold.

(4) The space is occupied (domain knowledge). Forestar (majority-owned by D.R. Horton) exists to buy, entitle and develop lots for builders. Five Point, Howard Hughes, land-banking funds (Millrose, Varde, JEN Partners, Hearthstone) and post-2008 distressed buyers (Cerberus, Kennedy-Wilson era) absorbed the REO zombie-plat inventory from 2010 to 2015. Scattered Florida antiquated-subdivision paper lots are worked by mass-mail, tax-delinquent 'land flipper' operators, and assembly (2.1M lots across 2,600+ subdivisions with fragmented owners, per the FL Senate report) is the bottleneck, not information.

Net: proving is expensive (12-36 months, $100k-1M), so a relaxed C3 lever exists, but ML's incremental edge over Zonda data plus brokers is maybe 1.2-1.5x. That earns C3=3.
verifiers.killer: The 'illegible signal' is mostly legible and already sold. Subdivision lot-status data (stalled, future or vacant-developed lots) comes from vendors like Zonda and John Burns, and plat dates and zoning sit in county and GIS fields. A Forestar-style lot developer and land funds already work this niche. The 2008-era REO mispricing window is closed, and entitlement alone yields only about 2-6x. So ML has no proprietary edge in an occupied, low step-up rung.

verifiers.evidence:
The search budget was already used up, so WebSearch returned nothing. All the evidence below comes from fetching the finalist's own cited sources directly with WebFetch.

(1) The physical step dominates. Acres.com gives a same-county example of $3,000 vs $18,000 per acre (6x), and says the gap "exists for a reason." It states that infrastructure (roads, utilities, grading, permits, environmental review) "can exceed the land purchase price," and that rural utility extensions alone cost "tens of thousands to over $100,000." The claimed 10-30x needs horizontal development, which is bespoke, capital-heavy construction. That is the same failure mode as the geothermal counter-example.

(2) The market spread between raw and build-ready land is modest, not 10^3. Realtor.com data via MortgagePoint (Apr 2026): raw land rose +86.5% since 2019 and fell -2.4% YoY. Build-ready land rose +53.3% since 2019 and fell -1.1% YoY. The all-listing median was $62,365/acre in Q1 2026, which means 'raw land' in growth markets is not priced near zero.

(3) The hidden right is weak in law. Dawe v. City of Scottsdale (Ariz. S. Ct.): recording a subdivision plat "without more" creates no vested right. The land stays subject to later, stricter zoning until substantial work or construction begins. So a stale plat is not a latent asset the regulator already approved, and the '50-70% because the jurisdiction approved once' premise is unsupported.

(4) The right is legally buyable, but not cheaply at scale. The Florida Senate Interim Report 2005-120 counts more than 2.1M vacant lots in about 2,600 antiquated subdivisions. It says acquiring them is "a formidable task" because of "numerous absentee owners... located worldwide." It also says owners have "little incentive... to sell based on low property taxes and their expectation of a higher appraised value." Local power to vacate plats on its own motion (s.163.280 F.S.) was repealed in 1985. A 1986 proposal would have required owning 60% fee title before replatting, and nothing has passed since 1985. So assembly runs into holdouts with no statutory override, and the sellers are not mispricing out of illegibility.

(5) Single-owner stalled tracts can be optioned through ordinary land purchases, so the right is bought, not claimed first-come. But the 2009-2012 REO desks that priced them as raw land are largely gone, and today's institutional holders and land brokers price entitlement status.

(6) No hard exclusion applies: this is not drilling or prospecting, and the company would own the asset rather than sell a service.

Net: a rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work exists only as an entitlement-only sale, worth about 2-5x. The rung that pays 10-30x is dominated by physical construction.
verifiers.killer: The step-up the pitch relies on (10-30x) comes from horizontal lot development, roads, sewer and water, whose cost Acres.com says can exceed the land price. That is the bespoke, physical-dominated step that sank the geothermal-in-coal-mines idea. If you strip it out and sell entitlement-only land, the uplift is about 2-5x. The right is also weaker and less buyable than claimed. Under Dawe v. Scottsdale a recorded plat alone vests nothing. Florida's 2.1M antiquated lots are held by worldwide absentee owners with "little incentive to sell," and no plat-vacation power has existed since its 1985 repeal. The cheap REO-desk supply from 2009-2012 has largely been absorbed.

verified.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
verified.one_line: Option farmland next to substations ML predicts have load headroom; prove with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter; sell powered land to data-center developers. Rescore of powered brownfields with a real purchase discount.
verified.fatal_flaw: The value step-up comes from the utility's firm capacity commitment, and the utility gives that to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral (AEP's 85% take-or-pay for 12 years), not to whoever reads the data first. Study results are non-binding and lose value as others join the queue, and tariffs are now built to filter out speculative flippers. So the 100x jump needs heavy capital and upgrade risk rather than an ML-found hit. Discovery is a minority of the rung, and incumbents already screen the same fairly legible grid data.
verified.step_up: Unproven: farmland in Licking County, OH sells for about $10-15k/acre, and options run about $50-300/acre/yr. Proven: Meta paid more than $1.1M/acre near Columbus in 2025. In Northern Virginia, entitled land without power sells for about $4M/acre and powered land for at least $6M/acre (Avison Young via Data Center Knowledge). So land goes up about 70-100x, and the option premium goes up 10^3x or more. But that jump goes with committed load (an ESA plus collateral), not with a study. A study or a non-binding will-serve letter alone probably gets about 2-5x.
verified.hit_rate_capex: A study costs about $50-250k per site (Texas SB6 set a roughly $100k large-load study fee), so proving clears the C3 expense bar. Base hit rate: AEP Ohio had about 13 GW of load-study requests after its tariff, and only 5.6 GW signed ESAs (E&E News). That puts the hit rate around 40% from study to firm contract, which is inside the relaxed 30-70% band. ML ranking substations by headroom could plausibly give about 1.3-1.6x on cost per proven site against naive screening. (1) RIGHT. Buying the right is legal and can be done at scale. The State Revenue Office (sro.vic.gov.au/understanding-windfall-gains-tax) says the tax started on 1 July 2023 and is charged when land is rezoned, not when it is sold. It is 62.5% on the part of the uplift between $100k and $500k, and 50% of the whole uplift once the uplift is $500k or more. So in Victoria the state takes about half of the rezoning step-up. Because the owner bears the liability at rezoning, an option deal must either pay the owner more or the optionee absorbs the tax. Either way the realistic net multiple roughly halves, from about 2-6x to about 1.5-3x. NSW adds the Housing and Productivity Contribution and the state and local infrastructure contributions per lot. That figure comes from background knowledge; the NSW page fetch returned 404, so it is unverified here.

It takes 2-6 years and AUD $0.5-3M of specialist studies (flood, bushfire, biodiversity, traffic), gateway work, exhibition, panel hearings and negotiation of infrastructure contributions. The Kempsey case ran from 2021 lodgement to a 2023 revised proposal, and gateway extensions are routine (Central Coast extension paper). This work is political and procedural advocacy, not discovery. Structurally it looks like the geothermal counter-example, where executing the bespoke step is harder than picking the site. Picking the parcel is about 20-30% of the work, not 80% or more.

(4) EXCLUSIONS. Not a hard exclusion: no drilling or prospecting, and the company would own the option and realise the uplift itself rather than sell a service. But the capitalised buyers (Stockland, Mirvac, Lendlease, Frasers, Peet) also option land and run rezonings in-house, so they are direct competitors for the same rung.

That fails C1 in the same way as the geothermal counter-example. Meanwhile the right is only cheap where the hit rate collapses, because parcels inside published growth areas already trade at hope value. Victoria's Windfall Gains Tax, in force since 1 July 2023, takes 50% of any rezoning uplift of $500k or more at the moment of rezoning, cutting the already modest 2-6x step-up to about 1.5-3x net.

However, each approval is written directly into a legible field, the zoning status or a published board vote, which is the pattern of regulators writing in the answer. Power availability, the main driver of value, sits mostly in non-public utility load studies.
verified.right_bought: Options are bought from farmers, but those owners are not unable to read the market. Developers are already offering 6-10x farmland value unsolicited, sellers widely know a data center premium exists, and some families refuse $26M offers. Tract and brokers run the same playbook, so there is little purchase discount for being able to read the data.
verified.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) and data center developers or REITs (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, Tract). They are deeply capitalised and actively buy entitled, powered land.
verified.ladder: The ladder runs: entitled land, then powered land (utility agreements and substations), then a powered shell, then a developed campus, then operating or leasing data centers, possibly with power generation behind it. The rungs above are real and enormous but crowded with heavily capitalised incumbents (Tract, QTS, Digital Realty).
verified.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 helps, because rising opposition pushes approvals to ~40-60% on expensive $50-300k, multi-year attempts. But the zoning-only step-up is ~3-30x, sellers already know the premium, and power rather than zoning drives value, so C1, C2 and C4 stay weak.

The prices below therefore come from the two pages I could reach, the finalist's own cited figures, and figures I knew from before this conversation, which are marked as such.

(1) The proven-right price is real. Datacenterwatch.org/report says Amazon's Warrenton, VA site was a "$39 million, 42-acre plot", which works out to about $0.93M/acre. The fb.org Market Intel page says land in high-demand areas "can reach millions of dollars per acre" and links to a figure of $4M/acre in Ashburn. (2) The unproven-right price is not near zero. The finalist cites Kentucky farmland at about $6k/acre (USDA 2024) and pre-rezoning developer offers of about $35-60k/acre (LEX18/TweakTown, which returned 403 so I could not check it). Landowners already price in the data center option.

(3) The step-up:
- Raw farmland to fully entitled, powered land in Northern Virginia: about 30-60x (roughly $20-30k up to $0.9-1M/acre). Most of that comes from Dominion transmission and fibre access, not from the zoning vote.
- Zoning alone, measured from the already-raised option strike: about 3-10x in secondary markets (strike around $30-60k/acre against entitled sales around $100-300k/acre, recalled ranges for Tract-style deals, not checked).
- Best case on option capital: an option premium of roughly $1-3k/acre plus $50-300k of entitlement cost spread over 200-500 acres puts about $2-4k/acre at risk for a spread of about $100k/acre, or roughly 25-50x. That is still well below 10^3-10^4x.

(4) Buyers are real and capitalised: hyperscalers, QTS/Blackstone, Vantage and Tract. But they mostly sign land contracts that are contingent on rezoning and do the entitlement themselves. They pay the full price only after power is confirmed, not immediately on a zoning hit, so a pure-zoning middleman has a thin role.

(5) The report gives no total project count, so no approval rate can be worked out. Its executive summary counts 6 projects blocked (about $18B) and 10 delayed (about $46B). Market size could not be verified this session. My unverified estimate is a few hundred large data center land sales per year in the US, worth roughly tens of billions of dollars, mostly concentrated in about 10 power-rich markets.
verifiers.killer: The step-up from zoning alone is about 3-10x off a strike price that farmers have already raised to 5-10x farmland value because developers make offers before any rezoning. Even counted as leverage on option capital it reaches only about 25-50x. The 30-60x jump in Northern Virginia comes from power and fibre, not from the rezoning vote. Capitalised buyers usually sign contracts contingent on rezoning and carry the entitlement themselves, paying the full price only after power is confirmed. So nothing near a 10^3x step-up is realised at once on a zoning hit, and the right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the market.

What ML could still add is prediction before options are signed, from staff reports, minutes and opposition signals. But the strongest predictors are already tracked and aggregated:
- Data Center Watch (datacenterwatch.org/report) keeps a continuously updated database of activist groups, petitions and the officials blocking or delaying projects. Its first report counted 142+ groups (42 in Virginia), 23+ petitions with 31,000+ signatures, 16 projects blocked or delayed, and $64B at stake; later updates cited by the finalist reach 843 groups and 45 projects / $68B. The database's public accessibility is unclear: the page says contact info@ or the PDF. It names zoning-law tracking as future work, so a per-county outcome tracker is not fully commoditised yet.
- Paces (paces.com) sells an AI agent plus power and permitting reports that 'find viable sites, de-risk development' for power and data center developers; named customers include Qcells and Demeter Land Development. This is an AI layer over the county permitting and ordinance data. Unverified from memory: Paces is VC-funded and uses LLMs to extract ordinances.
- LandGate's site menu lists Data Center Siting, Data Center Due Diligence, Offtake Capacity, Available Transfer Capacity, Fiber and Power Pricing. Vendors already package the power and fiber signal, which carries most of the value.

(2) The space is occupied by capitalised players running exactly this own-the-asset playbook:
- Tract does option, assemble and entitle, then sell powered land to hyperscalers. Background knowledge, unverified because tract.com did not load: Tract holds tens of thousands of acres and has raised large sums.
- Unverified: PowerHouse, Prologis, EdgeCore, Rowan, many land funds, and local brokers. Developers make unsolicited offers of 6-10x farmland value before any rezoning (finalist's tweaktown/LEX18 and USDA KY ~$6.2k/acre figures).

But the lift ML adds over a broker or Paces-style baseline that already sees opposition groups, moratoriums and board votes is probably ~1.2-1.5x at best, not >=1.5x over the status quo. Power availability lives in non-public utility load studies, which planning text cannot reach.

(4) Step-up. The zoning-only increment from an already-bid price is ~3-10x (best ~10-30x), far below 10^3.

(5) There is no purchase discount from illegibility. Sellers know the premium (the family that refused $26M).
verifiers.killer: The legibility gap is already closed. Approvals are published board votes. Opposition is tracked and aggregated by Data Center Watch. AI permitting and power-risk reports already exist (Paces) alongside power and fiber siting data (LandGate). Tract and other capitalised land developers already run the option-entitle-sell model. Landowners get 6-10x offers before rezoning, so there is no discount to capture. The step-up from zoning alone is ~3-10x, and power, which ML over planning records cannot see, drives most of the value. ML over planning minutes gives at most a marginal edge in an occupied space.

Search limit: the shared web-search budget for this turn ran out before my first query (both searches returned "budget used up"). Of the two direct fetches I tried, the tweaktown source returned 403. The fb.org source worked. So this verdict rests on the finalist's own sources, the fb.org page and background knowledge I could not re-check online here; none of the knowledge-only figures below were confirmed with sources in this session.

(1) Can the right be bought cheaply? Legally, yes: farmland options are an ordinary contract. Cheaply, from owners who cannot read the data, no.
- AFBF (fb.org) says that as parcels are rezoned or merely considered for rezoning, "farmland takes on value tied to future development". So the speculative premium is already priced in before any vote.
- The same page says data center land in high-demand areas reaches "millions of dollars per acre". It links to a report of Ashburn residents being offered $4M/acre, though that figure appears only in the link's URL, not the article text.
- The finalist's own figures say Kentucky owners already receive unsolicited offers of $35-60k/acre against about $6k farmland, and a family turned down $26M. Sellers know the premium.
- Background knowledge, not checked online: in Prince William County's Digital Gateway (about 2,100 acres), the landowners organised themselves, pursued the rezoning and marketed the land to QTS and Compass, as I recall at roughly $1M/acre or more. The owners captured the entitlement step-up; no outside optioner did.
- Background knowledge, not checked online: a court later voided that rezoning on procedural grounds, so even a "hit" can be undone after closing.
- Taken together, the information asymmetry this frame needs (sellers unable to read the signal) does not exist.

(2) Is the proving step trivial? No. Value depends on power, not zoning.
- The finalist itself admits power is the main value driver and that utility load studies are not public.
- Background knowledge, not checked online: utilities now require large-load tariffs with minimum-demand or take-or-pay commitments from creditworthy customers. Examples I recall are AEP Ohio's data center tariff (about 85% minimum demand billing) and Dominion's proposed new large-load rate class (GS-5).
- If that holds, a land-holding entity cannot credibly sign those commitments. Power needs substations and transmission lead times of years, often studies plus deposits in the millions, and usually a named end-user.
- That makes the dominant step bespoke, physical and capital-heavy, structurally like the geothermal counter-example rather than a cheap exploratory drill.
- Rezoning without power yields roughly the 3-10x step the finalist reported, not 10^3.

(3) Hard exclusions: none triggered. It is not drilling or prospecting, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service.

(4) Data: the outcome is written into a legible public field (the board vote or zoning status). Opposition signals are visible in local news and organised groups (Data Center Watch counts 843 groups). Brokers and Tract-type players already run this screen. The ML edge is limited to picking which counties to pursue.

Scores under the relaxed rubric:
- C3 = 3. Proving is expensive ($50-300k plus 1-2 years of carry, about 40-60% approval), so the lever exists. But ML over minutes likely gives about 1.2-1.5x, because the decisive variable (power) is not in the data.
- C5 = 3. The ladder above (powered land, shell, campus, operations) is real but crowded.
verifiers.killer: The model only works if sellers cannot read the signal and the proving step is cheap paperwork. Neither holds. Farmland owners already see the data center premium and capture it themselves. In Prince William's Digital Gateway, from memory and not confirmed online here, owners organised their own rezoning and sold at about $1M/acre, and the rezoning was later voided in court. AFBF notes that land gains value as soon as rezoning is merely considered. The value-making step is power, not zoning. It needs years of utility studies and deposits, plus, as I recall but could not verify here, minimum-demand or take-or-pay commitments under large-load tariffs that only a creditworthy end-user can sign. That makes the dominant step bespoke and capital-heavy, like the geothermal counter-example, and leaves zoning alone with only a ~3-10x step-up.

verified.name: Air-permitted behind-the-meter power pad for DC campuses
verified.one_line: Option industrial or ag parcels on interstate gas laterals, prove a PSD/Title V or minor-source air permit for 100-500MW of onsite turbines or engines plus a gas tap agreement, and sell the permitted, fuel-secured pad to off-grid AI campus developers.
verified.unproven_right: Land option near pipeline laterals from owners unaware that attainment status and dispersion profile make the parcel permittable.
verified.proving_step: Air dispersion modelling, PSD/Title V application and approval, pipeline tap or precedent agreement: about $300k-1.5M and 12-24 months; about 40-65% success.
verified.proven_buyer: Off-grid AI campus developers, hyperscalers and IPPs building bridge power (Crusoe, xAI-type builders, Williams-style deals).
verified.public_data: State air permit databases and scanned permits (TCEQ, ODEQ, PA DEP), EPA RACT/BACT/LAER Clearinghouse, EPA Green Book nonattainment maps, PHMSA and FERC pipeline filings, EIA gas pipeline data.
verified.rough_step_up: About 10-40x on site value; depends on gas-for-DC demand persisting.
verified.frame: The rung is: an optioned parcel plus an air permit plus a gas tap, sold as a pad ready for behind-the-meter power. Nothing physical is built inside the rung. It is all paperwork, dispersion modelling and negotiation. But the work is mostly proving (permit engineering and pipeline negotiation), not ML-driven discovery. Finding a parcel in an attainment area next to a lateral is maybe 20-30% of the work. The buyer is clearly capitalised: Pacifico got a 7.65 GW TCEQ permit for GW Ranch (Pecos), then the ~8,000-acre site was sold to Amazon. One catch: the permit's value depends on turbine supply and firm gas capacity, which the rung does not secure.
verified.step_up: Unproven: West Texas or Midwest industrial/ag land at ~$2-5k/acre. Proven: a Pecos TX 770-acre '2.4 GW energy campus' is listed at ~CAD 168M, which I calculate as ~CAD 218k/acre (~US$160k/acre). That is roughly 30-80x, but it is an asking price, not a closed sale. Benchmark: Northern Virginia powered land at $6M/acre vs $4M/acre for land with entitlements but no power (Avison Young via DatacenterKnowledge). That is only 1.5x between entitled and powered. Overall ~10-50x, so C2 = 3.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Per the candidate: $300k-1.5M and 12-24 months per attempt, 40-65% success. That meets the relaxed expense bar. But a Texas seller's listing claims expedited TCEQ permitting in 60-90 days for SCR-controlled units. So in permissive states the permit is cheap and fast, and failures come mostly from gas capacity and turbine availability, not siting. ML could pick parcels in attainment areas with headroom on laterals and few nearby PSD increment consumers. A plausible gain is ~1.2-1.5x on cost per proven pad, not clearly >=1.5x. C3 = 3.
verified.data: Mixed. EPA Green Book nonattainment areas, EIA and PHMSA pipeline maps and RBLC BACT entries are already legible GIS or database fields. Lateral capacity and tap feasibility are partly hidden in FERC filings and in negotiations with operators. Scanned state permits (PA DEP, ODEQ) are illegible, but they mostly record precedent, not the outcome for a new parcel. Landowners near laterals are cheap to option, but rural owners in Texas and Ohio know about the data center boom, and brokers are already marketing 'energy campus' land. The edge is thin. C4 = 2.
verified.right_bought: Purchase or lease options on industrial or ag parcels next to interstate gas laterals in attainment counties, bought from farmers and industrial owners. A pipeline precedent or tap agreement is negotiated, not bought.
verified.buyer: Hyperscalers (Amazon bought GW Ranch), off-grid AI campus developers (Crusoe, xAI), IPPs and midstream companies building bridge power (Williams for Meta in New Albany, OH, 200 MW).
verified.ladder: Strong: permitted pad, then turbine and engine procurement and EPC, then an owned onsite IPP selling power under a PPA, then powered shell or campus developer, then a gas-integrated compute or energy platform. Each rung is large. C5 = 4.
verified.fatal_flaw: The binding constraint is not the permit. Gas turbines have ~5-year backlogs (GE Vernova sold into 2030, Mitsubishi sold out through 2028, 260-week lead times), and firm pipeline capacity is also scarce. Air permits are written for specific equipment and are fast to get in Texas (60-90 days expedited). A permitted pad with no turbine slot or firm gas is not where the scarce value sits. Buyers like Amazon, Crusoe and Williams permit for themselves around the turbines they have secured, so the step-up goes to whoever holds equipment and gas, not to the holder of the paper.
verified.one_line_reason: The ladder is real and the buyer is capitalised, but this is permitting and siting work, not ML discovery over illegible data. The scarce input is turbines and gas, not the permit, so the expected step-up (~10-50x) and the ML lift (~1.2-1.5x) are both modest.

verifiers.evidence:
I found no closed sale of a 'permitted pad' (land plus air permit plus gas tap, nothing else) at a disclosed price, so neither the step-up nor the buyer is verified.

(1) The headline comp does not show a pad being sold. The Amazon / GW Ranch (Pecos, about 8,000-8,400 acres) price was not disclosed in any source I found (DCD, Baxtel, letsdatascience, aiweekly). Amazon bought the land, but Pacifico appears to keep the 7.65 GW (5,000 MW nominal per TCEQ) gas project and sell Amazon its power. Pacifico's money comes from a power deal, a higher rung, not from flipping a permitted pad.

(2) Landowners are already getting the step-up before any proving. In Hill County TX, developer RCM Hill signed contracts in 2025-26 for more than 800 acres at more than $80M, about $100k/acre. That is 14x the $7,100/acre appraisal (KWTX, 30 Jun 2026). Owners near power and gas know about the boom, so the 'unproven right bought cheaply' assumption fails.

(3) The big per-acre premiums go to grid power, not to paper permits:
- Bitdeer paid about $500k/acre for 200 acres in Milam County (CoStar).
- A Claros broker puts power-ready TX sites at about $800k/acre, vs $2.5-10k/acre without power studies (Bisnow).
- Northern Virginia: powered land at $6M/acre vs $4M/acre entitled but unpowered, only 1.5x (Avison Young).
None of these is the value of an air permit alone.

(4) Permits are cheap, fast and plentiful, so they are not the scarce input:
- TCEQ has issued many data-center gas permits up to 500 MW within about a month. One for 206 generators was applied for Dec 23 and granted Jan 14 (States Newsroom).
- At least 38 TX data centers have had simplified on-site generation permits since 2024. Many sit just under the 100 tpy NOx threshold, e.g. Vantage at 99.8 tpy (Floodlight via Forklog).
- Cleanview counts 59 US data centers planning about 90 GW of their own generation, but only about 2 GW was commissioned by mid-2026. Permitted but unbuilt paper is abundant. Turbines (backlogged to 2028-2030) and firm gas are what is scarce.

(5) The market is small. Bisnow counts only 16-20 US data center site sales per quarter of every kind (about $3.3B in Q1 2026). Behind-the-meter gas pad sales are a small subset, probably dozens a year at most.

My estimate for a permit-only pad: land at $5-10k/acre in a contested market, with the permit plus tap adding perhaps 3-20x. Much of the jump to about $100k/acre is already paid to landowners before any proving. That puts it under the ~30x bar, which is not 10^3. In Texas the proving step is weeks and low cost, so it fails the relaxed C3 expense bar. PSD/Title V in nonattainment-adjacent or stricter states (PA, OH) is expensive, but no buyer-price evidence turned up there either.
verifiers.killer: The value is not in the permit. Texas issues behind-the-meter gas permits for up to 500 MW within weeks under simplified procedures. 59 data-center projects plan about 90 GW of on-site generation, but only about 2 GW is commissioned, so the scarce inputs are turbines and firm gas, not paperwork. Landowners already get about 14x appraisal ($100k/acre in Hill County) before any proving. I found no closed sale of a permit-only pad. The one flagship case (GW Ranch) has an undisclosed price, and Pacifico appears to monetise it through a power sale to Amazon, not by flipping the pad. The realisable step-up is likely under 30x, and much of it already goes to the landowner.

verifiers.evidence:
DATA IS ALREADY LEGIBLE AND SOLD BY VENDORS. LandGate sells a parcel-level data-center screening product: gas pipeline locations, diameters, status and operators; gas offtake points (it calls them the gas-side equivalent of substations); compressor stations; 30-year well-level production forecasts tied to midstream; and a dedicated EPA non-attainment layer by pollutant and severity, stated to show 'how much room remains before major source review'. It has a parcel search filtering by distance to pipeline and offtake capacity, export/API access, and an 'off-market listings direct from landowners' channel (landgate.com/btm-natural-gas, /energy-markets/data-centers, /news/air-permitting-for-data-centers..., /news/the-fastest-path-to-data-center-land-off-market-listings...). Enverus and TGS market similar 'gas assets positioned to power AI data centers' analytics. Cleanview tracks every behind-the-meter project: 46 projects / 56 GW in Feb 2026, then ~59 projects / ~90 GW, ~75% gas. Public Citizen runs public trainings on finding and tracking TCEQ data-center air permits, so permit status is a searchable public record. The screening signal (attainment, lateral proximity, offtake) is a commodity layer, and the outcome (permit granted or not) sits in a legible state status field. That is exactly the failure mode the rubric warns about.
PROVING IS NOT EXPENSIVE OR RISKY IN THE KEY STATE. In January 2025 TCEQ created a non-rule Air Quality Standard Permit for natural-gas EGUs (tceq.texas.gov egu_sp). It makes the permit largely a template exercise, and TCEQ approved GW Ranch at 7.65 GW. The real failure modes are firm gas and turbine slots, and ML over public files does not improve either.
SPACE IS CROWDED WITH CAPITALISED PLAYERS DOING THE SAME RUNG: Pacifico (GW Ranch, permitted, sold to Amazon); Fermi America (Carson County TCEQ permits); Beacon Data Centers (2.4 GW Dove Creek application); Thunderhead Energy Solutions (11 sites, 23 GW, seeking air exemptions); RPower + Wise Asset (3,000+ acres of DFW 'natural gas powered land', with permitting included); LandBridge + NRG (1.1 GW Reeves County, air permit filed) and LandBridge/PowerBridge (3,400 acres, 2 GW); APR Energy (800 acres, Pampa, 400 MW approved); New Era Energy & Digital (Ector County, Vistra PPA, calls itself 'permitted powered land'); TerraVolt (Idaho, pre-permitted, BTM gas); Hedgehog/Idemitsu (Navarro County, 600 MW); Kodiak Gas (BTM recip engines); NextEra + Exxon; Chevron + TPL/Microsoft.
LANDOWNERS ARE NOT NAIVE. Texas Pacific Land, LandBridge and EagleRock actively market their Permian surface to data-center developers, and TPL paid ~$10k/acre for 10,000+ acres near Abilene. The 'cheap option from owners who cannot read the data' premise fails, and the unproven baseline is already raised, so the step-up is ~10-20x off asking prices.
verifiers.killer: The siting signal (attainment status, pipeline and offtake proximity, permit status) is already packaged as commercial GIS layers by LandGate, Enverus and Cleanview, with an off-market landowner channel built in. Texas made the air permit a standardised template (the NG EGU standard permit, January 2025). At least 12 capitalised developers (Pacifico, Fermi, Thunderhead, RPower/Wise, LandBridge/NRG, APR, Beacon, New Era, TerraVolt, Hedgehog, and others) plus sophisticated landowners (TPL, LandBridge) are already running this exact rung. There is no illegible-data edge, no naive seller, and the scarce inputs (turbines, firm gas) sit outside what ML can find.

verifiers.evidence:
LIMIT: this turn's shared search budget ran out after 2 searches (the harness's 200-search cap per turn), so the case below rests on 2 searches, 1 fetched TCEQ PDF and the finalist's own sources. Where I rely on regulatory knowledge without a source, I say so.

(1) The rung has one proof point, and its price is unknown. Pacifico's GW Ranch got its TCEQ permit for 7.65 GW of gas generation on 26 Jan 2026 (BusinessWire, Enerdata). Reports disagree on whether Amazon bought the site or is financing the plant, and none give a price or say how much capacity is contracted (aiweekly, energytech). There is no closed-sale comparable for a 100-500 MW 'permitted pad' as a standalone product. The only priced data point is still an asking price on a LoopNet listing.

(2) Air permits are not portable paper. To transfer a TCEQ NSR permit under 30 TAC 116.110(e), the new owner must accept every permit condition and every representation, with the same pollutants and emission quantities (TCEQ ownership-change filing 37589-tc). BACT, and therefore the permit, is tied to the specific turbine or engine model. A buyer holding different turbines, which is the scarce input, has to amend or re-permit. From my regulatory knowledge, not verified this turn: under 40 CFR 52.21(r)(2), a PSD permit lapses if construction does not start within 18 months. So the 'proven' asset decays unless the buyer already holds equipment.

(3) The fast permit route is not the step being proved. The TCEQ standard permit for natural gas electric generating units covers only spark-ignited engines. It excludes turbines, allows at most 6 engines and 400 operating hours per rolling 12 months, and sets property-line setbacks. That makes it backup or peaking power, not 100-500 MW of baseload campus power. The 'cheap and fast' TX route therefore does not reach the product's scale. The PSD/Title V route is expensive, but it is engineering and modelling work, not discovery.

(4) The value-bearing rights cannot be bought from owners who fail to read the data. Firm transport and the tap are allocated by the pipeline operator under its FERC tariff or an open season, at regulated rates. You win them by negotiating and paying, not by optioning them cheaply from someone uninformed. Brokers already market 'energy campus' land (the LoopNet Pecos listing), so landowners are not unaware.

(5) The physical step is trivial only because the rung leaves it out. The geothermal-style bottleneck (building a bespoke 100-500 MW plant, plus 5-year turbine backlogs per the finalist's own sources) sits with the buyer. The buyer also controls the value: Amazon, Crusoe and Williams permit around turbines they have already secured.

(6) Exclusion check: no hard exclusion applies. A gas tap is not exploration drilling, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service. Not excluded.

Revised scores: C1=2 (the rung exists on paper, but proving/discovery is well under 80% of the value and the permit is not freely saleable). C2=2 (the 10-40x figure rests on one asking price; with equipment-specific permits that lapse, the realisable premium is more like 3-10x). C3=2 (PSD is expensive, but the ML lift on cost per proven pad is under 1.5x: attainment status, pipelines and RBLC entries are already legible, and failures come from gas and turbines). C4=1 (the outcome inputs are legible GIS and database fields, and the scarce right is a tariffed allocation). C5=4 (the ladder is real). Total 11.
verifiers.killer: The scarce rights are firm pipeline capacity and turbine slots. Pipelines allocate capacity under FERC tariffs and open seasons, so it is not bought cheaply from uninformed owners, and turbine slots sit with the buyers. The air permit is written for specific equipment, transfers only on its original representations (30 TAC 116.110(e)), and, from regulatory knowledge not verified this turn, PSD permits lapse 18 months after issue without construction. A paper-only permitted pad therefore loses most of its value unless the buyer already owns matching turbines. That makes it a negotiated input to someone else's plant, not a discrete rung that holds a 10^3-10^4 step-up.

verified.name: Cryptic Clusters / Legacy Actinomycete Libraries: orphaned natural-product collections re-read for novel clusters
verified.one_line: Acquire mothballed pharma and academic actinomycete/fungal natural-product strain and extract libraries cheaply, sequence them, ML-rank silent biosynthetic gene clusters for novel high-value chemotypes (anti-Gram-negative, antifungal, ADC payloads), and ferment or express the top few to prove a compound.
verified.fatal_flaw: The proving step is both the dominant cost and the dominant failure mode, which inverts Terranox's 95-5 discovery/physical ratio into roughly 25-75: 11-32% of expressed clusters yield any detectable compound at $50-200k and 6-24 months each, and a commercially viable chemotype is <1-2% per cluster, so ML can only re-rank the cheap part and cannot touch the expensive part. This is exactly the geothermal-in-abandoned-coal-mines failure. Compounding it, the discovery edge is already commoditised: antiSMASH/antiSMASH-DB/BiG-FAM/MIBiG publicly novelty-score nearly every public BGC, and private collections are made legible by $50-200/isolate sequencing that any buyer can run, so there is no durable illegible-data moat and the sellers are sophisticated specialists rather than owners who cannot read their own asset.
verified.step_up: Right side: physical legacy libraries change hands for storage cost or effectively nothing — Sanofi transferred ~110,000 strains (~80,000 actinomycetes, ~70 years of industrial screening) to Fraunhofer IME in 2020 as a shared-resource transfer with no sale price; Ginkgo acquired Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform (>135,000 strains, >4M predicted BGCs) in 2019 on undisclosed, plausibly low-single-digit-million terms as a cast-off asset; Deinove licensed 400 of Naicons' ~45,000 strains, price undisclosed. Call the unproven right ~$10-100 per strain-equivalent, i.e. near zero. Proven side: a preclinical natural-product antibacterial or ADC-payload asset with in vivo proof-of-concept licenses in the low tens of millions upfront in a good case (single-asset preclinical anti-infective deals typically $1-20M upfront plus milestones); ADC payload/linker platform deals go higher but are platform, not single-compound, deals. So ~100-1000x on the right itself, which is C2 = 3 — but, crucially, the step-up is NOT immediate on a hit: it arrives only after the expensive expression-isolation-structure-assay-in-vivo chain, not at the moment of proving existence. A cluster shown merely to express a novel scaffold with no potency data moves value maybe 10-30x, not 10^4x.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving is genuinely expensive, which is what the relaxed C3 rewards. Detection of any compound from a heterologously expressed silent cluster: 11-32% across four large-scale studies (2023 review, PMC10727000). Across 50 studies Jan 2018-Jun 2023, only ~63 new natural-product families emerged in total. Probability a given silent cluster yields a novel compound with commercially relevant potency, selectivity and developability: my estimate <1-2%. Cost per proving attempt: $50-200k and 6-24 months per cluster (consistent with CRO/biofoundry refactoring plus isolation, structure elucidation by NMR/MS, and assay panels); a full isolate-to-structure-to-in-vivo package is my estimate $0.5-2M per serious candidate. Comfortably above the ~$50k / years-per-attempt bar. ML lever: ranking clusters by predicted novelty and by predicted expressibility in a chosen heterologous host plausibly lifts "yields a detectable novel compound" from ~15% to ~30%, i.e. ~2x on cost per proven asset — a full-strength lever by the relaxed standard, so C3 rises from near-0 under the strict rubric to 4. It is 4 rather than 5 because a large part of that ranking is already done for free by public tools (see C4), so the *marginal* ML lift over an incumbent using antiSMASH + BiG-SLiCE is much smaller than the lift over naive random picking.
verified.frame: The sellable rung would be "a legacy strain/extract library plus one novel-chemotype compound proven to exist and hit a target," sold or licensed to a pharma/biotech partner. But inside that rung, discovery (sequence + ML-rank silent BGCs) is roughly 20-30% of the work and the "physical step" (refactor/express/ferment, isolate, elucidate structure, assay for potency, selectivity, developability) is 70-80% — the opposite of Terranox's 95-5 split. The physical step is neither trivial, cheap nor abstracted: 11-32% of heterologously expressed clusters yield any detectable compound, and each attempt is $50-200k and 6-24 months. There is a capitalised buyer (big pharma buys anti-Gram-negative and ADC-payload assets), but it buys a validated hit/lead, not a ranked cluster list, so the buyer sits several expensive rungs above the discovery output. C1 = 2 (buyer exists; discovery share and physical-step triviality both fail).
verified.data: The underlying data is partly public and partly private, but the key failure is legibility of the OUTCOME, not of the raw data. Genomes of public strains are in NCBI; antiSMASH, antiSMASH-DB, BiG-FAM/BiG-SLiCE and MIBiG already auto-annotate essentially every public BGC and attach a novelty/distance-to-known score — i.e. the regulator-equivalent has already written the answer into a legible field, exactly the failure mode prior hunts identified. The genuinely illegible asset is the *unsequenced* private legacy collection (freezer vials, paper screening logs, 1960s-80s fermentation records), and there is real latent value there — but sequencing is cheap (~$50-200/isolate), so any acquirer can make it legible in weeks, which means the illegibility is a temporary and purchasable condition, not a durable moat. Owners (Fraunhofer, Naicons, university collections, ex-Sanofi/Merck/Pfizer archives) are specialists who can read the data as well as the acquirer can; they are not naive sellers. C4 = 2.
verified.right_bought: Right bought: physical strain/extract collections plus the IP and freedom-to-operate to commercialise compounds derived from them — acquired by asset transfer, licence, or by taking over a mothballed collection's custody and storage costs. Price is near zero to low single-digit millions for 10^4-10^5 strains. This part is real: the right is cheap and the step-up on a validated compound is large. The problem is that the right conveys optionality on a very expensive, low-yield proving process rather than on a cheap, decisive one.
verified.buyer: A capitalised buyer exists and is well funded: large pharma and anti-infective-focused biotech buying preclinical-to-Phase-I anti-Gram-negative, antifungal and ADC-payload assets, plus non-dilutive funders (BARDA, CARB-X, AMR Action Fund) who pay for anti-infective development. But the buyer buys a compound with target engagement and in vivo data, not a proven-existent cluster — so the buyer is two or three rungs above the rung this company would win, and the company must fund those rungs itself.
verified.ladder: Clear rungs above: proven compound -> lead optimisation -> IND -> clinic -> commercial product, and horizontally a strain-library-as-platform business. A winner could in principle become a large pharma company, so the ladder is real. But each rung is capital-intensive, slow and failure-prone in a way mine-building is not — climbing it means becoming a drug developer with ~10-year, ~$1B+ per-approval economics, so the smallest rung does not cheaply bootstrap the whole chain. C5 = 3.
verified.one_line_reason: Relaxed C3 genuinely rescues only the hit-rate leg (proving is expensive and ML plausibly gives ~2x on cost per proven asset, so C3 goes from near-0 to 4), but the structural defects are untouched: the expensive, low-yield wet-lab proving step dominates the work instead of discovery, and the discovery answer is already written into free public novelty scores while private collections are cheaply sequenced by anyone — so total 14/25 and the fatal flaw stands.

The transaction evidence below is from my own knowledge of anti-infective and ADC dealmaking up to mid-2026, flagged as unverified-this-round; the candidate's own cited figures are used where they cut against it.

PROVEN RIGHT (price received) — this is where the lens breaks the thesis, in two places.

(a) There is no transaction at the rung the company would actually win. "Silent cluster expressed, novel scaffold confirmed to exist" has no buyer and no price. I know of no class of transactions in which a validated-but-unoptimised novel natural-product scaffold, without potency/selectivity/in vivo data, was bought for cash. The first real market is lead-to-IND, which is 2-3 rungs and (candidate's own number) $0.5-2M per serious candidate above the proving step. Terranox's defining property — the 10^4 step-up lands the instant the drill core assays — is absent: nobody pays on existence.

(b) The buyer at the top of the antibacterial ladder is demonstrably NOT capitalised, which is fatal because anti-Gram-negative is the candidate's headline chemotype. The clearing prices for FULLY DE-RISKED, FDA-APPROVED novel antibacterials in 2019-2020 were: Achaogen (plazomicin, approved 2018, >$1B lifetime spend) sold in Chapter 11 for ~$16M; Melinta (four approved antibiotics) reorganised into Deerfield's hands for roughly $140M of new money; Tetraphase (eravacycline, approved) acquired by La Jolla for ~$14M cash plus CVRs after a bidding contest in the tens of millions; Aradigm and Paratek followed the same pattern (Paratek ~$462M including CVRs was the outlier). Big-pharma exits — Novartis, AstraZeneca, Sanofi, Allergan — removed the acquirers. If an APPROVED antibiotic clears at $14-16M, a preclinical scaffold two rungs below cannot be worth the low tens of millions upfront that the candidate assumes; realistic upfronts for preclinical/lead-stage antibacterials are $0-5M with the value in back-loaded milestones (e.g. Entasis-Zai Lab-style regional deals at ~$5M upfront). CARB-X ($1-5M), BARDA and the AMR Action Fund are non-dilutive funders and equity investors in clinical-stage companies — they do not BUY the asset, so they never realise a step-up for the owner.

(c) ADC payloads: here the buyer is real and rich, but the transactions are platform/linker deals on clinically validated chemistry, not purchases of a novel cytotoxin. Araris (Taiho, ~$400M upfront + ~$740M milestones) and Synaffix (Lonza, ~€100M upfront + milestones) sold conjugation/linker platforms; the payloads in essentially every approved or late-stage ADC are known chemotypes (auristatins, camptothecins/DXd, maytansinoids, PBDs, calicheamicin). I am aware of no transaction where a novel natural-product payload scaffold alone commanded a material upfront — payload novelty has repeatedly been a liability (tox, index) rather than a priced asset.

STEP-UP ARITHMETIC: library acquisition $0.1-2M; ML-ranked proving at the candidate's own $50-200k and ~15-30% detection per cluster means ~$0.3-1.3M of attempts per expressed novel scaffold, then $0.5-2M more to reach a licensable in vivo package, with <1-2% of clusters reaching commercial relevance. Gross against acquisition cost looks like 10-100x only if you ignore the proving spend; measured as value-on-capital-at-risk, which is the only honest comparison to Terranox's $1/ha → $10,000/ha, it is roughly 3-10x and arrives 3-7 years later. Under the lens's own threshold (refute if under ~30x) this fails.

MARKET SIZE: preclinical-stage novel-mechanism antibacterial licensing transactions with disclosed cash upfronts run at single digits per year globally, and the pool of acquirers is shrinking, not growing. That is not a market a "capitalised buyer pays at once" claim can rest on. Contrast: mine developers buy proven uranium ground routinely and pay cash on drill results.
verifiers.killer: An FDA-APPROVED novel antibacterial clears at $14-16M (Achaogen/plazomicin ~$16M in Chapter 11 after >$1B spend; Tetraphase/eravacycline ~$14M cash to La Jolla), so the terminal buyer for the candidate's headline chemotype is not capitalised — and nothing is paid at all for the rung the company would actually win, since no one buys a "novel scaffold proven to exist" without potency and in vivo data. VERIFIED THIS SESSION (one source; this turn's shared web-search budget was exhausted before my other queries ran, so the remaining points are reasoned from the candidate's own numbers rather than freshly sourced — flagging that explicitly):

1. The physical proving step is the dominant failure mode, confirmed first-hand. Fetched PMC10727000 (2023 review of heterologous expression of silent BGCs): success rate of getting ANY detectable compound from an expressed cluster "varied from 11% to 32%" across four large-scale studies — Gummerlich 2020 11% (4 products detected, only 2 produced in enough quantity to isolate), Enghiad 2021 16% (7/43 BGCs gave HPLC peaks), Libis 2022 24% (15/58), Ayikpoe 2022 32% (27/83 RiPP BGCs gave mass features). One outlier (Wang et al.) reached 67% only by screening multiple hosts, i.e. by multiplying the wet-lab cost per cluster. Across 50 studies from Jan 2018 to mid-2023 the entire global field produced ~63 new natural-product families. The review gives no cost or time figures, so the candidate's $50-200k / 6-24 months per cluster remains its own estimate, uncorroborated.

Read against the lens: the detection step is not merely expensive, it is the step where the asset is actually proven, and it is a bespoke per-cluster wet-lab build (refactor, host selection, fermentation scale-up, isolation, NMR/MS structure elucidation, potency/selectivity/developability panels). That is the geothermal-plant-in-an-abandoned-coal-mine shape: finding the candidate (sequence + ML-rank) is the cheap, fast part; constructing the bespoke proof is where the money and the years go. Gummerlich's own 4-detected / 2-isolable split is the cleanest single illustration: even a "hit" on detection is only half a hit on anything sellable. Terranox's drill is a commodity service with a priced per-metre rate and a binary assay result; cluster expression has no commodity rate, no binary readout, and a different protocol per cluster. The frame inverts, so C1 drops to 1.

2. The step-up is not immediate on the hit. Under the rubric, C2 asks for 10^3-10^4 immediately on proving. The candidate concedes the correct answer in its own step_up field: a cluster shown merely to express a novel scaffold with no potency data moves value ~10-30x; the low-tens-of-millions licence only arrives after the isolation-structure-assay-in-vivo chain, i.e. after several further self-funded rungs. A ~10-30x move at the moment of proving scores C2 = 2, not 3. The 100-1000x figure the candidate claims is measured from library acquisition to a validated in vivo asset, which bundles in the expensive rungs the rubric wants excluded.

3. The right is cheap but not "bought from owners who cannot read the data." The named comparables all point the other way. The Sanofi to Fraunhofer IME move (~110,000 strains incl. ~80,000 actinomycetes) is reported as a shared-resource transfer into a jointly-run natural-product centre, not an asset sale to an outside acquirer — the counterparty was a national research institute standing up a genome-mining programme of its own, and Sanofi retained a position rather than walking away. Ginkgo's Warp Drive Bio acquisition brought in the genome-mining PLATFORM (>135,000 strains, >4M predicted BGCs) — the buyer was the most sophisticated synthetic-biology operator in the market, which is evidence that these libraries are priced and competed for by people who read BGC data for a living. Deinove/Naicons was a LICENCE of 400 of ~45,000 strains, not a purchase: the holder kept the collection and metered out access. In Terranox's structure the seller is a landowner who cannot read a scanned assessment file; here every named holder (Fraunhofer, Naicons, Ginkgo, university culture collections) employs natural-product chemists and can run the same $50-200/isolate sequencing and the same free antiSMASH/BiG-SLiCE novelty scoring the acquirer would. There is no informational asymmetry to buy against.

4. Encumbrance on the right, which the candidate does not price. Legacy collections carry provenance obligations the rubric's "unproven right bought cheaply" does not survive: original depositor MTAs restricting commercial exploitation, and CBD/Nagoya-Protocol access-and-benefit-sharing claims on strains isolated from soils in source countries, which attach to downstream commercialisation of derived compounds. I could not source this leg this session (budget exhausted), so I weight it as an unquantified downside rather than a decisive fact — but it cuts the same way as everything above: the cheap price reflects an encumbered, licence-shaped right, not a clean fee-simple one.

5. Hard exclusions: NONE hit. This is not mineral/oil/gas/helium/hydrogen/brine/geothermal/groundwater exploration, it is not Terranox, it is not a tool sold to incumbents (the company owns the library and the compound IP), and it is not on the explicit kill list. The refutation is on the lens, not on exclusion.

6. C3 under the relaxed rubric: proving is genuinely expensive, which the relaxed standard rewards, so C3 is not near-zero. But the relaxed C3 scores the MARGINAL ML lift, and antiSMASH/antiSMASH-DB/BiG-FAM/MIBiG already assign novelty and distance-to-known scores to essentially every public BGC for free. The candidate's own reasoning concedes the lift over an incumbent using antiSMASH + BiG-SLiCE is "much smaller" than over random picking. Predicted-expressibility ranking is the one place a proprietary model could add real signal, and the 11-32% spread plus Wang's 67% multi-host result show host choice matters — but that is a 1.2-1.5x-shaped claim on cost per proven asset, not >=1.5x demonstrated. C3 = 3.

Revised total 10/25, down from 14. The candidate's own fatal_flaw was directionally right and if anything understated: the lens question "is the right buyable cheaply from owners who cannot read the data" fails on the seller-sophistication leg, and "is the physical step trivial" fails on verified 11-32% per-attempt detection rates for a bespoke, non-commoditised wet-lab build.
