verified.name: Floodway Narrowing for Urban Infill Parcels
verified.one_line: Buy urban and suburban parcels made near-worthless by sitting in the regulatory floodway, where no-rise rules ban building. Use ML to find floodways drawn from coarse old models or pre-channelisation topography, fund a corrected floodway model and LOMR, and sell now-buildable infill land to multifamily developers.
verified.unproven_right: Fee purchase of floodway-encumbered infill lots and remnant parcels, often tax-delinquent or estate-held, at 1-5% of comparable land value.
verified.proving_step: Corrected HEC-RAS encroachment model with current channel survey and LiDAR, community concurrence, then FEMA LOMR: about $100-400k and 18-30 months; about 30-50% success on ML-selected reaches.
verified.proven_buyer: Multifamily, build-to-rent and REIT-backed infill builders in supply-constrained Sun Belt metros.
verified.public_data: FEMA NFHL floodway layers versus 3DEP LiDAR, scanned FIS floodway data tables, DOT and municipal channelisation and culvert-replacement records (channel changed, map did not), tax-delinquent rolls, assessor data.
verified.frame: The rung is: buy floodway-encumbered parcels, get a LOMR floodway revision, and sell the now-buildable land. Discovery (finding reaches where the floodway is drawn too wide, from coarse models or pre-channelisation topography) is maybe 35-50% of the work. The rest is not trivial or abstracted. It needs a new HEC-RAS encroachment model and channel survey, a community finding under 44 CFR 65.7 that 'no practicable alternative' to revising its adopted floodway exists, notice to affected owners and adjacent jurisdictions, state approval where the state has floodway jurisdiction, FEMA review, and local adoption. Floodway width is an allocation along a whole reach under a surcharge cap (60.3(d)(2)). Narrowing it for my parcel can raise flood elevations on neighbours, so proving is a political and regulatory negotiation, not a drill hit. Capitalised buyers (multifamily, build-to-rent, REIT-backed builders) exist.
verified.step_up: The claimed ~20-100x (about $0.50/sqft to $20-60/sqft) is overstated. Land moved out of the floodway stays in the 100-year flood fringe (SFHA). It still needs flood insurance, elevated floors and often no-net-fill compensation. Houston requires floors 2 ft above the 500-year level and zero net fill across the 500-year floodplain; Harris County requires 24 in above the 500-year level, with no fill to reach elevation in the 100-year floodplain. Residential floodplain discounts are only ~4.6% in the LSE meta-analysis (Beltran et al. 2018), but for vacant fringe land the mitigation cost cuts net value. A realistic net step-up is ~10-30x, which fits the 10-100x band.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. The candidate puts it at $100-400k and 18-30 months per reach. Search found only an informal ~$4k LOMR review fee, plus a note that engineering fees vary widely and floodway no-rise work can mean full HEC-RAS modelling. The candidate's base success rate on ML-selected reaches is 30-50%. Comparing FEMA NFHL floodway layers with 3DEP LiDAR and DOT culvert and channelisation records to find mis-drawn reaches could plausibly lift success 1.5x+ over picking parcels naively. Under the relaxed C3 that is a near-full lever. I scored 4, not 5, because success depends heavily on community and neighbour politics, which ML cannot predict.
verified.data: Floodway status is a legible field in the NFHL. Whether the floodway is wrong is not: that sits in scanned FIS floodway data tables, old effective models, LiDAR differences and scattered DOT and municipal channel records, so the outcome is not pre-summarised. Incumbents, though, already do LOMRs one parcel at a time as a standard developer and civil-engineering tool. The edge is systematic screening, not unreadable data.
verified.right_bought: Yes. These are fee purchases of tax-delinquent, estate-held or remnant floodway lots from owners who cannot evaluate the hydraulics, so the right is bought cheaply. The catch is that the parcels are often thin strips along channels. Even when the floodway is narrowed, the buildable area may be small or bounded by setbacks and the flood fringe, and the inventory in infill metros is limited.
verified.buyer: Multifamily, build-to-rent and REIT-backed infill developers in supply-constrained Sun Belt metros. They are well capitalised, but they will discount for flood-fringe insurance, elevation and fill-mitigation costs, and for reputational risk after Harvey.
verified.ladder: The ladder runs: buy land, then entitle it (LOMR), then develop and own multifamily, then possibly do district-scale channel and flood-control improvements that unlock many parcels at once. That is a real-estate developer ladder. Its top is a big developer, not a trillion-dollar chain, and the base is capped by how many mis-drawn floodway infill parcels exist.
verified.fatal_flaw: A floodway is not a property of one parcel. It is a reach-wide allocation under a surcharge cap. To narrow it, the community must find no practicable alternative, notify affected owners and jurisdictions, accept higher flood elevations on others, and formally adopt the change. Even after a win, the land stays in the 100-year fringe with elevation and no-net-fill burdens. So the proving step is political and regulatory, not a discovery hit, and the step-up is capped well below 10^3.
verified.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive and an ML lever is plausible, but approval is reach-wide, needs community buy-in and shifts flood risk onto neighbours, and the de-floodwayed land stays flood fringe, so discovery is not the dominant work and the net step-up is about 10-30x.

A plausible net is ~$5-20/sqft, a step-up of roughly 5-30x, below the lens's 30x threshold. Only the finalist's own upper-bound case reaches ~100x, still under 10^3.

Market size, unverified estimate from memory: FEMA processes on the order of several hundred to ~1,000+ LOMRs a year nationally. Most are developer-driven fill or channel projects, not narrowings of a mis-drawn floodway on remnant infill lots. Transactions of exactly this type plausibly run tens per year across Sun Belt metros. The buyer class (multifamily, build-to-rent and REIT-backed infill builders) is real and capitalised, but no evidence shows them buying de-floodwayed fringe strips at full infill comparables.

Supply problem: much urban floodway land in the Sun Belt is publicly owned after flood-control buyouts. FEMA HMGP and Harris County Flood Control District buyout parcels are deed-restricted to open space in perpetuity, which shrinks the purchasable inventory further.

- C1: 1. Proving is regulatory and political work across the whole reach, not a discovery hit.
- C2: 2. Net step-up is ~5-30x.
- C3: 3. Proving is expensive and there is some ML lever, but the outcome is dominated by community concurrence.

That puts net value at roughly 5-30x the floodway purchase price, not 10^3x. No transaction evidence shows a capitalised buyer paying full infill comparables immediately after a LOMR. (2) The structural bias runs against narrowing [BK]. NOAA Atlas 14 raised design rainfall sharply in Texas and the Gulf: Houston's 100-yr 24-hr rainfall went from about 13 in to about 17-18 in. Remaps in the target metros are therefore widening floodplains and floodways, not narrowing them.

(3) 44 CFR 65.7 (fetched, customsmobile) works against urban infill specifically. Where BFEs do not change, the requester must 'modify the original hydraulic model to include all floodplain encroachments since the existing floodway was developed'. The combined effect must stay within the 60.3(d)(2) surcharge [BK: 1.0 ft nationally]. Built-out urban reaches have usually used up that surcharge through decades of fringe fill, so infill floodways are the hardest to narrow. Several states [BK: IL, IN, MI, MN, NJ, WI] cap surcharge at 0.5 ft or less, some at 0.1 ft or zero. The rule also needs community 'no practicable alternatives' findings, notice to affected owners and adjacent jurisdictions, and state approval.

(4) The 'channel changed, map did not' sub-thesis is closed by rule [BK]. Under 44 CFR 65.3 a community must submit new technical data to FEMA within 6 months when a physical change affects BFEs. Flood-control districts and DOTs routinely file the LOMR for their own channel projects, so stale-map gaps after channelisation are short-lived and the public sponsor captures them.

(5) Competition: CLOMR/LOMR floodway modification for land reclamation is a standard practice line at civil and hydraulic firms [BK: Halff, Freese and Nichols, LJA, Kimley-Horn, Dewberry]. Floodway status is a legible field in the NFHL.

(6) Proving is expensive [BK: $100-400k of H&H modelling; FEMA LOMR review fees run several thousand dollars]. But ML's marginal lift is small once BLE and remap data are free and public, so C3 drops to about 3.

verifiers.evidence:
Limits on this check: the shared web-search budget was used up before my searches ran, so both returned nothing. I fetched three primary sources directly. Points not marked as sourced come from domain knowledge and are flagged.

(1) The regulatory process is the proving step. I quoted 44 CFR 65.7 from customsmobile.com:
- 65.7(a): a floodway can be revised only after "the community has determined that no practicable alternatives exist to revising the boundaries of its previously adopted floodway". The community makes that finding at its own discretion. The parcel owner cannot buy it.
- 65.7(b)(1)-(3) and (c): every floodway revision, even one with no change in base flood elevations, needs either a public notice of the community's intent to revise or a statement that "all affected property owners and adjacent jurisdictions were notified". Where the state has floodway jurisdiction, it needs state notification and state approval.
- 65.7(c): the modified model must "include all floodplain encroachments made since the existing floodway was developed". The combined effect must stay within the 60.3(d)(2) surcharge cap (1 ft federally). If the original floodway already used the full surcharge and encroachment has happened since, there is little or no room left to narrow it, unless the hydraulics have truly improved.
- 65.7(d): a professional engineer must certify the analyses, and a professional engineer or licensed land surveyor must certify the topography.

(2) FEMA fees, from fema.gov's "Flood Map-Related Fees" page: a LOMR for a channel, culvert, hydrology or combination costs $8,000 online or $8,250 on paper; a CLOMR costs $6,500 or $6,750. The FEMA fee is small. The cost is the engineering and survey work plus 18-30 months of process. The candidate's $100-400k total is plausible but I did not verify it. That likely clears the >=$50k bar, so C3 is not refuted on cost.

(3) The FEMA MT-2 page says Form 1 (Overview and Concurrence), which requires a community official's signature, "is required for all Letter of Map Revision and Conditional Letter of Map Revision requests". The community has to sign off before FEMA will look at the request.

(4) Domain knowledge, not verified this round: many of the cheapest vacant floodway lots in flood-prone Sun Belt metros are FEMA or HMGP buyout parcels. 44 CFR 80.19 deed-restricts these to open space in perpetuity, so they cannot be developed whatever the map says. Large floodway holdings are also owned by flood control districts. Tax-delinquent lots go to competitive auction, and land banks do not sell them at 1-5% of value at scale. Several states set floodway surcharge caps far below the federal 1 ft, which leaves little to reallocate.

Lens verdict:
- The fee right is legal and cheap per parcel. But the binding right is the community's discretionary floodway revision, plus the absence of objections from the neighbours whose flood elevations rise. Neither can be bought.
- The mandatory public notice to all affected owners also exposes the edge before the win: neighbours either object or reprice their own lots.
- No construction is needed, so this is not as bad as bespoke geothermal. But the proving step is a political entitlement process. A discovery hit is not what proves the asset.
- No hard exclusion applies: the company owns the land, does not sell a service, and does no drilling.

Scores:
- C1 cut to 1: discovery is well under 50% of the work.
- C2 kept at 3: about 10-30x net once fringe mitigation is paid for.
- C3 = 3: proving is expensive, but politics caps the ML lever.
- C4 cut to 2: the data really is illegible, but the cheap right is not the binding one, notice leaks the edge, and much of the inventory is deed-restricted.
- C5 = 2: the ladder tops out as a real-estate developer.
verifiers.killer: The right that matters cannot be bought. Under 44 CFR 65.7(a) the community must make a discretionary finding that 'no practicable alternatives exist' to revising its floodway. Under 65.7(b)(1) and (c), every revision requires public notice to all affected property owners and adjacent jurisdictions, and state approval where the state has floodway jurisdiction. Owning a cheap floodway lot buys the chance to lobby a city, which has to agree to raise flood elevations on neighbours who have just been told about the plan. The proving step is a political entitlement process, not a discovery hit, and much of the cheapest inventory is FEMA buyout land deed-restricted to open space for ever (44 CFR 80.19, not verified this round).

verified.name: German Bauerwartungsland: picking farmland ahead of a Bebauungsplan
verified.one_line: Option arable land at farm prices next to built-up areas in German growth regions. Pick fields by reading Gemeinderat minutes, Flächennutzungsplan change procedures and Regionalplan settlement allocations to predict which will be zoned. Fund the Bebauungsplan as Vorhabenträger under a städtebaulicher Vertrag and sell Bauland to developers, who pay the step-up.
verified.unproven_right: Option or purchase of Ackerland at about €5-10/m² that the Flächennutzungsplan does not yet designate as building land. Owners are farmers and Erbengemeinschaften who cannot follow about 11,000 Ratsinformationssysteme.
verified.proving_step: Planning studies and the Bebauungsplan procedure (environmental report, compensation measures) under an urban development contract. About €200k-€1M and 2-5 years, plausibly 30-60% success on picked sites. Screen out municipalities that use Zwischenerwerb or Einheimischenmodelle, which cap the private uplift.
verified.proven_buyer: Bauträger and Projektentwickler (Vonovia development arm, Instone, regional developers) and logistics developers; raw building land in growth regions trades at about €150-500/m².
verified.public_data: Ratsinformationssysteme minutes and Beschlussvorlagen (PDF), Flächennutzungsplan amendment notices in Amtsblätter, Regionalplan settlement areas, BORIS standard land values (price current status, not future zoning), ISEK and housing needs reports.
verified.frame: The rung is Baulandentwicklung: option Ackerland, push it through FNP and Bebauungsplan, sell Rohbauland. It can be sold, and German land developers already do this work. Discovery (picking the field) is maybe 20-35% of the effort. Most of the work is political and procedural, and picking the field does not make it easy. That work is: lobbying the Gemeinderat, the Umweltbericht, Artenschutz surveys, Ausgleichsflächen, negotiating the städtebaulicher Vertrag, and assembling several owners (Erbengemeinschaften) into one plan area. This is close to the geothermal counter-example, where executing the bespoke step is harder than finding the asset. There is a capitalised buyer (Bauträger and Projektentwickler), so the frame half-works.
verified.step_up: The headline figure is €5-7/m² Ackerland to €150-500/m² finished Bauland, about 30-60x. Three things cut that down. (1) Erschlossenes Bauland is not the output of this rung. Erschließung costs about €50-100/m², and 25-35% of the gross area is lost to roads and green space. (2) Municipal capture under SoBoN-style § 11 BauGB contracts often takes up to about 2/3 of the planning uplift (Berlin's cooperative model explicitly tests the burden against the uplift). (3) Once the FNP designates the land, Bauerwartungsland already trades at 25-60% of the Bauland value (McMakler), so the price climbs in steps and does not jump on a single hit. The realistic net step for a private owner, from Acker to sold Rohbauland, is about 10-25x. A forum example: a developer offered €11.50/m² against a €25/m² Bodenrichtwert in Sachsen-Anhalt in 2022.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about €200k-1M and takes 2-5 years per site (the candidate's own estimate, consistent with typical B-Plan costs), so it clears the 'expensive' bar. The base hit rate on picked sites is plausibly 30-60%. Under the relaxed C3, ML that reads Ratsinfo minutes and Regionalplan allocations could pick better sites before options are signed. But the zoning decision is a local political choice, often made years later, and it depends on council majorities, Flächensparziele (the 30 ha/day target) and the municipality's own land-policy model. Local developers and the farmers already track these signals in person. I estimate the lift at about 1.2-1.5x, not 2-3x. No source was found that quantifies it.
verified.data: The data is public and genuinely illegible: about 11,000 Ratsinformationssysteme of PDF minutes, Amtsblatt notices, and scanned Regionalplan maps. But the key outcome signals are fairly legible. Regionalplan settlement allocations and FNP designations are published maps. Once land is in the FNP it is priced as Bauerwartungsland, so the regulator effectively writes the answer into a status field, and the edge only exists before the FNP stage. Rights are bought, not free first-come, which is good. But owners are not naive. Farmers are advised by Bauernverband and topagrar. Option contracts with Nachbewertungsklauseln are standard, and topagrar notes that the option contract itself can be treated as evidence of Bauerwartung. Municipalities hold Vorkaufsrecht under §§ 24-25 BauGB.
verified.right_bought: Option or purchase of Ackerland at about €5-10/m² before FNP designation. Farmers often negotiate uplift-sharing (Nachzahlung) clauses that claw back much of the gain.
verified.buyer: Bauträger, Projektentwickler, logistics developers and municipal land funds. They are capitalised and active. In many growth municipalities, though, the municipality itself is the required counterparty at a capped price.
verified.ladder: The ladder exists: land development, then Erschließung, then Bauträger home building, then build-to-rent and portfolio ownership (the Vonovia scale). Each rung above this one is a commoditised, low-margin, crowded construction business in a market that is down cyclically. The discovery edge does not carry upward.
verified.fatal_flaw: A municipal political decision gates the step-up, and growth-region municipalities increasingly design that decision to deny the uplift to private holders. Münster, Potsdam, Ulm, Braunschweig and others only start a Bebauungsplan in the Außenbereich if the city first owns at least 50% of the land, bought at a 'very low Bauerwartung' price. Elsewhere, SoBoN-style contracts capture up to about 2/3 of the uplift. These are exactly the growth regions the thesis targets. So the private optionholder often cannot realise the step-up, and the proving step is politics and permitting rather than discovery.
verified.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the proving step is expensive, but the net step-up is only about 10-25x after Erschließung and municipal capture. The proving work is political and procedural rather than discovery, and growth-region municipalities increasingly require that they buy 50%+ themselves at Bauerwartung prices before zoning, which blocks private capture of the uplift.

verifiers.evidence:
Web search budget was exhausted after the first call, so this rests on directly fetched sources, chiefly the Brandenburg MIL "Arbeitshilfe Baulandstrategien" (data from the Oberer Gutachterausschuss Brandenburg, 2019), plus topagrar and Destatis.

(1) Real transaction ratios, Brandenburg 2014-2018 (Tabelle 2):
- Werdendes Wohnbauland with nicht qualifizierte Bauerwartung (no FNP) averaged 16% of the baureif Bodenrichtwert in the Berliner Umland (45 contracts) and 22% in the weiterer Metropolenraum (53).
- Qualifizierte Bauerwartung (FNP designation or B-Plan draft) averaged 29% / 32% (124 / 134 contracts).
- Rohbauland (B-Plan rechtsverbindlich) averaged 54% / 50% (213 / 191 contracts).
- Farmland averaged about €1.00/m² across Brandenburg and €1.27/m² in the Berliner Umland.
- Baureif BRW for individual housing in the Berliner Umland was €220/m² in H1 2019.

(2) Implied step-ups:
- Pure Acker (€1.27) to Rohbauland (0.54 × 220 = €119): about 90x gross. That holds only if a field that later gets zoned can be bought at agricultural price.
- Land with any recognisable Bauerwartung, the very edge-of-settlement fields the ML would pick, already trades at 16% (about €35/m²). From there to Rohbauland is only about 3.4x.
- From the FNP stage (29%) to Rohbauland is about 1.9x.
- The price rises in stages (16% → 29% → 54%), not as a single jump on one hit.

(3) topagrar uses a similar ladder from experts: 15-40% of the baureif price at the village edge with no planning, 25-50% with the FNP adopted, 35-60% at the B-Plan Aufstellungsbeschluss, 50-70% once the plan is publicly displayed. In its worked example the municipality offered €20/m² against €270/m² baureif, and the expert valued the field at €81/m².

(4) Municipal capture, from the Arbeitshilfe's worked example (Abb. 24):
- Anfangswert €60, baureif €210. Costs are €147/m² net: planning €10.90, infrastructure €46.10, Ausgleich €3, social infrastructure €87.20.
- Under the 2/3 Kappungsgrenze, the planning beneficiary keeps €50/m² of a €150/m² uplift. Without the cap it keeps €2.80/m².
- So even with a perfect pick, the private holder's net gain is about 1/3 of the gross uplift, and most of the capital at risk is proving and contribution capex, not land.

(5) Buyer and volume:
- Developers do buy Rohbauland, so the buyer is real.
- But the hottest region in eastern Germany (Berliner Umland) logged only about 43 Rohbauland contracts a year, and the weiterer Metropolenraum about 38.
- Destatis puts average German baureif land at €271.86/m².

Net assessment: the realistic step-up for an ML-picked, edge-of-settlement field is about 3-25x after Bauerwartung pricing, staged price discovery and capture. Gross 50-90x appears only for fields bought truly at agricultural prices.
verifiers.killer: Gutachterausschuss transaction data shows the market prices Bauerwartung before any FNP decision. In the Berliner Umland, unzoned fields with any development expectation sold at an average 16% of the baureif value, about €35/m², not €1.27/m² farm value. FNP-stage land sold at 29% and Rohbauland at 54%. So from the kind of edge-of-settlement field an ML model would pick, the realistic step is about 2-3.4x, and it comes in several steps rather than one jump. The 50-90x headline appears only when a field is bought at pure agricultural price. Even then, 2/3-capped § 11 contributions leave the private holder about 1/3 of the gross uplift: €50 of €150/m² in the state's own worked example. Developer demand is also thin, at about 40 Rohbauland contracts a year in the hottest region. The net step is well under the 30x threshold.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch limit (200 calls per turn) was already used up when I started, so neither of my searches ran. Everything below comes from fetching known URLs directly, plus domain knowledge I flag as unverified.

(1) The decisive point: the outcome signal is already in the price, through a standard valuation scale that farmers' advisers use. topagrar (2020, with a lawyer's input) gives the stages of Bauerwartungsland as a percentage of the baureifes-Land price:
- 15-40% at the edge of town before any Flächennutzungsplan exists
- 25-40% once an FNP is prepared (25-50% if designated for housing)
- 35-60% after the council resolves to start a Bebauungsplan
- 50-70% once the B-Plan is publicly displayed

In topagrar's own example, the appraiser values an un-zoned 2.4 ha edge-of-town field at no less than 30% of the regional €270/m² Bauland price, i.e. €81/m². The municipality had offered €20/m², and the article advises the farmer to hire a certified appraiser (0.5-1% of value), check BORIS, and insist on conditional contracts with Nachbewertungsklauseln. It also notes that an option or re-valuation clause can itself count as evidence of Bauerwartung.

So the field the thesis targets (ag land next to built-up areas in a growth region) does not trade at the €5-10/m² farm price. Its realistic entry price is about €40-100/m² (15-40% of €250), and Rohbauland after Erschließung and the 25-35% area loss is about €150-200/m². That makes the realistic step-up roughly 2-5x, not 30-60x. The only land that really trades at farm prices is land the market sees as far from development, which has a low hit rate and long horizons.

(2) Legibility: the large value jumps sit exactly at legible public stages: FNP designation, Aufstellungsbeschluss and öffentliche Auslegung, all published in Amtsblätter and on BORIS. Regionalplan Siedlungsbereiche are published maps. OParl (oparl.org) is a standard JSON API that exposes 'alle öffentlichen Daten des Rates' for participating Ratsinformationssysteme, so council documents are partly machine-readable already. XPlanung is the legally binding data standard for Bauleitplanung (xleitstelle.de), which makes finished plans structured data. Project-intelligence vendors (ibau, DTAD) sell construction projects tracked from the 'Diskussion/Vorplanung' phase. That leaves ML a thin window: reading pre-Aufstellungsbeschluss council chatter that local actors already follow in person.

(3) Competition, from domain knowledge, not verified this round: logistics developers (Panattoni, Garbe, VGP, Goodman, Dietz) and residential Grundstücksentwickler routinely option Ackerland and run vorhabenbezogene B-Pläne as Vorhabenträger. Municipal and state land agencies (Zwischenerwerb; Münster SoBoN, Ulm, Potsdam, Braunschweig) take the uplift in the very growth regions targeted.

(4) The proving step is expensive (€200k-1M, 2-5 years), so C3 survives at about 3 under the relaxed rubric. But the 'hit' is a political decision, and ML is unlikely to beat local developers' relationships by more than 1.2-1.5x.
verifiers.killer: The buy price is not near zero. German valuation practice already prices un-zoned edge-of-town fields at 15-40% of the Bauland value before any FNP exists, and topagrar's own example values one at €81/m² rather than €7-20. Farmers are coached to hire appraisers and to insist on Nachbewertungsklauseln, and the option itself counts as evidence of Bauerwartung. Each later step (FNP, Aufstellungsbeschluss, Auslegung) is a legible public stage that re-prices the land. So the net capturable step-up is about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4, and the ML edge exists only in a thin window before the first council resolution, a window crowded with logistics developers, Grundstücksentwickler and municipal Zwischenerwerb programmes.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch quota for this turn was already used up when this verifier started, so no new web searches were run. Evidence below comes from fetching the finalist's own cited sources directly, plus text extracted from the Brandenburg PDF.

(1) The right is not cheap where it matters. Owners already price the Bauerwartung. topagrar gives the Bauerwartungsland value as a share of baureifes Land at each stage: 15-40% for land at the edge of town with no planning that the FNP does not show as residential; 25-50% once the FNP shows it as residential; 35-60% after the Aufstellungsbeschluss; 50-70% after public display of the Bebauungsplan. The Brandenburg Arbeitshilfe Baulandstrategien (2020, citing the Oberer Gutachterausschuss) puts average agricultural land at about €1.00/m², and €1.27/m² in the Berliner Umland. Yet werdendes Bauland traded at 16-54% of the baureifes-Land Bodenrichtwert, against roughly €220/m² for single-family Bauland and €389/m² for multi-storey in the Umland. A field next to the built-up area of a growth region therefore sells for roughly €35-90/m², not €5-7/m². The claimed 30-60x only exists on fields far enough out that nobody expects zoning, and those are the least likely to be zoned. From a correctly priced un-designated edge field to Rohbauland the step is about 2-4x. From pure Acker it is about 10-25x net, after a 25% Erschließung deduction (the Arbeitshilfe uses a 0.75 net-to-gross ratio) and municipal capture.

(2) Municipalities legally capture or block the uplift. topagrar summarises BGH case law: a municipality that bears the planning risk may keep the value increase, "oft bis zu 50 bis 70%". The Brandenburg Arbeitshilfe recommends making municipal Zwischenerwerb "in Gänze oder in Teilen" a precondition for drawing up a B-Plan, with the purchase made before the FNP change. Its Ulm case study shows the city buying land decades ahead and holding it under a recorded Wiederkaufsrecht. In the growth regions the thesis targets, the private optionholder is designed out of the uplift.

(3) The option contract itself creates a valuation problem. topagrar says the appraiser notes that options, withdrawal rights and uplift claims can themselves count as concrete signs of Bauerwartung. Nachbewertungsklauseln are standard; in topagrar's worked example the seller ends up with at least 30% of the €270/m² Bauland value, which is €81/m².

(4) The proving step is not trivial. It consists of council politics, the Umweltbericht, Artenschutz surveys, Ausgleichsflächen, the § 11 contract and assembling Erbengemeinschaften into one plan area. This is the bespoke-execution pattern of the geothermal counter-example; finding the field is not the hard part.

The finalist hits no hard exclusion: it is not drilling or prospecting, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service. C3 stays at 3 under the relaxed rubric: proving costs €200k-1M over 2-5 years and the plausible lift is 1.2-1.5x. No source was found that quantifies the lift.
verifiers.killer: The cheap unproven right does not exist where the step-up does. Fields at the edge of town in growth regions already trade at 15-40% of the Bauland price before any FNP designation (topagrar, Brandenburg Gutachterausschuss), against €1-1.27/m² for plain farmland. Municipalities can legally keep 50-70% of the uplift (BGH, per topagrar) or make their own Zwischenerwerb a precondition for the B-Plan (Brandenburg Arbeitshilfe). The option contract itself can count as evidence of Bauerwartung. That leaves a realistic 2-4x step on correctly priced land, and the gating step is political and procedural, not discovery.

verified.name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
verified.one_line: Take abandoned-in-place pipelines and easements from operators carrying decommissioning liabilities; ML over easement instruments proves broad 'any substance' assignable scope and continuity; sell to CO2/H2 trunkline and fiber developers.
verified.fatal_flaw: Proving title does not create the value and is not where the difficulty lies. Corridors fail on all-parcels-must-pass continuity, easement lapse or reversion (now being written into state law, as in Nebraska LB1186 and Missouri HB 706), bespoke physical requalification, and a stalled CO2/H2 buyer. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode. And the owners can read their own easements and do the good conversions themselves (Tallgrass Trailblazer).
verified.step_up: The basis is near zero or negative, because the operator carries an abandonment liability (my estimate: about $10-50k/mile to abandon in place). Proven value is about $100k-1M/mile to a CO2 developer if the pipe also requalifies (new CO2 build is about $2-4M/mile, with ROW about 10-20% of that; my estimate, not sourced), or about $5-50k/mile capitalised for fiber. That is a ~10-100x step-up, and it is not realised when proving succeeds. It comes only after requalification and once a shipper commits. New laws also threaten the basis: Nebraska LB1186 would revert easements to the landowner within 3 years after a line stops operating, and Missouri HB 706 would treat an easement as abandoned after 10 years of non-use.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap for each parcel (my estimate: about $300-2,000 for title review) but expensive for a corridor: hundreds to thousands of parcels cost roughly $100k-1M+ per corridor attempt, so it clears the relaxed ≥$50k bar. My estimate is that 20-50% of parcels carry broad, assignable language. Corridor success is roughly that rate raised to the power N, so the binding constraint is holdouts and gaps, not choosing the right corridor. ML reading the instruments can cut review cost per parcel and screen corridors before acquisition, plausibly a 1.2-2x gain in cost per proven corridor. That gain is diluted because requalification and holdout cure costs dominate. I give C3 a 3, up from below threshold under the strict rubric.
verified.frame: The rung is acquiring an abandoned-in-place pipe plus its easement chain and proving the corridor is assignable and continuous for CO2, H2 or fiber. Legal discovery is only about 30-50% of the work in that rung. The rest is getting every parcel to pass (holdouts, lapsed easements, scope litigation one parcel at a time), physically requalifying the pipe (PHMSA conversion, integrity testing), and finding a buyer. The CO2 and H2 buyers are currently stalled. The physical step is not trivial, and the real conversions so far were done by the incumbent owner: Tallgrass moved 392 miles of Trailblazer from gas to CO2 itself.
verified.data: The easement instruments are recorded in county deed records, scanned and scattered, which makes them public but illegible. That is a genuine fit. But the operator owns the easements, holds its own land files and can read them, so the seller is not blind to the data. The rights also cannot be bought cheaply apart from the pipe and its liability. Landowners and state legislatures are actively pushing reversion, so the right may be void exactly when it is transferred.
verified.right_bought: You would buy the idle pipe and its easements, with the abandonment liability, from midstream operators. Nominal price is near zero, but you take on the liability and the regulatory exposure. Owners who hold good corridors convert them themselves (Trailblazer is the example).
verified.buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Tallgrass, Summit-type projects, many stalled by permitting and landowner opposition), H2 developers (early-stage and capital-light), and fiber long-haul and middle-mile builders (capitalised, but they pay low ROW values).
verified.ladder: The ladder above is strong: corridor ownership, then operating the CO2/H2 transport pipeline as a midstream operator, then sequestration hubs and fiber and power co-location in the corridors. Midstream is a very large industry, so the path to a big company exists if the first rung works.
verified.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the lever to a moderate 3, because proving a whole corridor is expensive. The frame still fails: discovery is not 80% of the work, the step-up needs physical requalification and a stalled buyer, and sellers are not blind to the data.

verifiers.evidence:
Limits on this check: the shared web search budget for this turn was already used up, so no searches ran. Direct fetches of all five finalist sources (S&P Global, RBN Energy, Nebraska Examiner, Missouri House PDF, Energy Institute) returned HTTP 403. The verdict therefore rests on facts I knew before this session, and the dollar figures below are partly my own estimates, not sourced transaction prices.

1. Unproven right price. No public market prices idle pipe plus easements as a separate asset. Midstream assets sell on EBITDA multiples. Idle lines move either inside portfolio deals or as liabilities near scrap value. The basis is about zero or negative, but no comparable transactions exist to anchor it.

2. Proven right price. No public transaction shows a third party paying a premium for an easement chain that had been "proven" for CO2, H2 or fiber. The real conversions were done by the incumbent owner on its own pipe:
- Tallgrass moved Trailblazer, 392 miles, from gas to CO2 itself (the finalist's own source).
- Williams Communications pulled fiber through retired Williams gas pipelines in the 1990s (WilTel).
- El Paso/Kinder Morgan converted gas lines to oil service themselves.
Fiber right-of-way is capitalised at low values; railroad and utility fiber licences are a few dollars per foot per year. That puts a fiber step-up at ~10x at best.

3. CO2 value. The ceiling is the right-of-way share of a new build: roughly $200-600k/mile if the pipe also requalifies under PHMSA. It is not realised when title is proven. It needs requalification spending plus a committed shipper.

4. Buyer reality and market size.
- Navigator CO2 cancelled its Heartland Greenway project in Oct 2023.
- Summit Carbon lost its South Dakota permit in 2023, and South Dakota then banned eminent domain for CO2 pipelines in 2025.
- Wolf Carbon withdrew its Illinois application.
- H2 trunkline buyers are pre-revenue.
The capitalised buyers that pay at once are either fiber builders (low price) or the incumbent itself (which cuts out the middleman). I estimate deals at maybe 0-5 per year in the US, not a liquid market.

5. Reversion bills. Nebraska LB1186 (3-year reversion) and Missouri HB 706 (10-year non-use abandonment) cut the basis exactly when the pipe sits idle.

Net: the realisable step-up is ~5-50x, and it is gated on later physical and commercial steps. It is not a 10^3-10^4x jump paid at once on a hit. That is below the ~30x refutation threshold on a realised, immediate basis, and the buyer is stalled or not real for the high-value case.
verifiers.killer: No public transaction shows anyone paying a step-up price for a third-party-assembled, title-proven abandoned pipeline corridor. Every real conversion (Tallgrass Trailblazer to CO2, Williams/WilTel fiber in retired gas pipe, Kinder Morgan/El Paso gas-to-oil) was done by the incumbent owner on its own pipe. The high-value CO2 buyers have collapsed: Navigator cancelled in 2023, Summit was blocked in South Dakota and lost eminent domain there in 2025, and Wolf Carbon withdrew. Fiber, the buyer that does have capital, pays right-of-way values of only ~10x basis. The realisable step-up is about 5-50x, comes only after requalification and a shipper commitment, and happens in a handful of deals a year at most.

The points below come from background knowledge and the finalist's own cited facts. Under the instruction to default to refuted when the key claim cannot be supported, this verdict holds regardless.

By the finalist's own account, owners convert the good corridors themselves: Tallgrass moved 392 miles of Trailblazer from gas to CO2 through a FERC abandonment and conversion, so the counterparty saw and used the value.

(2) The underlying status is already legible. Pipeline location, operator and status (in service, idle, abandoned) are mapped in PHMSA's NPMS and reported in PHMSA annual reports. Commercial pipeline GIS vendors (Rextag, Enverus, Mapsearch-type products) package this for developers. So screening which corridors exist and are idle is a lookup table, not an ML edge.

(3) Easement reading is already a commercial service. Right-of-way land-services firms and title-abstraction vendors, increasingly LLM-assisted, already read easement scope. (4) The outcome is not decided by the text. Whether an easement can carry fiber or CO2 under 'any substance' language gets settled in landowner litigation, parcel by parcel. The fiber-in-railroad and fiber-in-pipeline ROW class actions of the 1990s and 2000s, including settlements over telecom fiber in pipeline easements, show courts often read scope narrowly. New reversion laws push the same way (Nebraska LB1186 proposal; Missouri HB 706: abandoned after 10 years of non-use). An ML read of the instrument predicts a legal fight; it does not prove the right.

(5) The proving step is not mainly legal. The value depends on PHMSA requalification and integrity testing and on a shipper committing. CO2 trunklines (Summit, Navigator) were cancelled or stalled over landowner and permitting opposition, so the capitalised buyer is weak exactly where the step-up is largest.

On C3: corridor review clears the relaxed $50k-or-more cost bar. But the ML lift applies only to the legal-review share of the cost per proven corridor. That share is minor against requalification and holdout cure, so the realistic gain is about 1.1-1.3x, which scores 2.

Revised scores: C1 1 (discovery is under 50% of the work in the rung; the physical step is not trivial). C2 2 (value is not realised on a proving hit; about 3-10x before requalification). C3 2. C4 1 (illegible only to outsiders, not to the seller; status legible in NPMS and vendor data; the right comes with liability, it is not cheap). C5 4 (the midstream ladder is real).
verifiers.killer: The seller, the pipeline operator, keeps the easement files in its own land department, maintains them actively and can read them. Idle and abandoned status is already public in PHMSA NPMS and sold by pipeline GIS vendors. The good corridors are converted by their owners (Tallgrass Trailblazer). So there is no blind seller and no data edge. Whether the right holds is decided by landowner scope litigation and reversion laws, not by reading the instrument better.
sources: NOTE: WebSearch budget exhausted (shared 200-call limit) and all WebFetch attempts on cited sources returned 403; nothing was verified live

verifiers.evidence:
Evidence was limited. The shared web-search budget for this turn was already used up (the 200-call limit), so no new searches ran. Direct fetches of the finalist's own sources (S&P Global on Trailblazer, RBN on Trailblazer, Nebraska Examiner on LB1186, Missouri HB 706 PDF) all returned HTTP 403, so the finalist's sourcing is unverified. One fetch succeeded: Wikipedia on Marvin M. Brandt Revocable Trust v. United States (2014). The Supreme Court held that 1875-Act railroad rights-of-way are easements that are extinguished on abandonment and leave the land "unburdened". Nothing reverts to the grantor-government. This is the doctrine behind the takings-claim wave over corridor reuse. The rest of this assessment rests on established law and industry knowledge, not new citations.
(1) Right not cheaply buyable as a clean asset. Under common law, an easement for a specific use terminates on abandonment, meaning non-use plus intent. An operator that has abandoned a pipe in place has created the very facts that let landowners claim termination. The finalist's own cited bills (Nebraska LB1186 reversion about 3 years after cessation; Missouri HB 706 abandonment after 10 years of non-use) would write this into statute. So the right decays exactly when it becomes available at a discount. Buying it means taking the pipe, the abandonment liability and the litigation risk, not a cheap option.
(2) Sellers are not blind. Midstream operators keep land and ROW departments with full easement files. The data is illegible to outsiders but legible to the seller, and the counterparty reads it best. The finalist's own example, Tallgrass moving 392-mile Trailblazer from gas to CO2 service, shows owners convert the good corridors themselves.
(3) Scope is already contested law. Fiber or new-substance use beyond the granted purpose is a well-known basis for landowner class actions, as in the railroad and utility ROW fiber cases of the 1990s and 2000s. So 'any substance' language is litigated parcel by parcel, not proven by reading.
(4) The physical step dominates. Converting to CO2 or H2 needs PHMSA conversion-of-service requalification (49 CFR 192.14 / 195.5): integrity testing, ILI, and checks for dense-phase pressure rating, fracture arrest and hydrogen-embrittlement suitability. Old gas pipe often fails these. The work is bespoke and the cost is engineering-scale, the same pattern as geothermal in coal mines. This point is from industry knowledge, not a fetched source.
(5) The step-up (~10-100x at best) is realised only after requalification plus a committed shipper, not when title is proven. CO2 trunkline buyers are stalled.
No hard exclusion applies: this is not drilling, and the company would own the asset. Under relaxed C3, corridor proving costs over $50k, but ML gives about 1.2-1.5x at most, because the binding costs are holdouts, cure and requalification.
verifiers.killer: The right decays at the moment it becomes cheap. Abandoning the pipe in place is itself the trigger for easement termination under common law (Brandt-style reversion, plus the statutory reversion bills). The operator selling it holds and can read the full easement file. Even a clean corridor is worth little until a bespoke, expensive PHMSA requalification of old pipe and a committed CO2/H2 shipper exist. So legal discovery is a minority of the rung's work and the physical step dominates, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode.
sources: https://nebraskaexaminer.com/?p=1428 (cited by finalist; 403 on fetch, unverified)
49 CFR 192.14 and 195.5 conversion-of-service rules (from knowledge, not fetched)

deep.name: Reviving zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats)
deep.memo:
# Zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats): feasibility deep-dive

*Note: the shared WebSearch budget ran out before this agent made its first search. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch reads of primary sources (SEC 10-Ks, the Florida Senate report) plus the finalist's cited pages. Unsourced figures are marked as estimates.*

## Frame of reference
The rung is a stalled or antiquated plat turned into entitled, serviceable land. Proving it is mostly legal and records work: a vested-rights determination or replat, a development agreement, and will-serve letters. The trouble is that the buyers who pay real money buy *finished* lots. Forestar, D.R. Horton's lot arm, spent **$595.3M on land acquisition and about $1.1B on land development** in FY2025 ([Forestar 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1406587/000162828025053125/for-20250930.htm)). So physical horizontal work (roads, sewer, grading) is about two thirds of the capital in the rung builders pay for. That is the geothermal counter-example's failure mode. A rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work does exist (sell entitled, unimproved land), but its buyers pay cost plus carry.

## Step-up ratio
- **Unproven:** a stalled-plat lot-equivalent at about $5-15k (estimate, from the pitch). Raw land is not priced near zero: the national median is $62,365/acre, and raw land is up 86.5% since 2019 against 53.3% for build-ready land ([MortgagePoint/Realtor.com](https://themortgagepoint.com/2026/04/23/prices-for-raw-land-has-surged-a-whopping-87-since-2019/)).
- **Entitled, mostly unimproved:** about $34k per homesite. Millrose bought Rausch's roughly 25,000 homesites for about $859M ([Millrose 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2017206/000201720626000002/ck0002017206-20251231.htm)).
- **Finished:** $108,400 average Forestar lot price ([Forestar 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1406587/000162828025053125/for-20250930.htm)). Millrose implies about $113k per homesite ($16.1B over 142,139 homesites).
- A same-county raw-versus-developed example gives 6x ($3k vs $18k/acre), and utility extension alone costs "tens of thousands to over $100,000" ([Acres.com](https://www.acres.com/blog/raw-land-vs-developed-land)).
- **Net for the proving rung: about 2-5x.** Raw to finished is about 10x, but only after you pay for the development.
- **Transactions per year:** Forestar sold 14,240 lots in FY2025. Total US builder lot takedown is about 1M a year (estimate). The zombie or uncertain-vesting slice is a small fraction of that (estimate).

## Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Capex:** about $100k-1M and 12-36 months per vested-rights determination or replat (estimate, from the pitch). Forestar says municipalities "were frequently delayed in granting the proper approvals" and have broad discretion over conditions.
- **Base hit rate:** 50-70% (estimate, unverified). Weakened by *Dawe v. Scottsdale*, which holds that a recorded plat alone vests no rights ([case brief](https://www.lexplug.com/casebrief/dawe_v_city_of_scottsdale_67cb06bf99e747a38d58393b)).
- **With ML:** screening plats for partly built infrastructure, released bonds, live development agreements and utility capacity could avoid dead options. Plausible gain is about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven asset (estimate). It is capped because council votes and holdout owners cannot be predicted from documents.

## Data source
- **Datasets:** county recorder plat books, recorded development agreements, planning and council minutes, improvement-bond release records, tax-delinquency rolls and aerial imagery, in AZ (Maricopa, Pinal), FL (Lee, Charlotte, Marion), NV, ID and TX.
- **Why it is illegible:** the records are scanned and spread across agencies.
- **Is the outcome already summarised?** Partly. Zonda and John Burns sell subdivision lot-pipeline status to builders (domain knowledge, not fetched). Plat dates and zoning sit in county GIS fields. The Florida Senate report says the 2.1M lots in about 2,600 antiquated subdivisions are undeveloped because of "lack of infrastructure" and fragmented absentee ownership, which is a known assembly problem rather than an information gap ([FL Senate report](https://spikowski.com/documents-LehighAcres/FloridaSenateReportOnAntiquatedSubdivisions.pdf)).

## How the right is bought
- **Single-owner stalled tracts:** a non-recourse purchase option with earnest money, the same structure Forestar uses ([10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1406587/000162828025053125/for-20250930.htm)).
- **Antiquated subdivisions:** buy hundreds of tiny lots from absentee owners. Florida proposals required 60% fee-title ownership before a replat, and owners have "little incentive to sell" ([FL Senate](https://spikowski.com/documents-LehighAcres/FloridaSenateReportOnAntiquatedSubdivisions.pdf)).
- **Uplift kept:** if the company sells entitled land at the about-$34k/homesite level, it keeps the entitlement gain, perhaps $15-25k per lot (estimate). Forestar's whole buy-entitle-develop-sell chain earns about a 21.9% gross margin ($1,662.4M revenue against $1,298.9M cost of sales).

## Capitalised buyer
Lennar, D.R. Horton and Pulte buy through option and takedown programs, and land bankers such as Millrose and Varde fund the land. Millrose's takedown price is its own acquisition cost plus the development budget, at an 8.5-11% yield, with no independent appraisals ([Millrose 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2017206/000201720626000002/ck0002017206-20251231.htm)). The buyers are real, but neither pays a jackpot.

## Integration ladder above
Entitlement, then horizontal development (Forestar-style), then land banking (Millrose), then vertical homebuilding and master-planned communities, then mortgage and title. These are very large markets, but capital-heavy and cyclical.

## Who else does this
- Forestar, majority-owned by D.R. Horton
- Builder land teams and Land Advisors Organization
- Land bankers: Millrose, Varde, JEN Partners
- Florida paper-lot mass-mail "land flippers"
- Post-2008 distressed funds, which absorbed the REO-desk zombie inventory from 2010 to 2015 (domain knowledge)

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. In Pinal County, AZ, pull 200 plats recorded 2004-2009 that have fewer than 20% of lots improved. Use the assessor parcel roll to find vacant lots.
2. Hand-label each plat's current status from the planning portal and bond-release records.
3. Compare recent recorded sale prices of vacant lots in plats labelled "revivable" with plats labelled "dead", and with entitled-land comps.
4. Call five land brokers to ask whether they already track these plats.

**Kill if:** the revivable-versus-dead price gap is under 2x, or if more than 80% of the status is already in GIS or broker knowledge.

## Verdict (relaxed C3)
- **C1 = 1.** The buyers pay cost plus carry, and the high-value rung is mostly physical construction.
- **C2 = 2.** About 2-5x for entitlement alone.
- **C3 = 3.** Proving is expensive, but ML gains are about 1.2-1.5x because local politics and holdouts cap them.
- **C4 = 2.** The data is illegible but partly summarised and sold. Rights are buyable, but antiquated lots need slow, holdout-prone assembly.
- **C5 = 4.** A real, very large homebuilding ladder.

**Total: 12/25. Not excluded, but weak.** The step-up that matters comes from horizontal development (about $65k+ of the $108k Forestar lot, estimate based on its 2:1 development-to-acquisition spend), not from discovery.

deep.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
deep.memo:
## Powered-Land Options: round-4 feasibility check

**Search note:** the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this task ran, so I could not run any new searches. The evidence comes from fetching 8 pages directly: the finalist's sources, LandGate, Interconnection.fyi and the Texas SB6 bill text. Figures marked (est.) are my estimates.

### Frame of reference
The rung is: option farmland near a substation, prove "power is coming" with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter, then sell to a data-center developer. The frame breaks because the proof the buyer pays for is **committed load**, not a study. Altus Group (80 deals checked) found "committed utility load was the strongest predictor of land pricing" ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). Committing load means signing an ESA, posting collateral and accepting take-or-pay terms. AEP Ohio requires an 85% minimum demand over 12 years plus a 3-year exit fee ([mgrid](https://mgrid.org/2025/12/03/aep-ohio-data-center-tariff-sets-national-precedent-after-30-gw-interconnection-surge/)). That step is capital-heavy and the utility controls it. Discovery is about 20-35% of the rung (est.). This is the same failure as the geothermal counter-example: the physical/financial step is the hard part.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** Licking County, OH farmland sells for $10-15k/acre ([Acres](https://www.acres.com/blog/meta-expands-ohio-footprint-679-million-invested-1345-acre-data-center-campus)). In low-cost markets, unpowered land is about $10k/acre ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). An option costs about $50-300/acre/yr (est.).
- **Proven price, by type of proof:**
  - **Power path established** (infrastructure plus utility relationships): "six figures per acre", about 10-30x ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).
  - **Committed load:** Meta paid more than $1.1M/acre in 2025, after the AEP transmission commitments, about 70-100x farmland ([Acres](https://www.acres.com/blog/meta-expands-ohio-footprint-679-million-invested-1345-acre-data-center-campus)).
  - **Northern Virginia:** entitled unpowered land is about $4M/acre and powered land at least $6M/acre, so power adds about 1.5x ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).
- **Location premium is captured before any proof:** Meta paid about $123k/acre in 2019, before any power proof, so farmers near known demand already capture about 10x ([Acres](https://www.acres.com/blog/meta-expands-ohio-footprint-679-million-invested-1345-acre-data-center-campus)).
- **Buyers pay in tranches against delivered megawatts:** Plug Power sold its Graham, TX site to Stream for $50M plus up to $26.5M contingent on the load finally established ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).
- **Transactions per year:** 80 verified in August alone, and about $6B of land bought in H1 2026, up 79% ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). That suggests about 600-1,000 deals a year (est.).
- **Step-up that can be credited to a study alone:** about 2-10x (est.).

### Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Study cost:** Texas SB6 sets a flat screening-study fee of at least $100,000 ([SB6](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)).
- **Real proving capex:** Plug/Stream put up a $6.5M deposit to Oncor plus a $7.75M letter of credit for 164 MW, about $87k/MW ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). This clears the "expensive" bar easily, but the money is collateral, not discovery spend.
- **Base hit rate:** no source gives a measured study-to-ESA rate. AEP's queue fell from 30 GW to 13 GW once commitments were required ([mgrid](https://mgrid.org/2025/12/03/aep-ohio-data-center-tariff-sets-national-precedent-after-30-gw-interconnection-surge/)), then to 5.6 GW ([E&E](https://www.eenews.net/articles/has-ohio-found-a-way-to-predict-the-power-needs-of-data-centers/)). That is 19-43% survival, but it measures speculators dropping out, not site quality.
- **Lift with ML:** ranking substations by headroom against a naive "230 kV line within X miles" screen gives about 1.2-1.4x on cost per proven site (est.). The voltage tier is already a legible price driver: 230/500 kV sites trade at about 2.4x 138 kV sites ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).

### Data source
- **Named datasets:** utility hosting-capacity maps, IRP load forecasts, ISO/utility generation queues (Interconnection.fyi tracks 44,281 requests from 50+ ISOs and utilities, [link](https://www.interconnection.fyi/)), and FERC Form 715 (CEII-restricted; the FERC page returned 403 to my fetch).
- **Why it is not illegible:** LandGate already sells "Available Power" offtake capacity for "every substation in the US", plus substation-level queues ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)). So the answer to "where is headroom" is already a packaged field.
- **Where the outcome actually lives:** large-load ESA status is private between the utility and the customer, and capital commitment decides it, not data.

### How the right is bought
- **From whom:** farmers.
- **Legal mechanics:** a purchase option or a ground-lease option, recorded as a memorandum.
- **Price:** near agricultural value, but the gap is closing. LandGate's PowerLeads marketplace sells "ready to sign deals with landowners" ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).
- **Site control:** SB6 requires the requester to show site control through ownership, a lease or another legal interest the PUC accepts ([SB6](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)). An option may not qualify without PUC acceptance (est.).
- **Share of uplift kept:** if the company sells at the study stage, it keeps roughly the 2-10x on option value. To capture the 70-100x it must post per-MW security and sign the ESA itself, which means becoming a capital-heavy developer.

### Capitalised buyer
Real and deep-pocketed:
- Hyperscalers. Meta paid $566M for 514 acres ([Acres](https://www.acres.com/blog/meta-expands-ohio-footprint-679-million-invested-1345-acre-data-center-campus)).
- Developers. SDC paid $615M for 97 acres, and Stream bought Plug Power's Graham site ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).
- Utilities. Dominion paid $45M for about 14 acres ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).

### Integration ladder above
The rungs go: option, then study, then ESA plus collateral, then entitled powered shell, then campus developer, then on-site generation or a utility-like power provider. The ladder is real, and it could lead to a very large company.

### Who else does this
- LandGate (data plus landowner marketplace, [link](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).
- GridTracker / Interconnection.fyi ([link](https://www.interconnection.fyi/)).
- Powered-land developers Tract, Cloverleaf and EdgeCore. These are named from background knowledge: tract.com returned empty or 404 to my fetches.
- Brokers such as Avison Young.

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
Run a backtest in ERCOT/Oncor:
1. Pull 2024-26 county deed records for parcels that sold at 10x or more above farmland value.
2. Score candidate parcels three ways:
   - (a) a naive screen: 230 kV or higher within 2 miles,
   - (b) LandGate's "Available Power" layer (demo account),
   - (c) an ML headroom model built on public queues and IRPs.
3. Kill the idea if (c) does not beat both (a) and (b) by 1.5x in precision at the top 50 parcels.

In parallel, phone 10 farmers near the flagged substations for option quotes, to measure how much of the purchase discount is left.

### Verdict under the relaxed rubric
| | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 1.5 | The buyer pays for committed load, and the utility allocates it against collateral; discovery is a minority of the rung. |
| C2 Step-up | 2.5 | About 2-10x for a study, 10-30x for a power path; 70-100x only with an ESA. |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 2.5 | Proving is expensive, but ML gives about 1.2-1.4x against a kV screen and LandGate (est.). |
| C4 Data + right | 1 | Headroom is already sold as a field; options can be bought, but the discount is closing. |
| C5 Ladder | 4 | Real ladder up to campus developer and power provider. |
| **Total** | **11.5 / 25** | **Not excluded, but it fails the frame test.** |

The relaxed C3 helps a little, but the step-up still comes from committing capital to the utility, not from discovery. Unless the backtest shows ML beating LandGate by 1.5x or more, kill this finalist.

deep.name: Australian rural-to-urban rezoning (NSW, SEQ and Victorian growth corridors)
deep.memo:
## Frame of reference
The company would buy an option over broadacre rural land on a growth front, get it rezoned, and sell it as englobo land to a master-planned community developer. Under the rubric this is a sellable rung and the buyer is real. The problem is the work mix. Choosing the parcel is about 20-30% of the effort (estimate). The rest is a planning proposal or scheme amendment: specialist studies, council and state advocacy, exhibition, panel hearings and negotiating contributions. That proving step is not cheap, short or hidden. It is political and procedural, which makes this look like the geothermal counter-example: carrying out the bespoke step is harder than finding the site.

## Step-up ratio
**Hard limit on this run:** the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this deep-dive started. All three searches I tried were rejected. The figures below come from direct fetches of known URLs and the finalist's own sources. Several fetches failed (NSW DPHI pages 404, Planning Panels Victoria and Stockland 403). Prices are mostly from 2018 and need a refresh.

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Land likely to be added in the next Melbourne growth-boundary expansion (hope value) | AUD $125-250k/ha | Cushman & Wakefield, quoted in https://www.beefcentral.com/?p=151472 |
| Unplanned land inside the growth boundary (Beveridge, 600 ha, $220M, 2018) | ~$367k/ha | same |
| Zoned residential parcel (Gisborne, 75 ha, $61.1M) | ~$815k/ha | same |
| Development-land benchmark (Biggin & Scott, H1 2018) | $2M/ha | same |
| Austral, Western Sydney (41 ha, $100M guide, 2023, flexible commercial zoning, not residential) | ~$2.4M/ha | https://www.realcommercial.com.au/news/western-sydneys-largest-ever-land-parcel-includes-100m-guide |
| True farm value | ~$10-100k/ha | estimate |

- **Gross step-up for parcels a model would actually pick** (hope value to zoned): about 6-16x.
- **In Victoria:** Windfall Gains Tax applies at rezoning. It is 62.5% of uplift between $100k and $500k, and 50% of the whole uplift above $500k. The owner at rezoning pays, and it can be deferred to the next dutiable transaction (https://www.sro.vic.gov.au/understanding-windfall-gains-tax). That roughly halves the net gain.
- **In NSW:** the Housing and Productivity Contribution plus s7.11 local charges cost tens of thousands of dollars per lot (estimate; the DPHI page returned 404).
- **Net step-up:** about 2-6x after proving cost and carry (estimate). The 10³-10⁴ needed is not reached.
- **Transactions per year:** dozens of englobo deals across Melbourne, Sydney and SEQ (estimate, unverified).

## Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Capex:** about AUD $0.5-3M and 2-6 years per proposal (estimate from the finalist's sources). NSW gateway deadlines are routinely extended (https://engagement.yourvoiceourcoast.com/sites/default/files/2021-09/background_information_-_gateway_determination_extensions.pdf).
- **Hit rate:** no published success rate found. 30-60% inside investigation areas is plausible (estimate). The register does publish "Made" and "Withdrawn" stages, so a base rate could be computed (https://www.planningportal.nsw.gov.au/ppr).
- **ML lift:** about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven parcel (estimate). Which parcels get zoned first is set mostly by published servicing and sequencing plans and by lobbying, not by hidden signals in documents. The VPA publishes an interactive precinct status map and a 10-year greenfields plan (https://www.vpa.vic.gov.au/).

## Data source
- **Datasets:**
  - NSW Planning Proposal register (stages from Under Assessment through Made or Withdrawn)
  - Planning Panels Victoria reports
  - council business papers
  - VPA status map
  - ShapingSEQ investigation areas
  - water-authority growth servicing plans
  - flood studies
  - the Government Gazette
- **Access:** all public.
- **What is illegible:** gateway conditions, panel reasoning and refusal grounds, which sit in PDFs.
- **What is not:** the outcome is summarised in a structured register stage, and the leading indicators (growth boundaries, investigation areas, PSP sequencing) are published maps. Developers' acquisition teams already read them, and Landchecker sells the zoning layers (https://landchecker.com.au/). This fails the rubric's "outcome not already summarised" test.

## How the right is bought
- **From whom:** pastoral or family owners.
- **Mechanism:** a call option or put-and-call option, with a fee of about 1-5% (estimate). The owner consents to the proponent lodging the proposal.
- **Price:** owners near growth fronts already charge hope value. Cushman & Wakefield's $125-250k/ha and CBRE's "notable premium" for farms just outside the boundary both say so (Beef Central). Cheap farm-value options exist only well outside published growth areas, where hit rates and timelines collapse.
- **Share of uplift kept:** after the option strike, Victoria's Windfall Gains Tax (which owners will push into the strike price) and contributions, the company keeps perhaps 30-50% of the gross uplift (estimate).

## Capitalised buyer
Stockland, Mirvac, Lendlease Communities, Frasers, Peet, AVJennings, Satterley, ID Land and land funds. They pay immediately for zoned englobo land (Beef Central). But they also option land and run rezonings in-house, so the buyer is also the main competitor for the rung.

## Integration ladder above
Above zoned englobo land sit civil works and subdivision, then lot sales, then built-form housing, then master-planned communities and retail or community assets. A Stockland-scale ASX outcome is possible. The market is domestic, cyclical and capital-intensive, so this is not a trillion-dollar path.

## Who else does this
Every major master-planned community developer's acquisition team, specialist rezoning syndicates and land-bank marketers, and agents openly selling "rezoning upside" parcels. Data and AI tools such as Landchecker and Archistar (https://www.archistar.ai/) sell the legible layers. None of them appears to predict rezoning outcomes.

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Scrape the NSW planning proposal register for Greater Sydney and the Hunter, 2019-2025, covering Made and Withdrawn proposals.
2. Pull each proposal's gateway determination PDF.
3. Train two models to predict Made versus Withdrawn and time-to-made:
   - a baseline that uses only published layers (growth area, servicing plan, LGA);
   - a model that adds features extracted from the PDFs.
4. Kill criterion: if the PDF features add less than 0.05 AUC, or under 1.2x on implied cost per made proposal, stop.
5. In the same two weeks, interview 3 land agents for current hope-value prices in investigation areas.

## Verdict (relaxed rubric)
| Criterion | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 1 | Buyer exists, but discovery is under 30% of the work and the proving step is advocacy |
| C2 Step-up | 2 | About 6-16x gross, 2-6x net |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 2 | Proving is expensive, but the likely ML lift is about 1.1-1.3x |
| C4 Data + right | 1 | Outcome sits in a structured register stage, indicators are published maps, owners price in hope value |
| C5 Ladder | 4 | Real ladder, but domestic and cyclical |

**Total: 10/25. Not excluded, but killed.** The step-up is already priced in, and Victoria's Windfall Gains Tax takes about half of whatever is left. The proving step is the hard part, not discovery. The signal is already published, and the buyers compete for the same rung.
